News.title: ‘Honeymoon items’ worth £500 stolen from couple as they were getting married – as CCTV released
News.content:
WEDDING WOE ‘Honeymoon items’ worth £500 stolen from couple as they were getting married – as CCTV released







Next

A NEWLY married couple were the victims of a parcel theft after items worth around £500 they bought for their honeymoon were stolen.

Cops have released CCTV images of three people they wish to speak to after the deliveries were swiped from a communal hallway within an apartment complex in Hove, Sussex.

The parcels were taken from the Pinnacle Apartments, School Road, in the early hours of Friday (October 16).

Sussex Police said: “The couple had received notifications to inform them that their items had been delivered – but when they returned from their wedding, every package had disappeared.





“The parcels contained clothes with a value of around £500.

“If you know who this trio are, or have information which may help with our investigation, please call 101 and quote serial 1150 of 16/10.”

News.title: Family pay tribute to ‘loving’ dad, 53, found dead in flat as son, 33, charged with murder
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

'BIG HEART' Family pay tribute to ‘loving’ dad, 53, found dead in flat as son, 33, charged with murder







Next

A FAMILY have paid tribute to a “loving” dad found dead in a flat – as his son is charged with murder.

Michael Anthony Ward, 53, was found at the property in Holyhead, North Wales, in the early hours of Saturday (October 17).

His family said in a statement: “Our father was a loving family man with a big heart.

“He will be greatly missed.





“We would ask for our privacy to be respected at this difficult time whilst we process our loss.”

Michael was found in the property at Llys Watling on London Road at around 2.40am.

Enquiries into the circumstances surrounding the death are ongoing.

Martin Ward, 33, has since been charged with the murder of his father.

He will appear before Caernarfon Crown Court today.

Anybody with information that could assist our enquiries should contact police via webchat or by calling 101, quoting reference 26000852942.

News.title: Brit holidaymaker, 34, suffers ‘traumatic head injury’ after plunging 32ft from cliff edge at popular Algarve beach
News.content:
HOLIDAY HORROR Brit holidaymaker, 34, suffers ‘traumatic head injury’ after plunging 32ft from cliff edge at popular Algarve beach







Next

A BRITISH has been left seriously injured after plunging 32ft from a cliff at a Portuguese holiday hotspot.

The horror fall occurred near to the scenic Amado Beach, a popular spot in the Algarve that attracts surfers from across Europe.

Firefighters had to be deployed to rescue the 34-year-old, who was then airlifted to Faro hospital with severe head injuries.

Local firefighters’ chief Antonio Angelo said after the rescue: “The victim fell from a height of around ten metres and suffered a traumatic brain injury.





“He was conscious, but his speech was incoherent.”

A friend of the injured Brit guided emergency responders to the spot where the accident occurred.

The alarm was raised around 3.30pm and 20 firefighters were involved in the rescue operation, along with the ambulance service helicopter and Lagos Maritime Police.

Rescuers said he had been using old cables attached to the rocks employed by fishermen to access a steep, rocky area near to the beach when one of them broke.

There has been no additional information on the man’s condition in hospital.

The area where the fall occurred is not a roped rock climbing destination and it was unclear why the Brit had been descending the cliffs there.

The beach is located in Aljezur, about an hour and 15 minutes drive west of Faro International Airport, and sits within the Costa Vincentina park.

It is close to the spot where a British professional surfer went missing during a stand-up paddle boarding excursion in July.



The 28-year-old Great Britain junior star Arran Strong vanished in the Atlantic Ocean near to the picture-postcard resort of Arrifana, a short drive up from the Algarve, on July 27.

Arran was born in the UK but had been based in Portugal for several years.

Jose Maria Pyrrait, a friend who Arran was with when he disappeared, wrote in an emotional Facebook goodbye at the time despite his pal’s body not being found.

He said: “Today was a day of irreparable loss and profound sadness.

“Arran was like a son to me. Since he was 10 years old, he trained with me and spent weekends and holidays with me.



“As I used to tell his mother, he was like the child of divorced parents.

“My love for him was like the love for another son that life had given me.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Strangely enough, he always told me he would die young. Right now, I feel a deep pain. The only faint comfort is that he departed at sea, the place he loved most.

“He was young, with a pure and kind heart, but he is gone. I feel empty and exhausted, but life goes on.”

News.title: Why is it so dark this morning?
News.content:
Next

ANYONE dragging themselves out of bed in total darkness has the changing seasons to thank as winter draws ever nearer.

Sunrise is creeping later and later each morning, while the sun is disappearing earlier in the evening.



Why is it so dark in the morning?

The main reason is the Earth’s tilt – our planet spins on an axis tilted at around 23.5 degrees as it travels around the Sun.

During autumn, the Northern Hemisphere, which includes the UK, becomes tilted further away from the Sun.



That means fewer hours of daylight, with the sun rising later and setting earlier as winter approaches.

And cloudy skies can make the mornings feel even gloomier.



What time does the sun rise today?

According to Timeanddate, the sun rises in London at 7.34am on Wednesday, October 21.

In Edinburgh, sunrise is at 7.56am, while Belfast has to wait until 8.04am.

The exact times vary depending on where you live, with the sun currently rising around two minutes later each morning in the capital.

However, it starts getting light before sunrise during a period known as twilight, when the sun is still below the horizon.



When will mornings start getting lighter?

Fortunately, there is some temporary relief on the horizon.

At 2am on Sunday, October 25, the UK will switch from British Summer Time (BST) to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), moving the clocks back an hour to 1am.

London’s sunrise will move from 7.39am on Saturday to 6.41am on Sunday, although sunset will also shift from 5.48pm to 4.46pm.

The change doesn’t create any extra daylight – it simply moves an hour of it from the evening to the morning – but the brighter monrnings won’t last very long.

The shortest day of the year falls on Monday, December 21, when the winter solstice takes place.



Although the days begin lengthening after that, sunrise actually continues getting later for a little longer.

In London, it won’t reach its latest time of approximately 8.06am until the end of December.

Can darker mornings affect your sleep?

Natural light helps regulate the body’s internal clock, which influences when we feel sleepy or alert.

The NHS explains that melatonin, a hormone involved in sleep, is produced after dark and decreases during daylight hours.

Reduced sunlight may also contribute to seasonal affective disorder (SAD), a form of depression usually experienced during winter.



Symptoms can include low mood, tiredness, difficulty concentrating and sleeping more than usual.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The NHS recommends spending time outdoors during daylight, exercising regularly and maintaining a consistent sleep routine.

Some people also use light therapy lamps to simulate daylight.

News.title: Beloved high school student, 15, thrown from car & killed after crashing into tree as one more dead & 3 fight for life
News.content:
SMASH TRAGEDY Beloved high school student, 15, thrown from car & killed after crashing into tree as one more dead & 3 fight for life







Next

A BELOVED high school student has died after being flung from a car during a high-speed crash that killed one more.

Three other passengers, all teenagers, are fighting for their lives after the vehicle veered off a Michigan road and hit a tree.



Jordyn Bigham, 15, and the 16-year-old driver, who has not been named, were pronounced dead at the scene after being thrown from the car.

Her sister Jada Bigham, 16, and two others, 15 and 17, survived but were rushed to hospital with serious injuries.



Jada is still fighting for her life in critical condition, according to a GoFundMe set up to support her and Jordyn’s family.

Loved ones wrote: “She faces a long, difficult road to recovery ahead, requiring extensive medical treatments, surgeries, and ongoing care.”



The two other wounded are reportedly in critical but stable condition, according to NBC affiliate WOOD-TV.

Police are now investigating what caused the horror crash, which happened at around 3.20am on October 18.

“The Kalamazoo County Sheriff’s Office extends its deepest condolences to the families and friends of the students who lost their lives,” police said.

“Our thoughts are also with the injured students, their loved ones, and the students, teachers, and staff of Mattawan High School during this difficult time.”



Christina Norris, Jordyn and Jada’s grandma told WWMT that the sisters were “inseparable”.

She said: “Where there was one, there was both. They didn’t go anywhere without each other, hardly ever.”

The fundraiser supporting their family has so far raised nearly $70,000 (£52,300).

The appeal reads: “Their mother is now carrying a heavy burden that no parent should ever have to face: mourning the loss of one daughter while standing by the hospital bed of another.

“Without medical insurance, the family is overwhelmed by the immediate cost of funeral and memorial expenses for Jordyn, as well as the rapidly accumulating medical bills for Jada’s life-saving care.



“Because Jada requires round-the-clock support, their mom is unable to work during this critical time.”

A makeshift memorial with flowers and balloons has been set up near where the crash happened.

Mattawan High School – where the victims studied – has also launched a crisis team to offer support to students and staff.

The man has since been bailed after being held on suspicion of rape, theft and fraud by false representation.

A police cordon was put in place at the Old Catton car park during the investigation.

News.title: Moment brave builders confront samurai sword-wielding thug and fight him off with spirit level – as attacker, 32, jailed
News.content:
Next

THIS is the shocking moment brave builders take on a samurai sword-wielding thug, armed only with a spirit level.

Aaron Messenbird, 32, approached a group of people hanging around a van and threatened them while swinging the blade about, in Milton Keynes on July 30 at around 9.05pm.



He also “raised the weapon in a threatening manner,” the police said.

During a struggle, Messenbird’s victim sustained injuries to his hands, including a damaged tendon requiring specialist treatment, as well as injuries to his ribs.



Two builders then intervened, one holding a spirit level, causing Messenbird to flee the scene.

Messenbird was later spotted walking along Silbury Boulevard while still armed with the sword.

He was arrested on August 5 and charged the next day.

Investigating officer PC Jordan Buchanan-Kay, of the Central Milton Keynes Neighbourhood Policing Team, said: “This was a violent and unprovoked incident in which Messenbird threatened members of the public with a potentially lethal weapon before assaulting a man who had stepped in to protect others.



“The victim suffered painful injuries, including damage to a tendon in his hand, as a result of Messenbird’s actions.

“I would also like to acknowledge the bravery of the members of the public who intervened and helped prevent this incident from becoming far more serious.

“Their actions undoubtedly contributed to protecting others from harm.

“However, we would always urge people not to put themselves in danger when confronted with somebody carrying a weapon.

“The safest course of action is to move to a place of safety and call 999 immediately, providing as much information as possible to help officers respond quickly.



“I am pleased that Messenbird has been given a custodial sentence and hope this outcome provides reassurance to the victims and the wider community that violent offending involving weapons will not be tolerated.”

Messenbird, of Milton Keynes, was sentenced to 12 months’ imprisonment at Aylesbury Crown Court on October 14.

He pleaded guilty to threatening a person with a bladed article, possession of a bladed article in a public place and assault occasioning actual bodily harm (ABH).

News.title: Migrants let off paying visa fees more than 76,000 times since Labour came to power
News.content:
Next

MIGRANTS have been let off visa fees more than 76,000 times since Labour took office, analysis shows.

Application charges worth at least £96.2million were waived after arrivals said they did not have the means to pay the £1,407 fee.



Each waiver is now worth up to £3,994 per adult, covering the £1,407 application fee and a £2,587 NHS surcharge for 30 months of leave.

However, not all applicants receive waivers for the NHS fee, although no breakdown is published.



Applicants must show they are destitute, that paying would leave them unable to afford food or housing, or that it would harm a child’s wellbeing.

The waivers were brought in after a string of human rights court rulings found it unlawful to charge people for human rights applications they could not afford.

A record 33,737 people applied to be let off in the first three months of this year, more than double the 13,669 who asked at the end of 2023.

Another 33,393 joined the queue between April and June, the second highest quarter on record.

Stats show officials are now struggling to keep up with the surge in applications, with 50,257 of those applications still waiting for a decision.

Just 478 of the 33,737 requests made in the first three months of the year were dealt with inside the Home Office’s 20-working-day target.



Official figures show 70,916 waivers were handed out in Labour’s first 18 months alone, up 57 per cent on the 45,101 in the final 18 months of the last Conservative government.

Applications began soaring in early 2024, when the health surcharge jumped from £624 to £1,035 a year.

Waivers are open to partners and parents on the 10-year family route, people who have built a private life in the UK, and failed asylum seekers later given leave on human rights grounds.

Small boat migrants and those granted asylum are already not required to pay a visa surcharge.

Those on the 10-year route must reapply every 30 months, so the same migrant can be let off up to four times before they can apply for settled status.



A further 2,353 waivers went to families applying to join relatives from abroad in Labour’s first 18 months.

Nigerians, Indians and Pakistanis top the nationalities granted extensions on the family and private life route since July 2024, with 21,220, 19,402 and 16,679 grants respectively.

But the Home Office does not publish which nationalities are most likely to receive the waivers.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Home Office said it did not recognise the figure.

A spokesman added that the waiver acceptance rate was lower than below the election and was still falling.

News.title: Lawyer caught by BBC offering to make illegal worker penalty 'go away'
News.content:
A solicitor has been secretly filmed by the BBC explaining how he could make a Â£45,000 illegal-working fine go away.

Mohammad Alias Yousaf - also known as Alias - made the claim to an undercover reporter, who was posing as a mini-mart owner facing a fine for employing an illegal worker.

The Bradford-based solicitor told his potential client he could avoid paying the fine, if he could find someone overseas prepared to declare themselves the owner of the mini-mart.

Alias has denied ever providing such advice to anyone, or giving false information to the Home Office.

At least Â£150m is currently owed to the government in uncollected illegal-working fines, according to Home Office figures obtained by the BBC.

In response to our investigation, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced a review of the way such fines are issued and collected.

In a statement, she said she wanted to thank the BBC "for exposing those who undermine our rules".

Many business owners do not take the fines seriously, a law enforcement official has told us anonymously.

She told us she had seen immigration fine notices, "some worth Â£40,000, stuffed in a box" on a mini-mart counter.

When she had asked a member of staff if the business owners intended to pay, she said she had been told: "'It's got nothing to do with me.'"

News.title: King praises Strait of Hormuz peace efforts at glittering banquet
News.content:
The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran in February, killing the country's supreme leader and sparking the ongoing Iran war.

The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most vital shipping lanes, has been effectively closed since then.

King Charles, Queen Camilla, Prince William and Catherine and Princess Anne were among the royals on duty at Windsor for the state visit.

It was the first state banquet for Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was seated next to the Omani academic and novelist, Jokha Alharthi.

It was a table laden with elaborate candelabra and polished decorations, with five glasses per setting, and even the surface of the salt had an imprint of the cypher of King Charles.

The hot summer meant a bumper crop of pomegranates in the Windsor Castle gardens, and the fruits were placed on the table alongside the floral decorations.

The King's speech, delivered to 160 guests in English with some quotes in Arabic, expressed his approval that his son Prince William had worked on an expedition project alongside the Sultan's son.

"There can be few happier symbols of success than a living relationship being passed from one generation to the next," said the King.

News.title: Why does Elon Musk want to merge Tesla and SpaceX?
News.content:
Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.

Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."

The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.

With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5tn (Â£1.1bn) and SpaceX at $2tn (Â£1.5tn), a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.

Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.

News.title: Schools should recognise antisemitism as distinct form of harm, review says
News.content:
Earlier this month, the BBC was given rare access inside a Jewish school in Hertfordshire, where pupils and staff operate under tight security, amid heightened concerns about antisemitism.

Spencer Lewis, the executive headteacher of Yavneh College, said that security was an "innate part" of his role.

"When you come in in the morning, there are high gates, high fences, lots of security cameras. We have four full-time security staff. And it sort of just becomes part of what you do," he said. "We think about it a lot."

Staff and pupils told the BBC they have become so used to these measures that they barely notice them anymore.

Lock-in - or "in-vacuation" - drills for dealing with intruders have become second nature, even to the youngest pupils.

"It's a bit scary sometimes, but you know you're safe," said Livi, a Year 6 pupil.

"It's sad that we can't be equal to everyone else, but people don't like us just because of the way we are," added her classmate, Sadie.

A group of a dozen older pupils who spoke to the BBC said that while they feel safe inside school, hearing about antisemitic attacks in the UK, including reports of pupils at other Jewish schools being harassed on their commute and at sports fixtures, has left them feeling targeted.

Some said that they were reluctant to wear skullcaps or necklaces featuring the Star of David â a Jewish symbol â outside school.

"Other religions get to be out and wear their necklaces and be proud - I don't get why Jewish people can't do it as much," said Year 9 pupil Ilan.

In response to the recommendations, the government is also expected to encourage schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)'s working definition of antisemitism, although it cannot make it compulsory.

The definition is supported by mainstream Jewish organisations and has been adopted by 47 countries, including the UK, as well as most British universities.

However, some of the IHRA definition's examples of antisemitic behaviour have proven controversial.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said that adopting the IHRA definition would provide schools with a tool "to deepen understanding of contemporary antisemitism".

In a statement, a spokesperson told the BBC: "Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children's safety, and will strengthen accountability."

He added: "We have advocated these measures be accompanied by other steps including improving education about Jewish life and ensuring schools maintain their duties in relation to political impartiality."

Bell, who is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland, heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across state and independent schools, as well as from community organisations.

The Department for Education has declined to comment before the review is published.

News.title: Giant tunnel proposed to clean up Windermere's sewage problem
News.content:
A Â£3.6bn proposal to stop sewage being discharged into Windermere, England's largest lake, has been unveiled.

The plans, which are backed by the local water company United Utilities and clean water campaigners, would see a tunnel up to 12 miles (19km) long built to transport sewage away from the lake.

At the moment both raw sewage and treated effluent are discharged into Windermere and campaigners say that is why parts of the lake have been turning green each summer, so-called algal blooming.

It is now up to the government to decide if the plan can be further developed, and if the Â£3.6bn price-tag is acceptable.

The Lake District is a Unesco World Heritage site and attracts close to 18m visitors each year.

Windermere is at its heart, with the lake holding around 300bn litres of water. That is so big that it can take 9 months for water entering one end to reach the other.

News.title: Tighter rules planned to protect people from cosmetic surgery that goes badly wrong
News.content:
Only properly trained professionals will be allowed to offer high-risk cosmetic procedures like liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), vampire facials and chemical peels, under long-awaited government plans for England in 2027.

The government said it wanted to "drive cosmetic cowboys out of the market" and shield people from treatments "that can go badly wrong".

Currently, there are no restrictions over who can carry out these 'no scalpel' procedures, which can harm or kill if not performed safely.

Under the new rules, high-risk procedures for under-18s will also be banned, and rogue providers will face new criminal offences and fixed fines of up to Â£4,000.

News.title: 60 years on: The Aberfan disaster through the eyes of those who survived
News.content:
"I heard this tremendous sound, like a hurricane. It was so overwhelming, I knew something was coming, but didn't know what.

"Then this mass of black came crashing through the window, hurling me from the front of the classroom to the back.

"I woke up to find the classroom was no longer the classroom. The roof had caved in on us, and we were completely buried.

"I couldn't see my legs, I thought they had gone.

"A pupil in front of me was trapped, and he had blood trickling down his head. Another one was trying to get through the roof to get help.

"My head was cut open, and I couldn't move my hand as it was stuck in the cracked wall.

"I pinched the hand of a child near me to see if it would move. It didn't.

"Then I heard someone shout 'I'm going to smash the window' and saw my grandfather.

"I started to cry and will never forget the look in his eyes knowing I was alive.

"I'd broken my femur, my leg was just swinging and my shoes had gone.

"'I'll buy you all the shoes you need,' my mum said as she greeted me outside.

"My parents then ran off to find my siblings.

"I was later told Carl and Marylyn had died, and all my friends had gone as well.

"My life changed forever."

News.title: UK government expected to approve Jackdaw gas field
News.content:
The UK government is expected to announce a long-awaited decision on whether to approve the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.

It is widely believed in Westminster that Jackdaw will be approved but that a decision on the Rosebank oil field off Shetland will not yet be made.

The question of whether to approve the two sites has become hugely politically significant and has been delayed for several months.

Multiple Whitehall sources have told BBC News the government would make an announcement on Jackdaw on Wednesday morning with the Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh expected to address MPs in the afternoon.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has spoken repeatedly of the need for a "flexible" approach to energy and is believed to be in favour of drilling more where licensing already exist in the North Sea.

Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to issue any new oil and gas licences in the North Sea but to honour existing ones such as Jackdaw.

News.title: Two men re-arrested on suspicion of assisting Iran intelligence after RAF Fairford incident
News.content:
Two men have been re-arrested after an incident near RAF Fairford last month, counter-terrorism police have said.

A 24-year-old UK national, and a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, are being held on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service under Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023, with police saying the investigation relates to Iran.

Police had been alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the US airbase in Gloucestershire in the early hours of 27 September - a major incident was subsequently declared and dozens of homes evacuated.

Seven men in total have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.

Gloucestershire Police said it had received a call about "three suspicious vehicles" travelling towards RAF Fairford at 00:45 BST on 27 September.

A bomb disposal team was deployed to the village to examine a number of vehicles.

Petrol was found in three vans near the airbase and five men were arrested.

They had been initially arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and then further arrested on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act.

Police later said they did not find "improvised explosive devices".

The re-arrests announced on Tuesday relate to a 24-year-old man who was initially arrested on 27 September near the base and a 25-year-old who was arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts days later on 1 October in the borough of Westminster.

The other five men - who also include a 22-year-old British national arrested in Westminster on 6 October - remain on police bail.

The head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said: "This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement.

"Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it."

The officer added that national security investigations can take time to progress due to their sensitive nature.

"Our specialist teams have been working tirelessly to interrogate the many lines of enquiry involved in this hugely complex investigation," he said.

Days after the incident, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC there were "strong indications" Iran had played a part in the incident.

He did not provide further details at the time.

Iran has previously denied any involvement.

RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.

In the week after the incident, it emerged that the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details.

Vice-President JD Vance said it was done out of an "abundance of caution".

News.title: Tory MP questions government advisor's position after wife's Palestine Action post
News.content:
Conservative MP Alicia Kearns has raised concerns over whether Jonathan Powell, the National Security Advisor, can remain in his post following his wife's references to Palestine Action on social media.

The shadow home affairs minister has written to the prime minister questioning whether Powell's position is still tenable, despite the Metropolitan Police concluding no action was necessary over his wife's, Sarah Helm, comments.

A Downing Street spokeswoman told the BBC: "These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity."

Posting on X last Thursday, Helm wrote: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action," responding to a discussion about the author Sally Rooney.

The Normal People writer announced last week that her books will not be supplied to UK booksellers after she announced she would use her royalties to support Palestine Action.

The Met investigation into Helm's post found "it did not meet the criminal threshold" and the matter was dropped on Saturday.

But Kearns has written to Andy Burnham about the handling of sensitive national security information, asking whether the government has investigated the posts and whether he retains full confidence in his adviser.

She told the BBC: "We cannot have the NSA's wife tweeting about what decisions her husband has or hasn't made."

Palestine Action was proscribed as a terror organisation last year, making it a a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years imprisonment to belong to or support the group.

An appeal against the proscription of Palestine Action is due to be heard by the Supreme Court next month, external, in a battle that has now gone on for more than year.

News.title: Woman says she 'couldn't speak or breathe' during alleged rape by Russell Brand
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

A woman who says Russell Brand raped her at his home in London told police she "couldn't speak or breathe" during the alleged attack, a jury has heard.

The 51-year-old entertainer is accused of raping the woman in 2009 after meeting her at London's Hammersmith Apollo, where he had been performing as a stand-up comedian.

Brand faces seven charges in the trial in total - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies all the charges.

In video evidence of her speaking to a police officer, the woman said she performed a sex act on Brand at the London theatre after being invited for drinks following the show.

She said she gave him her phone number, explaining she was "a massive Russell Brand fan" and a "massive comedy fan" at the time.

After that night, she said Brand messaged her and she went to his house in Hampstead knowing they would have sex.

But she said a consensual encounter became rape when Brand started having anal sex with her and ignored her pleas for him to stop.

She said when she arrived at his home, Brand told her she needed to have a shower "because my hair smelled funny". He then asked her to brush her teeth.

"I was trying to make a joke of what he was making me do", she said. "All of those things made me feel, 'I don't like this'."

The woman said a short while after getting on his bed, she was turned over. It was then she said she was allegedly raped.

She told police: "From the very moment it happened, I felt I had willingly gone there and from what his reputation was, what did I expect?"

She said Brand "hurt me and harmed me, and when I asked him to stop, he didn't". She added: "The horror in anyone that I told was not enough to make me believe I didn't deserve it."

The woman said she told friends and family afterwards, and went through sexual health tests - believing that she had contracted a disease from Brand.

Earlier on Tuesday, another woman who claims Brand sexually assaulted her described the alleged attack as "frenzied" and "violent".

That complainant alleges Brand assaulted her at the Choice FM radio studios in central London in the mid-2000s.

She said she came out of a small room in the building to find Brand outside.

"He said 'aye aye'," she told the jury. "He grabbed me by my face, started to kiss me, and when he was kissing me he started pushing me - his body against me."

The woman continued: "He was kissing me, it was very frenzied. There was no time for me to even understand what was going on.

"He was running his hands over my body and I had my back against the wall at that point."

From behind a blue screen, the woman described the kiss as "sloppy" and "very, very rough", when asked by the prosecution barrister about the alleged attack.

"His hands at the same time were all over me," she said. "He touched my bum, my breasts, his body was pressed up against me."

The woman said she pushed him off and swore at him.

She said there were several people with him who she claims didn't say anything about what happened after the alleged assault.

The woman - now in her 50s - said she had never met Brand before and that she believed he'd been in the building because he was on Channel 4 show Big Brother's Big Mouth.

She told the jury: "His whole body was pressed against me - the kisses were hard and sloppy and going down my neck.

"His hands were moving so much - the reason I used the word frenzied was because it was violent. He just wasn't stopping."

She said she felt "dirty" after the encounter and "never told anybody", adding: "I felt shocked and stunned, shaken."

News.title: Audit regulator looking into Manchester City accounting
News.content:
The UK audit regulator has confirmed it is leading inquiries into accounting irregularities at Manchester City.

The Financial Reporting Council confirmed in a letter to the House of Commons business select committee it had taken over "regulatory consideration" of the case from the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales on 30 September.

No formal investigation has started, but the FRC is making inquiries into the case.

It comes after Manchester City were found guilty by an independent commission of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, including by artificially inflating the club's financial position by more than Â£900m. City are appealing the verdict.

The FRC has greater resources, and greater powers, to apply sanctions if it does find evidence of violations. It routinely oversees accounting standards at bigger institutions such as listed public companies, but not football clubs.

The FRC can look into the conduct of BDO, Manchester City's auditors, to ask whether the audit was in line with the rules.

It can also apply sanctions to individuals such as directors or employees of the Etihad club, if they are members of professional accountancy bodies.

BDO is the UK's fifth-biggest accounting firm, but claims to be a market leader in football, advising more Premier League and Championship clubs than any other firm.

The independent commission which looked into Manchester City found that the club gave a "misleading impression" of the scheme used to disguise the origin of shareholder funds injected into the club to its auditors, who were "unaware" of the scheme.

Manchester City have said they will appeal against the commission's decision, arguing that it contains "material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

Liam Byrne, chair of the business select committee, called for greater powers for the FRC to look into similar cases.

He wrote on X: "The regulator's letter exposes gaps in its ability to compel evidence from the club and pursue directors who fall outside its disciplinary rules.

"This raises serious questions about the powers available to hold companies and directors to account.

"The government has a responsibility to explain why reforms to close these gaps were abandoned - and what will now be done to strengthen accountability."

BDO declined to comment.

News.title: BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra broadcast channels to close
News.content:
BBC Three, which is aimed at young audiences and launched hits such as Fleabag, Normal People and Gavin & Stacey, previously moved online in 2016, but was reinstated as a TV channel in 2022.

BBC Scotland launched as a channel in 2019, broadcasting a variety of Scottish programming including news, sport, documentaries and entertainment.

However, some of the shows that air on the two networks, such as Two Doors Down on BBC Scotland and Sort Your Life Out on BBC Three, are repeats of episodes originally broadcast on other more mainstream BBC channels.

Both networks currently only broadcast TV programming in the evenings, although BBC Scotland simulcasts BBC Radio Scotland during the rest of the day.

The BBC said that the network's nightly programme Reporting Scotland: News at Seven will not move to BBC iPlayer and will cease when the linear channel closes.

Audiences will continue to be served by BBC Scotland's wider news offering, including Reporting Scotland, The Sunday Show, Radio Scotland Breakfast, Debate Night and Scotcast, the corporation said.

While Radio 4 Extra does air some original programming, its schedule is predominantly made up of archive content, much of which is available on BBC Sounds.

Sir Peter Bazalgette, former chairman of ITV and production company Endemol, told BBC News: "This is a modest and pretty well-judged package.

"The essence of it is it protects the spending on content, it really cuts money in the distribution of programmes, and it really had to happen because the BBC has lost 30% of its revenue in 10 years."

But entertainment trade union Equity said Tuesday's announcement "does not signal a thriving BBC, and we are concerned about the UK's preeminent public service broadcaster's ability to meet its duties to the fullest".

Affected staff were told about the changes on Tuesday, although the proposed closure of BBC Scotland and BBC Three had been reported by some media outlets in recent weeks.

The BBC is aiming to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - almost one in 10 - in an attempt to save Â£500m over two years as it faces "significant financial pressures".

Around 550 job closures have already been announced in news, while more than 30 job cuts have so far been announced for BBC Sport.

The newly appointed director of BBC News, Rachel Jupp, announced on Tuesday that a further Â£5.5m of savings were being proposed, which would represent the closure of around 100 roles.

Meanwhile, several high-profile BBC TV series have been cancelled altogether in recent weeks.

RuPaul's Drag Race UK, Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live at the Apollo, Football Focus, Ski Sunday and Radio 4âs The World Tonight and You & Yours are among the programmes the BBC has dropped so far.

News.title: Google resolves cloud outage affecting UK banks and websites
News.content:
Google Cloud says it has resolved disruption at its UK cloud site which caused an outage affecting UK banks, businesses and the courts.

The company, one of a few large cloud computing firms whose infrastructure and services underpin many online platforms, reported an "issue with multiple services" at its London data centre complex "europe-west2" early on Tuesday.

Revolut, Lloyds Bank and HSBC were among popular UK services that confirmed disruption on Tuesday morning, after thousands of reports of problems were raised by users online.

The tech giant apologised to those affected and thanked customers for their patience.

"We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event," a Google Cloud spokesperson said in a statement on Tuesday evening.

"Services have been restored."

They added that the company would publish an analysis of the incident on its service health dashboard, external, where it provides customers with updates about the status of its cloud services globally.

Cloud computing giants like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud make their services available to clients in local or regional sites around the world, which they call "regions", containing their data centres.

In updates to its service dashboard on Tuesday morning, Google Cloud had said a number of its cloud services were "experiencing elevated errors and intermittent network failures in europe-west2 region" - its UK cloud facility in London.

It later said that the issues had stemmed from a "power event" within one of its smaller data centre zones, europe-west2-b.

These seemingly affected a host of popular UK platforms and services, with customers flagging issues with sites including Royal Mail, DPD and e-bike service Forest.

The HM Courts and Tribunals Service also said it was aware of an issue affecting the video platform used for remote hearings.

News.title: Man, 26, charged with woman's murder
News.content:
A man has been charged with the murder of a woman who was stabbed to death in a street in Manchester.

Lawrence Johnson, 26, of Dorking Avenue, has been charged with the murder of Alisha Samuels, also 26, and the attempted murder of a man following the incident on Thursday.

He has been remanded in custody and is due to appear at Manchester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

Det Ch Insp Justin Bryant said officers were continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding Ms Samuels' death and to provide answers for her family.

Police are still appealing for information.

Det Ch Insp Bryant said: "I'd like to thank those that have called and supported our investigation thus far. Your reports are always taken seriously and prove vital to our work.

"I urge others who may have information, no matter how small, to please come forward."

News.title: Hungary’s Magyar vows accountability for Orbán era while holding firm on migration
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, defeating Viktor Orbán in a landslide election was only the beginning. Less than six months into his term, his new government is pursuing former officials he accuses of corruption and abuses of power.

In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday, Magyar, 45, said efforts to recover assets that were allegedly misused under his predecessor were underway, but that the push for accountability must follow the rule of law that Orbán's government often flouted.

“The Hungarian people obviously want to see results in holding those responsible accountable, punishing them and recovering stolen property,” Magyar said from his central Budapest office.

During Orbán's rule, he said, Hungarians "experienced that this wonderful country, which was a high achiever when we joined the European Union in 2004, became one of the poorest and most corrupt member states in Europe.”

Magyar’s center-right, pro-European Tisza party defeated Orbán’s far-right Fidesz in April, ending 16 years of rule admired by the global nationalist right for its antagonistic approach to the EU and strong stance against immigration and the “liberal mainstream.”

Orbán’s self-described “illiberal democracy” dismantled checks and balances and enriched allied business figures, largely through awarding them lucrative EU-financed state contracts. Concerns over corruption and democratic backsliding prompted the bloc to begin withholding billions in funding to Hungary in 2021.

New government pursues asset recovery

Before the election, Magyar promised to bring those responsible for past abuses to justice and to recover public assets misused under Orbán. Recent polls show a large majority of voters expect him to fulfill that pledge.

Magyar's government established the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, which holds investigative and prosecutorial powers to pursue cases of misused public funds. Magyar called the office a “superauthority” that can enlist police, prosecutors and the national tax authority “so that it doesn’t take years to uncover a complicated corruption case.”

Magyar has also applied to join the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, which investigates crimes involving EU funds, reversing Orbán’s longstanding refusal to participate.

While several former officials have already been detained on suspicion of corruption-related offenses, Magyar acknowledged there is pressure for quicker results.

“I feel the impatience,” he said. “But everyone must understand that we want to build a rule of law state, a democratic country, a country that complies with EU and fundamental rights, and that takes time.”

“I try to tell people that it’s not the first 10 minutes of mafia movies and crime films that are the most exciting, but the middle and the end,” he said.

Holding firm on migration

Rapid reforms targeting corruption and bolstering judicial independence helped secure the EU’s announcement in May that it would unlock 16.4 billion euros (around $18.4 billion) for Hungary that it had frozen under Orbán.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will visit Budapest on Friday for the 70th anniversary of Hungary’s 1956 anti-Soviet revolution in another sign that the bumpy relationship with the EU is turning a corner.

But the rapprochement has not erased differences over migration.

Magyar said his administration would retain Orbán-era immigration and asylum policies, including escorting migrants who entered irregularly back across the southern border into Serbia. The fences with razor wire along the border, erected by Orbán in 2015 to keep out migrants and asylum seekers, will also stay in place.

In 2024, the European Court of Justice fined Hungary 200 million euros ($225 million) plus 1 million euros ($1.1 million) daily for failing to comply with a 2020 ruling on its asylum and removal practices.

Magyar said that since that ruling, “there is a completely new political environment" in the EU concerning immigration, and that Hungary had “already lost one billion euros because of this punishment, and I don’t think that’s right.”

He expects an agreement ending the fines by the end of the year, and linked the dispute to negotiations on the EU’s next seven-year budget, which requires unanimous approval from member states.

“I don’t believe that there can be a common EU budget until this problem is solved,” he said.

Rebuilding ties with Ukraine

Magyar has also sought to repair relations with neighboring Ukraine after Orbán repeatedly blocked aid to Kyiv and held up EU sanctions against Russia, all while maintaining cordial ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In a turnabout from Orbán's hostile approach to Kyiv, Magyar's government has expressed solidarity with Ukraine and designated Russia a national security threat. But he has maintained Hungary's demand that Ukraine protect its ethnic Hungarian minority’s right to education in its mother tongue.

While Orbán's government had failed to secure such a change, Ukraine’s parliament last week expanded minority-language education rights alongside Ukrainian following weeks of bilateral consultations.

Magyar called the passage of the law “a chance to open a new chapter in Ukrainian-Hungarian relations," which he said for many years have been "very frosty.”

He welcomed other Ukrainian gestures, including acknowledging Soviet Ukraine’s responsibility for the deportation and torture of Hungarians between 1944 and 1946, which he said was “an important step toward reconciliation.”

Still, Magyar opposes accelerated EU membership for Ukraine — advocated by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and numerous EU leaders — saying accession must be merit based and that he does not believe a country at war can join the bloc.

“It undermines the credibility of the European Union if you put some (prospective) member countries on a fast track,” he said.

Taxing wealth, raising benefits

At home, Magyar’s proposed 2027 budget combines tax cuts for lower earners with a new wealth tax, reflecting his criticism that Orbán’s economic policies divided Hungary into two groups: “Well-to-do, wealthy people, oligarchs and their circles, and then all the rest.”

The government expects an annual 1% tax on net wealth above 1 billion forints ($3.1 million) to affect about 15,000 people and raise 200 billion forints ($617 million), helping finance tax cuts for around 2 million lower earners. The rate would rise to 1.5% on wealth above 100 billion forints ($308 million).

The government also plans to double child allowances, whose basic rate is around $37 monthly for a one-child family and has been unchanged since 2008. It will also more than quadruple the monthly minimum pension from around $88 — which Magyar called “inhumane” — to around $370.

“That doesn’t make me a socialist. That doesn’t make me a leftist. This is called humanity. This is called social justice,” Magyar said.

News.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak leaves grieving families struggling with fear and stigma
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

When a schoolteacher in eastern Congo learned that five of her family members had been diagnosed with Ebola, she was “deeply shaken,” fearing the worst from a disease that carries stigma and is seen by some in her community as evil.

Two of her relatives — her brother and his wife — died of Ebola in July at a treatment center in Ituri province, the epicenter of the deadliest outbreak in Congo's history.

The 34-year-old teacher, who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity for fear of being stigmatized, said grief and stress over the loss of her relatives led her to seek treatment at a mental health clinic.

After two months at the clinic, the teacher said she was feeling better but worried about her future. “Will these people still be there for me?” she said of her relatives in Bunia, capital of Ituri.

Her experience highlights a burden rarely talked about in the fast-moving Ebola outbreak: the psychological toll on relatives coping with loss, fear and rejection in communities already scarred by years of rebel violence.

The outbreak is spreading at an unprecedented rate under some of the most challenging conditions imaginable, fueled by mass population movements, violence, mistrust and poor working conditions for frontline health workers. Caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus for which there's no approved vaccine or drug, the outbreak has killed at least 4,600 of the 9,500 people infected. The World Health Organization has said that it continues to outpace efforts to track and slow it.

The mental toll that comes with Ebola

Losing relatives to disease outbreaks is always difficult, but responders say grief can be especially severe with Ebola in a country where the disease is viewed by many as evil due to rumors and misconceptions. The risk of transmission also limits contact with the patients even after death, depriving families of closure and the opportunity to observe their preferred burial rites.

The psychological effects of past Ebola outbreaks can persist long after the immediate crisis, according to WHO, often taking the form of anxiety and mood disorders.

This is Congo’s 17th Ebola outbreak and has spread to eight provinces, coinciding with an escalation of decades-long conflict in the east between government forces and rebels.

Experts say the outbreak has compounded the trauma for many across the region. The medical response has focused largely on treating and containing the disease, with little to no attention to the mental health of those affected.

“There are so many areas (in eastern Congo) already devastated by war, crisis and severe malnutrition" and Ebola has worsened the condition of vulnerable populations and their mental health conditions, said Mirella Riccardi, a mental health specialist with Doctors Without Borders, known by its French name Médecins Sans Frontières.

‘It felt as though we were living all alone’

The Congolese teacher recalled that her family felt abandoned by neighbors when her relatives began showing symptoms consistent with Ebola, including fever, vomiting, diarrhea and muscle pain.

Neighbors stayed away until Ebola responders came to take the sick to a clinic and disinfect their house afterward.

“It felt as though we were living all alone because of the illness,” said the teacher, who did not contract the disease. “It has caused severe trauma within our family.”

She also lost someone she had regarded as a father and said many others in their Bunia neighborhood have also died.

“Many people initially assumed that their symptoms were due to poisoning or malaria. Only later did they realize that they could be Ebola,” she said.

The Samelo mental health facility in Bunia, where she was admitted, said it had received up to 350 patients, a surge it attributed to the Ebola outbreak.

“Grief, fear of infection, social isolation and a succession of deaths can leave families and communities lastingly vulnerable,” said Katembo Vyaluva Anicet, the head nurse at the facility.

Five months into the outbreak, health authorities remain alarmed. More than 70% of new cases involved people who were not among known contacts, while at least 60% of deaths occurred outside treatment centers as of early October, government data showed.

The teacher has been discharged from the mental health facility but returns often for follow-up checks. Her three other infected relatives survived, and her husband said she feels much better.

But fear of Ebola persists within her family and among her neighbors.

“This has reignited fear and tension within the community,” she said. “Now, everyone is wondering how this disease will end.”

___

Ope Adetayo contributed from Lagos, Nigeria.

____
