World.title: Can Tinubu campaign without campaigning?
World.content:
By LANRE OGUNDIPE

There is something intriguing about President Bola Tinubu’s approach to the 2027 presidential campaign. He appears determined not to conduct the election as though the business of governing Nigeria can be suspended for the sake of campaigning. Rather than carry his campaign physically from one rally to another, he is placing considerable responsibility on governors, party officials, ministers, legislators and political allies to take the message into the country. At first glance, this could look like a candidate stepping back from the electorate. I see something more calculated. Tinubu may be testing whether the political organisation he has spent decades building is now strong enough to campaign on his behalf. That is the real question.

The 2027 election may be the first major test of whether Tinubu can turn a presidential campaign from a candidate-centred operation into a system-wide political enterprise. If he can, it would say something important about the sophistication of his political organisation. But it would also expose the limit of political engineering: an organisation can carry a message into every state, but it cannot determine whether citizens believe the message.

Tinubu is not an accidental politician. He has spent decades learning the mechanics of power, from the difficult years of opposition politics to the construction of the Lagos political machine, the coalition that eventually became the APC, the struggle against an incumbent federal government and, finally, the presidency. He understands something many politicians learn too late: a serious political organisation cannot depend entirely on the physical presence of one man. The APC’s latest campaign structure suggests that this is precisely the calculation. The revised presidential campaign council places all 32 APC governors in charge of the presidential campaign in their respective states. It also reaches beyond the APC itself, assigning campaign responsibilities to Nyesom Wike in Rivers and the Federal Capital Territory, Chukwuma Soludo in Anambra and Ademola Adeleke in Osun. Tinubu remains at the centre of the structure, with Vice President Kashim Shettima and APC national chairman Nentawe Yilwatda as his principal deputies.

This is more than a distribution of campaign duties. It is an attempt to make the campaign a network rather than a procession behind one candidate. The President governs from Abuja. Governors take the political argument into the states. Ministers defend the administration. Legislators mobilise their constituencies. Party officials coordinate the structure. Political allies outside the APC widen the coalition. Tinubu is effectively asking whether the political system he has assembled can do much of the campaigning traditionally expected of the presidential candidate himself.

There is historical precedent for such an approach, but the lesson from history is more nuanced than the simple proposition that delegation works.

Richard Nixon’s 1972 re-election offers the closest parallel. His campaign allowed him to spend substantial time governing while surrogates carried the message across the country, and he went on to win 49 of 50 states. But the organisation worked because it was operating in a favourable political environment. Jimmy Carter’s defeat in 1980 showed the reverse. His limited campaigning during the Iran hostage crisis was only one element in an election already shaped by economic dissatisfaction, political fatigue and Ronald Reagan’s challenge. Four years later, Reagan benefited from an improving economy that allowed his record to become a powerful campaign argument in its own right.

Nigeria has its own cautionary history. Shehu Shagari’s 1983 re-election demonstrated the reach of incumbency and party organisation, but the controversy surrounding that election remains a reminder that political strength and democratic legitimacy are not interchangeable. The lesson is simple: political organisation can amplify a favourable political environment. It cannot manufacture one. That is where the Nigerian reality becomes decisive for Tinubu.

A governor can explain the administration’s reforms. A minister can defend its policy choices. Party officials can mobilise supporters and political allies can broaden the coalition. But Nigerians will not assess the 2027 election solely through political speeches. They will also assess it through the cost of feeding their families, moving to work, paying rent, keeping the lights on, sending children to school and dealing with insecurity. This is where public hardship deserves careful treatment. Hardship is politically powerful, but it is not politically deterministic. Nigerians can endure painful reforms if they believe the pain is temporary, necessary and producing visible results. They can also reject an administration that tells them the future will be better when their experience of the present offers little evidence of improvement. The real political question, therefore, is not whether Nigerians have suffered. They plainly have. It is whether enough Nigerians will believe that the suffering is producing a destination worth reaching. That is why the President’s own argument about reform matters. Tinubu has repeatedly maintained that Nigerians have endured necessary sacrifices and that the foundations for a stronger economy are being laid. He has also acknowledged the crucial next step: the benefits of reform must increasingly be felt in the daily lives of ordinary Nigerians.

By 2027, that will no longer be merely an economic argument. It will be an electoral proposition. Are Nigerians better off? The answer will not be determined by how convincingly the governors explain the reforms. Nor will it be determined simply by how angry critics are about them. It will be determined by whether citizens can see and feel enough improvement to conclude that the sacrifice was worth it. If food becomes more affordable, transport less punishing, electricity more reliable, security stronger, jobs more available and purchasing power better, the administration’s record may begin to campaign for itself. The governors and other surrogates would then have something much stronger than a talking point. They would have lived evidence. But if household hardship remains stubbornly dominant, the political calculation becomes much harder.

A government can have respectable macroeconomic indicators and still struggle to persuade citizens who cannot reconcile those indicators with the arithmetic of their homes. That is not necessarily proof that the reforms have failed. It is proof that economic reform and political legitimacy do not always move at the same speed.

This is where Tinubu’s political sophistication will face its most serious test. Governors are not merely campaign operatives. They are politicians with their own futures, successors to produce, factions to manage, alliances to preserve and political debts to repay. Their interests may overlap with Tinubu’s, but they are not identical to his. The deployment of 32 governors therefore gives the ruling party extraordinary political reach while simultaneously creating a complex web of state-level calculations. Tinubu’s long political apprenticeship becomes significant here. His political strength has arguably never rested principally on speechmaking. It has rested on political engineering: building coalitions, identifying useful alliances, accommodating competing interests and keeping a broad political structure together long enough to achieve an objective.

The inclusion of politicians outside the APC can therefore be understood as an extension of that philosophy. The coalition is less about ideological purity than electoral arithmetic.

That is politics as Tinubu has practised it for decades. But political sophistication carries a danger of its own. Those who command a political structure can begin to confuse the strength of their organisation with the strength of their argument.

The 2027 electorate will not be a meeting of governors. It will be millions of individual decisions. A voter may cheer at a rally and vote differently. He may support the direction of the reforms but dislike their consequences. He may believe that the sacrifice is finally producing results. Or he may conclude that he has sacrificed enough. Those decisions cannot be read reliably from the size of a crowd, the number of governors behind a candidate or the prominence of the people assembled on a campaign platform. This is why Tinubu does not necessarily need to be everywhere. But he needs to be present where the political argument is most difficult. He needs to explain the choices his government has made, defend its record, answer its critics and, above all, demonstrate that he understands the distance between a reform that looks successful on a government balance sheet and one that feels successful in a Nigerian household.

That may ultimately determine whether his unconventional campaign strategy becomes a masterstroke or a miscalculation. If the political environment is improving, the governors can amplify it. If citizens are beginning to feel relief, the campaign can give that relief a political narrative. If hardship remains the dominant experience, however, political organisation will have a much harder task. It can explain hardship. It can ask for patience. It can present the promise of tomorrow. It cannot erase the experience of today. The machine can carry the message. It cannot determine whether Nigerians believe it. That is the real test of Tinubu’s 2027 strategy. And when the campaign finally gives way to the ballot, the most carefully constructed political architecture in the country will still have to confront the one variable it cannot organise away: the independent judgement of the Nigerian voter.

•Ogundipe, a public affairs analyst, wrote in from Abuja.

World.title: Again, Another Non-Nigerian Brings Ebola into Abuja; FG Says Don’t Panic, Stay Vigilant
World.content:
• Govt confirms first case in Abuja, activates emergency response

•44 close contacts identified as tracing begins

• Medical sciences academy seeks implementation of high-alert protocols

•Urges Nigerians to avoid handshakes, unnecessary physical contacts

Emmanuel Addeh and Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja





The federal government yesterday confirmed one case of Ebola disease in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), with the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare revealing that it has activated emergency public health response, including the commencement of contact tracing.

Also, the Academy of Medical Sciences of Nigeria (AMSN) yesterday noted with concern the reported case, but commended the prompt commencement of contact tracing as well as the isolation of the patient and the in-tensified surveillance already underway.

The Academy further recommended the immediate and nationwide implementation of high-alert protocols, draw-ing on the proven measures that enabled Nigeria to contain Ebola in 2014 and to respond to COVID-19 in 2020.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), the epicentre of the disease, has recorded thousands of cases and deaths as health authorities intensify containment efforts. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, had heightened regional concerns over cross-border transmission, prompting increased surveillance, contact tracing and isolation measures.

Specifically, as of October 20, 2026, at least 4,605 people have died from the ongoing Ebola outbreak in Central and East Africa, according to the US Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), with one death reported in Kenya and two in Uganda.

Besides, the CDC has recorded 9,582 confirmed cases across the affected countries, with investigations and reporting still ongoing. For comparison, the DRC’s 2025 Ebola outbreak, which was declared over on December 1, 2025, recorded 45 deaths from 64 confirmed and probable cases, representing a case fatality rate of 70.3 per cent.

Ebola is a severe and often fatal disease transmitted through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people or contaminated materials. The Bundibugyo strain responsible for the 2026 outbreak is particularly con-cerning because there is no approved vaccine or specific treatment for this strain, making early diagnosis, iso-lation, supportive care and contact tracing essential to containing its spread.

But in the statement conveying the news on the Ebola case, the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Wel-fare, Prof. Ali Pate, said the patient was a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria on an international flight from Uganda.

She was said to be asymmetric and Ebola usually takes about three weeks for symptoms to develop.

And thankfully, Abuja has very well equipped medical laboratories capable of meeting the challenge.

According to the minister, the woman was admitted to a private hospital in the FCT where she received care for several days before diagnosis was confirmed. The statement added that she is currently in isolation and receiv-ing medical care.

Pate said the Federal Ministry of Health and the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and (NCDC) are working closely with FCT Health Services Secretariat and other relevant authorities to contain the infection and prevent further spread.

“Contact tracing has commenced with 44 close contacts identified presently, with public health teams identifying and monitoring people who may have been exposed, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts,” he said.

He added that surveillance has been intensified and hospitals are receiving immediate support to strengthen infection prevention and control measures.

The federal government called on all public and private healthcare facilities nationwide to be on high alert. It urged healthcare workers to maintain a high index of suspicion, promptly identify and isolate suspected cases, observe strict infection prevention and control measures, and immediately report suspected cases.

The government also issued advisory on what Nigerians should know and do. It said Ebola spreads through direct contact with blood or body fluids of sick people or contaminated materials, and cannot spread before symptoms begin.

It advised Nigerians to remain calm but vigilant, practice regular hand hygiene, avoid contact with body fluids of suspected cases, watch for symptoms including fever, severe weakness, headache, vomiting and diarrhoea, and report possible exposure immediately.

It further urged those contacted during tracing, including airline passengers, to cooperate and avoid rumours and stigma.

“Our assurance to Nigerians (is that) Nigeria successfully contained Ebola in 2014, and we have the experi-ence and public health systems to respond to this case,” Pate said, noting that investigations are ongoing and updates will be provided.

The first known case of Ebola in Nigeria was in a traveller called Patrick Sawyer, exposed in Liberia. On July 17, 2014, while under observation in a Monrovia, Liberia, hospital for possible Ebola, the patient developed a fever and, while symptomatic, left the hospital against medical advice.

Despite advice against travel, on July 20 he flew by commercial airline from Monrovia via Accra, Ghana, to Lomé, Togo, then flew to Lagos. On arrival in the afternoon of July 20, he was acutely ill and immediately transported to a private hospital where he was noted to have fever, vomiting, and diarrhea. During hospital admission, the patient was queried about Ebola and said he had no known exposure; he was initially treated for presumed malaria.

Based on the patient’s failure to respond to malaria treatment and his travel from an Ebola-affected country in the region (2), treating physicians suspected Ebola. The patient was isolated and tested for Ebola virus infection while local public health authorities were alerted about a suspected case of Ebola. A blood specimen sent to Lagos University Teaching Hospital was confirmed positive for acute Ebola virus infection. The index patient died on July 25.

Meanwhile, the AMSN has recommended the immediate and nationwide implementation of high-alert protocols, drawing on the proven measures that enabled Nigeria to contain Ebola in 2014 and to respond to COVID-19.

“These should include: Enhanced screening at airports, seaports and land borders, particularly for travellers from affected countries. (Also) strict infection prevention and control in all public and private health facilities, with adequate personal protective equipment for health workers, rigorous contact tracing, monitoring and follow-up with sustained, accurate public communication through official channels,” it stated.

The academy, in a statement by the President, Prof. Osato Giwa-Osagie; Foundation President, Prof. Oladapo Ashiru and Head of Rapid Response Committee, Prof. Boaz Adegboro, pointed out that health workers must maintain a high index of suspicion, promptly isolate suspected cases and report them immediately to public health authorities.

“The public should understand clearly that Ebola is not an airborne disease. It spreads through direct contact with the blood or other body fluids of a person who is sick with Ebola or has died from it, or through contact with materials contaminated by those fluids. A person with Ebola cannot spread the disease before symptoms begin.

“As a simple and effective precaution, the Academy advises all Nigerians to avoid handshakes and other un-necessary physical contact, including hugging, during this period. We encourage the use of non-contact greet-ings,” the group said.

For information or to report a suspected case, it urged members of the public to call the NCDC toll-free number 6232, which it said is available 24 hours a day as well as seven days a week.

“The Academy stands ready to support the federal government and all stakeholders with expert advice as the response continues,” the group emphasised.

World.title: Gbajabiamila: Draft of National Policing Bill Now Ready, Undergoing Legislative Review
World.content:
• Expected back from justice ministry by October 30 for onward transmission to president

•Submitted along with 29 consequential amendment bills

• Delta approves amendment for state police, to write National Assembly

Deji Elumoye in Abuja and Omon-Julius Onabu in Asaba





The presidency, yesterday, disclosed that the draft of the 2026 National Policing Bill was ready.

Chief of Staff to the President and Chairman of the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, Hon. Femi Gbajabiamila, made the disclosure, in a release.

Gbajabiamila said the group had completed the drafting stage of its assignment and had formally submitted the bill, together with 29 consequential amendment bills, to the Federal Ministry of Justice for legislative drafting review and validation.

He said the submission to Attorney General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Lateef Fagbemi, took place on Monday, October, 19, in line with the working group’s work plan.

The chief of staff explained that the ministry’s review would ensure that the bills conformed to legislative drafting standards and conventions, and did not conflict with existing laws.

He said the Ministry of Justice was expected to return the validated draft bills to the working group on or before Friday, October 30 for final consideration before their presentation to President Bola Tinubu, which would mark the conclusion of the group’s mandate.

Gbajabiamila said, “The proposed National Policing Bill seeks to establish the constitutional and legislative framework for a dual policing structure, comprising a Federal Police Service and State Police Services.

“The Working Group remains committed to a rigorous and transparent process that will deliver a comprehensive legislative proposal for consideration by the president and subsequent transmission to the National Assembly.

“The work on preparing the National Policing Bill is proceeding alongside the ongoing consideration of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026 by the States Houses of Assembly, which must be completed before the bill is transmitted to the National Assembly.”

The presidency had last Thursday hinted that the National Policing Bill would be transmitted to the National Assembly within two weeks.

Gbajabiamila told newsmen after the steering committee’s meeting at State House, Abuja, “The National Policing Bill is more or less ready for transmission to the National Assembly.

“We will probably have one more meeting after this to cross the t’s and dot the i’s and make sure every area is covered. So, we are 90 per cent ready. The governors have one or two observations, and we should be ready in about a week or so.”

He described the bill as “the most consequential bill of the administration so far”, adding that it has undergone strenuous exercises in the last few weeks since the working group’s steering committee began deliberations on August 3.

Commenting on the possibility of the states dragging their feet on the passage of the Sixth Constitution Alteration Bill (State Police), especially against the backdrop of the information that only about six states had passed the amendment, out of the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Gbajabiamila affirmed that there was a “national consensus” among Nigerians on the need for the amendments.

“I see no reason why anyone will want to have a rethink on it,” he said.

Members of the committee present at Thursday’s meeting held at the conference hall of the Chief of Staff Office at State House, Abuja, included Chairman of Nigeria Governors’ Forum and Governor of Kwara State, AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq; Governor Dapo Abiodun of Ogun State; Governor Uba Sani of Kaduna State; Inspector General of Police, Tunji Disu; and Attorney General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, represented by Solicitor General and Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Justice, Mrs Beatrice Jedy-Agba.

Others were Chairman, Policy Advisory Committee, Justice Abdullahi Liman (rtd); Head, Nigeria Police Reform Secretariat, Professor Olu Ogunsakin; Special Adviser to the President on National Assembly Matters (House of Representatives), Dr. Lanre Smart; Senior Special Assistant to the President on Planning and Research, who also doubles as Secretary of the Committee, Nnadubem Moghalu; the representative of President of Nigerian Bar Association; and Assistant Inspector-General of Police (AIG) Abraham Nabhon Thomas, representing the National Security Adviser, among others.

Tinubu had on July 7 inaugurated the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill to prepare the legal framework for the implementation of state police across the country.

The working group’s inauguration followed National Assembly’s passage of the Constitution Alteration (State Police) Bill, 2026, in which the president proposed a dual policing structure comprising the Federal Police Service and 36 State Police Services.

Tinubu had stated that while the constitutional amendment created the framework for state police, the National Policing Bill would provide the legal structure for its implementation.

He said, “The Constitution Amendment Bill establishes the framework for dual policing, but it does not operationalise it. That work is left to the National Policing Bill.”

According to him, the proposed legislation would address issues necessary for a smooth operationalisation of the state police system.

Tinubu stated, “The proposed National Policing Bill will include provisions on minimum policing standards, state readiness certification, federal-state coordination, accountability, human rights safeguards and fiscal conditions.”

The president said the committee would produce an implementation-ready draft bill immediately after the constitutional amendment process.

“The Working Group has been constituted to produce a technically robust, implementation-ready draft National Policing Bill for transmission to the National Assembly,” Tinubu said.

He said the committee was necessary to avoid delay after the State Police bill was passed.

“We must not wait until the constitutional process is concluded before beginning this important assignment,” he said.

Delta Approves State Police Amendment

Delta State House of Assembly, yesterday, approved the Sixth Alteration Bill of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999 (as amended) to give legislative muscle to the proposed State Police Services in the country.

The approval followed deliberation on a letter from the National Assembly seeking the consideration and concurrence of the 36 States Houses of Assembly in the ongoing constitutional amendment process.

Speaker, Hon. Emomotimi Guwor, read the letter on the floor of the Assembly, outlining the objective of the bill, which sought to provide a constitutional framework for the establishment of State Police Services while preserving the Nigeria Police Force as the Federal Police Service.

Majority Leader, Hon. Emeka Nwaobi, said the proposed amendment aimed to guarantee security of life and property through a dual policing system, allowing states to establish and fund their own police services to address rising cases of insecurity, particularly at the local level.

The lawmakers generally agreed that the bill would strengthen local intelligence gathering, improve response to security challenges, create employment opportunities, and help tackle insecurity at the grassroots more effectively.

Support for the bill was unanimous, with all 23 members present at plenary affirming their support.

While commending the members for their patriotism and overwhelming support for the bill, Guwor stated that the establishment of State Police would ensure a safer environment and engender the desired development of Delta State.

He stated, “Distinguished colleagues, I commend you for approving the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, in line with Section 9 sub-section (2) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as altered).

“This is a significant step towards the establishment of State Police in Nigeria. It brings us closer to a policing system that is more responsive to our communities, improves intelligence gathering, and strengthens our capacity to tackle security challenges.

“For Delta State, this reform holds great promise for protecting lives and property, sustaining peace and creating a safer environment for investment and development in line with the M.O.R.E Agenda of our amiable Governor, His Excellency, Rt. Hon. (Elder) Sheriff Francis Orohwedor Oborevwori.”

The speaker thereafter directed Clerk of the House, Mr. Otto Aghoghophia, to communicate the resolution of the Delta State House of Assembly to the National Assembly appropriately.

Earlier, the legislators observed one-minute silence in honour of former governor of Delta State, Dr. Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan, who died on Monday, October 19, three days to his 72nd birthday.

World.title: Tinubu, Awolowo’s Family Mourn as Afenifere Leader, Pa Fasoranti, Dies at 100
World.content:
• President describes elder statesman as an icon and beacon of principle

•Says Nigeria will sorely miss his voice of wisdom, moral authority, and fatherly counsel

•Aiyedatiwa, Falae, Sanwo-Olu, Bamidele grieve

Deji Elumoye, Sunday Aborisade in Abuja, Sunday Ehigiator in Lagos and Fidelis David in Akure





President Bola Tinubu and the Chief Obafemi Awolowo family, yesterday, paid glowing tributes to Afenifere leader, Pa Reuben Fasoranti, who died at the age of 100.

Tinubu, in a tribute, praised the late patriarch and elder statesman as a principled icon and one of the Awolowo progressive family’s last great titans.

According to him, Nigeria will sorely miss Pa Fasoranti’s voice of wisdom, moral authority, and fatherly counsel.

Tinubu, in the 13-paragraph release, stated, “I received with profound sadness the news of the passing of Pa Reuben Famuyide Fasoranti, our father, patriarch, elder statesman, and foremost Afenifere leader, who died at the glorious age of 100.

“On behalf of the federal government and the people of Nigeria, I commiserate with the Fasoranti family, the good people of Akure Kingdom, the government and people of Ondo State and South-west Nigeria, and the entire Afenifere family.

“Pa Fasoranti was an icon, a beacon of principle, and one of the last great titans of Chief Obafemi Awolowo’s progressive family.

“His life, spanning a century, was a lesson in integrity, discipline, selflessness, and unwavering commitment to the Yoruba people and the unity and progress of Nigeria.”

The president added, “From his days as an educationist and principal, to his stewardship as Commissioner for Finance in the old Western Region, and later as the leader of Afenifere, Baba never wavered in his belief in true federalism, social justice, and a Nigeria that works for all.

“Baba made immense contributions to this country and, at the risk of his life, fought for the democracy we enjoy today.

“Pa Fasoranti distinguished himself in every respect: in his disciplined, Spartan way of life, his belief in principles, and his commitment to noble causes.”

Tinubu said, “Our nation will sorely miss his voice of wisdom, moral authority, and fatherly counsel, especially now, when we need his guidance most.

“I recall Baba’s centenary on May 11 this year, when we celebrated not just longevity, but a legacy of honour. He lived a fulfilled life and left indelible footprints in the sands of time.

“I also recall his prayers and counsel when I came to his residence in Akure in 2022 to inform him of my decision to contest the presidency. Pa Fasoranti told me I would be President in his lifetime, and God answered his prayer.”

Tinubu stated, “I had hoped Papa would also be around with us for my second term to witness the full dawn of economic growth and prosperity in the land.

“But we must thank God for Pa Fasoranti’s long life of service, grace and fulfilment.

“May his gentle soul rest in perfect peace. May God comfort all who mourn him and grant his family the fortitude to bear this great loss.”

Aiyedatiwa, Falae Hail Afenifere Leader as ‘One-in-a-Thousand-Years Man’

Fasoranti, who turned 100 years in May, died peacefully in his sleep at his residence, yesterday, October 20, according to his eldest son and Secretary to the Ondo State Government, Dr Taiwo Fasoranti.

Taiwo said the family had been looking forward to celebrating his father’s 101st birthday but had accepted his death as the will of God, describing his century-long life as one worthy of celebration rather than mourning.

He stated, “Baba passed on this evening around 4pm peacefully in his room, in his bed. Baba was 100 years old. He turned 100 in May, and we were all looking forward to his 101st birthday, but God knows best.

“I don’t count it as mourning, but I count it as a time to celebrate his longevity and his influence and impact in the lives of Nigerians, especially Yoruba people.”

He described his late father as a man of few words whose wisdom, firmness, and calm disposition left an enduring impression on those around him.

“My day starts with seeing him in the morning and seeing him when I get back from the office. No matter how late it is, he will still be up waiting for me to come in,” he said, recalling the close relationship they shared until his father’s death.

Fasoranti’s Passing is End of Awolowo’s Political Era, Late Sage’s Family Declares

The Awolowo family mourned the death of Fasoranti, describing his passing as the end of a remarkable era in the political history of Awolowo’s Titans, the Yoruba nation, and Nigeria.

The head of the Awolowo family and Chairman of African Newspapers of Nigeria (ANN) Plc, publishers of the Tribune titles, Ambassador Olatokunbo Awolowo Dosumu, made the assertion in a condolence statement issued yesterday.

Dosumu described Fasoranti as one of the last surviving titans of the political tradition established by the late Chief Obafemi Awolowo, stating that his commitment to the ideals of the late sage remained steadfast throughout his life.

Dosumu stated, “The passing of Chief Reuben Fasaranti at the venerable age of 100 marks the end of a remarkable era in the political history of the Yoruba nation and Nigeria.

“With his departure, we have lost, in a very real sense, the last of the titans of the Awolowo political tradition.”

Dosumu added, “Chief Fasaranti belonged to that extraordinary generation of leaders whose political convictions were rooted in principle, whose commitment to public service was steadfast, and whose loyalty to the ideals and philosophy of Chief Obafemi Awolowo endured through changing times and circumstances.”

He stated, “Throughout his long and eventful life, he remained steadfast in his commitment to the values of justice, equity, progressive governance and the advancement of the common good.

“Neither the passage of time nor the changing fortunes of politics diminished his dedication to the cause he embraced.”

Falae: He’s Exceptional Generational Man

Former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Chief Olu Fale, described the late elder statesman as his in-law, whom he had known intimately for more than 60 years and considered an extraordinarily rare figure in Nigeria’s political, religious, and social life.

“I’m going to describe Baba Fasoranti as an exceptional generational man, one in a thousand years,” Falae said.

He recalled that throughout their decades-long relationship, he had never witnessed Fasoranti quarrel with anyone or raise his voice at political meetings.

Falae said the late leader was always willing to mediate disputes and help parties reach peaceful resolutions.

He said, “In all that time, I’ve never heard him quarrel with anybody, shout at anyone, even in political meetings. He was always ready to mediate in any dispute brought to his attention.”

Falae said Fasoranti’s influence extended beyond politics to education, community development, and religious life, stating that his commitment to helping disadvantaged children was among the enduring examples of his selflessness.

He recalled that when Fasoranti was the founding principal of Iju/Itaogbolu Grammar School, he admitted pupils from poor backgrounds and allowed them to complete their secondary education on credit, with the opportunity to repay after leaving school.

“No one is perfect, but Baba is as near perfect a human being as I believe you can get in this fallen world,” Falae said, describing his death as a significant loss to Akure, Ondo State, and the Yoruba nation.

Aiyedatiwa: He Was a Beacon of Wisdom

Ondo State Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa, described Fasoranti as a patriarch and a beacon of wisdom, integrity and selfless service, whose contributions to the development of Ondo State, Yorubaland, and Nigeria would remain indelible.

In a telephone conversation, he said, “His counsel, fatherly guidance, and principled stand on issues of justice and good governance will be sorely missed.”

The governor commiserated with the Fasoranti family, the people of Akure Kingdom, and the state over the loss.

Sanwo-Olu: It’s End of an Era

Lagos State Governor, Mr. Babajide Sanwo-Olu, described the demise of Pa Reuben Fasoranti, leader of the pan-Yoruba socio-political organisation, Afenifere, as the end of an era.

Sanwo-Olu, who is Chairman of South-West Governors’ Forum, said the glorious exit of Pa Fasoranti, a respected elder statesman, educationist, and progressive, was a big loss to the Yoruba people and Nigeria at large.

In a condolence message personally signed, Sanwo-Olu described the late Pa Fasoranti as a committed leader and a symbol of wisdom, integrity, and selfless service who served the Yoruba people and Nigeria passionately.

He also commiserated with his Ondo State counterpart, Aiyedatiwa; the government and people of Ondo State, particularly the people of Akure Kingdom; the Fasoranti family; and members of Afenifere.

Sanwo-Olu stated, “Baba Fasoranti was a respected and passionate statesman whose contributions to education, leadership and public service remain indelible. He impacted many lives positively through courageous and uncompromising leadership. His commitment to public service and community development was commendable.

“Pa Fasoranti, during his lifetime, made a lot of positive impact in Yorubaland and Nigeria. He did great exploits as the leader of Afenifere by steering the ship of the pan-Yoruba socio-cultural organisation in the right direction.

“We cherish Pa Fasoranti’s commitment to fighting for truth, equity, justice, true federalism and good governance, which he championed for many decades during his lifetime.”

Sanwo-Olu added, “I pray for the repose of the soul of the late Pa Reuben Fasoranti. May God grant the deceased’s family, loved ones, and the Yoruba people the fortitude to bear the irreparable loss of the centenarian.

“On behalf of my family, the government and people of Lagos State, as well as my brother governors in the South-West, I commiserate with the Fasoranti family, Afenifere members and the entire people of Yorubaland over the departure of our respected leader and elder statesman, Pa Reuben Fasoranti.”

Bamidele: Fasoranti’s Death Robs Nigeria of a Patriot, Awoist

Leader of the Senate, Senator Opeyemi Bamidele, described the death of Pa Fasoranti as a monumental loss to Nigeria, saying the late elder statesman devoted his life to national development, progressive politics, and the pursuit of true federalism.

Bamidele, who expressed shock and sadness over the passing of the centenarian, said Fasoranti distinguished himself as a patriot and statesman who consistently placed the national interest above personal and sectional considerations.

In a condolence message, the senate leader said the late Afenifere chieftain left behind an enduring legacy of integrity, selflessness, and commitment to the unity and progress of Nigeria.

Describing him as a patriot par excellence, Bamidele said, “The late centenarian was a patriot par excellence, a statesman of uncommon integrity who consistently placed national interest far above personal or sectional considerations.

“As an educationist, school administrator and community leader, Baba Fasoranti impacted generations of Nigerians and left an indelible mark on our national development trajectory.”

World.title: CAS: Volatility, Contemporary Warfare Makes  Military to Build Relevant Doctrines
World.content:
Linus Aleke in Abuja

The Chief of the Air Staff (CAS), Air Marshal Sunday Kelvin Aneke, has said the volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity of contemporary warfare placed increasing demands on the military to develop relevant doctrines and innovative operational thinking to prepare personnel for complex security challenges.

He stressed that meeting these demands required not only capable aircraft and modern equipment but also sound doctrines, effective professional military education, informed operational planning and institutions capable of translating lessons from operations into improved combat effectiveness.

Speaking at the commissioning of new vehicles procured for the Air Warfare and Doctrine Centre (AWDC), the CAS commended the Commandant and the entire staff of the Centre for their continued efforts to advance the professional and intellectual capabilities of the Service.

Represented by the Chief of Logistics, Air Vice Marshal Henry Yurkusi, the CAS noted that the Air Warfare and Doctrine Centre occupied an important position in this process, adding: “The Centre’s responsibilities in doctrinal development, research and professional military education are central to our institutional growth.”

The CAS said the Centre’s output helped to shape how the Service understood air power, prepared its personnel and responded to emerging operational requirements.

“It is, therefore, important that the Centre has the necessary resources to support its activities and sustain the tempo required to fulfil its mandate. The vehicles being commissioned today represent a practical investment in that institutional capacity.

“Beyond their immediate transportation function, they will improve the Centre’s ability to coordinate official engagements, supervise activities, support training programmes and facilitate other institutional assignments.

“Their availability is expected to reduce mobility constraints and contribute to more efficient administration. While these vehicles may appear to be a modest addition to the Centre’s overall inventory, their value lies in how effectively they support the work the Centre was established to carry out.”

Air Marshal Aneke stressed that lessons emerging from operations must inform the development and review of doctrine, while training must remain responsive to the realities confronting aircrew and ground personnel.

“We must continually assess whether our concepts, procedures and institutional approaches adequately prepare the Service for present and future challenges.

“In this regard, I expect the Centre to sustain its efforts towards producing sound doctrinal products and competent personnel who can translate professional knowledge into operational advantage,” he concluded.

World.title: Oborevwori Visits Late Uduaghan’s Family, Otuaro, Omo-Agege, Mulade, Other Mourn
World.content:
Sylvester Idowu in Warri

Delta State Governor, Hon. Sheriff Oborevwori, yesterday, visited the family of former governor Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan, to offer his condolences, following his death on Monday at the age of 71.

Oborevwori, who was accompanied by his wife, Deaconess Tobore Oborevwori, and top government functionaries, described the late Uduaghan as a great leader whose contributions to the development of Delta State would remain indelible.

The governor had earlier joined family members and other dignitaries, including Uduaghan’s daughter, Orode, and former President of the Nigeria Football Federation, Amaju Pinnick, to receive the former governor’s remains at Osubi Airport.

Speaking during the condolence visit to Uduaghan’s widow, Mrs Roli Uduaghan and family members, Oborevwori said the outpouring of grief and the large number of people, who gathered to mourn the former governor reflected the impact he had made on many lives.

He recalled his relationship with the deceased, describing him as his former boss and a man who played a significant role in his political journey.

“He was my boss. He gave me the highest political appointment, Special Adviser, in 2007. That is something that really touches my heart. You are all aware that he supported me throughout this journey,” the governor said.

Oborevwori described Uduaghan as a calm, articulate and thoughtful leader who made significant contributions to the development of the state.

According to him, the number of people who turned out to receive the late governor’s remains and those who visited his family was evidence of the lives he had touched through public service and political appointments.

The governor had earlier signed the condolence register, wrote: “I am saddened by the demise of the former Governor, Dr Emmanuel Eweta Uduaghan. He was a great boss. I commiserate with his beloved wife, children, family members and Deltans over this great loss.

“May God grant the family the fortitude to bear the loss. Your impact in Delta can never be forgotten. Asamaigor, RIP.”

Also, the immediate past deputy governor of Delta State, Dcn. Kingsley Burutu Otuaro, described the death of Uduaghan as a major loss to Delta State and the Niger Delta acknowledging his contributions to governance, peace and regional development.

Otuaro, in a condolence message, said the death of the former governor had robbed the state of an experienced statesman whose leadership and commitment to the wellbeing of the people would remain part of Delta State’s political history.

“Dr. Uduaghan was more than a former governor; he was a father, an elder, a gentleman and a leader whose humility, wisdom and commitment to peace and development touched many lives,” Otuaro said.

Also, a former Deputy President of the Senate, Senator Ovie Omo-Agege, has expressed profound shock over the death of Uduaghan.

In a condolence message personally signed, Senator Omo-Agege described Uduaghan’s death as a profound personal loss, recalling their days together in the James Ibori administration.

“This is a profound loss. We served together under our leader, Chief James Ibori. He was Secretary to the State Government and I was Executive Assistant to the Governor. I knew him as calm in a crisis, loyal, humane and decent. He brought a doctor’s compassion into government.

“Our political paths later diverged, but our respect for each other never did. He remained a brother across party lines: a gentleman, a bridge-builder and a man of peace”, he said.

Similarly, the National Democratic Party (NDP) Candidate for the house of representatives in Warri federal constituency, Chief Mulade Sheriff, in a tribute described the passing of Uduaghan as a monumental loss to the state, Niger Delta and Nigeria as whole.

Mulade described his passing as the fall of an Iroko, the exit of a political colossus, and a monumental loss to Delta State, the Itsekiri Nation, the Niger Delta and Nigeria at large.

The Delta Unity Group (DUG) has also expressed deep shock and profound sorrow on the passing of Uduaghan.

In a statement issued by its National Publicity Secretary, Sir Sunny Areh, the group stated that Dr. Uduaghan’s transition was not just the loss of a former governor but the exit of a unifier.

“For us in DUG, this is not just the loss of a former Governor; it is the exit of a unifier. Dr. Uduaghan was Delta in its truest essence: An Itsekiri by birth, Urhobo by adoption, Isoko by bond, Anioma by love and Ijaw by service. In a state often divided by ethnic fault lines, he lived and led as a bridge. He belonged to all of us, and all of us belonged to him.”

World.title: 2027: AbdulRazaq Tasks Renewed Hope Youth Leadership on Tinubu, Others’ Polls
World.content:
Kwara State Governor, Alhaji AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, yesterday, urged the leadership of Renewed Hope Youth Engagement (RHYE) to mobilise youths across the 16 local government areas of the state for the electoral victory of President Bola Tinubu and other All Progressives Congress (APC) candidates in the 2027 elections.

AbdulRazaq made the appeal in Ilorin, during the inauguration of the Kwara State Chapter of RHYE, an initiative aimed at promoting youth participation in governance, political engagement and national development.

He advised the youths to strengthen grassroots engagement, promote peaceful political participation and communicate the programmes and achievements of the All Progressives Congress (APC) administration to the electorate.

He said the party’s objective ahead of the 2027 elections was to present its records, communicate its vision and secure the support of the people for President Bola Tinubu and other APC candidates.

“Our aspiration is to see Kwara record overwhelming votes for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and secure strong electoral support for all APC candidates, from the National Assembly to the State House of Assembly and other elective positions,” he said.

The governor stressed that achieving the objective required unity among party members, effective grassroots engagement, credible communication and a genuine connection with the people.

Represented by the state deputy governor, Mr. Kayode Alabi, AbdulRazaq said youths remained important partners in the development of the state, adding that their energy, creativity and determination were essential to building stronger communities and expanding opportunities.

Earlier, the RHYE State Coordinator, Nafisat Buge, said the inauguration was aimed at strengthening an existing structure committed to grassroots engagement and youth participation across Kwara.

In his remarks, the state Chairman of the APC, Mr Sunday Fagbemi, congratulated the newly inaugurated leadership of the Renewed Hope Youth Engagement (RHYE) in Kwara, expressing confidence that supporters would mobilise in large numbers to vote for their party.

World.title: Nigeria’s Vanishing Middle Class Exposes Deepening Economic Crisis, Declares Duke
World.content:
Ayodeji Ake

Presidential candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP), Donald Duke, has said the disappearance of Nigeria’s middle class reflected the deepening economic crisis in the country, warning that widespread poverty, unemployment and insecurity were pushing the nation towards state failure.

Duke, who spoke in an interview, yesterday, said many Nigerians who previously considered themselves financially stable were now struggling to meet their basic needs, leaving them vulnerable to economic shocks and emergencies.

He argued that the country’s economic difficulties had been compounded by shrinking businesses, inadequate job opportunities and a rapidly expanding population that the economy could no longer adequately support.

“The so-called middle class does not really exist anymore. Many of those we call middle class are only surviving from day-to-day. Let there be one serious emergency and they crumble,” he said.

The former Cross River State governor said the widening gap between the wealthy and the poor was an indication that Nigeria’s economy was failing to provide the conditions necessary for a decent standard of living.

“You have perhaps one per cent who are genuinely wealthy and then a huge number of people struggling around or below the poverty line,” he said.

Duke said the situation had become a major motivation for his decision to contest the 2027 presidential election, arguing that Nigeria could not afford to continue on its present path for another four years.

“I talk about the urgency of now because I don’t think we can go on like this for another four years,” he said.

He explained that his decision to seek the presidency was driven by the need to move beyond criticism of successive governments and offer solutions to the country’s worsening economic and social challenges.

“You get to a point in your life where you say, ‘Either I walk away or I do something.’ There is no guarantee that you will win. But I don’t want to look back and say that all these things happened and I did nothing,” he said.

World.title: Appeal Court Nullifies Zamfara North APC Senatorial Primary
World.content:
Onuminya Innocent in Sokoto

The Court of Appeal sitting in Sokoto has nullified the All Progressives Congress (APC) primary election for Zamfara North Senatorial District for gross non-compliance with party guidelines and the Electoral Act.



The judgment was delivered yesterday by Justice Tunde Oyebamiji Awotoye, who upheld the earlier decision of the Federal High Court, Gusau, which had in August 2026 voided the primary election.



Justice Awotoye lambasted the APC for what he described as reckless declaration of Senator Sahabi Ya’u as winner despite clear violations of its own constitution and the Electoral Act.



The court held that the respondent, Hon. Abdullahi Shinkafi, proved his case beyond reasonable doubt, questioning how a senatorial district with 26,000 registered party members could return 70,000 votes for an aspirant.



According to the court, the figures presented by the party showed clear over-voting and irregularities that rendered the entire exercise invalid and liable to be nullified.



Justice Awotoye wondered why the party leadership ignored the obvious discrepancies and proceeded to declare a winner in an election that failed basic integrity tests.



The appellate court resolved all seven issues formulated for determination in the appeal against the appellant, Senator Sahabi Ya’u.



On the preliminary objection bordering on lack of jurisdiction raised by the appellant’s counsel, Popoola, SAN, the court held that the respondent had duly exhausted all internal dispute resolution mechanisms of the party before approaching the court.



The court also dismissed the argument on statute bar, holding that the suit was filed within time and was entertained on its merit in line with extant laws.

Reacting, counsel to the respondent, Bello Galadi, described the decision as a victory for the rule of law and democracy.



Galadi said the judgment would serve as a deterrent to political parties and politicians who undermine internal democracy and violate their own rules.

Also, Hon. Shinkafi thanked the judiciary for living up to its billing as the last hope of the common man, describing the judgment as freedom from political captivity.



He argued that the judgment was a victory against marginalisation and prolonged dominance, noting that Senator Ya’u has spent 16 consecutive years in the Senate while Kaura Namoda has monopolised the seat since the return to democracy in 1999.

World.title: Gogo ‘too rich’ for old-age grant still fighting SASSA
World.content:
80-year old Anna Mampe Ndlovu is fighting SASSA over being deemed 'too rich' for her old-age grant. Image: AI augmented, for illustrative purposes only

Meet old-age grant recipient, Anna Mampe Ndlovu, from Vereeniging. She’s 80 years old and recently told a media outlet that she hasn’t received her government pension for several months. That’s because, according to the agency, she’s ‘too rich’ to continue receiving it.

Allegedly, after an old-age grant review, income from a cash investment left by her late husband pushed her over the eligibility limit. The thing is, according to the gogo, he never named her as a beneficiary, so, she says she has seen none of it. “I’m not receiving a cent. I’m suffering,” said Ndlovu.

GOGO ‘TOO RICH’ FOR OLD-AGE GRANT

Meanwhile, the South African Social Security Agency tells a different story. Spokesman Lungelo Mkamba says its system shows payments were processed from July 2025 to March 2026. Ndlovu’s old-age grant has not been terminated and someone else must be receiving her money. Therefore, he urged her to visit her nearest SASSA office to rectify the situation. The Auditor-General’s recent findings peg ineligible SASSA payments at R1.33 billion last year, including R211 million to so-called deceased recipients.



Nevertheless, the dispute is a good reminder of how the system works and what elderly beneficiaries can do to stay aligned. Just this month, on 9 October, the agency confirmed it was intensifying grant reviews, eLife certification and biometric enrolment. It reminds old-age grant recipients that the money, “is not an unconditional entitlement.”

WHAT TO DO IF YOU’RE EVER IN THIS SITUATION

New SASSA minister Dina Pule has not rubber-stamped October top-ups and billions is being wasted on ineligible beneficiaries. What’s next? Image: File

If you find yourself in a similar situation, what can you do?

Make sure your contact details are up to date and respond to every SASSA request.

If contacted for a review, eLife certification or biometric enrolment, go on the date given.

Tell SASSA about changes to income, assets, marital status, address or bank details. Inheritances and investments can count against you in your means test.

Check your payments. If your grant is missing, ask SASSA immediately to confirm bank details, and when the last payment was made.

Watch your account for deductions you don’t recognise (typically unauthorised funeral policy debit orders).

Keep all paperwork. Retain ID, bank statements, estate documents and reference numbers.

Visit your local SASSA office or phone 0800 601 011. Don’t wait to ask questions that could rectify the matter.

But what do you think? Have you had your old-age grant reviewed recently? How did the process go? Please share your thoughts in the comments section below …

World.title: How South Africa’s disability grant compares with Botswana’s
World.content:
People living with disabilities in South Africa and Botswana receive financial assistance from their respective governments, but the monthly payments differ significantly.

South Africa’s disability grant increased to R2 400 per month in April 2026, while Botswana’s Disability Cash Transfer programme provides different amounts depending on the beneficiary group.

How much South Africa pays in disability grants

According to SAnews, South Africa’s disability grant increased from R2 315 to R2 400 per month in April 2026.



The grant is administered by the South African Social Security Agency (SASSA) and is intended for eligible people whose physical or mental disabilities prevent them from working.

According to the South African government, applicants must be between 18 and 59 years old and meet the prescribed income and asset limits.

Applicants must also undergo a medical assessment to determine their eligibility. The grant can be temporary or permanent, depending on the expected duration of the disability.



What Botswana pays in disability cash transfers

Botswana operates a Disability Cash Transfer programme for eligible people with disabilities.

In March 2025, DailyNews, Botswana’s government newspaper, reported that beneficiaries in Kanye District received different monthly amounts of P550, P700, P830 and P850.

The report did not provide a breakdown explaining which disability categories corresponded to each payment amount.



Earlier, in December 2023, Botswana’s assistant minister for local government and rural development said people with severe and profound disabilities received a monthly disability cash transfer of P600.

These figures reflect different reporting periods, so the latest published district-level rates should not automatically be treated as a uniform national payment. Botswana’s government assesses applicants to determine their eligibility for disability benefits.

How the two disability grants compare

South Africa’s maximum monthly disability grant is R2 400, while Botswana’s reported monthly disability cash transfers range from P550 to P850 (R660 to R1 020).



The programmes also have different eligibility requirements and payment structures.

The amounts alone do not establish which country provides better overall support, as the cost of living, access to other social assistance programmes and individual needs also matter.

For people with disabilities and their families, understanding the eligibility rules and available benefits is an important part of accessing government assistance.
