03

What to See & Do

WEDNESDAY IN RIO

TODAY’S PICK — CENTRO CULTURE Spend the wet afternoon inside the free Banco do Brasil cultural centre Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil sits at Rua Primeiro de Março 66, an easy walk from Uruguaiana or Carioca metro stations. It is open Wednesday to Monday from 9am to 8pm, and entrance and exhibitions are free, which makes it the smartest indoor plan for a showery Wednesday. The 1906 building is part of the draw, so allow two unhurried hours inside.

OUTDOORS — LOW-KEY AND LEAFY Parque Lage works if the rain eases Parque Lage in Jardim Botânico is open daily from 8am to 5pm and costs nothing. Keep today’s outdoors slow: the seafront will be wet and the sea is not a wise call with storms around.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Lapa for live music when the rain clears Lapa is Rio’s best-known district for live samba and choro after dark. Check each venue’s own page for tonight’s line-up and opening time before you go, as programmes change at short notice.

MATCH DAY — FLUMINENSE AWAY Fluminense play Palmeiras in São Paulo tonight Fluminense are in São Paulo for the second leg of their Copa Libertadores semi-final against Palmeiras, kicking off at 9:30pm Brasília time. Palmeiras lead 2-1 from the first leg at the Maracanã. Flamengo host Estudiantes at the Maracanã on Thursday at 9:30pm in the other semi-final, after a 0-0 first leg in La Plata.

BUSINESS — A STRONG TUESDAY Brazilian stocks rally, the dollar eases The Ibovespa, Brazil’s main stock index, rose 1.57% to 208,296 on Tuesday, and the dollar eased 0.11% to R$5.0278. For expats with money in Brazil, the practical point is the exchange rate: R$5.0278 per US dollar at Tuesday’s close. Brazil’s mid-month inflation reading (IPCA-15) is due on Friday, with a forecast of 0.43% for the month.

THE WEEKEND ROUND Election Sunday, then a drier week The presidential runoff is on Sunday 25 October, and polling stations are open from 8am to 5pm. Keep plans flexible and carry your voting documents if you are a registered voter. Saturday still carries a 50% chance of rain, so check the forecast again on Friday.

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

The Metrô and the VLT light-rail line are the quickest ways across Centro in the rain. Metrô Line 1 serves Uruguaiana and Carioca stations near CCBB.

With rain expected from late morning, ride-hailing demand usually rises at peak hours, so allow extra time.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

In Centro, lunch counters serve a prato feito, the plate of the day, at midday. Confeitaria Colombo on Rua Gonçalves Dias is the historic café stop near the CCBB.

For dinner, Lapa and Botafogo have many casual bars and restaurants within walking distance of a metro station.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a compact umbrella and a light layer, as the day is warm and humid.

Most places accept cards and Pix, Brazil’s instant payment system, but keep a little cash for small kiosks.

After dark, keep phones out of sight when leaving the metro, especially around Centro.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

Centro and Botafogo are where many newcomers find coworking spaces and café meetups.

On a rainy day, a café with reliable wifi is the easiest way to meet people and get work done.

08

Game Day

FOOTBALL

Fluminense play Palmeiras in São Paulo tonight at 9:30pm, and bars in Rio are likely to show the match.

Flamengo host Estudiantes at the Maracanã on Thursday at 9:30pm, so expect a busy Maracanã area and crowded Metrô trains that evening.

09

WEEK IN FIGURES

The Ibovespa, Brazil’s main stock index, rose 1.57% to 208,296 on Tuesday, and the dollar eased 0.11% to R$5.0278.

Brazil’s IPCA-15 inflation reading follows on Friday 23 October, forecast at 0.43% for the month and 4.73% over twelve months, against 0.70% and 4.47% previously.

The Selic, Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, stands at 13.75% ahead of the 3–4 November Copom decision.

World.title: Latin American Pulse for Wednesday, October 21, 2026
World.content:
Latin America mood today: Brazil is wary before Sunday's runoff, Mexico resigned to high rates, Chile hit by storms and Argentina closing legal chapters.

Rio Times · Latin America

Key Facts —Brazil Wary pride and election nerves as Meta’s Oversight Board criticises recurring moderation failures, while an FGV study says lower deforestation avoided up to R$192 billion (about US$38 billion) in climate damage. —Prediction markets Polymarket traders put Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning the 25 October runoff at 79.9% and Lula’s at 20.5%, as of 11:01 p.m. ET on Tuesday, 20 October. —Mexico Resigned patience as 25 of 36 analysts in the Citi survey expect Banxico to leave interest rates unchanged through 2027, with the peso seen at 18.20 per dollar at year-end. —Chile Frayed nerves as the government suspends classes in ten Santiago communes under a red alert and La Florida extends the closure. —Argentina Legal endings and industrial strain as a court opens insolvency proceedings for textile industrialist Teddy Karagozian and a US judge formally closes the YPF case. —Colombia Steady institutions as the coffee federation says it will renew its fund contract for ten years, while a mobile office helps earthquake victims in Chocó.

The Continent’s Mood Today

The region is jittery about politics, weather and money, but steadier than the headlines suggest. Brazil’s stock market rose 1.57% on Tuesday and Mexico’s 0.36%, while Chile’s slipped 0.42%.

Four days before Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday 25 October, much of the region’s attention is on one vote. Elsewhere, courts, central banks and storms set the mood.

Brazil — Wary Pride Under a Digital Cloud

Meta’s Oversight Board, the company’s independent review panel, said on 20 October that it sees recurring failures in how Meta moderates election content in Brazil. Meta had admitted that a technical error removed the ad account of President Lula’s campaign and that a global incident blocked post view counts on 7 October.

The board said Meta errs both by enforcing its rules too loosely and too rigidly, and it asked for transparent and consistent moderation. The criticism lands four days before the runoff, in a country with a long memory of online manipulation.

There was also a long-term gain. A study by the Brazilian Institute of Economics at the Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV Ibre) estimates that lower Amazon and Cerrado deforestation since 2023 avoided 1.49 billion tonnes of greenhouse gases.

Economist Bráulio Borges puts the avoided climate damage for Brazil at between R$67 billion and R$192 billion (about US$13 billion to US$38 billion), and at R$1.16 trillion (about US$231 billion) worldwide. Inpe, the national space research institute, recorded falls of 41.8% in the Amazon and 23.8% in the Cerrado between August 2025 and July 2026.

For a foreigner living in Brazil or holding assets there, this means separating election-week noise from slower gains such as lower deforestation.

What Prediction Markets Say

Traders on Polymarket, a prediction market, put Flávio Bolsonaro’s chance of winning the 25 October runoff at 79.9 percent and Lula’s at 20.5 percent at 11:01 p.m. ET on Tuesday, 20 October. About US$189.8 million had been traded on that market.

These prices are bets by traders, not polls, and they can move within minutes of a debate or a new survey. The official result will come from Brazil’s electoral court, the TSE.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Mexico — Resigned to a Tight-Money Winter

A Citi survey published on 20 October found that 25 of the 36 analysts polled expect Banxico, the central bank, to leave its policy rate unchanged for the rest of 2026 and through 2027. Analysts now see the dollar ending 2026 at 18.20 pesos, up 20 centavos from their forecast 15 days earlier.

Mexico’s stock market closed up 0.36% at 69,259 and the peso was little changed at about 18.43 per dollar. Retail sales for August are due today at 13:00 Lisbon time, and mid-month inflation follows on Thursday.

For a foreigner or asset holder, this means expecting high interest rates to last and a peso that analysts now see weaker than a few weeks ago.

Chile — Rain, Mud and Frayed Nerves

On Tuesday 20 October the government suspended classes in ten communes of the Santiago Metropolitan Region, including Las Condes and La Florida, because of a red alert linked to a new frontal system. The measure covered all schools in those communes.

La Florida’s municipality then extended the suspension for its municipal schools and kindergartens to Wednesday 21 October, and its mayor asked the education ministry to rethink the reopening. The dispute follows the mudslide that hit Las Condes on 8 October.

For a foreigner or asset holder in Chile, the practical risk is disruption from storms and slides. The IPSA stock index fell 0.42% to 10,926 on Tuesday.

Argentina — Courts Close Chapters, Industry Feels the Strain

A court in La Rioja opened preventive insolvency proceedings (a concurso preventivo) for Teodoro “Teddy” Karagozian, a leading textile industrialist, La Nación reported on 20 October. His case will be handled together with that of Hilado SA, another company in the TN Platex group.

Separately, US judge Loretta Preska formally closed the YPF case in New York and voided her 2023 judgment of more than US$16 billion against Argentina, Infobae reported on 20 October. She was following a March appeals court ruling, and Burford Capital’s petition to the US Supreme Court is still pending.

For a foreigner holding assets or living in Argentina, the YPF ruling reduces a large legal risk but is not yet final. The textile insolvencies show how strained local industry remains.

Colombia — Steady Institutions, Disaster Relief

Germán Bahamón, general manager of the National Coffee Federation, has said the federation will renew for another ten years its contract to administer the National Coffee Fund, and that the sector is “working hand in hand” with the government. The current extension expires on 11 December, so the new government must sign the contract.

Colfondos, one of Colombia’s pension funds, sent a mobile office to Quibdó, the capital of Chocó, from 19 to 21 October to help people affected by the earthquake. It offers advice on early withdrawal of severance savings and on other benefits.

For a foreigner in Colombia, the coffee contract signals continuity in a core export sector, while the relief work shows the scale of the disaster response.

The Shared Mood

The continent is caught between institutions that keep working and pressures that keep building. Brazil’s Meta dispute, Mexico’s tight-money outlook, Chile’s storms and Argentina’s insolvencies all point to the same feeling: people want to believe in progress, but they are tired.

The deforestation gains and court rulings are real. The strain of polarisation, weather and tight money is also real, and for a foreigner the practical rule is to respect the resilience without mistaking it for calm.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened with Meta and Brazil’s election?

Meta’s Oversight Board said on 20 October that it sees recurring moderation failures in Brazil’s election, including a technical error that removed Lula’s campaign ad account and a global glitch that blocked view counts on 7 October.

What do analysts expect from Mexico’s central bank?

A Citi survey published on 20 October found that 25 of 36 analysts expect Banxico to leave its rate unchanged through 2027, and they see the dollar at 18.20 pesos at the end of 2026.

Why were classes suspended in Santiago on 20 October?

The government suspended classes in ten communes of the Santiago region because of a red alert linked to a new frontal system, and La Florida extended its closure to 21 October.

What happened in the YPF case on 20 October?

US judge Loretta Preska formally closed the case in New York and voided her 2023 judgment of more than US$16 billion against Argentina, while Burford Capital’s petition to the US Supreme Court is pending.

World.title: Guyana father reportedly confesses to throwing 6-year-old who couldn’t swim to drown after spiritual advisor told him the boy wasn’t his
World.content:
Guyana father reportedly confesses to throwing 6-year-old who couldn’t swim to drown after spiritual advisor told him the boy wasn’t his

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 45-year-old father in Guyana has reportedly confessed to killing his six-year-old son by throwing him into the water, knowing he could not swim, after allegedly being told by a spiritual advisor that the child was not biologically his.

Bharrat Jaikarran is accused of killing his son, Orlando Jaikarran, whose decomposing body was discovered early Tuesday morning, October 20, in a canal at Bath Settlement, West Coast Berbice. The boy had been missing since October 14.

According to the Guyana Chronicle, Jaikarran reportedly told investigators that he had consulted a pujari, a Hindu religious officiant who conducts religious ceremonies and may also provide spiritual guidance. He claimed the spiritual advisor told him Orlando was not his biological son, although that allegation has not been independently verified.

Investigators were reportedly told that Jaikarran rode his motorcycle to an area near the sea dam, left it there and returned home to collect Orlando. He allegedly took the child back to the location and threw him into the water despite knowing that the six-year-old could not swim.

The father reportedly admitted knowing that a neighbour had surveillance cameras but believed his movements would not raise suspicion because Orlando frequently accompanied him on early-morning fishing trips.

According to News Room Guyana, police obtained information from the father that led them to the child’s body. Investigators also reviewed surveillance footage reportedly showing the father travelling with the child before returning alone.

Jaikarran had initially reported Orlando missing and denied harming him. However, as investigators gathered evidence, he reportedly confessed to the killing and provided information that led police to the location of the boy’s remains.

The tragedy has sparked outrage in Guyana, with Minister of Human Services and Social Security Vindhya Persaud condemning the killing and warning against religious figures who make harmful claims under the guise of spiritual guidance.

The case has also raised concerns about the influence of spiritual beliefs and the devastating consequences of acting on unverified claims.

Jaikarran remains in police custody as investigators continue their investigation. A post-mortem examination is expected to establish Orlando’s cause of death.

World.title: Triple murder trial of Christian Espat and Michael Brown delayed until 2027 as prosecution introduces new evidence
World.content:
Triple murder trial of Christian Espat and Michael Brown delayed until 2027 as prosecution introduces new evidence

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The long-awaited triple murder trial of Christian Espat, 31, and Michael Brown, 25, has been postponed until January 2027 after the prosecution sought to introduce additional cellphone evidence just days before the proceedings were scheduled to begin.

The two men appeared before Justice Nigel Pilgrim in the High Court on Tuesday, October 20, in connection with the October 2023 shooting deaths of three-year-old Amarie Esmeralda Rodriguez, her father Delmar Rodriguez, and Carlos Leonardo Chi in San Pedro Town.

The prosecution informed the court that additional digital evidence had emerged following discussions with a witness. The evidence reportedly includes cellphone records, a forensic report and photographs that the Crown considers crucial to its case.

Defense attorneys Dickie Bradley and Leeroy Banner, representing Espat, and Dr. Lynden Jones, representing Brown, objected to the late disclosure, arguing that they needed sufficient time to independently examine the material.

Jones told the court that he received notice of the additional evidence late Friday, October 16, and raised concerns about discrepancies in the number of photographs disclosed. He also questioned why digital files reportedly obtained in 2023 carried modification dates from October 2026.

Although Justice Pilgrim acknowledged that the evidence was being introduced unusually late, he ruled that the prosecution could submit it, emphasizing the importance of allowing relevant forensic and digital evidence to be considered in determining the accused men’s guilt or innocence.

The judge subsequently scheduled another case management conference for December 3, 2026, and set the trial for January 19 to 29, 2027, declaring that it would proceed on those dates “come hell or high water.”

The October 22, 2023 shooting in San Pedro’s San Pedrito area also left several other people injured. Espat and Brown were subsequently charged with three counts each of murder, attempted murder and use of deadly means of harm.

The trial has faced previous procedural disputes, including a June 2026 ruling allowing two prosecution witnesses to testify virtually after they expressed fears for their safety.

Justice Pilgrim also invited defense attorneys to submit bail applications on behalf of their clients, who have remained on remand since 2023.

Both men were further remanded to the Belize Central Prison pending the next hearing.

World.title: 19-year-old Adam Reynolds charged in violent $89,900 Burrell Boom home invasion after stolen SUV recovered
World.content:
19-year-old Adam Reynolds charged in violent $89,900 Burrell Boom home invasion after stolen SUV recovered

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old Ladyville resident has been charged with aggravated burglary following a violent home invasion in Burrell Boom Village during which four armed intruders allegedly tied up a businessman and escaped with nearly $90,000 in cash and valuables, including his SUV.

Adam Abraham Reynolds, a labourer of Vista Del Mar, Ladyville, appeared before a Belize City magistrate on Tuesday, October 20, where he was arraigned on a single count of aggravated burglary in connection with the October 14 attack on a 53-year-old businessman at El Chiclero Resort.

According to police reports, the man was asleep inside his condominium around 4:50 a.m. when he was awakened by loud noises. An intruder allegedly jumped onto his bed and pressed a pillow against his face. As he struggled, a second man entered and struck him with an object resembling a firearm, causing an injury to his face.

The businessman was then restrained with duct tape around his hands, feet and mouth while three intruders ransacked his residence. The men allegedly escaped with $30,000 in cash, two gold chains valued at $12,000, two cellphones, a television, a surveillance system and a burgundy 2017 Toyota Rush valued at $45,000. The total value of the stolen property was reported at $89,900.

Police subsequently located the stolen SUV in Santa Familia Village, Cayo District, on October 15. Investigators allege that Reynolds was inside the vehicle when officers approached, but sped away before crashing and abandoning it.

Usher later positively identified the recovered vehicle as his property.

During an October 16 police briefing, Assistant Superintendent Stacy Smith confirmed that two persons of interest had been detained and that investigators were seeking another individual in connection with the burglary.

Reynolds reportedly surrendered to police on Monday, October 19, in the presence of an attorney. During Tuesday’s court appearance, he requested additional time for his attorney to arrive, but the arraignment proceeded after approximately two hours without counsel.

The charge remains an allegation, and Reynolds has not been convicted. Investigations into the involvement of the other alleged intruders continue.

World.title: International News: World Food Programme to cut food assistance for 500,000 people in Gaza
World.content:
International News: World Food Programme to cut food assistance for 500,000 people in Gaza

By Zoila Palma: The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) will suspend monthly assistance to approximately 500,000 people in Gaza because of a funding shortfall, the agency announced on Monday.

The reduction means that about 1.1 million Palestinians, roughly half of Gaza’s population, will continue receiving monthly food or cash assistance, down from the 1.5 million to 1.8 million people reached each month since the October 2025 ceasefire.

Shaun Hughes, the WFP’s country director, told AFP in East Jerusalem that the assistance had been a lifeline for families struggling to survive. He stressed that the cuts were not caused by a lack of humanitarian access to deliver food, but by insufficient funding. The agency’s decision comes as many Palestinians continue to face displacement, insecurity and difficult living conditions, with the United Nations estimating that 1.2 million people have lost their homes.

Under the revised assistance programme, families receiving food will get one parcel instead of two, along with a smaller bag of wheat flour.

Meanwhile, approximately 75,000 families receiving cash assistance will see their monthly payments reduced from 1,250 shekels, about US$400, to 750 shekels, or roughly US$240.

Hughes said conditions in Gaza remained severe, with daily airstrikes, continued displacement and widespread homelessness.

Recent assessments indicate that 1.4 million people, or about two-thirds of the population, remain acutely food insecure and require assistance to survive.

World.title: Saudi finance minister promises to review delayed US$77 million solar energy loan for Belize
World.content:
Saudi finance minister promises to review delayed US$77 million solar energy loan for Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño says he personally raised Belize’s long-delayed solar energy financing arrangement with Saudi Arabia’s finance minister during meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.

Briceño explained that he attended a small gathering involving several high-level participants, including the Saudi finance minister, where he took the opportunity to raise concerns over the delayed project.

According to the Prime Minister, the Saudi official was not fully familiar with the details but assured him that he would examine the matter.

Briceño expressed optimism that the discussion could help move the project forward.

Belize signed a US$77 million financing agreement with the Saudi Fund for Development in August 2023 to support the construction of a 60-megawatt solar energy project.

However, as Breaking Belize News reported in August, Minister of Public Utilities Michel Chebat confirmed that no funds had been disbursed three years after the agreement was signed.

Chebat previously attributed the delays to procurement requirements, engineering consultations and procedures imposed under the Saudi financing arrangement.

The government has also discussed restructuring the project to combine solar generation with battery storage.

While Briceño described his conversation with the Saudi finance minister as encouraging, he did not announce a specific date for disbursement or the start of construction.

World.title: PM blames two-year delay in battery storage project on disputed iguana sanctuary claim
World.content:
PM blames two-year delay in battery storage project on disputed iguana sanctuary claim

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño has again criticized bureaucratic delays at the World Bank, claiming that a dispute involving an alleged iguana sanctuary in San Pedro held up a major electricity storage project for approximately two years.

Speaking after returning from international financial meetings in Bangkok, Briceño said the government had been pursuing World Bank financing for battery storage facilities capable of supplying approximately 40 megawatts of electricity.

According to the Prime Minister, the project was delayed after concerns were raised that land earmarked for the development was being used as an iguana sanctuary.

Briceño disputed the claim, describing the person occupying the property as a squatter, and said World Bank officials were embarrassed when he explained the circumstances during their meeting.

He argued that the delay had serious consequences for Belize’s energy security.

The Prime Minister explained that battery storage would allow Belize to purchase cheaper electricity from Mexico during periods of low demand, particularly in the early morning hours, store the power and use it during peak consumption periods.

He suggested that the project could have helped Belize avoid some of the electricity supply problems it has experienced.

The World Bank announced the US$58.4 million Belize Energy Resilience and Sustainability Project in February 2025. The initiative includes battery energy storage systems at four strategic locations to improve electricity reliability and reduce dependence on imported power.

Briceño said the government is continuing discussions to resolve the outstanding issues while pursuing greater energy independence through solar and other renewable sources.

World.title: PM seeks extension of World Bank agriculture project as March 2027 deadline approaches
World.content:
PM seeks extension of World Bank agriculture project as March 2027 deadline approaches

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Prime Minister John Briceño says Belize is requesting an extension of a World Bank-funded agricultural development project, warning that complicated administrative requirements have delayed its implementation.

Speaking following his return from Bangkok, Briceño explained that the project is intended to assist small farmers in adapting to climate change through improved agricultural practices and technology.

However, he complained that the World Bank’s requirements and approval procedures have made it difficult for Belize to complete the necessary work within the prescribed timeframe.

The Prime Minister said he raised the matter directly with two World Bank vice presidents during his overseas meetings.

The project is scheduled to conclude in March 2027, but Briceño said the government has made the case for additional time to ensure that farmers benefit from the initiative.

According to the Prime Minister, a World Bank technical team is expected to visit Belize shortly to review implementation, assess the project’s successes and consider the government’s request for an extension.

The Climate Resilient and Sustainable Agriculture Project, approved in March 2022, aims to improve agricultural productivity and encourage the adoption of climate-smart farming practices. World Bank records identify March 31, 2027, as its scheduled closing date.

Briceño expressed optimism that the government’s discussions would help secure more time for the project, although no extension has yet been confirmed.

World.title: Former CMU worker details university’s accounting, banking systems
World.content:
Campus of Caribbean Maritime University in Kingston (Photo: CMU)

A former senior member of staff of the Caribbean Maritime University (CMU) is expected to continue testimony regarding the school’s finances on Wednesday, with information on the now-defunct CAP-YES programme, in the fraud trial of former CMU boss Fritz Pinnock along with former education minister Ruel Reid and their co-accused.

The witness, appearing before Senior Parish Judge Sanchia Burrell at the Kingston and St Andrew Parish Court on Tuesday, testified how money came into and left certain bank accounts controlled by the university between 2016 and 2019, including accounts for payroll, CAP (Career Advancement Programme) and CAPYES (Career Advancement Programme – Youth Empowerment Services) programme, among others.

The department in which they worked was guided by the FAA (Financial Administration and Audit Act) and PBMA ( The Public Bodies Management and Accountability Act), the witness said, adding that it oversaw payroll, including salary deductions for CMU employees; accounts receivable, which dealt with collecting money owed to the school; and accounts payable, which dealt with any money the school owed to vendors or debt obligations.

While testifying, the witness indicated that the weekly accounts payable process included the submission of documentation verifying the debt obligation, which would be entered on CMUs system and included in an aged payables report. Any vendors to be paid by the school would then be selected from that report.

When pressed on what type of vendors this included, the witness listed utility entities, suppliers of goods to the school’s tuck shop and others undertaking special projects.

The witness also told the court that the school received a monthly subvention from the Ministry of Finance through the Ministry of Education that was deposited to a specific bank account.

When asked where that subvention was funded from, to their understanding, the witness said “from taxes”.

That account, the witness said, was used as a flow-through to other bank accounts, including payroll accounts.

The witness also touched on the operations of the school’s canteen or tuck shop, which had multiple accounts associated with it. The witness testified that cash proceeds would be deposited into the accounts and canteen vendors paid from it, adding that when enough cash was not in the account to pay vendors, the canteen would be provided with an advance by CMU, which would also go to the account.

The school also received money from the government for the operation of the CAP and CAP-YES programmes, deposited directly into accounts set up by CMU, the witness told the court. The witness said accounts were used for expenses associated with CAP and CAP-YES, including paying some salaries as well as stipends for students in need and other initiatives.

CAP, which is carried out at institutions across the island, was intended to provide technical, vocational, and academic training to youth, and CAP-YES was a programme offshoot attached specifically to the Caribbean Maritime University (CMU).

CAP and CAPYES were shuttered at the Caribbean Maritime University in 2020 with instructions to complete the course for those already in training and take in no further applicants.

During testimony, the witness identified Pinnock as the former head of the university, pointing out his striped shirt and orange tie. Pinnock, who has sought leave to take notes during the trial, did not react visibly at being identified. He was represented by a junior of his attorney in the matter, Hugh Wildman.

Pinnock, Reid and their co-accused, Reid’s daughter Sharelle Reid and wife Sharen Reid and Councillor Kim Brown Lawrence’s are before the court on a 35-count indictment, accused of participating in a scheme with others unknown that siphoned off more than $25 million from the Ministry of Education and CMU.

They have pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Issues with disclosure were also put before Burrell in the courtroom on Tuesday with defence attorney Linda Wright, who represents Reid, Carolyn Chuck, who represents Sharelle and Kevon Johnson, who holds for Brown Lawrence’s attorney Oswest Senior Smith, all rising to express concern.

Wright maintained that more documents relating to certain witnesses, including the witness scheduled to be called that day, had been shared by the prosecution at a late hour, thus creating challenges for the defence to go through the documents and take instructions from their clients.

Wright maintained that this was not a “trial by ambush”, describing the disclosure as untidy.

The prosecution maintained that the documents in relation to Tuesday’s witness were not new and that any late disclosure of new documents was not a deliberate effort on its part.

Burrell, who reminded counsel to exercise care around disclosure, is expected to grant a brief adjournment in relation to the issue.

World.title: NWC seeks 51 per cent tariff increase
World.content:
Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The National Water Commission (NWC) has applied to the Office of Utilities Regulation (OUR) for a 51 per cent tariff increase, a move that could affect its approximately 500,000 customers.

Acting NWC President Kevin Kerr told the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) on Tuesday that the application was submitted to the OUR last Friday, adding that the regulator is expected to make an announcement shortly.

Kerr said the proposed increase is tied to an investment plan designed to secure funding for the company’s priority projects.

He warned that if the OUR does not approve the full 51 per cent increase, the NWC would have to revise its investment plan.

Kerr also noted that members of the public would have an opportunity to provide feedback through a consultation process before the OUR makes a determination on the application.

The NWC has argued that the increase is necessary to bring its revenues in line with its expenses. The commission last received a tariff increase in 2019.

NWC Chief Financial Officer Fabian Christie told the committee that the company’s revenue position had deteriorated over time, particularly in relation to customer payments.

He said the proposed increase was needed to keep pace with rising operating costs, including energy expenses.

World.title: 11 things only a Queen’s girl would know
World.content:
In this file photo, Miss Jamaica World 2010 Chantal Raymond strikes a pose with a group of students from the Queen's School.

From the famous ‘Holy Ground’ to the lizards roaming the school grounds, The Queen’s School had its own quirks, traditions and unwritten rules, according to the St Andrew-based institution’s alumni community.

Based on Observer Online’s discussions with past students, here are 11 things that will have any Queen’s girl reminiscing about life at the institution.

1. Holy Ground

Holy Ground never looked or felt particularly holy, so why was it called that in the first place? That remains a question worth asking. One thing was certain: students know the spot well, as it was reserved for devotions and, on occasion, punishment. It was hardly the place anyone wanted to visit for the wrong reasons!

2. Big Tree

Big Tree was one of the most recognisable landmarks on the school grounds. Towering over the area, it served as an outdoor lunchroom, complete with concrete tables and chairs where students gathered to eat, chat and socialise. And when all the seats were taken, the tables became seats, too. Rules or no rules, a girl had to find somewhere to sit!

3. The Hall

The Hall was the designated space for music and drama classes, but it doubled as a favourite hangout for several cliques. Getting students to leave was sometimes a task in itself, particularly for Mr Heriage, who old girls remember having had his hands full trying to get everyone out. For some, it was a classroom; for others, it was the place to catch up with friends.

4. Etheline Aiken

Legendary former principal who served as headmistress from 1976 to 1992. It was under her stewardship that The Queen’s School won the 1978 Girls’ Athletic Championship. Former students remember her as being strict, holding students accountable and requiring them to behave as proper young ladies. But, at the same time, she was well-loved.

5. The ‘iguanas’

Queen’s had lizards in every shape, size and colour imaginable. They were so plentiful that it sometimes seemed there were more lizards than students on the grounds. Whether perched somewhere in plain sight or scurrying across the grounds, these reptiles were a familiar part of the school environment.

6. The ‘Chiney’ shop across the road

The wholesale across the road was a popular stop before and after school. From bag juice and cake soap to rags and socks, it supplied students with a range of essentials. Despite repeated warnings not to cross the road to visit the shop, students somehow found themselves making the trip day after day.

7. Smithy, aka Mr Smith

When it came to Mr Smith, there were two sets of students: those who were lucky enough to be in his class and those who wished they were. Affectionately known as Smithy, he brought a distinctive personality and energy to Mathematics and Accounts lessons, making the subjects enjoyable. His famous Mathematics marathons were another highlight, giving students plenty to remember long after the lessons ended.

8. Reverend Pointsette’s prayers

Reverend Pointsette’s devotions could feel especially long when students had to stand in the blazing sun. Some would deliberately arrive late in the hope of missing part of the session, while her voice coming over the speaker in the afternoon was often met with collective sighs across the school. Those prayers may not have been everyone’s favourite part of the day then, but their value is something many have come to appreciate with time.

9. The in-school vendors

Every form seemed to have its own go-to vendor, making it easy to find a snack or treat after lunch. But the offerings went well beyond food. From haberdashery items and CDs to clothing, these enterprising young women catered to a variety of student needs. Even better, some have since registered their businesses and are thriving in their entrepreneurial ventures, showing that the hustle extended well beyond the school gates.

10. Mrs Keane-Dawes

Another long-serving principal, Mrs Keane-Dawes made it her duty to monitor the school gates in the mornings, earning her reputation as the school’s very own gate police. Strict but understanding, she commanded respect while ensuring students remained disciplined and focused. Her firm approach, balanced with compassion, helped create an environment in which students were encouraged to excel.

11. The standpipe

The standpipe, originally used to water the school grounds, often became a busy wash-up station shortly before the morning bell. Girls would gather to wash their faces and freshen up, with cake soap and soap dishes in abundance. With just 15 minutes to go before classes, the area could become quite crowded as everyone tried to get ready in time for the school day.

– Carlysia Ramdeen
