World.title: Where is the outrage?
World.content:
Minister of religion Lisean Gordon delivering the sermon during the Heritage Week Thanksgiving Service at the Greater Highway Church of Christ Apostolic in Caterwood, Trelawny, on Sunday. Looking on are Mayor of Falmouth C Junior Gager (left) and moderator Leisa Dawson. (Photo: Horace Hines)

CARTERWOOD, Trelawny — Minister of religion Lisean Gordon has criticised what she described as the public’s readiness to demand justice when police officers use force, but silence following the killing of two members of the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) last Friday.



Preaching under the theme ‘Let the Children Know’ during a Heritage Week Thanksgiving Service at the Greater Highway Church of Christ Apostolic in Caterwood, Trelawny, on Sunday, Gordon said the lack of comparable demonstrations demanding justice for the slain cops reflects a troubling imbalance.

“They may be somebody’s father, somebody’s son. Nobody came out because we have placed in the heart of ungodly people that we are allowing them to take over this country, all in the name of politics,” said Gordon as she addressed the service hosted by the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC) in Trelawny and the Trelawny Municipal Corporation.

Two members of the JCF’s Special Operations Branch, Corporal Trevoy Shaw and Constable Devoney Rose, sustained fatal gunshot wounds during a firefight with men who had barricaded themselves inside a house in the Five Miles area of St Catherine on Friday.

Three civilians, Errol Hussey, his son Malique Hussey, and nephew Javoun Cogle, also died in the incident while a 10-year-old girl was left nursing a gunshot wound.

Delivering the sermon, Gordon condemned the tendency to vilify members of the police force without knowing the circumstances surrounding an encounter, and charged that media coverage and circulating recordings often fuel premature judgements.

Gordon linked the hostility towards law enforcement personnel to a broader erosion of respect for authority, and contended that political allegiance is encouraging Jamaicans to excuse behaviour they might otherwise condemn.

“There is something called the hidden curriculum, which we sometimes forget about. The hidden curriculum: What they see us do is what they will do,” said Gordon, who is also an educator.

She also took issue with verbal attacks against political leaders, including Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness and Opposition Leader Mark Golding, warning that adults risk normalising disrespect among children who observe and absorb their behaviour.

“This disrespect that we put up with…because we are affiliated to a party, and to politics, it must stop. Disrespect is disrespect, and everybody who leads us needs to be respected, whether they are on the Opposition side or they are on the ruling side,” declared Gordon.

She argued that while children are taught to assert their rights, adults are neglecting the importance of responsibility and accountability.

“But we teach them about their rights, but no longer teach them about their responsibility,” Gordon said as she insisted that parents and other adults must uphold discipline, principles, and respect rather than retreat from the challenges of raising the younger generation.

She warned that Jamaica faces a dangerous escalation of disorder if the erosion of these values continues, describing the threat as a storm more severe than Hurricane Melissa.

“I am afraid of what is coming to Jamaica. There is a storm coming that is worse than Melissa… It’s called a storm of lawlessness, it’s called the storm of disorder, and it’s coming towards us. It’s worse than a Category 5,” said Gordon.

The minister of religion urged Jamaicans to reflect on the values they are passing on to their children as she argued that a meaningful inheritance extends beyond material possessions.

Meanwhile, mayor of Falmouth C Junior Gager, in his remarks, called on Jamaicans to preserve the legacy of the national heroes through their everyday actions rather than limiting remembrance to speeches and ceremonies.

“Our national heroes stood firm in the face of adversity, injustices, challenges, and paved the way for the freedom and opportunities we enjoy today,” Gager said.

He urged citizens to serve their communities, stand up for what is right, invest in young people, and work together to build a better Jamaica.

Gager also underscored the Church’s role in strengthening families and communities through prayer, mentorship, compassion and outreach, helping young people embrace their heritage and recognise their potential.

World.title: Ochie ‘Lovers Rock’ gets Hollywood pop-in
World.content:
Jimmy Fallon, host of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon on NBC, hangs out with Steve James, promoter of Lovers’ Rock: A Night of British Reggae on Friday in Ocho Rios, St Ann.

A Hollywood power player showed up at Lovers Rock: A Night of British Reggae last Friday.

Jimmy Fallon, host of The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon on NBC, surprised the packed house at Ocean’s 11 Bar and Restaurant in Ocho Rios, St Ann.

Fallon popped into the venue with Wayne Jobson, the Jamaican impresario who is an influential figure in the Southern California reggae scene.

Steve James, who started ‘Lovers Rock’ earlier this year, was surprised when the American comedian appeared.

“I was very shocked! We had received an indication that he might attend, but there is a big difference between hearing that someone may show up and actually seeing them there,” he told the Jamaica Observer. “When we saw him we were pleasantly surprised and delighted. His attendance was certainly an unexpected highlight of the evening.”

James said Fallon mingled with patrons, most of whom are fans of lovers’ rock, the genre that emerged in the United Kingdom during the late 1970s and early 1980s.

Since 2014 Fallon has hosted his late-night talk show, which is consistently one of the top-rated in the United States.

Beres Hammond also attended Lovers Rock: A Night of British Reggae, which saw a performance from singer/bassist Lloyd Parks.

The South Florida-based James, who hosts the Real Rock Radio show, led the line-up of selectors who played songs that defined the lovers’ rock movement. Others manning the turntables were Martin Mitchell; Twinn Spinn from Fetedayzradio.com; DJ Jacko from King Jammy Sound System; Buppy C from Vibes FM London; and Lady Gee, formerly of Choice FM London and Vibes.

“The atmosphere was fantastic! Many patrons expressed how much they had missed hearing this kind of music. For them, it was more than just a night of entertainment; it was a nostalgic journey that transported them back to their days in the UK,” said James, who is considered an authority on lovers’ rock.

The genre produced several stars, most of whom were born in the United Kingdom to Jamaican parents. They include Janet Kay, Peter Hunnigale, and Maxi Priest.

Lovers Rock: A Night of British Reggae was first held during Reggae Month last February at Pon Top Seafood Grill and Bar in Kingston. The second staging took place at the same venue in May.

The fourth is scheduled for Kingston in February.

World.title: Netball Jamaica boss talks up Sunshine Girls’ chances in Horizon Series
World.content:
Jamaica’s Sunshine Girls will face England’s Roses in the four-Test Horizon Series, with the first two games set to be played in England on November 21 and 22 at the Copper Box Arena. The Sunshine Girls will then welcome England to Jamaica on December 5 and 6. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

NETBALL Jamaica (NJ) President Karen Baugh has promised entertainment galore as the Sunshine Girls look to tackle England’s Roses in the Horizon Series next month.

The four-Test series was announced at a press conference held at S Hotel in New Kingston on October 13, 2026. The first two games are to be played in England on November 21 and 22 at the Copper Box Arena.

The Sunshine Girls are set to welcome the Roses to Jamaica on December 5 and 6.

“When Jamaica and England meet on a netball court you can expect intense competition, a bit of drama, excitement, and if Jamaica has anything to do with it, a little extra flair,” Baugh said.

“…This is much more than just two netball matches… it is an international sporting event, a celebration of our Sunshine Girls, and an opportunity to showcase the best of Jamaica netball and Brand Jamaica. This is definitely a rivalry worth watching.”

The Horizon Series — contested in honour of netball icons Molly Rhone of Jamaica and Jean Hornsby of England — began in 2024 with a classic.

Baugh recalled her favourite match, one she ranks alongside the 2026 Commonwealth Games win over Australia.

“That first match here against England, [in] the last second, we were leading by one and Shanice [Beckford] literally ran down the clock to prevent them from scoring again — and we won in the last second to tie the series. We went on to win the last game and won the series 2-1,” she said.

That Jamaica team had trailed 1-0 after the England leg — drawing the first, losing the second — before coming home to win the series.

In 2025 Hurricane Melissa forced the cancellation of the Jamaica leg, and England won the two matches played in England.

“The trophy, our trophy, is currently in England so we have a question to settle in 2026: Will the Rhone Hornsby Trophy be coming home?” Baugh asked.

In a historic first, Jamaica’s men’s team, The Suns, have been invited by England Thorns to play the curtain-raiser in London.

“It is a great opportunity for the male players to showcase their talent, and we wish The Suns every success in what is promised to be an exciting contest,” Baugh said.

Baugh said that for the home leg of the series, fans will get two matches for the price of one. England’s Roses Pathway team will tour Jamaica for a three-match series against the Jamaica Development Squad.

The first match will be on December 3, with the other two serving as curtain-raisers on December 5 and 6.

“You want to come really early. You want the place to be electric,” Baugh said.

Baugh said that the series forms part of preparations for the 2027 World Cup in Australia and comes on the back of a stellar year.

At the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, the Sunshine Girls won silver, stunning world number one Australia 46-45 in the semi-final before going down to New Zealand in the final.

“That was a statement to the world that Jamaica is among the very best in world netball,” Baugh said.

World.title: READY TO COMPETE
World.content:
Jamaican winger Jamone Lyle (centre) is expected to feature prominently for Jamaica at the FIFA Under-17 World Cup in Qatar in November. Here he is seen dribbling away from Canada’s Eloi Breton (right) and Ulrich Zamble during the Concacaf Under-17 Qualifiers encounter between Jamaica and Canada in Costa Rica on February 11, 2026. (Photo: JFF Media)

WITH the FIFA Under-17 World Cup now less than 30 days away, national under-17 Head Coach Wendell Downswell says the group have had to make the most of a less-than-ideal preparation period as they look to ensure they’re ready to compete at the tournament.

The young Reggae Boyz are set to make their third appearance at the global eventwhen it kicks off in Qatar on November 19. Jamaica have been drawn in Group E with European giants Italy, Ivory Coast and Uzbekistan.

The team booked their spot back in February at the 2026 Concacaf U-17 Qualifiers. However, they haven’t been able to secure international matches since.

Downswell, though, says they have made the best of the options available to them.

“It’s not been the ideal preparation that we have had because we were not able to get an international game; we were exploring at least two international games,” he

told the Jamaica Observer.

“However, we have been having camps — probably about four to five with the core of the players — which is good. And what we do is we prepare them in such a way that we use the Premier League teams and the Tier 2 teams as part of the measuring stick to see where we are in terms of the necessary preparation, and the boys have been responding very positively.”

“The coaching staff have explored all the possibilities to stretch these players somewhat similar to opposition that we’ll be up against in the tournament itself. So, hopefully this level of preparation, this kind of limitation that we have, will be of utmost significance for us going forward.”

Downswell says the technical staff have been closely keeping track of all the players they intend to select for the squad. However, he says several factors, including the ongoing ISSA Schoolboy Football, season haven’t made life easy.

“We release them and then some of them come back, [and] some come back with injuries here and there, knocks here and there,” he said. “[But] we have been having conversations with them. We have another camp coming up on the 6th and we have been having dialogue with the schools, so they won’t be released from the 6th up to our departure on the 14th.”

Downswell, who previously guided Jamaica’s U-17 team to the 2011 World Cup, says the players have been put through extensive preparation on and off the field, ahead of the tournament.

“We’ve put in place tactical preparation and the mental aspect of the players to get them fully focused regarding this task ahead. We have placed a lot of emphasis on the mental aspect of preparation, and the players have been responding in a positive way,” he said.

“Also, the whole preparation going in[to] international [games] — how we play the first 10 minutes, 5 minutes, the various tactical manoeuvres that we have done for the players to assimilate and adapt from a tactical standpoint — these are some of the things that we have been working on.”

Jamaica struggled in their two previous World Cup appearances, exiting at the group stage in 1999 and 2011 without recording a win in six matches.

Donwswell, though, is confident these young Reggae Boyz can break that trend and create history for the country. “I’m very upbeat, very enthusiastic about going, and at the same time our intention is to compete,” he said.

“Our first game’s against Italy [so] what we will do, the fact that we haven’t gotten much international exposure, so to speak, since February, [the plan] is using each game as part of our preparation and hoping that it lends itself in such a way that we are able to come out of the zone and take it from there.”

The squad, which is expected to feature new senior Reggae Boyz Jahmarie Nolan and Jamone Lyle, is set to be finalised by the first week of November.

World.title: Brussels goes looking for billions to fund Ukraine
World.content:
With Washington’s support for Kyiv increasingly uncertain, Brussels is looking to its allies to help keep Ukraine afloat. The price tag: €70 billion.

On today’s show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Kathryn Carlson discuss how the EU hopes to persuade Canada, Britain and Japan to help foot the bill — and whether closer trade and defense ties could be part of the bargain.

Then, Germany’s far-right AfD leader Alice Weidel is in Strasbourg to present her vision for a radically different European Union.

And who owns your face and voice in the age of AI? As deepfakes become increasingly convincing, MEPs are pushing for new protections.

If you have a question or comment, don’t hesitate! Message us on our WhatsApp here or at +32 491 05 06 29.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

World.title: EU to press Canada and UK for more Ukraine funding
World.content:
The EU has committed to a €90 billion loan for 2026 and 2027, intended to cover about two-thirds of Ukraine’s needs. Brussels had expected other partners — including Canada, Japan, South Korea, Australia and Norway — to provide another €45 billion, but much of that money has been slow to arrive as other governments have yet to firm up or disburse the support Brussels expected.

While calls to help Ukraine defend itself are not new, the projected 2027 bill has grown as Russia intensifies its assault, the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran drives up costs and Washington shifts toward positions more favorable to Moscow — leaving Europe and other allies to shoulder more of the cost of keeping Kyiv afloat.

Brussels is heading into negotiations about closer economic and defense ties with London and Ottawa. Diplomats and EU officials said they do not expect a formal bargain, but that support for Kyiv from the EU’s partners is likely to shape the political climate around the talks. Like others in this article, they were granted anonymity to speak about the sensitive diplomacy.

European Council President Antonio Costa, Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the European Council Summit in Brussels on Oct. 16. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga/AFP via Getty Images

The EU has also raised Ukraine’s 2027 financing needs at meetings of the International Monetary Fund, the G7 and the G20, as well as with Gulf Cooperation Council countries.

“During my meetings in Bangkok, the need to secure financial support for Ukraine in 2027 was a prominent topic,” European Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis told POLITICO, referencing last week’s IMF and World Bank Group meetings. He said he called for “broad burden sharing and stressed the importance of international partners each doing their part as Ukraine continues fighting Russian aggression.”

All the EU officials and diplomats stressed that the push was not a criticism of the U.K. or Canada, both of which are strong supporters of Ukraine. The point, they said, is that Kyiv’s needs have grown.

World.title: Maybe it’s personal: Europeans worry Trump just likes Putin more than Zelenskyy
World.content:
As they scratch their heads for explanations for Trump’s latest turn against Ukraine, some European officials and diplomats think it comes down to the president’s personal preferences, as much as his country’s political aims.

“I do think it’s a personal thing,” said former British Cabinet minister David Lidington, now distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a leading security think tank in London. “Trump is self-centered — his personal predilections for dictators and autocrats, his desire to give opportunities to U.S. businesses … are very important parts of his motivation.”

In private, EU officials agree. “Trump doesn’t like [Ukrainian President Volodymyr] Zelenskyy. He just doesn’t like him,” said one government official who has observed both men closely. “That makes it harder to get the U.S. to help on peace. Everything is a rational business deal with Trump, until it’s not.”

A diplomat from an EU country — granted anonymity, like others in this report, to discuss sensitive matters — said the inconsistent Trump could change his mind again and reverse recent moves against Ukraine. The U.S. president has chopped and changed on many issues, “except one thing,” the diplomat said. “He seems to be supportive of the Russians.”

“He’s been critical of Ukraine, the EU, NATO, but hardly ever said anything critical about Putin. It is striking. We have to deal with an administration that seems to be more pro-Russian than anything else,” the diplomat said.

The White House didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Poland’s government votes to ease abortion laws in challenge to conservative president
World.content:
Still, neither bill would allow abortion on request up to 12 weeks of pregnancy, as Tusk's Civic Coalition promised during the 2023 election campaign. The multi-party coalition includes many conservatives and lacks agreement on the liberalization going this far.

Both bills now move from the lower chamber, or the Sejm, to the Senate, where they seem poised to pass, but their eventual fate remains uncertain. President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of the nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) party, said before his election in 2025 that he would not sign legislation easing abortion rules.

“By refusing to sign [the abortion] legislation, the president is hurting people," Włodzimierz Czarzasty, speaker of the Sejm, said Tuesday before the votes. "If he wants to hurt women, he will hurt them. I think women will see that and hear that.”

Tusk's coalition government will likely keep turning up the heat on the president and PiS if Nawrocki blocks the liberalization, as he has said he would.

Overriding a presidential veto requires a three-fifths majority in the Sejm that the Tusk-led coalition doesn’t have. The proposals that passed Tuesday lingered in a parliamentary committee for two years before surfacing, spurred by the campaign heating up 12 months before the next general election, slated for late 2027.

Overturning restrictions

At the parliamentary level, ending criminal penalties for helping women with abortion passed with 217 votes in favor, 213 against and three abstentions. The other bill won a slightly clearer majority of 233 for, 203 against and a single abstention.

World.title: Europe’s conservatives have 2 new targets in their campaign to weaken EU climate laws
World.content:
Both policies are central pillars in the EU’s effort to reduce its planet-warming emissions. A successful repeal of ETS2 in particular would be a blow to EU climate goals, as it covers around 40% of the bloc’s greenhouse gas emissions.

But it would also be a major victory for conservative and pro-business lawmakers and national governments that have been campaigning for less stringent EU climate laws in the name of industrial competitiveness.

Ax the tax

The EU Emissions Trading System, launched in 2005, requires power plants and factories in sectors like steel, chemicals and cement to acquire carbon allowances for every ton of carbon they emit. The total number of allowances is reduced each year, eventually reaching zero.

ETS2 applies the same idea to suppliers of fuel for transport and heating from 2028.

The cap-and-trade scheme will be a powerful tool for reducing emissions from these highly polluting activities. But many policymakers worry it will raise the cost of gasoline, diesel and natural gas and add to voters' cost-of-living pressures.

Nine national delegations of the EPP — the Polish, Spanish, Italian, French, Romanian, Croatian, Slovenian, Slovak and Estonian — are now calling for ETS2 to be repealed, according to draft amendments obtained by POLITICO. “ETS2 should be deleted,” the amendment, sponsored by Polish EPP lawmaker Adam Jarubas, argues.

World.title: Ed Miliband’s clean energy company is being split apart
World.content:
Set up by then Energy Secretary Ed Miliband, the government backed GBE with £8.3 billion of fresh funding. Its purpose at the time seemed clear. “Great British Energy will own, manage and operate clean power projects,” Miliband pledged, “and generate energy in its own right.”

Labour officials familiar with GBE plans told POLITICO in 2024 local projects would get around £3 billion of its total budget, while the rest would go on helping the company establish itself in the market, including by taking stakes in wind and solar projects.

Yet now experts can’t agree on what, exactly, GBE is for.

How to spend it

Miliband’s GBE pitch to the public was ambitious.

The company would allow Britain to become a bigger player in its own clean energy market in Labour’s dash to hit green goals, he said. Referencing huge state-owned companies in Denmark and France, he told Channel 4 News weeks after the election that GBE was “not going to become Ørsted or the generation arm of EDF overnight. But that is the long-term vision.”

Soon after GBE passed into law, though, former Chancellor Rachel Reeves reassigned £2.5 billion of its budget to help developers design small-scale nuclear power plants and prep sites where those mini-nukes will eventually go.

World.title: US to offer Putin face-to-face talks with Zelenskyy and Trump
World.content:
Vladimir Putin attends an event in Moscow on March 18, 2025. | Pool photo by Maxim Shemetov via AFP/Getty Images

Steve Witkoff will fly to Russia for discussions about peace proposals on Wednesday.

U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff will offer Vladimir Putin direct talks with President Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy in an effort to secure a ceasefire.

The proposal for three-way leaders’ negotiations on a peace proposal, the first such summit since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, was announced at a press conference Tuesday after talks in Norway between Zelenskyy and Witkoff.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who hosted the talks, said Witkoff will travel to Russia Wednesday and set out proposals for peace terms, including the idea of a three-way summit between the leaders. The meeting in Oslo came after days of high tensions between Ukraine and the U.S. president.

World.title: China threatens retaliation if UK follows the EU on tariffs
World.content:
A worker inspects an electric car at a Zeekr factory on Meishan Island in Ningbo, China on April 18, 2025. | Hector Retamal/AFP via Getty Images

China urged Britain to follow World Trade Organization rules and warned it against copying Brussels’ approach, arguing that tariffs on Chinese EVs would be discriminatory.

LONDON — Beijing has threatened to retaliate if the U.K. raises tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, aligning with the European Union.

Responding to POLITICO’s story that Britain was looking to act in “lockstep” with the bloc to counter China’s market dominance in electric cars, a spokesperson from the Chinese Ministry of Commerce said: “If the U.K. insists on imposing restrictions on Chinese electric vehicles, China will resolutely retaliate and safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese industries.”

The U.K. is currently working with its European partners to avoid a 10% electric vehicle tariff from the beginning of next year, when stricter rules of origin under the Brexit trade deal kick in.

World.title: What is Spain’s DANA weather phenomenon and is climate change making it worse?
World.content:
A storm in eastern Spain has killed five people and left cars and streets submerged in water, and the DANA weather system is behind it.

 

Storm Adam dumped 700 litres of rain per square metre in just 24 hours in some areas of the Valencia region. Floodwaters swept away parked cars, submerged roads and cut off residents, some of whom had to be airlifted to safety by emergency crews.

The coastal resort of Oliva was one of the areas worst hit by Sunday night’s storms. A 79-year-old woman was found dead in her home, while a man suffered a fatal heart attack at a local campsite. The third victim was a man who drowned while swimming at a beach in Sagunto. Firefighters in neighbouring Catalonia also reported the death of a woman who fell into a rain-swollen stream.

Storm Adam is reminiscent of the sudden downpours that devastated Valencia in 2024, when some areas saw a year’s worth of rain in just 24 hours. 200 people lost their lives, making it one of the worst flood-related disasters in Europe since the late-1960s and the worst in Spain for many decades.

The government came under heavy criticism for the lack of warnings to the public about what was to come. Thankfully they appear to have learnt their lesson: warnings were sent to mobile phones before Storm Adam hit, urging people to avoid travelling, stay away from rivers and ravines, and seek shelter on higher ground or on the upper floors of buildings.

The 2024 storm introduced many Europeans to a weather phenomenon that often hits Spain: DANA. What is it and is it becoming more deadly as the climate warms up?

What is a DANA?

DANA stands for ‘Depresión Aislada en Niveles Altos’. It’s not easy to translate into English but it essentially means periods of heavy rain, stormy weather and a sudden drop in temperatures.

The bigger the temperature difference, the bigger the storm. This is why the worst DANAs are usually at the end of summer in September and October, and are more likely to happen in parts of southern and eastern Spain.

Put simply a DANA is a very intense wind current that forms when it breaks away from a polar jet, a sort of pocket of cold air surrounded by warmer air that can move around and cause extreme weather. It’s the meeting of hot and cold air fronts causing extreme weather.

Southeastern Spain is particularly vulnerable to DANAs because it’s where the Atlantic and Mediterranean meet, meaning that cold air fronts can meet warm air fronts at certain times of year. It’s also an area where mountains favour the formation of storm clouds and therefore rainfall.

DANA is increasingly used in everyday language in Spain

Some Spanish people now use the term DANA to refer to a big storm, but this hasn’t always been the case.

For many years Spaniards have used the phrase ‘gota fría’, literally meaning ‘cold drop’, The Local Spain explains. But as technology has advanced, and it has become easier to predict and understand the weather, meteorologists say that DANA is a more useful term because it’s more specific.

On its website, Spain’s meteorological agency Aemet explains that: “The term gota frìa is a relatively old concept and has been superseded over the years. New ways of understanding tropospheric processes and new observational tools have made us revise and redefine the ideas linked to these isolated pockets of cold air at higher levels.

“We believe that the concept of DANA, which we associate with the Anglo-Saxon term ‘cut-off low’, is more accurate and realistic than that of gota fría. As the concept of a gota fría is not very precise and incomplete, it is understood that it should be replaced by a more modern one.”

Is climate change making DANAs worse?

The Valencia floods in 2024 made worldwide news, with many shocked by the scale of loss and devastation in a wealthy European country. Much analysis followed, with climate scientists asking what role global warming played.

It was confirmed that a DANA was to blame and that global warming very likely made it worse.

“No doubt about it, these explosive downpours were intensified by climate change,” Dr Friederike Otto, lead of World Weather Attribution at the Centre for Environmental Policy, Imperial College London, said in 2024.

The floods were caused by a ‘cut-off low pressure storm system’ that had migrated from an unusually wavy, stalled jet stream. This system then got stuck over the region, pouring down a year’s worth of rain in eight hours.

Unusually warm sea surface temperatures, made much more likely by human-caused climate change, and our warming atmosphere, however, directly impact how much rain these storms can hold. The ground in many parts of eastern and southern Spain had also been left less able to effectively absorb rainwater following severe drought.

A rapid partial analysis done by Dr Otto’s group of international scientists suggested that human-caused climate change made Spain’s rainfall around 12 per cent heavier. It also found that the weather event the region experienced was twice as likely.

Though it isn’t a full, detailed attribution study, they said climate change is the most likely explanation for the extreme downpours.

“With every fraction of a degree of fossil fuel warming, the atmosphere can hold more moisture, leading to heavier bursts of rainfall. These deadly floods are yet another reminder of how dangerous climate change has already become at just 1.3°C of warming,” Otto adds.

World.title: Trump’s embrace of Putin roils Europe, but not enough to break with the US
World.content:
The rift between Europe and the United States over Russia's war on Ukraine has plunged to a new depth as Donald Trump doubles down on his embrace of Vladimir Putin, jolting an alliance that was already treading on thin ice.

 

Over just two striking weeks, the US president has struck a diesel deal with his Russian counterpart, eased economic sanctions on Moscow, called for new elections in Ukraine and dismissed the legitimacy of its president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom Trump said was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin.

Zelenskyy, increasingly defiant, has denounced the diesel deal as a "historic mistake" and cautioned that other US-Russian agreements related to gas flows, banking, chemicals and the immobilised assets would be next in line.

Ukraine has identified sudden limits on the use of the Starlink satellite technology and US-made weapons deliveries.

"I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate," Zelenskyy told Bloomberg in remarks that revived the long-running dread that Trump and Putin would conspire to thrash out a backroom deal that ends in Kyiv's surrender.

Moscow's pitch for a trilateral meeting with Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping further fuelled those fears.

"I would do it. Not so much for Ukraine, because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," Trump said when asked about the trilateral.

The rapid succession of events has caught Europeans off guard, who, after previous setbacks, believed they had learned to navigate Trump’s unilateral style of diplomacy.

Once again, they find themselves blindsided and undercut by a close ally that is willing to make overtures to Russia without demanding a single concession in return.

"We want to leave no doubt about our position towards Ukraine, and at the same time, we know that the Americans have other interests," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said last week at the end of a two-day summit in Brussels.

In a swipe at Trump, French President Emmanuel Macron denounced the "ambiguities" of some leaders and warned: "Capitulation is weakness. Weakness is danger."

Italy's Giorgia Meloni deplored the diesel deal as a "very risky choice" that legitimises Moscow and weakens sanctions. Denmark's Mette Frederiksen lamented that "we, the Western alliance, are in a worse position now than we were a few days ago".

On Tuesday, High Representative Kaja Kallas upped the anteand explicitly accused the US of pushing Ukraine to "surrender on Putin's terms".

Conscious coupling

Yet despite the criticism and widespread indignation, Europe remains unwilling and perhaps unprepared to break away from Trump and pursue an independent course.

Brussels, Berlin, Paris and London still prefer to maintain an active, even if precarious, channel with Washington to influence its thinking as much as possible, as shown in their participation in the latest round of US-led peace talks in Miami and later in Oslo.

"Europe will live with the consequences, and that's why we need to see a more unified Europe at the table," Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.

For Kyiv, the European presence has become indispensable to offset the White House's Russian-friendly slant. Zelenskyy has repeatedly encouraged Europe to develop a parallel channel with Russia, but Moscow has shown no interest.

Though Trump's latest actions prove the European push has been limited at best, the thinking remains unchanged: the seat at the table must be preserved at all costs.

"We have to move forward, because we also know cooperation with the US is essential for Ukraine to fight its war. Everybody knows the volumes that are part of the diesel deal are low," a senior diplomat said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

"So keep calm and carry on. Deplore and continue. But no over-dramatisation either. That's in none of our interests."

Some officials find reassurance in the belief that Trump’s rapprochement with Putin is largely motivated by a desire to deflect responsibility for high fuel prices ahead of next month's midterm elections, in which opinion polls show his Republican Party will lose.

Trump claims that Ukraine's successful strikes on Russia's oil refineries are to blame, but energy experts agree his war on Iran is the chief culprit of the oil market turmoil.

"We have dialogue, and we'll continue to have dialogue. It has taken us to positive results in what our interests are concerned," a senior official said. "This is the best way."

Yet there is a growing recognition that Europe and the US have fundamentally diverged in their approaches to Russia, with differences that may prove impossible to reconcile.

EU leaders at the summit in Brussels. AP Photo

Europe, for now, bets on sanctions to cripple the war machine, long-term decoupling to avoid vulnerable dependencies and strict diplomatic isolation. Although some far-right and far-left parties question this logic, the strategy is widely shared.

The US, by contrast, is dangling economic incentives for Russia to engage in the peace negotiations. These reportedly involve an early partial release of sovereign assets and the resumption of gas flows to Europe, both of which Europe has already rejected. Deals related to Lukoil and nuclear technology are also said to be in the works.

European officials contend the American approach is flawed because it ignores Putin's fixation with territorial conquest, the core reason why he launched the invasion. No deal, however lucrative, can replace Ukraine's annihilation in Putin's mind, they say.

Washington's invitation to Putin for the G20 summit in Florida, which a dozen European leaders are scheduled to attend, is another sign of glaring discrepancy.

As Trump moves closer to Putin, the ideological gap between the two sides of the Atlantic is unlikely to narrow any time soon. If anything, it could deepen even further, raising serious questions about what might happen when the peace process reaches the endgame and allies are called to make joint decisions of exceptional significance.

Maria Shagina, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, says the White House's actions are designed to pressure Europe into relinquishing its pressure front and accommodating the US stance on Russia.

"The more fundamental question is whether Europe can sustain an independent sanctions strategy over the longer term. The EU and the UK retain considerable economic leverage over Russia, but can they translate that leverage into effective and sustained pressure on Moscow without US participation?" Shagina told Euronews.

"The challenge is not simply whether Europe possesses sufficient economic power, but whether it has the political will, institutional capacity and strategic coherence to deploy that power independently of Washington, something that until now has been inconceivable."

World.title: A chilled stay: Europe’s coolest ice, snow and igloo hotels to visit this winter
World.content:
This winter, the coolest holiday destinations may just be where the temperature barely hovers above freezing.

 

In Europe, there are various ice, snow and igloo hotels which offer guests the charm of a winter fairy tale: icy accommodation set against the Northern Lights in a snow-covered escape.

But the experience begins long before check-in. Many seasonal hotels rely on ice harvested from nearby rivers and lakes, while others use fresh snow to preserve a year-round frozen retreat.

Here are some of Europe's coolest "properties" to keep on your radar this winter season and beyond.

Snowhotel 365, Bjørnevatn, Norway

Located at Snow Resort Kirkenes in northern Norway, Snowhotel 365 offers guests a unique experience with each room being hand-carved by international ice sculptors – so no two rooms are alike.

Although indoor temperatures hover around -4C, each room comes with a thermal sleeping bag and access to the property’s heated lounge, sauna and showers. As an all-inclusive Arctic adventure, each stay also includes breakfast and a three-course dinner.

Here, the winter fun doesn’t have to end when the weather takes a warmer turn. Guests can check in year-round, even in the middle of summer.

Each year, 30 tonnes of ice and fresh snow are used to preserve and renew the property. Over time, as the snow turns into solid ice, the hotel's walls, ceilings, and sculptures develop new textures and shapes.

An art suite at ICEHOTEL ICEHOTEL

ICEHOTEL, Jukkasjärvi, Swedish Lapland

Each winter, as the Torne River freezes, artists and sculptors from around the world gather to mould ICEHOTEL anew.

For five months of the year, starting in December, guests can check into its temporary rooms or art suites before it melts back into the river again.

Temperatures in the ice rooms hover around -5C, however, each room is kitted out with reindeer hide blankets and sleeping bags to keep guests warm. Meanwhile, the art suites are individually designed with a selection of artists bringing their creativity to life.

ICEHOTEL also offers a range of dining concepts, including an “ice menu” where dishes are served on plates made of ice from the river.

Arctic SnowHotel, Rovaniemi, Finnish Lapland

In Rovaniemi, the capital of Finnish Lapland, the winter season from 15 December until the end of March sees the grounds blanketed by snow, with rivers and lakes freezing. It also means the Arctic SnowHotel opens its doors for guests to stay the night.

Since 2008, a “new hotel” of ice and snow has been moulded each year at this popular attraction, where 20 rooms can host as many as 70 guests.

A suite at Arctic Snowhotel Arctic Snowhotel

Guests can choose from a double suite that sleeps two, all the way up to a family room that sleeps up to six guests.

The cool experiences also continue at the Ice Restaurant, where meals are served on an ice plate. While the Ice Chapel offers an unforgettable setting for those seeking a space for spirituality.

Arctic SnowHotel also has a resident “Northern Lights Watcher”, who keeps an eye on the skies and ensures no guest misses the magical display of the auroras.

Sorrisniva Igloo Hotel, Alta, Norway

Alta in Norway is home to Sorrisniva – the world’s northernmost igloo hotel.

Harvesting ice from the Sierravannet mountain lake, it takes 250 tonnes of ice and 7,000 cubic metres of snow to build the igloo hotel each year under a special theme.

After being rebuilt, guests are welcome to stay from 20 December to the end of March, with rooms and suites to choose from. With no two seasons ever being the same, each winter, ice sculptors turn the suites into their canvas – designing the furniture and room’s ice sculptures.

For adventure travellers, snowmobiling across the Finnmark plateau, chasing the Northern Lights, snowshoeing and husky sledging are among the itinerary of activities to try.

Iglu-Dorf Zermatt, Switzerland

In the Swiss Alps, Iglu-Dorf Zermatt is rebuilt each winter at 2,700 metres on the ski slopes above the car-free resort.

At this remote mountain location, guests can stay in hand-carved igloos linked by snow corridors, from 19 December to 4 April, with the igloos’ temperature remaining around freezing point.

Exterior of Iglu-Dorf Zermatt, Zermatt Switzerland Iglu-Dorf GmbH

During the daytime, the outdoor terrace is a shared dining space that serves Swiss cheese fondue, alongside a selection of other snacks and hot and cold beverages.

Beyond Zermatt, overnight stays are also possible across other Swiss igloo villages, including Davos and Gstaad, as well as further afield in the German Iglu-Dorf on the Zugspitze and in Kühtai near Innsbruck in Austria.

World.title: From ‘sleepmaxxing’ to rising temperatures: getting a good night's sleep is getting harder
World.content:
Sleep allows our bodies to repair tissue, clear brain waste, and consolidate memories — something essential for wellbeing and health.

 

However, rising temperatures, digital technology and round-the-clock working are increasingly disrupting sleep.

And it is not for individuals alone to address this, researchers warned in a paper published in the Journal of Sleep Research. They are turning to European governments to address the social and economic conditions that determine whether people can get sufficient, restorative sleep.

"We're seeing a perfect storm of challenges for sleep health across Europe,” the co-lead author of the paper, Fran Pilkington-Cheney, lecturer in Psychology and Sleep at Nottingham Trent University (NTU), said in a press release.

“People are aware that sleep matters, but few recognise how factors such as climate change, technology, shift work, urban environments and misinformation are combining to affect how well we sleep.”

Therefore, the authors call for “shifting away from individualised approaches toward coordinated, systems-level action across policy, healthcare, education, industry, and environmental planning” to address the major challenges for getting a good night’s sleep.

Those are climate change and urban environments; unequal access to sleep medicine; the rapid expansion of digital health technologies; online misinformation; and a culture of constant connectivity that leaves less time for rest, according to the paper.

Climate and inequality

Among the mix of environmental, technological and societal pressures that are making it harder for people to get sleep, rising temperatures are emerging as a particular concern.

Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent, and increasingly hot nights can interfere with the body's ability to cool down, delaying sleep and causing more frequent awakenings.

Urban pollution, traffic noise and artificial light at night add to the problem, while climate-related anxiety and extreme weather events can further undermine mental health and sleep.

The effects are unlikely to be distributed equally. People living in poorly insulated homes, those unable to afford cooling and people in overcrowded accommodation face greater difficulties maintaining comfortable sleeping conditions. Refugees and displaced people may also be exposed to excessive heat, noise, artificial light and a lack of privacy.

Technology presents another challenge. Wearable devices and sleep-tracking applications could help people identify potential problems and allow clinicians to monitor patients remotely, particularly in rural areas with limited access to specialists.

But consumer devices are not necessarily accurate enough to diagnose sleep disorders, and their results can cause unnecessary anxiety.

The paper highlights “orthosomnia”, a term describing an excessive preoccupation with achieving supposedly perfect sleep measurements.

The researchers also warn that social media trends such as “sleepmaxxing” can encourage rigid routines, unproven remedies and excessive self-monitoring.

Meanwhile, online influencers and AI tools can spread misleading health advice, making it harder for people to distinguish scientific evidence from commercial promotion.

Work is part of the problem

Europe's 24-hour economy is also placing pressure on sleep.

Shift workers, healthcare staff, transport workers and people in precarious employment may have limited control over their schedules, while remote working and after-hours messages can blur the boundaries between professional and personal life.

The report cites estimates that 21% of workers across Europe engage in shift work, with night shifts presenting particular challenges to the body's natural sleep-wake cycle.

The researchers advocate stronger protections for workers, more predictable schedules, better fatigue-management systems and workplace practices that protect time for rest.

“Without wider co-ordinated action, these pressures are likely to become more significant in the years ahead,” Pilkington-Cheney said.

World.title: Elon Musk backs SpaceX-Tesla merger as rocket firm turns profit
World.content:
Elon Musk said on Tuesday that he would back a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, as his rocket and AI company reported its first quarterly profit since going public, driven by deals to rent out computing power to AI firms.

 

Asked about a possible tie-up on a call with analysts, Musk said he felt he was “tap dancing through a minefield”, but that a combination would be “a good idea”.

Shares in SpaceX shot up nearly 5% in after-hours trading following the comments.

Musk said special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla had been established to study the idea at the request of shareholders.

He added that he could not take part in their talks because he had a conflict of interest.

Musk is chief executive of both companies and also serves as chairman and chief technology officer of SpaceX.

He owned 48.4% of SpaceX as of 30 June, according to a regulatory filing, and controls more than 82% of its voting power through shares carrying enhanced voting rights.

He holds about 20% of Tesla.

The committees have not agreed on the terms of any deal, and there is no guarantee they will, Musk said, cautioning that it would be overstating the position to treat a merger as a certainty.

Any deal would need the backing of a majority of all Tesla shares, not just those voted, which Musk called “quite a high hurdle”.

He said the two companies could benefit from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and space-based computing.

His remarks came after SpaceX posted net income of $4.4 billion (€3.8bn) for the July–September period, compared with a loss of $1.1 billion (€0.95bn) a year earlier.

Revenue jumped 161% to $14.6 billion (€12.6bn). The quarterly results follow a bumpy start on Wall Street.

SpaceX began trading on the Nasdaq on 12 June after an IPO priced at $135 a share that raised about $85.7 billion (€73.9bn).

Its first earnings report as a listed company showed second-quarter revenue of $7.8 billion (€6.7bn) and a net loss of $541 million (€466m).

The AI division, which SpaceX now calls “Super Intelligence”, drove the turnaround. Super Intelligence is US President Donald Trump's preferred term for AI.

The unit's revenue rose more than ninefold from a year earlier to $7.6 billion (€6.6bn), overtaking the Starlink satellite internet business as the company's largest source of sales.

Cloud computing

SpaceX credited new cloud services agreements, wider adoption of its Grok chatbot and its acquisition of Cursor, an artificial intelligence coding start-up.

SpaceX's cloud customers include Anthropic, which agreed in May to pay nearly $45 billion (€38.8bn) over three years for computing power at SpaceX's Colossus data centres.

Google signed on in June, agreeing to pay $920 million (€793m) a month from October through June 2029.

The AI unit reported an operating profit of $431 million (€371m), compared with a loss of $1.7 billion (€1.5bn) a year earlier.

As with other AI companies, spending remains heavy.

SpaceX invested $19.6 billion (€16.9bn) in the quarter, of which $16.4 billion (€14.1bn) was invested in AI, bringing capital spending for the first nine months of the year to $48 billion (€41.4bn).

Its computing capacity reached 1.7 gigawatts, up from 0.6 gigawatts a year earlier.

Musk said he was “fairly confident” that SpaceX could bring an additional 10 gigawatts of computing capacity online in 2027.

That would come on top of the approximately 2.5 to 3.0 gigawatts it expects to have running by the end of this year.

He added that power, cooling and electrical equipment were “somewhat of a limiting factor”.

Revenue at the Starlink satellite internet unit grew 69% to $5.2 billion (€4.5bn), and consumer subscribers reached 13.6 million.

Average monthly revenue per consumer, however, fell to $69 (€59) from $83 (€72) a year earlier.

SpaceX also completed the first revenue-generating flight of Starship, the giant rocket central to Musk's Mars ambitions and to deploying satellites at scale.

The flight carried 26 next-generation Starlink satellites into orbit.

World.title: Alberta’s “no” to separation gives Carney a boost as Trump pressure unites Canadians
World.content:
Voters in Alberta, Canada’s oil-rich province, on Tuesday overwhelmingly chose to remain in the country, giving Prime Minister Mark Carney a boost in his push for national unity as US President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats rally Canadians around their flag.

 

With about 90% of voting areas counted, 75% backed staying in Canada, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.

“Don’t mess with Canada. President Trump is watching this,” said Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation.

The referendum was not a direct vote on independence. A “yes” result would have set Alberta on a path toward a later vote on leaving Canada.

Carney: “A great result for Canada”

“It’s a great result for Canada that Albertans have chosen unity,” Carney told reporters in Ottawa before a Cabinet meeting on Tuesday.

He argued that the quarter of voters who supported starting the separation process did not all necessarily want independence. In his view, only a smaller “hard core” favours leaving. Some voters have said they backed the question to send Ottawa a message rather than to break away.

Carney said he spoke with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Tuesday morning about the results and about closer federal-provincial cooperation, including on immigration.

Mark Carney arrives for a meeting of the federal cabinet on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. (Justin Tang /The Canadian Press via AP) AP Photo

Some voters said they backed the separation question without wanting Alberta to leave. Edmonton voter Shawn Campbell said he voted to begin the process to send a message: “It sends a message to Ottawa that Albertans are not happy.”

Others criticised the vote itself. Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, objected to spending money on a “referendum on a referendum” rather than on healthcare. With Trump threatening Canada, he said, “It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united. Instead, we’re fighting among ourselves.”

If you need to cut for length, drop Malka’s healthcare point and keep only the Campbell quote. If you’re running long-form, the full section is fine, and you can restore Khowaja.

Alberta premier rules out another referendum

In a televised address Tuesday night, Smith welcomed the outcome and promised not to call another separation referendum while she is premier.

“Yesterday, Albertans voted overwhelmingly in favour of remaining a province of Canada,” Smith said. “The voter turnout was historic and a powerful testimony of the passion Albertans feel for our country and our province.”

Supporters react to voting results at the pro Canada watch party in Edmonton, Alberta Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. (James Maclennan/The Canadian Press via AP) AP Photo

She said Alberta would keep pushing Ottawa for more provincial autonomy, but that disputes would be resolved through Canada’s political and legal institutions, not through separation.

Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters: “Don’t mess with Canada. President Trump is watching this.”

Separatists concede defeat, but not the cause

Meanwhile, Alberta separatist organiser David Parker acknowledged the scale of the loss.

“Independence feels far away, and we should not pretend this was not a defeat,” he wrote on social media.

Still, separatist leaders insisted they would carry on. At a referendum-night gathering at an Edmonton restaurant, the crowd fell silent as the results came in.

“We’re not going anywhere,” said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project. “We’ve dominated the conversation in the last year. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.”

Rath had said before the vote that he would be thrilled with 30% support. He also said he wanted Smith removed as leader of the United Conservative Party (UCP) and believed the party could splinter, possibly producing a new pro-independence party.

From fringe cause to lasting movement

Alberta is home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves. It is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold, with a political culture that has long had more in common with the American West than with much of Canada. Resentment toward the federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but it has not traditionally translated into broad support for independence.

Former Premier Jason Kenney noted that separatist parties historically drew only 1% or 2% of the vote. He said anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilise activists who later embraced the separatist cause.

Trump’s trade war and his threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney build support in Alberta, a province where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular.

World.title: New Romanian prime minister Luca Niculescu and Cabinet members sworn in
World.content:
Romania on Tuesday swore in a new cabinet following a vote that ended a months-long political impasse.

 

Prime Minister Luca Niculescu, an independent diplomat, won 280 votes in favour of his proposed cabinet, with 58 against. He plans to start work immediately, with a large budget deficit at the top of his agenda.

President Nicușor Dan nominated Niculescu, 55, a diplomat and former journalist, on 5 October, the president’s fourth pick for the job, after three earlier nominees failed to form a government.

Niculescu was widely expected to succeed after securing pledges of support for a minority government from the Social Democrats and other parties. He has reportedly reached a deal with several parties for six months of backing while a longer-term agreement is negotiated.

Speaking in Parliament after the vote, he thanked lawmakers for trusting his Cabinet.

“I present a governing programme, a team, and a commitment to work toward several clear objectives,” he said. “And I want to tell the Romanian people, from the very start, what kind of government this will be. A government that brings funds and investments into the country.”

The political crisis gripped Romania since May

The political crisis has gripped Romania since May, when then-Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan was ousted in a no-confidence motion. The motion was filed jointly by the Social Democratic Party, which had been part of his governing coalition, and the Alliance for the Unity of Romanians party. Bolojan’s government had pursued strict austerity measures.

Bolojan took office in 2025 with the aim of ending one of Romania’s worst political crises since the end of communism and of reducing a massive budget deficit.

Related Three parties to attempt to form new cabinet following Romanian election

Romania has faced a long stretch of instability since the annulment of a presidential election in December 2024. The country has also struggled with rampant inflation and a technical recession. Last year, it recorded one of the highest budget deficits in the European Union.

Tuesday’s vote came weeks after lawmakers rejected a Cabinet proposed by Dan’s third pick, Siegfried Muresan. That failure prolonged the crisis and raised the prospect of early elections, at a time of regional security concerns linked to Russia’s war in neighbouring Ukraine. Romania is a member of both NATO and the EU.

Experts warn that tensions could flare again soon. Niculescu’s support rests on a six-month arrangement with several parties, and a longer-term deal has yet to be agreed.

World.title: Rising emissions and temperatures: The cost of Trump's climate retreat is now clear
World.content:
The world is set to breach the critical 1.5-degree temperature limit, with Donald Trump's US withdrawal from climate action worsening the outlook, according to a UN report. But there is a small silver lining.

For over a decade, scientists have warned the world must limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) to avoid the most severe consequences of climate change.

That goal is no longer within reach.

Decades of "insufficient" action on cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet means overshooting 1.5-degree temperature threshold is now "imminent and unavoidable," according to the United Nations Environment Program's (UNEP) annual Emissions Gap Report.

If current climate policies continue, temperatures will rise by an average of 2.8 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels within this century. But even if countries meet their new climate pledges, global warming is still projected to reach 2.6 degrees Celsius. Both scenarios would tip the world into a period of catastrophic weather extremes.

The projections reflect a gap between what governments promise to do and the action they are taking to curb emissions. Some 167 countries have submitted climate action plans to the UN, covering 83% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But those pledges to cut emissions fall far short of what is needed to limit warming.

Among the world's largest emitters, Indonesia, China and the United States saw emissions rise in 2025, according to preliminary estimates. The increase in the US "far exceeded that of all other countries," driven by a resurgence of coal — the dirtiest fossil fuel source — and rising electricity demand, partly linked to massive AI data center expansion.

The outlook has worsened in part because of US President Donald Trump's withdrawal of the United States from the historic Paris climate accord in which the world came together in 2015 to agree to halt climate change. The US is the second-largest annual emitter of climate-warping greenhouse gases.

Since Trump entered the Oval Office for a second time, his administration has taken a sledgehammer to climate policy, gutting environmental regulations and expanding oil and gas production.

"The main takeaway is simple — governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible," said Bill Hare, CEO of the global science and policy institute Climate Analytics, of the report.

What does overshooting mean for the planet?

Exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius even temporarily sets humanity on a dangerous course, as it increases the risk of triggering potentially irreversible or difficult-to-undo "tipping points," like the loss of coral reefs, long-term retreat of ice sheets, and the Amazon Rainforest turning into a grassland.

As ecosystems disappear and sea levels rise, these changes could trigger a deadly chain reaction, releasing more greenhouse gases and accelerating warming, dramatically increasing the likelihood of deadly extreme weather.

This summer alone, Europe recorded more than 32,000 excess deaths related to heat and nearly 1,500 people died in a flash floods in Nepal and Tibet, after climate change laid the groundwork for a glacier to collapse.

Residents carry their belongings salvaged from their damaged homes filled with mud and debris following a deadly glacier collapse in Nepal Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

But scientists maintain 1.5 degrees Celsius is not a magic number, and that every fraction of a degree of warming brings escalating risks. To reduce the risk of future damage, countries should still focus on rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels, the largest contributor to global climate change, and toward renewable energy like solar and wind.

Now the best-case scenario is overshooting 1.5 degrees Celsius for a short time before bringing temperatures back down quickly.

"Overshoot is not surrender," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a press statement. "We can still keep it as small and as short as possible — and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees before the end of the century."

How can the world limit overshoot?

UNEP lays out a scenario in which the world sees warming peak at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius around mid-century, before falling back to 1.5 Celsius by 2100. Getting there would require steep emissions cuts of 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.

It would also require removing 330 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and storing it in the ground. But recent studies have cast doubt on the feasibility and costs of the technology, as well as the nascent carbon removal industry's ability to scale as quickly as required to meet climate goals.

The UN warns any delays will make the challenge harder, saying that every five years that emissions remain at current levels adds about 0.1 Celsius to projected peak warming.

"We must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5 Celsius by the end of the century," Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP, said in a press release. "This is possible."

Climate policy works

Still, climate policies have proven effective in reducing emissions. The UNEP report draws on more than 200 studies that analyze how measures like carbon taxes, government climate targets, building codes and subsidies for low-carbon technologies are working.

Carbon-pricing schemes have been the most widely studied so far. China's pilot schemes reduced emissions by about 11%, while the European Union's emissions trading system saw an 8% cut, compared with projected levels without these policies.

"There are more opportunities than ever to accelerate action," according to the report, pointing to the boom in renewable energy since the adoption of the Paris Agreement a decade ago.

Pakistan's solar boom shields some from energy shocks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Global renewable electricity capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated, and solar build-out grew seven times faster. In 2024, more than 90% of renewable projects were cheaper than fossil fuel alternatives.

While total energy supply from coal, oil and gas has continued to rise, that's happened at a slower rate than was projected in 2015. And coal use is likely to peak and decline by the end of the decade.

"We have a wealth of success stories showing that emissions can be cut quickly," Andersen said. "It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies."

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

World.title: Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of Starlink in Ukraine — report
World.content:
Elon Musk "capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network," the Wall Street Journal reported.

Tech billionaire Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing US officials.

Kyiv uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the service means restricting the country's attack and defense missions against Russia.

Last week, Musk capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network, the report said, citing unnamed sources. The move rendered some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless, it added.

Two people told the Journal that Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public.

Some US officials, the report said, believed Musk acted unilaterally and that Trump did not specifically order retribution against Ukraine.

However, one person familiar with the situation said Musk spoke with multiple senior administration officials, including Trump, before imposing the speed cap.

Both Musk and Trump have expressed anger at Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries in recent weeks, which the president blames for high energy prices.

The report also comes after Trump's comments last week that he did not think either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access.

Musk had said that any limits on speed or use were decided by the US military or the president.

Musk, SpaceX, and the White House are yet to respond to the report.

US envoy Steve Witkoff is set to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday after what a US official called "constructive" talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway, as Trump said it was time for Ukraine to end the war.

World.title: UK fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks
World.content:
The UK is sending military support to Saudi Arabia as Iran-aligned Houthi rebels launch repeated attacks on the kingdom.

Britain will deploy Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom against increasing attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels, the UK government announced on Tuesday.

The aircraft will protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from drones and missiles, the Ministry of Defense said. They will not carry out offensive strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen.

"The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable," British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said.

He particularly condemned attacks on Riyadh's international airport, which has been targeted 20 times since the beginning of October.

Riyadh's international airport has seen a string of attacks claimed by the Houthis Image: Social Media/REUTERS

Strikes on the airport have killed at least 18 people and wounded hundreds this month, according to reports.

What additional military support is Britain providing?

The deployment follows a request from Saudi Arabia and expands military assistance announced by London in September.

Britain will also send an Atlas A400M military transport aircraft and military advisers. It has extended its offer to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi aircraft operating against the Houthis for another 90 days.

The announcement comes as Yemen's civil war continues to escalate following the collapse of a years-long truce in September.

Houthi attacks have increasingly targeted Saudi oil facilities and civilian infrastructure. The rebels have also imposed a naval blockade and attacked tankers, disrupting oil exports and pushing up energy prices.

Houthi rebels have targeted oil facilities in Saudi Arabia too [PHOTO: October 3] Image: REUTERS

Inside Yemen, authorities said a Houthi strike on Monday killed 58 people at a training camp for Saudi-backed government security forces.

Saudi Arabia and the United States accuse Iran of supporting the Houthis, an allegation Tehran denies.

How is the conflict affecting Saudi Arabia's economy?

Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, informally known as "Davos in the Desert," until 2027.

The event, originally scheduled for October 26-29, was expected to attract leading international financiers.

According to media reports, major banks and private equity firms had raised security concerns about attending the event.

The conference is a key part of Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract foreign investment and diversify its economy away from oil.

World.title: Portugal housing protests continue after police clear camps
World.content:
Demonstrators vow to continue their campaign to call for affordable housing in Portugal after police cleared tent camps and arrested at least 55 people.

Thousands of people rallied in Lisbon, Porto and other Portuguese cities on Tuesday evening, hours after police dismantled protest camps and arrested a total of 55 demonstrators.

The protesters vowed to continue their campaign against Portugal's deepening housing crisis, which has made buying or renting a home increasingly unaffordable.

Organizers said more than 1,000 people gathered in each of the two main protest locations, although police did not provide crowd estimates.



Protesters call for affordable housing as soaring property prices put pressure on residents Image: Pedro Nunes/REUTERS

In Lisbon's central Rossio square, demonstrators voted by a show of hands to re-establish their tent camp on Wednesday.

Police moves to shut down protest camps

Police launched coordinated operations in Lisbon and Porto shortly before 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Tuesday, after warning protesters that their camps were illegal.

Activists had occupied Lisbon's Rossio square since Saturday, setting up around 200 tents. In Porto, protesters had camped in Dom Joao I square for about 10 days.

Protesters set up tents in Lisbon's Rossio square before police moved to eject people from the central square on Tuesday [FILE: October 19, 2026] Image: Patricia De Melo Moreira/AFP

Authorities seized 228 camping structures during the operation.

In Porto, demonstrators dismantled their tents themselves after police threatened to intervene. In Lisbon, officers cleared the square as protesters formed a human chain.

Clashes subsequently broke out, according to footage broadcast by local television stations.

Carla Valadao, a spokesperson for the Lisbon camp, described the operation as "very aggressive."

However, Public Security Police superintendent Sergio Soares disputed that account, saying the eviction had been "calm, proportionate and appropriate, with no police charge."

All 55 people arrested were later released pending a court appearance in Lisbon on Wednesday.

Why are people protesting in Portugal?

Portugal is struggling with one of Europe's worst housing affordability crises.

Property purchase prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new leases have nearly doubled over the same period.

The problem is particularly severe in major cities such as Lisbon and Porto, where residents have also protested against excessive tourism and an influx of so-called digital nomads.

Protesters camp out in Porto [PHOTO: October 19] Image: Diogo Baptista/SOPA Images/IMAGO

Demonstrators accuse the center-right government of failing to address the crisis.

They are demanding the withdrawal of a bill that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. The proposed legislation has already passed its first parliamentary reading.

Debora Miranda, a 41-year-old communications consultant, told Reuters she joined the Lisbon demonstration to represent generations struggling with rising housing costs.

"If people don't feel at home, in every sense of the word, they can't move forward with their lives...enough is enough."

Jorge Paixao, a 19-year-old history student, described the situation as "a societal crisis."

He said his generation needed "the ability to live with dignity, start families and rejuvenate Portugal."

Portugal housing protest takes place amid demos around Europe

The demonstrations come amid growing anger over housing affordability and living costs across several European countries.

Protesters in Portugal have sought to align their movement with similar demonstrations in neighboring Spain.

In Madrid, activists maintain a tent camp to call for stronger action to tackle the housing crisis. The crisis was sparked by the eviction ofMaria del Carmen Abascal from her home.

Protesters call for stronger laws to protect renters [PHOTO: October 16, Madrid] Image: Bernat Armangue/AP Photo/picture alliance

The nearly four weeks of protests in Spain have contributed to political turmoil, leading to a snap general election being called for November 29.

Meanwhile, demonstrations over rising living costs have also taken place in France, Belgium and Italy.

Violence that erupted in France over the weekend on the sidelines of otherwise peaceful protests has raised concerns that similar unrest could spread to other countries facing comparable economic pressures.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

World.title: AfD's Alice Weidel to unveil plan to cut EU powers — report
World.content:
The far-right AfD will propose slashing powers of the European Union when it presents its policy paper on Wednesday, Politico reports.

Alice Weidel, the co-leader of Germany's far-right AfD, is expected to present her party's policy for the EU at the European Parliament on Wednesday.

According to a report from news outlet Politico , the AfD policy paper on the EU does not seek to exit the bloc or the eurozone at first.

The party rather wants to downsize the EU's powers and budget.

What's in the AfD policy paper?

Instead of direct European Parliament elections, the AfD would like to see delegates appointed by national parliaments.

The AfD would also limit the scope of the European Commission to purely administrative tasks and supplant the European Court of Justice with an arbitration tribunal.

The far right party would threaten to slash Germany's contributions to the EU budget.

Germany under the AfD would seek exemptions from EU regulations regarding issues such as migration and social policy. The AfD may also seek opt-outs of other areas such as agriculture and financial policies.

If the EU would not bend to the AfD's demands for reform, the party would then seek a German referendum on EU membership.

A referendum would be unrealistic, as it would require a constitutional amendment to the German Basic Law to take place. An amendment would require a two-thirds majority vote in both the Bundestag and upper house Bundesrat — an extremely high threshold to meet.

AfD eyes victory in next federal elections in 2029

The AfD hopes that it can implement its EU policies in 2029, when the next German and European elections will take place.

Recent German federal election surveys show the AfD in first place but it would have to form a coalition with another partner to establish a ruling majority government. That's difficult when other parties such as the conservative Christian Democratic Union refuse to have any cooperation with the AfD as part of a "firewall" policy.
