Li believes that Yugouliang’s remote location and climate make Lu’s vision of building a tourism industry here difficult to realize.

“I don’t have that kind of ability. No single institution or person can solve a problem this big on their own,” he said. Li has only been in the job for two years but admits that he already wants to leave.

During a recent yoga event, Li asked people to help with livestream sales of local farm products, but the results were disappointing.

The village Party secretary, Zhang Pengcheng, who took over from his father in 2021, said he has also tried encouraging residents to make short videos and livestream, but many struggle even to use smartphones, let alone speak standard Mandarin with viewers online.

Yet he sees the remaining yoga team as the “embers” to spark a tourism boom. In 2025, he organized a gala in which the team performed on ice beside a bonfire. A livestream of the event drew about 100,000 viewers.

But for now, the priority is improving infrastructure. In July last year, the township government and local businesses funded the opening of a guesthouse with room for up to 86 guests. It has yet to turn a profit. When Sixth Tone visited, its doors and windows were shuttered.

The village has also built a canteen for pensioners, with dishes starting at just 2 yuan. It was also temporarily closed in July because of a staff shortage.

Before stepping down, Jin earned a yoga instructor qualification in Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, and has since relocated to Zhangbei Town, about 60 kilometers from Yugouliang. She offers free classes to locals and teaches online six days a week.

Of the few residents still practicing yoga in Yugouliang, Zhang Xiying, despite her age, remains the most able and enthusiastic — though not for the village’s benefit, but for her own family’s.

“Exercise keeps me healthy,” she said, after wrapping up a practice session. “And I need to take good care of my old man.”

Additional reporting: Wu Huiyuan; editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Villagers practice yoga together on a summer afternoon in Yugouliang, Hebei province, July 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.title: New Robinsons Sports & Leisure unit to bring global concepts to the Philippines
World.content:
The new team will is set to shape global concepts and expertise around local interests and lifestyles

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by Robinsons Land Corporation and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

The hours we remember most are rarely the ones we planned down to the minute. A friendly match stretches into one more game. The last kilometer of a run reveals inner strength we didn’t know we had. Somewhere in a darkened theater, an entire audience holds its breath. And when those moments have passed, we carry something from them back into everyday life: a little more confidence, a deeper connection, the simple pleasure of feeling fully alive.

There is a Filipino word for that renewed energy: sigla. And Robinsons Sports and Leisure (RSL), Robinsons Land’s newest business unit, wants to make room for more of it for every Filipino. By bringing quality sports, recreation and entertainment experiences closer to where Filipinos live, work, shop and stay, RSL hopes to make these hours—our precious “me time”—a little more rewarding by fulfilling its promise, “For a Life That Moves You.”

RSL looks to the world for inspiration and to Filipino communities for direction. Its distinctly “glocal” approach brings international sports and leisure concepts and expertise closer to home, shaping them around local interests and lifestyles. The aim is to make these experiences relevant, accessible, and community-driven, giving Filipinos opportunities to discover something new and make it their own.

“The world is full of exciting ways to play, compete and recharge. We at Robinsons Land want to bring more of these experiences within reach of every Filipino and make them feel right at home here,” said Ramon Rivero, Robinsons Land’s chief strategist and RSL head. “That’s what “glocal” means to us: pairing international expertise with a real understanding of the communities we serve. A first-time player should feel welcome. Someone training seriously should have room to grow. Reeling senses after a night of live entertainment. And everyone should come away with more confidence, connection, and sigla.”

“Glocal” is a portmanteau combining global and local which describes the practice of living with a mindset that spans both worldwide and regional scales.

Bringing the action closer to home

Robinsons Land’s entry into sports and leisure builds on decades of experience developing places that are woven into Filipino daily life.

“For 46 years, Robinsons Land has built homes, workplaces, malls and hotels around the changing needs of Filipinos,” said Mybelle V. Aragon-GoBio, Robinsons Land president and CEO. “Sports and leisure give us another way to make sure that those developments become a part of every Filipino. We want our destinations to offer meaningful experiences worth making time for, with the quality and consistency that communities have come to expect from us.”

RSL is finding new possibilities within Robinsons Land’s existing developments. Rooftops and open areas can be transformed into courts and recreational spaces, bringing sports and leisure closer to where people already live, work and spend time together. A game after work or a weekend activity with friends can then seamlessly become a natural part of daily life.

Some will come to compete, others to learn, and still others simply for the pleasure of staying active and spending time with friends. RSL hopes to welcome them all, from curious beginners and weekend players to serious athletes and older adults discovering new ways to keep moving.

That spirit of participation will be on display on November 29, when the RSL Run Crew makes its debut at the AIA Rock ’n’ Roll Running Series Manila. Part of an international series that combines road racing with live music and entertainment, the event will bring runners together for a celebration of fitness and camaraderie along Manila’s historic streets.

Another opportunity arrives on December 7 with the public opening of GX Sports at Robinsons Galleria. The facility will feature two pickleball courts and an official HYROX Training Zone under the HYROX Training Club X (HTCx) concept. Equipped with race-standard equipment, a prescribed layout, and structured programming, the zone will help participants prepare for HYROX, the global fitness race combining running and functional workouts.

“The specialized training environment brings an internationally recognized fitness format within reach of Filipino enthusiasts, whether they are preparing for competition or looking for a new challenge,” adds Rivero.

In 2027, three GX Sports In Motion events will offer different ways to participate, giving people more opportunities to meet, compete and enjoy activities together. RSL will also continue developing the programming and partnerships that bring its facilities to life.

Pickleball takes a bigger stage

WORLD-CLASS FACILITIES. Helios Beta at Bridgetowne brings world-class pickleball facilities closer to Filipino communities, creating new spaces where recreation, competition, and connection come together

A friendly game and an international tournament begin the same way: someone steps onto the court.

At Bridgetowne, the fast-rising sport will take center stage when Helios Beta hosts the PPA Asia 500 Manila Open 2027. Operated by Kosmas Athletic Ventures Corporation (KAVC), the 14-court facility will bring international tournament action to an estate where residents, workers, and visitors can also make sports part of their everyday lives.

TOURNAMENT-GRADE. Designed to international standards, Helios’ tournament-grade courts are set to host top-level competition while serving as an everyday destination for players of all skill levels

Bridgetowne’s pickleball offerings will expand further with the development of the separate 25-court Helios Pickleball Center, a joint venture between Robinsons Land and KAVC. International expertise is helping shape the project, with KAVC tapping Johns Design & Consulting, the consultancy of professional pickleball players Collin and Ben Johns, as design consultant. The brothers’ experience competing at venues around the world will help inform the state-of-the-art facility’s planning, design, and events programming.

Beyond Bridgetowne, additional pickleball courts are planned for selected Robinsons malls and offices. Each new location can bring the sport within reach of another community, giving more Filipinos a chance to discover the game, improve their skills, and perhaps turn an occasional match into a weekly tradition.

From the court to the curtain call

The thrill of a close match, the magic of a live performance—there are many ways to bring people together. RSL is making room for more of them.

In Cebu, the approximately 1,850-seat NUSTAR Grand Theater is slated to open in 2028, expanding RSL’s offerings into live entertainment and culture. “NUSTAR Grand Theater will be the largest entertainment and cultural venue in the VisMin Region,” shares Rivero. He adds that RSL is looking forward to the venue for the grandest and best live entertainment to hit Philippine shores in the coming months.

Beyond the theater, RSL is exploring an even wider range of leisure possibilities, including sports and golf simulators, padel courts, flexible black-box spaces for entertainment and social activities, and wellness experiences. RSL will pursue these opportunities where demand is clear, the location is suitable and there is a strong potential for repeat participation.

“This deliberate approach supports Robinsons Land’s premiumization strategy, which seeks to make its destinations more distinctive, appealing and rewarding to visit,” says Rivero. This will translate to RSL developing thoughtfully designed facilities, engaging programs and forge specialist partnerships, with consistent high standards of quality, service and safety across locations and offerings shaped by the interests of each community.

The real test will come after opening day. Will people enjoy themselves enough to return? Will a new interest become a lasting passion, or a favorite activity find a regular place in someone’s week? These are the signs that an experience has found its way into people’s lives—and the measure of RSL’s success.

That is the promise behind RSL’s “glocal” vision: bringing the world’s possibilities closer to Filipino communities and giving people the freedom to make those experiences their own. An idea that began halfway around the world can become a favorite pastime, a familiar gathering place or a tradition shared among friends.

The game ends, the curtain falls, and everyone makes their way home—with a little more sigla than when they arrived. – Rappler.com

World.title: Signal No. 2 up in Batanes due to Super Typhoon Rosal
World.content:
ROSAL. Satellite image of Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) as of October 21, 2026, 10 am.

Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) maintains its maximum sustained winds of 215 km/h on Wednesday morning, October 21 — already its peak intensity, according to PAGASA

MANILA, Philippines – The country’s northernmost province of Batanes was placed under Signal No. 2 shortly before noontime on Wednesday, October 21, due to Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi).

Rosal was located 845 kilometers east of Northern Luzon as of 10 am on Wednesday, moving west northwest at a slightly slower 25 kilometers per hour from the previous 30 km/h.

The super typhoon maintained its strength, with maximum sustained winds of 215 km/h and gustiness of up to 265 km/h. It is already at its peak intensity, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA).

Rosal is still affecting parts of the country even though it will remain offshore. It will be closest to extreme Northern Luzon between Thursday, October 22, and Friday afternoon, October 23.

Below are the areas under tropical cyclone wind signals as of 11 am on Wednesday.

Signal No. 2

Gale-force winds (62 to 88 km/h), minor to moderate threat to life and property

Batanes

Signal No. 1

Strong winds (39 to 61 km/h), minimal to minor threat to life and property

Cagayan including Babuyan Islands

eastern part of Isabela (Maconacon, Divilacan, Palanan, Santa Maria, Cabagan, Delfin Albano, Santo Tomas, Tumauini, San Pablo, Ilagan City, San Mariano, Dinapigue)

Ilocos Norte

Apayao

northeastern part of Catanduanes (Pandan, Bagamanoc, Panganiban, Viga, Gigmoto)

There is a possibility of Signal No. 3 being raised, depending on Rosal’s track.

The northeasterly windflow and the periphery or outer bands of the super typhoon will also bring strong to gale-force gusts to the following areas:

Wednesday, October 21

Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Cagayan Valley, Bicol, Romblon, Aurora, Eastern Visayas, Siquijor, Bohol, Northern Mindanao, Caraga, Davao Region, Sarangani

Thursday, October 22

most of Luzon and Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Northern Mindanao, Agusan del Norte, Surigao del Norte, Dinagat Islands, Sarangani, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

Friday, October 23

most of Luzon and Visayas, Misamis Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Dinagat Islands, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

In the next 48 hours, Rosal may also trigger significant rainfall in at least four provinces in Northern Luzon. The following should watch out for floods and landslides:

Wednesday noon, October 21, to Thursday noon, October 22

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters): Batanes, Ilocos Norte, Apayao, Cagayan

Thursday noon, October 22, to Friday noon, October 23

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Batanes, Cagayan

On Wednesday, aside from the provinces mentioned above, Rosal may trigger moderate to at times heavy rain in Isabela and Catanduanes, as well as scattered rain and thunderstorms in the rest of Cagayan Valley, the rest of Bicol, the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, Ilocos Sur, Quezon, and Eastern Visayas.

Meanwhile, PAGASA updated its warnings for affected seaboards on Wednesday morning. Waves in portions of extreme Northern Luzon may now reach up to 9 meters or 29.5 feet high.

Up to very rough seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

Northern and eastern seaboards of Batanes; eastern seaboard of Babuyan Islands – waves up to 9 meters high

Northern and eastern seaboards of Cagayan – waves up to 8 meters high

Remaining seaboards of Batanes; northern seaboard of Babuyan Islands; remaining seaboard of Cagayan; northeastern seaboard of Isabela – waves up to 7 meters high

Remaining seaboard of Isabela – waves up to 6 meters high

Eastern seaboard of northern Aurora; northern and eastern seaboards of Catanduanes; northern and eastern seaboards of Polillo Islands; northern seaboards of Camarines Norte and Camarines Sur; northern seaboard of Ilocos Norte – waves up to 5 meters high

Remaining seaboard of Aurora; northern seaboard of Northern Samar; eastern seaboards of Albay and Sorsogon – waves up to 4.5 meters high

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Eastern seaboards of northern Quezon and Eastern Samar; remaining seaboard of Northern Samar – waves up to 4 meters high

Remaining seaboard of Ilocos Norte – waves up to 3.5 meters high

Seaboard of La Union; northern seaboards of Dinagat Islands and Siargao-Bucas Grande Island Group; remaining seaboard of Catanduanes; northern seaboard of Ilocos Sur; northern and eastern seaboards of Davao Oriental; northwestern seaboard of Pangasinan – waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate to rough seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Seaboards of Surigao del Sur and Surigao del Norte; southern seaboard of Davao Oriental; remaining eastern seaboard of Quezon; remaining seaboards of Ilocos Sur, Dinagat Islands, and Siargao-Bucas Grande Island Group – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Eastern seaboard of Davao Occidental – waves up to 2 meters high

ALSO ON RAPPLER

PAGASA expects Rosal to start gradually weakening on Wednesday afternoon. It may be downgraded to a typhoon by Thursday and into a severe tropical storm by Sunday, October 25.

Rosal is still projected to exit the Philippine Area of Responsibility by Friday evening or early Saturday morning, October 24. It entered PAR on Tuesday, October 20.

Rosal is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.

The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

World.title: In the Public Square: Nine years after Marawi seige
World.content:
Rappler columnist John Nery is joined by Drieza Lininding, chair of the Moro Consensus Group. Catch the episode on Wednesday, October 21, at 8 pm.

It has been nine years since the brutal siege of Marawi City came to an end. At the height of the siege, some 300,000 families were displaced. Today, thousands of “bakwit” remain in temporary shelters. And that is only the most visible of proud Marawi’s many wounds.

Why is it taking so long for these wounds to heal? And will all those responsible for wrecking Marawi ever be held to account?

World.title: Musk ordered slowdown of Starlink service used by Ukraine’s military – report
World.content:
ELON MUSK. Tesla CEO Elon Musk attends the 'A New Golden Age' summit at the US Institute of Peace, renamed The Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace by the Trump administration, in Washington, DC, USA, October 8, 2026.

The Wall Street Journal reports Elon Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public, while the president was campaigning last week

Elon Musk last week ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on, the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, October 20, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.

Musk, SpaceX and the White House did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. Reuters could not immediately verify the report.

Ukraine uses Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations. Restricting the satellite service hampered the country’s attack and air defense drone missions against Russia.

Musk and US President Donald Trump discussed the Starlink decision in a call soon after the slowdown became public, while the president was campaigning last week, according to the report, which added the two had also discussed the matter prior to the decision to throttle Starlink.

Reuters had reported exclusively that the order to limit the satellite system came from inside the White House.

Trump said last week he did not think either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access, while Musk said any limits on speed or Starship or Starshield use were decided by the US military or the president.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s relations with Washington have sunk to new lows after Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow. Trump has also told Kyiv to stop attacking Russian refineries and urged Ukrainians to replace Zelenskyy.

Zelenskyy, who is in Oslo in a bid to repair US relations, said on Tuesday he discussed issues including “the situation with Starlink/Starshield, which needs to be restored” with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Tuesday Washington had not pulled back Ukraine’s ability to access Starlink’s satellite network, but signaled the problem lay with the terms of service Kyiv needed to comply with. – Rappler.com

World.title: [In This Economy] Marcos’ unconstitutional budgets: Who will answer for them?
World.content:
The big question is: Will Congress and the Marcos administration account for the affected funds and change how they prepare the next budget?

The Supreme Court has delivered a damning verdict on how Congress and the Marcos administration have handled our national budgets in the past few years.

In a decision announced on Tuesday, October 20, the Supreme Court (SC) declared the 2024 and 2025 General Appropriations Acts (GAAs), or our annual budget laws, unconstitutional. It also struck down two provisions governing the release of unprogrammed appropriations (UA) in the 2026 budget.

This is a historic decision. It’s not every day that the Supreme Court declares GAAs unconstitutional. It also comes on the heels of the SC’s December 2025 decision ordering the return of P60 billion transferred from PhilHealth to the Treasury—done also to fund unprogrammed appropriations.

Note that the Court didn’t invalidate the entire 2026 budget, abolish all unprogrammed appropriations, or order the return of every past payment. Instead, the ruling—dated October 7 and written by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen—exposes serious defects in the way hundreds of billions of pesos were authorized in the past few years.

What went wrong, and what should happen next?

Budget inflation

Let’s start with the very concept of unprogrammed appropriations or standby spending authority that the government can use only when specified funding conditions are met. These differ from programmed appropriations, which already form part of the government’s regular spending plan.

In principle, unprogrammed funds can serve legitimate purposes. A foreign-assisted project, for instance, like a railway, may need spending authority contingent on an approved loan. The Supreme Court recognizes that such appropriations can be constitutional.

But just because a spending item is “unprogrammed” doesn’t mean it’s exempted from the Constitution’s budget ceiling. This is a key ruling in the decision.

Article VI, Section 25(1) of our Constitution says Congress may not increase the appropriations recommended by the President for government operations, set yearly in the National Expenditure Program or NEP. For instance, for 2027, the NEP set a P7.2 trillion budget, and Congress cannot exceed that.

What the Supreme Court made clear is that this ceiling should strictly include both programmed and unprogrammed appropriations.

Congress brazenly breached this ceiling in past years. For 2024, the President proposed about P281.9 billion in unprogrammed funds, but Congress raised that to P731.4 billion, amounting to an increase of P449.5 billion or roughly 159%. Hence, the standby allocation became about 2.6 times the original proposal.

The scale of the increase is really mind-boggling. Nearly half a trillion pesos in additional spending authority emerged from the budget legislation process. Programmed appropriations remained unchanged, so the UA increase also raised the combined total above the President’s budget ceiling.

With the 2024 budget ceiling breached, the Supreme Court declared the P449.5-billion increase (and, consequently, the 2024 budget law) unconstitutional. The 2025 budget suffered a similar defect through a P17.992-billion increase in the Department of Public Works and Highways’ Special Road Fund.

From where I sit, the Supreme Court decision is largely a constraint on Congress’ ability to play around with unprogrammed funds. This is the handiwork of Marcos’ allies and family members in Congress, including the former speaker Martin Romualdez (his first cousin), who orchestrated the anomalous budget increases.

But blame rests on the executive, too. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his budget officials—especially former budget secretary Amenah Pangandaman—must explain how budgets with these defects passed through executive scrutiny.

By the way, the ruling also raises questions about the 2023 budget, the Marcos administration’s first, when unprogrammed appropriations reached more than P807 billion. That budget was outside the consolidated cases, however.

Questionable financing

Through its recent decision, the Supreme Court also reaffirmed limits on when standby funds can be released.

The challenged 2026 special provisions allowed releases from unprogrammed appropriations when collections from a particular non-tax revenue source exceeded its target, or when a new revenue source produced collections.

Neither condition, by itself, guarantees that total government revenues have exceeded the overall target. The reason is that higher collections from one source—or revenues from a new source—can coexist with larger shortfalls elsewhere.

For instance, suppose the government expects P90 in taxes and P10 from other revenues, for a total of P100. Instead, it collects P80 in taxes and P15 from other sources. There’s a P5 windfall in the second category, but total collections are only P95.

If planned spending is P100, the financing gap is already P5. Authorizing another P5 of spending on the strength of the supposed windfall doubles that gap to P10.

Reaffirming its earlier Araullo ruling, the Supreme Court requires aggregate collections to exceed total revenue targets for the use of unprogrammed appropriations. It invalidated the two triggers found in the 2026 budget, but still allowed approved loans for foreign-assisted projects.

This makes a lot of sense from a fiscal standpoint. Additional spending without genuinely additional resources can mean more borrowing, higher interest costs, or less room for other services. Government borrowing can finance worthwhile investments, but the projects and financing must be assessed in tandem, not in isolation.

The spending of these funds also deserves scrutiny. The decision examines the broadly defined Support for Assistance to Government Infrastructure and Social Programs (SAGIP), which left actual project selection and allocation to the Executive after budget enactment.

Of roughly P200 billion in SAGIP allotment releases in 2024, about P155.9 billion went to public works, including P85.8 billion for flood control. These were authorizations to incur obligations, not proof of completed projects or corruption.

The Supreme Court itself says SAGIP “paved the way for the new pork barrel system.” It recounts the comments of an amicus curiae, UP School of Economics Professor Emerita Solita Monsod, one of my mentors. She explained before the court how infrastructure allocations had become embedded in budget preparation, with lawmakers proposing projects and a “parking fee” allegedly paid for projects outside their districts.

These observations demand investigation: Exactly which allocations financed useful infrastructure, and which financed ghost projects or kickbacks?

What now?

The main concern with the ruling is that it does little to recover what was already lost. It’s like shutting the tap after water has already gone down the drain.

A number of lawyer friends immediately pointed out that the Supreme Court applies the doctrine of operative fact, which allows certain consequences of an unconstitutional law to stand when undoing them would unfairly harm people who relied on the law in good faith.

Here, that protection is qualified: it covers irreversible programs, activities, and projects under the affected 2024 unprogrammed appropriations and challenged 2025 accounts, whose beneficiaries relied in good faith on the law’s validity. It doesn’t automatically clear every transaction or protect the officials responsible.

The ruling itself convicts nobody of plunder or graft. Those questions require separate proceedings and proof. But authors, proponents, and implementers of the unconstitutional budget provisions can’t simply invoke the protection of beneficiaries to escape scrutiny.

Moving forward, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) should publish a project-level accounting of affected funds, distinguishing amounts authorized, released, committed through obligations, and actually paid. Ongoing commitments also need prompt legal review so agencies know which activities can lawfully proceed.

Right now, Congress is finalizing the 2027 budget, and must be guided by the new Supreme Court decision. Specifically, the combined total of programmed and unprogrammed appropriations must stay within the constitutional ceiling.

Congress must also publish a reconciliation of changes to be made by the bicameral conference committee, which settles differences between the House and Senate versions. Every addition should have an identifiable purpose and financing basis.

The Supreme Court ruling is a win not just for budget watchdogs but for Filipinos at large. It gives government an opportunity to correct anomalous practices in recent years. But the big question is: Will Congress and the Marcos administration account for the affected funds and change how they prepare the next budget?

Note, too, that lawmakers wised up and shifted their pork projects away from unprogrammed funds toward programmed funds. The 2027 budget (for the last full year of the Marcos administration, right before the 2028 polls) is shaping up to be as corrupt and patronage-driven as ever.

Pork is here to stay, unless a radical shake-up in the political landscape changes how the budget is crafted and implemented. For Filipinos, bad budgeting is a double-whammy: we’re borrowing and paying for the corrupted amounts they stole from the public coffers. But we get nothing in return by way of quality public goods.

Ang hirap mahalin ng Pilipinas! (It’s hard to love the Philippines!)

– Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and COVID-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).

World.title: Three issues defining the 2026 US midterm elections
World.content:
DONALD TRUMP. US President Donald Trump gestures after his speech during the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas, Texas, USA, September 9, 2026.

US President Donald Trump's record-low popularity, voter concerns over affordability and a fierce immigration debate are shaping the November 3 US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress

WASHINGTON, USA – US President Donald Trump’s record-low popularity, voter frustration over the cost of living and a fierce immigration fight are shaping the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine whether Republicans keep control of Congress or Democrats gain the power to challenge his administration.

Republicans hold narrow majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of each chamber.

The outcome will hinge on a relatively small number of competitive races, but the campaigns are being shaped nationally by Trump himself and voter concerns over affordability and immigration.

Here is a look at the three issues defining the election:

Donald Trump

The president has put himself front and center in the closing stretch of the campaign cycle despite his record-low popularity, with upcoming rallies in Florida, Iowa, Michigan and Texas. Trump’s approval rating has fallen to an all-time low of 31%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll. Yet he has repeatedly urged voters to pretend he’s on the ballot, an effort that could motivate Democrats and independents to rally against his party despite the message being aimed at increasing turnout among Trump’s base.

Democrats have said Trump has broken his campaign promises to lower costs and end wars. They have vowed to tackle an affordability agenda to reduce Americans’ cost of living and hold the administration accountable for alleged corruption if voters give them control of either chamber.

Affordability

Voters have consistently ranked the cost of living as the top issue this election cycle. Half of registered voters surveyed in a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll cited the cost of living as the most important factor in how they will vote. In the same poll, voters highlighted health care, gasoline, food and housing as the top household bills lawmakers should focus on.

Republicans’ top legislative achievement was a tax cut extension that slashed roughly $1 trillion in spending for Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income Americans, and other health programs. Democrats last year forced a government shutdown over a failed effort to extend expiring health subsidies that benefited 24 million Americans.

Gas prices have spiked since the US and Israel launched military strikes on Iran in February. The national average price of gas is $4.28 — $1.20 higher than it was a year ago, according to AAA. The average cost of diesel is $6.32 — a $2.70 increase from a year earlier.

Grocery costs are up 1.8% over the past year, according to US Bureau of Labor Statistics data on consumer prices. Federal Housing Finance Agency data show home prices rose 2.1% over the past year. Congress passed a bipartisan housing bill earlier this year. It became law without Trump’s signature.

Immigration

Preliminary data from the Department of Homeland Security showed a 95% drop in migrants apprehended at the southwest border compared to former president Joe Biden’s administration. The agency said there have been no Border Patrol releases the entire fiscal year for the first time ever.

But fatal encounters with federal immigration agents have occurred in Maine, Minnesota and Texas. The backlash to the deaths of two US citizens in Minnesota pulled many Democrats in competitive primaries to the left this year, with some candidates calling for the impeachment of then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and others saying Immigration and Customs Enforcement should be abolished.

Democrats and Republicans sparred over immigration funding this year in a stalemate that forced Republicans to unilaterally pass a $70 billion bill to fund ICE and the Border Patrol for the remainder of Trump’s presidency. Republicans counter Democrats’ criticism by saying Democrats support open borders.

Federal immigration officials also raided the Washington home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota this month, drawing widespread condemnation from Democrats. A person familiar with the case against Omar told Reuters one potential aim of the investigation could be to strip her of US citizenship and deport her.

Other issues

Artificial intelligence and data centers, cryptocurrency, abortion and Israel could also influence voters in individual races. In Ohio’s Senate race, for example, Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown has labeled Republican Senator Jon Husted the face of data centers, and the crypto super PAC Defend American Jobs has spent more than $46 million to reelect Husted over Brown, a former US senator who chaired the chamber’s Banking Committee.

In Maine’s Senate race, Democratic nominee Troy Jackson is hoping voters don’t forget that Republican Senator Susan Collins helped confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, which later overturned the federal right to abortion. Collins is on the election ballot for the first time since the high court made abortion a state issue rather than a federal right.

In Michigan, Republican nominee Mike Rogers has indicated he would accept help from a pro-Israel super PAC that spent more than $30 million backing Democratic US Representative Haley Stevens in her unsuccessful primary against Abdul El-Sayed, who now faces Rogers in the general election. The group has already spent more than $280,000 on mailers against El-Sayed.

Earlier this week, Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection. – Rappler.com

World.title: France to deploy troops, admits to failures over weekend unrest
World.content:
PROTEST. Residents gather during a protest following a fire at the town hall in Limoges, France, October 18, 2026. Reuters

Targeted curfews are implemented to restore calm, with the government admitting to intelligence failures and static police deployments during the unrest

PARIS, France – France will reinforce police with troops and mount a huge security operation for more protests planned on Saturday, the government said on Tuesday, October 20, acknowledging failures in its response to last weekend’s violence.

“The deployment next Saturday (October 24) will be massive,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said, adding that the immediate priority was to restore order after rioting and looting swept Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities on October 17.

In a sometimes rowdy debate, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the military would be deployed alongside police, while the government pledged to overhaul tactics after widespread criticism that city centers had been left vulnerable.

Targeted curfews help restore calm

Framing the crisis as a choice “between violence and the Republic,” Lecornu blamed the unrest on far-left groups, who in turn have accused the government of underestimating public anger over high living costs and declining public services.

The turmoil shocked France because of both its scale and the apparent inability of police to contain it, inflaming tensions ahead of presidential elections next year with candidates from the far right and hard left performing strongly in polls.

Protests in other European countries, including Italy and Albania, have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading around the continent at a time when many nations, including France, are struggling with budget woes.

A night of relative calm in France followed targeted curfews imposed in several areas affected by the chaos, which the government said had helped reassert control. The localized curfews, some directed at children and teenagers under age 18, were extended to Tuesday night, police said.

Lecornu acknowledged shortcomings in the state’s response at the weekend, saying there had been intelligence failures, while police deployments had been too static and authorities had erred by not canceling planned police leave.

Nunez apologized for the mistakes. “I deeply regret what happened. I accept my share of responsibility,” he said.

Suspect arrested for Limoges town hall destruction

Parliament is setting up a commission of inquiry to establish the causes of the unrest, while authorities have assigned 200 investigators to identify and track down those involved in the street violence.

Police arrested on Tuesday a man suspected of starting a blaze that destroyed a historic town hall in the central city of Limoges during the rioting. Officials said he had been on a security watch list and belonged to an ultra-left group.

Sylvain Maillard, a Renaissance deputy for Paris, told Reuters some apps had become “a walkie-talkie system for rioters and looters.”

Underscoring the broad impact of the crisis, French borrowing costs rose further on Tuesday as investors fretted about the prospect of more unrest, with the yield on benchmark 10-year government bonds touching its highest level in 24 years.

Supermarket chain Carrefour said it had lost tens of millions of euros through theft and damage, warning that it faced an “unprecedented situation” because of the disorder.

France’s main student union UNEF has called for further protests on Saturday, pledging to maintain pressure on Macron’s government over what it says is a deteriorating and underfunded education system. “We carry on,” it said on social media.

Separately, groups identifying themselves as “Gilets Jaunes” (Yellow Vests) called for protest actions over rising fuel costs.

The yellow vest movement, largely inactive in recent years, sprang up in 2018 during Macron’s first term over plans to raise petrol taxes. Traffic blockades continued for months until the government made costly concessions it can ill afford now.

Italy faces new form of unrest, minister says

Northern Italian cities, including the financial capital Milan, were also hit by riots last weekend.

Though not on the scale seen in France, the unrest nonetheless jolted Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government, which was expected to introduce new security measures at a cabinet meeting on Tuesday.

Defense Minister Guido Crosetto described the disturbances as a form of “hybrid warfare” conducted through social media platforms such as TikTok, YouTube and other online networks.

“The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy are fundamentally different from those seen in other eras,” Crosetto wrote on X. “The West has yet to realize this or take any meaningful action in response.”

In Milan’s central Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, sportswear retailer On and a Levi’s store that were targeted during the unrest had reopened on Tuesday but remained boarded up. Luxury stores had restored merchandise to window displays after temporarily removing it for security reasons.

In Albania, protesters were expected to take to the streets of Tirana for a seventh consecutive day against the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama. – Rappler.com

World.title: Parts of Northern Luzon to be rainy as Super Typhoon Rosal speeds up
World.content:
ROSAL. Satellite image of Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) as of October 21, 2026, 4 am.

Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) is located 990 kilometers east of Northern Luzon at 4 am on Wednesday, October 21

MANILA, Philippines – At least three provinces in Northern Luzon are expected to have moderate to heavy rain on Wednesday, October 21, as Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) accelerated before dawn.

As of 4 am on Wednesday, Rosal was already 990 kilometers east of Northern Luzon, moving west northwest at 30 kilometers per hour from the previous 25 km/h.

The super typhoon had intensified further on Tuesday evening, October 20, with its maximum sustained winds reaching 215 km/h from 195 km/h. Its gustiness also went up to 265 km/h from 240 km/h.

Rosal remains unlikely to make landfall in the Philippines, but it will still have an impact due to its size and intensity. It will be closest to extreme Northern Luzon between Thursday, October 22, and Friday afternoon, October 23.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) released an updated rainfall outlook at 5 am on Wednesday, showing that the following provinces are expected to see significant rain:

Wednesday, October 21

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters): Ilocos Norte, Apayao, Cagayan

Thursday, October 22

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Batanes

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Ilocos Norte, Apayao, Cagayan

Friday, October 23

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Batanes

On Wednesday, aside from the provinces mentioned above, Rosal may trigger moderate to at times heavy rain in Batanes, Isabela, and Catanduanes, as well as scattered rain and thunderstorms in the rest of Cagayan Valley, the rest of Bicol, the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, Ilocos Sur, Quezon, and Eastern Visayas.

PAGASA also advised more areas to brace for strong winds from the super typhoon. Here are the areas covered by Signal No. 1 as of 5 am on Wednesday:

Batanes

Babuyan Islands

mainland Cagayan

eastern part of Isabela (Maconacon, Divilacan, Palanan, Santa Maria, Cabagan, Delfin Albano, Santo Tomas, Tumauini, San Pablo, Ilagan City, San Mariano, Dinapigue)

northern and central parts of Apayao (Calanasan, Luna, Santa Marcela, Flora, Pudtol, Kabugao)

northeastern part of Ilocos Norte (Pagudpud, Adams)

northeastern part of Catanduanes (Pandan, Bagamanoc, Panganiban, Viga, Gigmoto)

The highest possible tropical cyclone wind signal due to Rosal is Signal No. 2 or 3.

The northeasterly windflow and the periphery or outer bands of the super typhoon will also bring strong to gale-force gusts to the following areas:

Wednesday, October 21

Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Cagayan Valley, Bicol, Romblon, Eastern Visayas, Siquijor, Bohol, Northern Mindanao, Caraga, Davao Region, Sarangani

Thursday, October 22

most of Luzon and Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Northern Mindanao, Agusan del Norte, Surigao del Norte, Dinagat Islands, Sarangani, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

Friday, October 23

most of Luzon and Visayas, Camiguin, Misamis Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Dinagat Islands, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

Travel is becoming increasingly dangerous in more seaboards in Luzon on Wednesday, with the highest waves up to 8 meters or around 26 feet high.

Up to very rough seas (travel is risky for all vessels)

Seaboards of Batanes; northern and eastern seaboards of Cagayan including Babuyan Islands – waves up to 8 meters high

Remaining seaboards of Cagayan; seaboard of Isabela – waves up to 6 meters high

Eastern seaboard of northern Aurora; northern and eastern seaboards of Catanduanes – waves up to 5 meters high

Remaining seaboards of Aurora; northern and eastern seaboards of Polillo Islands; northern seaboards of Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, and Northern Samar; eastern seaboards of Albay and Sorsogon – waves up to 4.5 meters high

Up to rough seas (small vessels should not venture out to sea)

Eastern seaboards of northern Quezon and Eastern Samar; remaining seaboard of Northern Samar; northern seaboard of Ilocos Norte – waves up to 4 meters high

Eastern seaboards of Dinagat Islands, Siargao-Bucas Grande Island Group, and Davao Oriental; remaining seaboards of Catanduanes and Ilocos Norte – waves up to 3 meters high

Up to moderate to rough seas (small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible)

Seaboards of Ilocos Sur, La Union, Surigao del Sur, and Surigao del Norte; southern seaboard of Davao Oriental; remaining eastern seaboards of Quezon; northwestern seaboard of Pangasinan – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Eastern seaboard of Davao Occidental – waves up to 2 meters high

ALSO ON RAPPLER

PAGASA said Rosal can still strengthen further as it moves over the Philippine Sea on Wednesday morning, but it is likely to gradually weaken afterwards. It could weaken into a typhoon on Thursday and into a severe tropical storm by Sunday, October 25.

Rosal’s latest forecast track shows it is projected to maintain its west northwest direction on Wednesday, before heading northwest until Friday morning and recurving northeast by Sunday.

It may leave the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) by Friday evening or early Saturday morning, October 24.

Rosal, which entered PAR on Tuesday, is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.

The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

World.title: Thousands Flee as Regime Troops Push Into Myanmar’s Oil Hub
World.content:
Regime troops backed by airstrikes are pouring into Magwe Region’s Myaing Township as the battle for Myanmar’s oilfields escalates, forcing thousands of residents to flee.

Reinforcements from the Light Infantry Division in Pakokku, an hour to the south, are bolstering the offensive to seize territory — nicknamed “Anyar Dubai” for its oil wealth — from resistance groups.

Resistance forces have controlled the area since 2022, repelling repeated efforts to choke off their crucial revenue stream. However, a regime offensive backed by 1,000 troops gained a foothold on May 24, seizing the Well-2 oil field in Tae Gyi village.

The latest push began on October 18, when regime reinforcements arrived in Kamma town, Pakokku Township while gyrocopters bombed the nearby village of Ohntaw, killing five people, including children, and injuring four others.

On Monday, the troops arrived in Myaing’s Twinma village, controlled by regime-aligned militia, and set up camp there. According to Sayar Htwe from the Anyar Myay Civil Society Organization, up to 5,000 residents fled neighboring villages as airstrikes and troops advanced.

“We have no information on where the troops are heading, but we can assume they are reinforcements for Tae Gyi village,” Sayar Htwe told The Irrawaddy.

Regime troops suffered heavy losses in the three-month battle for Tae Gyi, where they are now encircled and entirely reliant on airdrops for ammunition and supplies.

On September 28, the regime reported that troops had seized 131 small-scale oil rigs in the area, torching some to prevent them from falling back into resistance hands.

On Monday, the Magwe resistance’s Anyar Myay Coalition urged the public to remain on high alert for airstrikes and attacks, as regime troops were mobilizing in Pakokku, Myaing and Pauk townships. It warned that regime troops camped in Tae Gyi had killed around 50 civilians and torched 600 houses since May.

World.title: Regional Body Expels Myanmar Regime’s Human Rights Fig Leaf
World.content:
The South East Asia National Human Rights Institutions Forum (SEANF), a regional umbrella group, has expelled a fig-leaf human rights body controlled by Myanmar’s military regime after it refused to cooperate with a compliance review.

SEANF on Monday said it has terminated the membership of the Myanmar National Human Rights Commission (MNHRC) because it is not an independent institution promoting and protecting human rights.

Established in 2007, SEANF now consist of just five national human rights commissions aiming to strengthen regional cooperation, from Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and Timor-Leste.

The decision, made on Oct. 1 and put into effect immediately, came at the 11th hour before Myanmar was to assume the umbrella group’s rotating chairmanship in 2027.

It follows a review of whether the MNHRC still met the Paris Principles standards for independence, effectiveness, and integrity, which SEANF uses to define a national human rights institution.

SEANF told the MNHRC in early September to respond, but the MNHRC refused, saying the review “did not comply with” the network’s procedural rules—a frequent fallback by the putschist regime in dealing with regional organizations of which it has fallen foul.

SEANF then decided unilaterally that the MNHRC “no longer satisfies the definition of a national human rights institution under amended Article 1 of the SEANF Rules of Procedure,” namely being independent to promote and protect human rights, it said in Monday’s statement. The decision was made in “a fair, transparent and evidence-based manner,” it added.”

The MNHRC was also kicked out of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) and the Asia-Pacific Forum (AFP) in 2025.

SEANF added the MNHRC can reapply for membership if it can demonstrate efforts to comply with the Paris Principles.

Established under the quasi-civilian Thein Sein administration in 2011 and once recognized as a “partially independent” body, the MNHRC went rapidly downhill when its leadership was replaced with regime loyalists after the 2021 coup.

It has since remained conspicuously silent about the regime’s glaring human rights violations while offering it a veneer of respectability and protection from scrutiny. Anecdotal evidence suggests that anyone coming to the MNHRC with a complaint could expect a knock on the door from the regime’s enforcers soon after.

Rights groups in Myanmar and beyond have long called its removal from global networks.

Prominent activist Khin Ohmar of Progressive Voice told the Irrawaddy that SEANF’s decision was “a long-awaited principled action” and “strips the criminal military junta-controlled MNHRC of regional legitimacy.”

“This decision sends a clear message that this body can no longer hide behind a SEANF membership card,” she added.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Bombs Civilians While Claiming Military Operations Serve Peace
World.content:
Framing its aerial bombardment of civilians as a peace initiative, the Myanmar regime continued aerial attacks across five regions and states over the weekend, killing over two dozen civilians.

Addressing humanitarian concerns raised in the media over the targeting of civilians, newly appointed Defense Minister Lieutenant General Yar Pyae, who is also chair of the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), claimed that the current military operations—a reference to the bombing of civilians in resistance-held territories—were conducted in the pursuit of peace.

He made the remark at the closing ceremony of an event marking the 11th anniversary of the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) in Naypyitaw on October 16.

At the event, the regime again called on ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) to join its purported peace talks while encouraging the People’s Defense Force (PDF), the armed wing of the civilian National Unity Government (NUG), to surrender.

Meanwhile, from October 16-18, the regime bombed civilian targets in Magwe, Sagaing and Mandalay regions and Rakhine and Chin states, killing at least 27 people and injuring 11, according to media reports.

On Friday evening, regime aircraft bombed a Starlink-based WiFi shop in Thitgyitaw Village in Yesagyo, Magwe Region. The attack on the shop, which locals rely on to bypass the regime’s restrictions and access the internet, killed at least 12, including two children aged 1 and 10, and injured two, the NUG said on Sunday.

The number of casualties was likely to increase as bomb damage was making it difficult to determine the number and identities of the dead, the NUG’s Human Rights Department said.

“This is a blatant violation of international humanitarian law and a war crime,” it said.

The operation was carried out by two Russian-made Mi-35 attack helicopters, two fighter jets from Magwe and Nyaung Oo, and two drones from the Pakokku-based No. 101 Light Infantry Division, the NUG said.

However, local media reported that at least 15 civilians were killed in the incident.

On the same day, the regime bombed Magyikan Village in Sagaing’s Myaung, injuring one.

The regime’s airstrikes continued on Sunday, as Y-12 utility aircraft bombed Arakan Army (AA)-controlled ethnic Rakhine villages in Rathedaung. Wai Hun Aung, a prominent ethnic Rakhine writer and aid worker, said five people were killed.

The regime also bombed a jetty in AA-controlled Paletwa, Chin State, on the same day, resulting in 20 casualties according to media reports, though there has been no official statement yet.

A regime drone attacked Shwebayet Village in Mandalay’s Singu Township on October 18, killing three people and injuring four women and girls, including a 5-year-old, the Singu People’s Defense Force reported on Monday.

Three regime gyrocopters bombed Ohntaw Village in Magwe’s Pakokku Township on Sunday, killing five including children and senior citizens. Local media reported that four were injured, including a 2-year-old.

At the NCA anniversary event, regime leader Min Aung Hlaing invited 2015 signatories that have been fighting the Myanmar military since the 2021 coup—the Karen National Union, Chin National Front and All Burma Students’ Democratic Front—to join his peace process. The regime demands that the PDFs surrender.

Lt-Gen Yar Pyae insisted the aerial bombing was conducted for peaceful purposes. “Some parts are military actions, while others are steps to achieve peace,” Yar Pyae said.

World.title: Detained Aung San Suu Kyi Receives UK Royal Package: Regime
World.content:
YANGON—Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi received a package from Britain’s King Charles III on Monday, authorities said, releasing the first pictures of the detained Nobel laureate in two months and describing her as a “special female prisoner.”

It is the first time Myanmar authorities have used the term to describe Aung San Suu Kyi, who was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitor ACLED.

The coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April following elections that did not include Aung San Suu Kyi’s party, and she was moved to house arrest soon afterwards.

Home Ministry officials met her on Monday to deliver a package of two books about soil, “one sealed envelope, and a sealed diplomatic communication sent by King Charles III of the United Kingdom to the special female detainee,” Myanmar’s presidential spokeswoman said on her Facebook page.

Britain is Myanmar’s former colonial power and the monarch is known to have a keen interest in gardening and the environment.

Accompanying the statement were two images of Aung San Suu Kyi meeting two men with their backs to the camera.

The pictures appeared to be in a similar room to the last released images of her, when she met a Red Cross representative in August, her first publicized meeting with a foreign official since her ouster.

Fact-checkers from AFP examined the latest photos and found no evidence of manipulation using Meta Generative AI or OpenAI tools.

Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained on charges rights groups say were concocted to return power to the military, which has historically ruled Myanmar since independence.

“I have been extremely lenient toward her,” Min Aung Hlaing said in an interview with Time magazine published last month.

In response to questions from AFP, the Foreign Office in London did not say whether British diplomats had sought to deliver the package in person, or been refused permission to do so.

Britain condemns what it describes as Aung San Suu Kyi’s “arbitrary detention” and calls for her immediate and unconditional release.

World.title: Myanmar Regime’s Sittwe Counteroffensive Hits the Rocks on Nga Pyi Island
World.content:
The Myanmar military’s push to land troops on Nga Pyi Island in Rakhine State’s Pauktaw Township has suffered fresh setbacks as the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) strikes regime vessels and tightens its siege on the state capital Sittwe.

Frontline sources said AA artillery hit another navy vessel off the island on Sunday, the third to be damaged in recent days. “The boat was struck and caught fire,” a local source close to the AA confirmed. Intense clashes are raging both on and around Nga Pyi Island as regime forces continue efforts to secure a beachhead despite mounting casualties.

Sources said commanders are driving conscripts forward in near‑suicidal assaults, but few have managed to reach land.

Since Oct. 7, the military has deployed more than a dozen gunboats and landing craft backed by airstrikes and artillery from encircled Sittwe, in an effort to seize the island. The move aims to break the AA’s blockade of the Kaladan River corridor and shield the navy’s Shwe Mingan base in Sittwe, which sits on a peninsula surrounded by water on three sides.

Nga Pyi Island is a key AA stronghold, blocking regime access upriver to AA-controlled Pauktaw and Ponnagyun townships.

“Junta soldiers keep coming despite heavy casualties, but few have made it to shore,” said a source close to the AA.

Meanwhile, AA columns have seized several regime outposts elsewhere in Sittwe and are pressing toward Shwe Mingan naval base and the Sittwe Regional Operations Command.

The assault on Nga Pyi was launched as advancing AA troops threatened to encircle the military’s Sittwe stronghold. Fighting has also intensified just down the coast in Kyaukphyu Township, where AA forces are attacking outposts near Taung Maw Oo naval base.

The AA controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships along with Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State, with the regime maintaining a foothold in Sittwe, Kyaukphyu, and the sparsely populated Manaung island.

A regime counteroffensive launched from neighboring Magwe, Bago, and Ayeyarwady regions is bogged down amid fierce resistance and heavy losses.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Defense Minister Claims Airstrikes Are Aimed at Achieving Peace
World.content:
Despite widespread domestic and international condemnation of the military junta’s airstrikes on civilian targets, newly appointed regime Defense Minister Lieutenant General Yar Pyae said the bombing operations were intended to achieve peace.

“Mainly, they [questions raised in the media] are based on human rights and humanitarian concerns regarding the bombings. From our perspective, the current military operations are actually steps taken to obtain peace,” Lt-Gen Yar Pyae, who also serves as chairman of the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), said during his closing address to a workshop marking the 11th Anniversary of the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) on October 16.

The military regime routinely bombs civilian targets in resistance-held territories in an effort to undermine anti-regime groups’ administration and to coerce them into joining its purported peace talks. The tactic worked well in northern Shan State and Mandalay Region, where it managed to force the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and its ally, the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), to stop fighting, agree to China-brokered ceasefires and hand over some seized towns.

The regime continues to use the tactic in other regions and states including Rakhine State, which is almost entirely controlled by the Arakan Army (AA), an ally of MNDAA and TNLA.

On September 28, the regime conducted an airstrike targeting the busy Indian Market in the AA-controlled town of Kyauktaw, killing at least 50 people. The attack drew fierce condemnation from the UN, the UK, ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights and various human rights organizations.

Since the 2021 military coup, the Myanmar military has consistently launched airstrikes across revolutionary strongholds, including the Anyar region (also known as the Dry Zone) and ethnic minority regions—targeting not only military sites, but also schools, hospitals, religious buildings and civilian homes.

Even as it makes peace overtures, the regime continues to engage in heavy fighting with the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) in Bhamo, and clashes are ongoing with the AA in Rakhine State. Airstrikes also continue to target civilians in the Anyar region, where People’s Defense Forces (PDFs) maintain a strong presence.

Amid the ongoing air raids on resistance-held areas, junta leader Min Aung Hlaing made what he called an unconditional peace invitation during the 11th NCA anniversary event in Naypyitaw on October 15. The regime nonetheless continues to pressure the PDFs—the main armed resistance groups across the country—to lay down their arms and surrender.

According to statements made during a press conference at the close of the NCA anniversary workshop, invitations to peace talks were extended to the KIA, but not to the AA.

Furthermore, Min Aung Hlaing stated on October 15 that if ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) wish to engage in politics, they must disarm and form political parties; if they wish to conduct business, they must do so legally; and if they wish to serve in defense, they must join the Border Guard Forces (BGF).

In 2009, the military heavily pressured EAOs to transform into Border Guard Forces. With few exceptions, however, the initiative largely failed.

The KIA, which is currently engaged in intense fighting with the military, was one of the major ethnic armed groups that refused to transform into a BGF at that time. During the Spring Revolution that erupted in response to the coup, the KIA earned the Myanmar military’s ire by providing military training, weapons and combat support to anti-junta PDF forces.

Similarly, following Operation 1027, the AA seized control of most towns in Rakhine State, including a regional military command center. Since then, the regime has launched several offensives to retake lost territory in the state.

While urging PDFs to surrender and asking EAOs to join the BGF, Min Aung Hlaing also told ethnic representatives attending the NCA ceremony that he would cooperate with those willing to work together on peace, while actively finding methods to handle those who refuse to cooperate.

World.title: Solar Mandate Crushes Myanmar Builders as Regime Chief’s Son Profits
World.content:
Contractors warn that a new regime mandate requiring installation of solar power systems in all high-rises and commercial buildings will send construction costs soaring in Myanmar. The directive further squeezes construction companies already pinched by a shortage of materials, import restrictions, and severe currency volatility.

The Yangon City Development Committee’s Engineering Department issued the order on October 1 as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

From November 1, all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar panels sufficient to power elevators and emergency lighting. For commercial buildings, solar systems must be integrated with power supplied by the Yangon Electricity Supply Corporation (YESC).

The order applies to existing projects, buildings under construction, and those awaiting Building Completion Certificates required for habitation.

“We have been handed the order at a time when prices of solar panels and related equipment are rising daily,” complained a Mandalay‑based builder. “Steel and cement prices are already soaring, so this adds yet another burden.”

Meanwhile, industry insiders warn of a scarcity of skilled technicians capable of installing large solar systems, creating technical and financial hurdles. “Household systems won’t power elevators, which require commercial‑grade solar systems,” the manager of a solar dealership explained. “Installation takes at least two months and costs around 100 million kyat.”

Solar imports to feed surging demand created by the new mandate are controlled by Aung Pyae Sone, son of regime chief Min Aung Hlaing.

Aung Pyae Sone swiftly cornered the lucrative market after his father’s regime waived tax on solar imports in April 2023 under the pretext of boosting the energy grid. His Venus Essential company also holds licenses to supply solar equipment for projects in Naypyitaw and planned 40-megawatt solar power plants in Taungdwingyi, Salin, Pakokku, Pauk, Chauk and Kyunchaung.

The solar mandate comes as regime energy rationing intensifies with more frequent rolling blackouts this year.

“They cut electricity during extreme heat, then order solar systems to be installed,” said a former political prisoner from Mandalay. “But only one company — belonging to the coup leader son — is allowed to import and sell the equipment nationwide. This is not aimed at solving the power crisis, but exploiting authority for personal profit.”

On October 5, the Electricity and Energy Ministry introduced rolling four-hour blackouts under the pretext of surging demand during the El Niño heatwave. Since then, households in Yangon, Mandalay and Naypyitaw have faced daily outages.

The power crisis has driven prices of solar panels and related equipment to record highs. In early August, a 500‑watt panel cost around 650,000 kyat. By mid‑October, the price had surged past one million kyat, putting solar systems beyond the reach of ordinary families.

World.title: An ‘All-for-Arakan’ Approach Is Needed to Address the Rohingya Refugee Crisis
World.content:
As resistance against long-term Rohingya presence in host countries grows, the refugees’ fate is back in the headlines. Malaysia is a recent example. Its government has yielded to growing hate speech against Myanmar refugees, and Rohingya in particular. In September, Malaysia and Myanmar negotiated a controversial repatriation agreement for 5,000 refugees that is not supported by the UN or its refugee agency. Resentment in India and Indonesia has also grown.

Following large-scale Rohingya returns from Bangladesh to Myanmar in the 1970s and 1990s, repatriation efforts started again in 2017, after the enforced flight of 750,000 Rohingya from Myanmar to Bangladesh. Initially, they were based on a Chinese offer to mediate between the two countries. Even though these and later efforts failed, Bangladesh’s pursuit of repatriation continues, and Malaysia has now joined in.

There are many reasons why the repatriation initiatives of the past 10 years have not been successful. A largely unmentioned one is that many initiators wrongly assume that traditional diplomatic relations between states can lead to meaningful dialogue and conflict resolution. This state-centric approach overlooks the key question at the heart of Myanmar’s decades-old volatility: how power and political authority are shared between Myanmar’s center and its highly diverse regions and ethnic nationalities. Moreover, since the country’s 2021 military coup, the regime in Naypyitaw has lost control over much of the country. In Arakan (Rakhine State), the birthplace of most Rohingya refugees—and where some 500,000 of them still live—the current regime has control over only three of the state’s 17 townships.

Today’s Myanmar is in transition. It is a country with multiple centers of authority. In some, local territorial control has been in place for decades; in others, it has been established since the military coup of 2021. These ethnic and regional authorities are not against a federal state as such. They are against the current federal union that is based on a constitution that concentrates significant power at the center, and particularly with the armed forces.

Right now, the key question is whether a new form of federalism can emerge, one that leaves a highly centralized system behind and, instead, focuses on existing and newly emerging centers of political authority. A long road lies ahead but in many parts of the country progress is clearly visible.

Arakan is a prime example. As the territorial dominance of the United League of Arakan/Arakan Army (ULA/AA) grows, particularly since 2023, it has been transforming into a central administrative authority with local administrative, security and judicial mechanisms. The Institute for Strategy and Policy in Chiang Mai recently reviewed the progress that has been made and concluded that “despite persistent challenges, a solid institutional framework is emerging”. But it also cautions that following rapid territorial expansion, a performance gap has emerged between public expectations and the administration’s delivery capacity.

A key reason for the delivery gap is that right now Arakan is a war zone with almost daily ground clashes between the AA and Myanmar’s armed forces, as well as attacks by Bangladesh-based Rohingya militias. Moreover, Arakan is now a prime target for attacks by Myanmar’s air force, which deliberately targets civilian structures with bombs of up to 500 pounds. The devastation on the ground is massive, with hundreds of civilians killed and maimed, while schools, markets, clinics and prayer houses have been destroyed. Physical infrastructure is also heavily affected, including by recent massive floods, leading to large-scale disruption of livelihoods and food security.

According to a recent report by the UN Development Programme, 68.4 percent of Arakan’s population (all ethnicities) experience multi-dimensional poverty, while a further 20 percent is at risk of falling into that category. Arakan’s current population is thought to stand at just over 2.4 million, while a Doctors Without Borders report in 2024 estimated that only 636,000 Rohingya remained in Arakan. Today that number will have fallen significantly, as approximately 150,000 more Rohingya have fled to Bangladesh since then.

To be clear, Rohingya repatriation from Bangladesh and other countries will take time. Refugees cannot return if armed conflict continues and before the underlying reasons for their flight have been addressed. To achieve this, a central role for both ULA/AA and the people of Arakan, including the Rohingya, is critical. But at the same time, various factions on the Rohingya side stand in the way of a united approach, particularly those supporting armed militias. Moreover, some of them have been used as a divide-and-rule tool by Myanmar’s military-backed regime.

Arakan’s problems are manifold and a broader vision of identity is critically important, one that acknowledges inclusion and equality as basic building blocks for a stable, secure and prosperous Arakan.

This understanding led the Rakhine Advisory Commission of 2016-17, chaired by former UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan, to focus on solutions to address the legitimate grievances and suffering of all Arakan’s diverse people. Its report and recommendations to Myanmar’s leaders remain highly relevant, based as they are on the central objective of developing conditions in Arakan that will lead to a peaceful, fair, harmonious and prosperous future for all communities. In 2018, the commission published a lessons-learned report focusing on how it operated in Myanmar’s highly politicized and complex context.

Obviously, much has changed since the report was released but it remains relevant, even after the National League for Democracy’s violent removal in 2021. It analyzes Arakan’s situation around three major crises: a security crisis, an economic and development crisis, and a human rights crisis. These crises persist and could form the basis for an all-of-Arakan approach.

Since 2017, the Annan report has been re-acknowledged annually by an overwhelming majority of the UN General Assembly and the UN Human Rights Council. Yet, no efforts have been made to establish how it might serve Arakan’s people under their current circumstances, and particularly since 2024, when most of Arakan came under the control of the ULA/AA.

Any process leading to a comprehensive plan for Arakan will be complex, not least because of the wide range of actors, functioning at diverse levels. In “The Dilemma of Hard Choices”, published in August, the Center for Arakan studies identifies the heterogeneity of agents as a key issue and adds that it is compounded by the problem of ownership, where most states, armed groups, civil society and international bodies each deflect overall responsibility while pursuing their own narrow strategic interests.

Precisely these diverging interests would make the Annan report a helpful starting point for dialogue. For good reasons, the commission’s recommendations are not highly prescriptive. Its general understanding was that, while basic principles of governance and human rights should guide the implementation process, details could be developed as part of dialogue processes. The report contains 88 recommendations on a comprehensive set of issues, ranging from economic and social development to freedom of movement, citizenship, health, access to justice, intercommunal cohesion, humanitarian access and internally displaced persons.

Obviously, dialogue cannot be based on the Annan report alone, but it could be a starting point. Additional questions must be raised to take account of developments since 2017. The first is the clarification of victimhood. Who are the victims of decades of oppression, persecution and violent conflict? A second is the “fog of war” that distorts a clear view of what is happening on the ground.

Obviously, it is not necessary to argue that the Rohingya are victims; that is accepted around the world. But what about the other communities in Arakan—the Rakhine, the Maramagyi, the Mro, the Chin, the Hindus and others?

They too are victims, yet their plight has been getting far less attention. They too have had their villages bombed and burned, their clinics, schools and livelihoods destroyed, while thousands are displaced in areas where relief goods cannot reach them. But their plight is not as widely documented. Acknowledgment that all Arakan’s people are victims could be a first step in reconciliation. And clearly, there are different degrees of victimhood and these too must be acknowledged.

The second point concerns the current “fog of war” and the urgent need to establish independent investigations. As in other places around the world, violent conflict, displacement and hunger obscure a clear view of developments on the ground. In such situations, deliberate disinformation thrives. We should not pretend that we have a clear view of what is happening in Arakan and in the refugee camps in Bangladesh. Lack of independent access and blocked internet facilities compound the problems.

Independent investigations will be needed to establish what has happened in Arakan and Bangladesh since 2017. While a significant body of research about the Rohingya exists, research on Arakan’s other communities remains scant. Moreover, research should also focus on disturbing allegations about what has been happening in Bangladesh. How did Rohingya militias manage to get a firm grip on the population in the refugee camps? Where did funding for their arms and operations come from? And how can large numbers of refugees and militia fighters continue to cross the Bangladesh-Myanmar border seemingly unnoticed?

Since 2018, the Independent Investigating Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) has been collecting and preserving evidence to facilitate criminal prosecutions of those most responsible for atrocity crimes. But it only shares its findings with investigative, prosecutorial and judicial authorities in national and international courts. As a result, a vast body of information remains inaccessible to the public. Moreover, IIMM’s mandate does not cover other truth-seeking needs, such as documenting and public acknowledgment of crimes through truth and reconciliation bodies and publicly accessible archives. These limitations underline the importance of establishing additional mechanisms to ensure that accountability is pursued as an integral part of transitional justice and reconciliation. This should be part of a comprehensive approach: an all-for-Arakan approach.

Using the Annan report as a credible starting point for dialogue could be a first step towards creating a better understanding of the needs of all Arakan’s people. Moreover, its repeated recognition by the UN General Assembly might help to rally much needed support for such an exercise at a time when resources are scarce.

Laetitia van den Assum is a former Dutch diplomat. She was also a member of the Rakhine Advisory Commission (2016-2017), chaired by Kofi Annan, former UN Secretary-General.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan’s Tourism Sector Grows 45% as Industry Revenue Rises
World.content:
