ASTANA — The number of people using tourism services in the Kyrgyz Republic reached 5.3 million in 2025, a 45.2% increase from the previous year, as the sector recorded growth in revenue, business activity and investment, according to an analysis by Finprom published Oct. 19.

The figure includes visitors who used organized tourism services, such as hotels, travel agencies and health resorts, as well as an estimate of visitors to private guesthouses and households. The latter accounted for 32.1% of the total, according to data from the National Statistical Committee of the Kyrgyz Republic cited by Finprom.

The organized tourism sector recorded approximately 3.7 million visitors in 2025. Of these, 2.9 million were Kyrgyz citizens and 770,000 were foreign visitors. The number of foreign visitors using organized tourism services increased by 30.5%, or approximately 180,000, compared with 2024.

These figures cover users of organized tourism services and should not be confused with the total number of foreign nationals entering Kyrgyzstan, which also includes people traveling for purposes other than tourism.

Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Russia were the leading source markets for inbound tourism, according to the report.

Tourism’s economic contribution increases

Tourism’s contribution to the country’s gross domestic product rose from 3.2% in 2021 to 3.8% in 2025. The government aims to increase the sector’s share of GDP to 7% by 2030.

Gross output in the tourism sector reached 136.8 billion Kyrgyz soms (US$1.56 billion) in 2025, up 26.8% from the previous year. The figure was 52.8 billion soms (US$603.8 million) in 2021.

Exports of tourism services approached $1.1 billion in 2025, an 8.1% annual increase. Retail trade turnover associated with tourism rose 41.6% to 74.6 billion soms (US$853.1 million). The total value of tourism services reached approximately 21 billion soms (US$240.1 million), around a quarter more than in 2024.

Accommodation providers, including hotels, hostels and other lodging facilities, accounted for 11.1 billion soms (US$127 million) of tourism services. Travel agencies generated 7.6 billion soms (US$86.9 million), while sanatoriums and other health resort organizations accounted for 2.4 billion soms (US$27.4 million).

Tourism service prices increased by 7.6% in 2025. The rise in the sector’s financial indicators therefore coincided with both expanding activity and higher prices.

Investment and tourism businesses expand

Foreign investment in the construction of tourism facilities in the Kyrgyz Republic reached $87.8 million in 2025, the highest level in recent years, according to Finprom. Investors from the Netherlands accounted for $63.9 million of the total.

The report identifies several major tourism development projects, including the Ramada by Wyndham Issyk-Kul sports and hotel complex, the Ala-Too Resort ski resort in the Ak-Suu district of the Issyk-Kul Region, the Mövenpick Ak Keme Issyk-Kul Resort and the Azimut park hotel in the Issyk-Kul Region.

The number of business entities operating in the tourism sector increased from 14,600 in 2021 to 20,700 in 2025.

The Issyk-Kul Region remains a key area for tourism development, including beach and winter sports tourism. The Osh and Chuy regions also contribute to the country’s tourism offering.

Regional air connectivity provides additional travel options. In summer 2025, Asman Airlines and FlyArystan introduced direct flights between Issyk-Kul and Almaty, with four weekly flights planned between the destinations during the summer season.

As the sector expands, its contribution to the economy will depend not only on visitor numbers but also on the development of tourism infrastructure and the quality of services available across the country.

World.title: Tokayev to Deliver Annual State-of-the-Nation Address on Oct. 28
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev plans to deliver his annual state-of-the-nation address on Oct. 28 in the first half of the day.

Tokayev announced the plans in a post on his X account on Oct. 20, saying he was working on the text of the address.

“I plan to deliver my annual state-of-the-nation address on Oct. 28 in the first half of the day. I am working on the text of this important document,” Tokayev wrote.

World.title: Central Asia is Shaping Terms of Cooperation With China, Experts Say
World.content:
ALMATY – Central Asian countries are increasingly shaping how China invests, builds infrastructure and develops technological partnerships in the region, challenging the perception that Beijing follows a single model of global engagement, experts said at an Oct. 20 discussion in Almaty.

Organized by the Almaty-based CAPS Unlock think tank and the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, the discussion examined how local governments, institutions and businesses influence China’s activities across different regions. Experts stressed that Central Asian states are not merely responding to China’s growing presence but are using their own development priorities and bargaining power to influence the terms of cooperation.

At the same time, intensifying competition between the United States and China could make it more difficult for countries in the region to maintain diversified international partnerships, even as global uncertainty creates new opportunities for them to advance their interests.

From a single China model to local adaptation

Carnegie launched the China Local/Global initiative nearly six years ago to study Chinese engagement across seven regions: Central Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Latin America, Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, and the Pacific.

Evan A. Feigenbaum, vice president for studies at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said the initiative was designed to examine how Chinese engagement differs according to local political, economic and institutional conditions.

“While that may be part of the story, it is very clearly not the whole story,” Feigenbaum said of the assumption that China imposes a uniform model on countries around the world. In many cases, he noted, Chinese actors adapt to local practices and partner with domestic stakeholders.

For Central Asian countries, the question is not only how to attract Chinese investment, but also how to ensure that cooperation supports domestic priorities, including economic growth, employment, technological development and the creation of higher-value industries.

CAPS Unlock Executive Director Aida Aidarkulova said the partnership was intended to bring regional expertise into international debates rather than simply introduce foreign perspectives to Central Asia.

“We believe such exchanges enrich everyone involved,” she said, describing the think tank’s broader goal as generating knowledge about Central Asia from within the region and contributing to a regional research agenda.

Investment is shifting beyond raw materials

Djoomart Otorbaev, former prime minister of the Kyrgyz Republic, emphasized that China’s economic engagement in Central Asia has evolved over the past three decades, with a growing emphasis on foreign direct investment, industrial localization and more structured approaches to borrowing.

“Engagement between China and Central Asia is not merely borrowing now, but a structural shift towards FDI, foreign direct investment, industrial localization, and far more disciplined sovereign borrowing,” Otorbaev said.

According to the figures cited by Otorbaev, accumulated Chinese foreign direct investment in Central Asia reached $56 billion by mid-2025, nearly doubling over the previous decade.

While raw materials accounted for approximately 68% of Chinese investment in the region a decade ago, that share has since declined to 54%. Manufacturing now represents 22%, while energy, including renewables, accounts for 12%.

“Today manufacturing accounts for 22% of Chinese FDIs in Central Asia. In energy, including renewables, 12%. This is industrial embedding to my classification,” he said.

Kazakhstan remains the largest single recipient of Chinese investment. Uzbekistan has emerged as an increasingly significant competitor for capital, Otorbaev said. He pointed to the expansion of Chinese investment in Uzbekistan as a reason for Kazakhstan to strengthen its own investment environment.

“Yes, we are competing very, very hard with each other to be better,” he said. “So now I think, with all my excuses, it is a wake-up call for Kazakhstan.”

“What we want from China is cooperation in new 21st century economies. China’s most disciplined expansion is happening in Central Asia,” he added.

U.S.-China rivalry puts pressure on regional choices

Feigenbaum cautioned, however, that the growing role of local governments could be challenged by intensifying strategic competition between Washington and Beijing.

“The way I would describe the change is the securitization of everything, by which I mean that every issue, including economic flows, goods, capital, people, technology, data, are being refracted by both Washington and Beijing through the prism of national security in their own competition,” he said.

“If you’re sitting in this region, as in most regions of the world, I often use a mathematical metaphor. The mathematical operations that matter are addition and multiplication, not subtraction and division,” he added.

He warned that the growing rivalry could make it harder for regional governments to maintain that flexibility.

Temur Umarov of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center similarly urged analysts to pay closer attention to political and economic changes originating within Central Asia.

“I do believe that we pay too much attention to what is happening outside of Central Asia, not so much to what is actually happening here,” Umarov said. “And I think that this is one of the biggest problems that we have as people who write, observe, and analyze events in Central Asia, because it is not just unfair, it is wrong.”

He said international developments, including the geopolitical shocks and U.S.-China tensions, influence the region, but should not overshadow the agency of Central Asian governments themselves.

“The initiative in that activity is not coming from Washington,” Umarov said, stressing that regional political leaders have used international uncertainty to attract attention and expand their diplomatic and economic options.

He added that a new generation of actors is emerging across Central Asia’s political institutions, businesses and civil society.

“It is actually happening on all of the layers of government or any other institution, body, company, business, NGOs. Everywhere you see the new generation appearing,” Umarov said, highlighting that the current international environment, despite its instability, creates opportunities for countries located between major powers to strengthen their own positions.

The discussion also featured how regional experience can inform policymakers beyond Central Asia, reinforcing the organizers’ argument that understanding China’s global role requires attention to local conditions rather than assumptions about a single, universal model.

World.title: Kazakhstan Begins $1.8 Billion Copper Smelter Project in Abai Region
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has launched construction of a $1.8 billion copper smelter in Aktogai, the Abai Region, with an annual production capacity of 300,000 tons of cathode copper, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev announced on Oct. 20.

Speaking at the launch ceremony via video link, Tokayev described the project as a major industrial initiative expected to strengthen Kazakhstan’s metallurgical sector, increase domestic processing and create more than 1,000 jobs.

The plant is being developed by KAZ Minerals Group, with Chinese company NFC serving as its engineering partner. The first copper cathode is scheduled to be produced in 2030.

“The capacity of the new enterprise will reach 300,000 tons of cathode copper per year. This will fully meet the needs of the domestic market. After the plant begins operations, Kazakhstan will enter the world’s top 10 producers of high-quality refined copper,” Tokayev said.

The facility will also produce metallic gold, silver and sulfuric acid. It is designed to cover the full production cycle, from ore extraction and processing to finished metal production, using its own copper concentrate as a raw material.

Tokayev said the project reflects Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to develop its mining and metallurgical industry and make more effective use of the country’s natural resources.

“Natural resources located beneath the ground belong to the people,” he said, adding that industrial projects should primarily serve the interests of Kazakhstan and its citizens.

Kazakhstan has more than 9,500 mineral deposits, extracts nearly 160 million tons of ore annually and produces around 3.5 million tons of copper concentrate, according to the figures cited by Tokayev. He also highlighted growth in the country’s manufacturing sector, whose output reached $60 billion last year. Over the past three years, 540 industrial projects have been implemented across Kazakhstan, creating approximately 50,000 permanent jobs, he said.

The new smelter is expected to increase the value added within Kazakhstan by processing domestically produced copper concentrate into refined metal rather than relying solely on the extraction and sale of raw materials.

Focus on technology and workplace safety

Tokayev called on the project’s shareholders and contractors to prioritize workplace safety, digitalization and the use of artificial intelligence in industrial operations.

“Applying advanced solutions contributes to higher productivity, improved workplace safety and effective prevention of industrial injuries,” he said.

He also stressed the importance of maintaining construction quality and meeting established deadlines, while thanking Kazakh specialists and Chinese partners involved in the project. Tokayev called on the government and local authorities to maintain close communication with workers and address their legitimate social needs.

The Aktogai copper smelter is expected to strengthen Kazakhstan’s domestic metallurgical capacity and support the country’s ambitions to expand industrial production and move toward higher-value processing.

World.title: Kazakhstan Eyes Greater ICAO Role Amid Global Aviation Challenges
World.content:
ASTANA — International Civil Aviation Organization Security Week 2026 kicked off in Astana on Oct. 20, bringing Kazakhstan’s bid for a seat on the ICAO Council, growing cybersecurity threats, aviation risks in conflict zones and prospects for direct flights between Kazakhstan and the United States into focus.

The three-day event has brought together more than 1,000 participants from 62 countries, including government officials, aviation regulators, airline executives and security experts.

“In 2027, ICAO will convene the third high-level conference on aviation security. The ideas that emerged from Astana will reach the global conversation as we prepare for it,” ICAO Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar said during the opening ceremony.

Beyond the conference’s contribution to global aviation security discussions, Salazar also addressed Kazakhstan’s bid to join the ICAO Council during a press briefing. The candidacy comes ahead of an extraordinary ICAO Assembly in Montreal on Nov. 19-20, when four additional members will be elected to the organization’s governing body, expanding it from 36 to 40 seats.

“The success of ICAO is always informed from the voices that every region of the world has in the ICAO Council. And in that regard, the aspiration of the candidature of Kazakhstan is very welcome and is very well rooted in the representation of the voices of the region,” he said.

Kazakhstan has been an ICAO member since 1992 and became the first Central Asian country to establish a permanent mission to the organization in 2024. According to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport, the country has achieved a 95.7% effective implementation score under ICAO’s aviation security audit framework, placing it among the world’s top 20 countries by this measure.

Salazar said Kazakhstan was among the countries with the highest levels of compliance with international aviation security standards, supporting its potential as a regional hub for passenger and cargo transportation. He identified workforce development as a key priority for maintaining those standards, noting that Kazakhstan already has regulations and technology in place but needs to continue investing in training and attracting qualified personnel.

From cyberattacks to conflict zones: aviation’s changing threats

Opening the event, Salazar called for a fundamental shift in global aviation security, warning that emerging threats are evolving faster than traditional regulations can respond.

“Threat actors are adaptive. They learn, they innovate, and they exploit new technologies faster than regulation has traditionally moved. (…) Digitalization connects every part of our operations, and with it every vulnerability. Supply chains grow more complex every day. Airspace that was routine yesterday can become dangerous overnight,” he said.

Salazar emphasized that aviation authorities must increasingly anticipate threats rather than respond only after incidents occur, relying on intelligence-led risk assessments, faster information sharing and closer coordination between governments and the industry.

“So the ambition for this week and for the year ahead of us is to move from reacting to anticipating,” he said.

He also warned that even attempted attacks can trigger far-reaching economic consequences, forcing flight diversions, causing delays and disrupting travel and business operations.

“That means foresight. It means risk-based decisions informed by intelligence, where we understand not only the threat but also the vulnerabilities and consequences that together determine the risk. And it means working together earlier and sharing information faster between states, within states, and with the industry,” said Salazar.

The conference agenda includes discussions on cybersecurity across airports, airlines and air navigation systems, artificial intelligence in security screening, risks to flights operating over or near conflict zones, and the protection of international cargo and mail supply chains.

Participants will also examine the effectiveness of aviation security audits, workforce development and the challenges of sustaining security modernization with limited resources.

Direct U.S. flights, aviation expansion

Speaking to reporters, Kazakh Vice Minister of Transport Talgat Lastayev said direct flights between Kazakhstan and the U.S. could begin in 2027, subject to regulatory approval and operational preparations.

“A few weeks ago, Kazakhstan was visited by a team of auditors from the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration [FAA]. There were approximately seven or eight inspectors who worked here for a week, and at the final briefing, they gave a fairly positive assessment of our civil aviation system and its compliance with international standards,” he said.

The FAA conducted its International Aviation Safety Assessment in Kazakhstan on Sept. 21-25, examining the country’s aviation safety oversight system and compliance with applicable ICAO standards. Lastayev said the official report is expected in November, with Kazakhstan aiming to secure authorization for flights to the U.S. by the end of 2026.

“We expect to receive a Dreamliner in December, a long-haul aircraft capable of operating such flights. Before it can enter service, flight crews and technical personnel need to accumulate a certain number of operating hours. I think that over the course of next year, provided all these conditions are met, we expect to launch a direct flight,” he said.

According to Lastayev, New York is being considered as the destination in the U.S, while Astana is the priority departure point in Kazakhstan. When asked whether the route would be commercially viable, he expressed confidence in its long-term profitability, citing growing economic and investment ties between the two countries. Ticket prices have yet to be determined.

World.title: Japan Eyes Middle Corridor to Expand Trade With Central Asia and Caucasus
World.content:
ASTANA – Japan is exploring opportunities to strengthen transport and trade links with Central Asia and the Caucasus through Kazakhstan’s Middle Corridor, with planned direct flights between Tokyo and Almaty and a proposed 719 million yen (US$4.7 million) project to modernize customs inspections at the Port of Aktau, reported the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ press service.

The initiatives were discussed at a conference in Tokyo on Oct. 19, attended by nearly 100 representatives of Japanese government agencies, the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the ROTOBO association and logistics companies.

The event focused on attracting Japanese investment into the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor, and improving transport connectivity between Japan, Central Asia and the Caucasus.

Japan’s State Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Kei Takagi highlighted the route’s strategic importance for diversifying international transport and logistics networks. He said the Middle Corridor offers additional opportunities to strengthen Japan’s trade and economic ties with countries across the two regions.

Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Japan Yerlan Baudarbek-Kozhatayev and Azerbaijan’s Ambassador Farid Talibov presented their countries’ transport development strategies and discussed ways to improve logistics efficiency and expand international transport cooperation.

Japan plans to support customs modernization in Aktau

Japanese companies have conducted trial shipments along the Middle Corridor to assess delivery times, transportation costs, customs procedures and the quality of logistics services. The findings provided practical insight into the route’s performance and areas where efficiency could be improved.

One initiative focuses on customs infrastructure at the Port of Aktau, a key link in Kazakhstan’s transport network across the Caspian Sea. Japan plans to support the installation of a stationary, large-scale X-ray scanning system. The equipment is expected to reduce cargo inspection times by approximately threefold, helping improve customs processing and the efficiency of freight movement through the port.

The project forms part of broader efforts to make the Middle Corridor a more competitive option for international cargo flows as countries seek to diversify transport routes.

Direct flights to connect Almaty and Tokyo

The conference also addressed the planned launch of regular direct flights between Almaty and Tokyo’s Narita International Airport by Air Astana. The first flight from Almaty is scheduled for Nov. 30, with the return flight from Narita planned for Dec. 1. The airline intends to operate the route twice a week using Airbus A321LR aircraft.

The flight is expected to take seven hours and 30 minutes. The service will establish Kazakhstan’s first regular direct air connection with the Japanese capital, creating another link for business, tourism and broader bilateral exchanges.

Air Astana’s Senior Regional Manager for South Korea and Japan, Adel Dauletbek, presented the prospects for strengthening air connectivity during the conference.

Digital infrastructure adds another dimension

Participants also discussed the development of digital infrastructure along the Middle Corridor.

Baudarbek-Kozhatayev highlighted the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic communication line, which was officially commissioned in Baku on Oct. 15 with the participation of Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev.

The project is intended to expand international data exchange and strengthen the resilience of digital communications between countries in the region. Together, the transport, customs and digital infrastructure initiatives reflect efforts to strengthen Kazakhstan’s role as a transit link between Asia and Europe while expanding economic cooperation with Japan.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Rybakina Extends Lead at Top of WTA Rankings
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina continues to lead the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) singles rankings, holding a lead of more than 1,600 points over her closest rival, Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus, while Kazakhstan’s Yulia Putintseva has climbed 13 places to 66th, according to the latest rankings.

Rybakina has 9,196 points, ahead of Sabalenka with 7,550. Russia’s Mirra Andreeva ranks third with 6,306 points. Americans Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff round out the top five with 6,235 and 5,974 points, respectively.

Putintseva now holds 969 points after improving her position by 13 places. At the recent WTA 1000 tournament in Wuhan, China, she advanced through the first round before losing to Russia’s Diana Shnaider in the second round.

Several other Kazakh players feature in the WTA singles rankings. Sonya Zhiyenbayeva is ranked 381st, followed by Zhibek Kulambayeva at 479th. Aruzhan Sagandykova holds 678th place, while Asylzhan Arystanbekova ranks 692nd and Ekaterina Dmitrichenko is 884th.

Kazakhstan also has a representative in the top 10 of the WTA doubles rankings. Anna Danilina has retained seventh place with 6,135 points. The doubles ranking is led by Czech player Katerina Siniakova with 11,260 points. American Taylor Townsend ranks second with 9,415 points, followed by Brazil’s Luisa Stefani with 9,220.

World.title: CICA’s Moment to Turn Confidence Building into Secure Connectivity
World.content:
The seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku on Oct.15 adopted the Baku Declaration, admitted Laos as the 29th member, extended Azerbaijan’s chairmanship through 2028 and appointed a new Secretary General. The CICA Charter, which would complete the forum’s transformation into a full international organization, was not yet adopted, and leaders called for continued work on it. The next two years are therefore the moment of graduation. How CICA defines its purpose in the charter will decide whether it becomes a working instrument or remains a dialogue club. We argue that the organization should make one link explicit, the link between conflict prevention and secure, efficient connectivity. The disruption of Asia’s transit corridors over the past year shows why this link cannot wait, and it is squarely in Kazakhstan’s interest.

A forum that kept its distance from hard security

Kazakhstan proposed CICA in 1992 because Asia had no common security structure, and it still has none. ASEAN, the SCO, the Arab League and the Gulf Cooperation Council each cover a subregion, while the continent’s most dangerous disputes run between states belonging to different groupings. CICA is the only format where India and Pakistan, Israel and Palestine, China and its maritime neighbours all sit together.

That breadth came at a price. Decisions are taken by consensus, and the forum has generally steered clear of conflict resolution. The notable exception came at the first summit in Almaty in June 2002, at the height of the India-Pakistan standoff after the attack on India’s parliament. Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Pervez Musharraf both attended, and while they did not meet directly, Vladimir Putin relayed messages between them on the margins. In 2004 members adopted a Catalogue of Confidence Building Measures that included military notifications and consultations on border incidents. In 2007, however, they agreed to begin with economic, environmental and human measures and to postpone the military-political ones.

Although military-political confidence-building measures have since been developed and implemented, their practical role in preventing disruptions to regional connectivity remains limited. Given the diversity of the membership, the caution is understandable. It has also left CICA without a role in the crises that now matter most to Asian trade.

A year of broken corridors

The past 12 months have shown how quickly conflict closes trade routes. The war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb.28, 2026 disrupted the International North-South Transport Corridor and the southern branch of the East-West route through Iran, cutting Central Asia’s shortest access to open water. Southern routes became unusable or uninsurable for extended periods, and freight was rerouted at higher cost.

Further east, Pakistan closed its five main trade crossings with Afghanistan after clashes in 2025, and a year later they remain shut. Trade between the two countries had been estimated at about $2.35 billion a year. The closure also halted transit of goods from China, Malaysia and Vietnam. Mediation by Qatar and Turkiye produced a ceasefire in October 2025, but fighting resumed and escalated to Pakistani air strikes on Kabul in February 2026. In May 2025 India and Pakistan had already exchanged strikes for four days.

All of these conflicts involve CICA members, and each struck at routes that Central Asia had been counting on. For landlocked economies, connectivity is a security question. A corridor is only as reliable as the most fragile border it crosses.

The Middle Corridor as the test case

The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or Middle Corridor, which runs from China and Kazakhstan across the Caspian to Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkiye, shows both the promise and the vulnerability. Volumes through Kazakhstan rose from 0.8 million tonnes to 4.5 million tonnes a year, and total corridor traffic reached 4.5 million tonnes in 2024, up 62%. The World Bank estimates that volumes could reach around 11 million tonnes by 2030. The disruption of routes through Iran has shifted more of the burden onto it.

The corridor’s growth has been underwritten by conflict management. The initialling of the Azerbaijan-Armenia peace agreement in Washington in August 2025 opened the prospect of new links across the South Caucasus, and the Kyrgyz-Tajik border treaty of March 2025 reopened crossings in the Fergana Valley. Yet the war in Iran underscored how quickly instability could spill into the South Caucasus segment. Baku, which hosted the summit and has coordinated CICA’s transport track since 2007, sits at the centre of this equation.

At the summit Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed two initiatives that point in the right direction. One is a CICA Transport Connectivity Strategy covering major routes, including the Middle Corridor. The other is a Mechanism for Preventive Diplomacy, which he justified with the line that peace is best built before crises emerge. The value lies in treating these 2 proposals as one agenda.

What CICA can do

First, CICA can make corridor security part of its confidence building work. The measures adopted in 2004 already provide for notification of military activity and consultations on dangerous incidents near borders. Applied to transit routes and border crossings, they would give governments and logistics operators earlier warning and a channel to contain incidents before they close a route.

Second, the organization can articulate a norm that trade crossings and third-country transit stay open during bilateral disputes. No member would surrender its position in a dispute, yet all would gain predictability. The Afghanistan-Pakistan border is the obvious first case. Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan, which trade with both sides and have their own plans for routes to Pakistani ports through Afghanistan, could coordinate such an effort. The obstacle is representation. Taliban authorities were not invited to the 2022 summit in Astana, and despite their efforts to take part, they were absent again in Baku, even though Afghanistan formally remains a full member and its seat is held in reserve. The Secretariat has nonetheless kept a channel open, holding its first informal consultative meeting on engagement with Afghanistan in August 2025, and expert-level work on border and transit issues does not require settling recognition.

Third, the Charter should write this linkage into CICA’s mandate. A charter that lists cooperation areas side by side will reproduce the old division between soft and hard issues. A charter that defines secure connectivity as a core purpose, with preventive diplomacy as one of its tools, would give the new organization a reason to exist that its members can measure.

Azerbaijan’s extended mandate

Azerbaijan’s first term strengthened the economic side of CICA. The 2025 implementation plan included 44 events, about 20 of them proposed by Baku, with a focus on transport digitalization, data protection and cybersecurity, and ministers established a Women Council and a Finance Summit. Security received less attention in the public record of the chairmanship, a limit of the consensus model more than of Baku. The extension through 2028 and the appointment of an Azerbaijani Secretary General give Baku the time and the institutional levers to close that gap and to steer the Charter negotiations toward the security-connectivity link. CICA would not replace bilateral negotiations or existing mediation mechanisms. Its contribution would be to facilitate voluntary consultations, improve communication among participating states and support practical arrangements for transit continuity. Such efforts would require the consent of the states concerned and, where relevant, cooperation with countries outside CICA.

Why it matters for Kazakhstan

CICA is a Kazakh initiative, and its Secretariat remains in Astana. Kazakhstan’s transit strategy rests on routes it does not control, from the Caspian crossing to the planned railway to Pakistan through Turkmenistan and Afghanistan. As a land-locked country like its other Central Asian neighbors, an effective transit corridor strategy must be a very high priority. At the summit Tokayev also outlined plans with Azerbaijan to raise volumes of Kazakh oil shipped through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline. Every one of these projects depends on predictable borders. An organization that can lower the risk of conflict along these routes would serve Astana’s interests more directly than any additional dialogue platform.

If CICA uses the 2026 to 2028 window to adopt a Charter that ties conflict prevention to secure connectivity, it can become the first Asian institution with a practical answer to the corridor disruptions of the past year. If the Charter instead codifies the existing separation of soft and hard issues, the organization will gain legal status without gaining relevance, and Asian trade will continue to depend on ad hoc mediation by outside powers each time a border closes.

The authors are Eldaniz Gusseinov, a Co-Founder and Head of Research of Nightingale Int., a geopolitical foresight and advisory firm focused on Central Asia and Greater Eurasia, and Andrew Kuchins, a Senior Fellow at the Center for the National Interest in Washington, who also teaches at Johns Hopkins SAIS.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Counterinsurgency: How the second Chechen war became a blueprint for Russian rule
World.content:
The second Chechen war

In these days of remembrance, the world is recalling Anna Politkovskaya, who was murdered 20 years ago. The gunmen have been identified, but those who ordered the killing have not. The motive, however, is clear: her work as a journalist. Above all, her reporting from Chechnya during the Second Chechen War, whose catastrophic consequences Russia has yet to confront or come to terms with.

Politkovskaya’s legacy consists of 500 articles published in Novaya Gazeta — 500 documents of an era that reveal what that war was.

Around the world, Politkovskaya is often remembered as Ramzan Kadyrov’s personal enemy. That characterization vastly understates the significance of her work in understanding modern Russia and how it arrived at a point of absolute inhumanity.

▇ Politkovskaya was no more an enemy of Kadyrov than she was of Putin. She was a pathologist of the war that brought them both to power.

Understanding her legacy without understanding how that war stripped us of our humanity is impossible.

We invite you to go back 27 years, to September 1999. That was when a country, frightened by terrorist attacks, placed its trust in Vladimir Putin, who promised to “wipe out” the terrorists. The terms of the bargain — freedom in exchange for security — included an expansion of presidential power. In the end, our shared future was at stake.

Based on an article by Novaya Gazeta Europe.

“Not for Publication”

In the summer of 2014, the hacker group Anonymous International hacked the email account of Igor Girkin, also known as Strelkov, one of the most prominent instigators and participants in the war in Ukraine, and handed his correspondence to journalists at Novaya Gazeta. Among the emails was a fictional story by Girkin titled Adventures of Scumbags. It describes in detail a day in the life of an FSB operative during the Second Chechen War, in which Girkin took part from 1999 to 2005.

Girkin writes: “Today we are supposed to head west, toward the city of Argun and the large ‘bandit’ village of Mesker-Yurt on the plains (…). Our contact, an armed local guide, is waiting in his car at the agreed meeting point. We move him into our vehicle and question him. Today, he is prepared to identify four houses where militants frequently take shelter or spend the night.”

The story ended as follows: “We dropped the local guide off in Argun and took Vovan to Khankala (…). Reporting, planning, organising…” Vovan was another FSB operative, while Khankala was the main base of Russian forces in Chechnya.

At first glance, there was nothing criminal about a story describing a meeting with a recruited Chechen informant. What was revealing, however, was a warning Girkin included in the email itself: “The story cannot be published because the people we detained usually disappeared without a trace after interrogation. Only those who were there by chance were released. The rest were [taken away] without trial…”

When Novaya Gazeta journalists asked Girkin’s press secretary, Anastasia Mikhailovskaya, to confirm his authorship, she replied: “If you publish it, there will be a scandal. You must not publish it. We will sue!”

Why was Girkin so afraid of the publication of a story about a war that had ended long ago?

A Catastrophic Miscalculation

Formally, the Second Chechen War began with secret decree No. 1255s, signed by President Boris Yeltsin on September 23, 1999. But the first link in the chain of events was the incursion into Dagestan’s Botlikh district on August 7, 1999, by forces led by Shamil Basayev and Khattab, a Saudi militant linked to al-Qaeda.

Nearly three years had passed since the Khasavyurt Accords ended the First Chechen War. Power in the de facto independent Chechen Republic of Ichkeria had become divided. Aslan Maskhadov, who had been legally elected president in 1997, faced opposition from Shamil Basayev, the best-known field commander and deputy prime minister. Alongside militants from the Middle East, Basayev sought to impose a strict Sharia-based regime rooted in Salafism, which was alien to local traditions. These ideas found little support among Chechens.

Basayev and Khattab were counting on Dagestan’s Salafists. During the 1990s, Sharia-based jamaats emerged in Dagestan, declaring autonomy from Russia’s secular system of government. The most significant enclave was considered to be the so-called Kadar Zone, comprising four mountain villages. But here, dreams of a caliphate collided with reality: the overwhelming majority of North Caucasus residents did not support an Islamic state. Unlike Chechnya, the republics of the region were not seeking independence either. The Dagestani poet Rasul Gamzatov put it this way: “Dagestan did not voluntarily join Russia, and it will not voluntarily leave it!”

The first to repel the militants were Dagestanis themselves. A popular militia forced Basayev’s and Khattab’s forces to retreat into Chechnya.

Russian authorities launched a military and police operation in the Kadar Zone. To divert Russian forces, Basayev and Khattab invaded Dagestan’s Novolaksky district. At the same time, the ideologues of the caliphate resorted to a far more terrifying tactic: bombing residential buildings in Russia. After an explosion destroyed a military dormitory housing servicemen’s families in Buynaksk, followed by the bombing of the first apartment building on Guryanova Street in Moscow, Basayev told Czech journalist Petra Procházková that these were “Dagestani bombs” that had exploded “in response to Russia terrorizing Dagestan.”

Basayev and Khattab were probably drawing on the precedent of Budyonnovsk, where the hostage-taking in May 1995 had shifted the balance in favor of the Chechen resistance. But this time, they made a catastrophic miscalculation. Basayev later categorically denied involvement in the bombings, but by then it was too late. The attacks shook Russia, unleashed a wave of hatred toward Chechens as a people, and gave the military an unassailable pretext for revenge.

Russia’s Response

From the first months of the campaign, Western analysts judged the Second Chechen War to be far more successful for Russia than the first. Many agreed with Anatoly Chubais, who declared that “the Russian army has been reborn in Chechnya.” The authorities and military had taken the lessons of the first war on board and were preparing for another.

There were no more reckless attempts to “take Grozny in two hours with a single airborne regiment.” The operation was led by experienced generals. Forces were built up gradually and methodically. Air power and artillery were deployed extensively and without restraint, including Grad multiple-launch rocket systems, self-propelled artillery and sustained, large-scale air strikes. According to estimates by Western specialists who studied the war at the Pentagon’s request, the air force accounted for more than 80% of all fire missions, while artillery accounted for 15–17%.

No targets were off limits to the military: not residential buildings, schools, hospitals or markets. Numerous reports by Russian and international human rights organisations attest to this. They are not the only evidence. The website of the state-run A. A. Kadyrov Memorial Glory Museum states: “Virtually all industrial, residential and transport infrastructure was destroyed. More than 80% of residential buildings in central Grozny and its neighbourhoods were completely destroyed or rendered beyond repair.”

This strategy resulted in enormous civilian casualties, but it also sharply reduced Russian military losses compared with the First Chechen War.

In the mountains, elite units were deployed to fight. Battles for strategically important gorges were deliberately scheduled for winter, when militants’ movements could be easily spotted from the air and the forests offered little cover. For the first time in Russian history, combat pay was increased severalfold and contract soldiers were offered social benefits. War became an attractive way to make a living.

But the conflict in the former Yugoslavia and NATO’s intervention had a greater influence on the “rebirth of the army” than Russia’s defeat in the first Chechen campaign. Western analysts were already warning that Chechnya had become a testing ground where Russia was rehearsing scenarios for future wars against external adversaries.

The Indian military expert and retired Major General Gagandip Bakshi compared Russia’s operation to the suppression of separatism in Jammu and Kashmir. In his view, the Balkans and NATO’s new mission beyond the alliance’s traditional area of responsibility had prompted Russia to revise its military doctrine and “conventionalise” the conflict in Chechnya.

“This is a full-scale military invasion in which [Russia] has disregarded international condemnation and transformed the conflict into a brutal, conventional war, where the laws of peacetime and human rights standards are no longer taken into account…”

Grozny became the symbol of this response. In 2003, the United Nations recognised it as the most devastated city on Earth since the Second World War.

From the NKVD to the FSB

On February 29, 2000, Lieutenant General Gennady Troshev, deputy commander of the Joint Group of Forces in the North Caucasus, announced the end of the military phase of the campaign. In five months, the army had brought all of the Chechen lowlands and a substantial part of the mountainous region under its control. Almost all major settlements had been destroyed. The exception was Gudermes, which was surrendered without a fight by the influential Yamadaev clan, which had switched sides to support Moscow.

Nearly half of Chechnya’s population — around 400,000 people — fled the republic. In Russia, no one was waiting to welcome them after the apartment bombings. People sought refuge in Ingushetia or risked crossing the mountains into Georgia in the depths of winter.

Tiny Ingushetia took in 240,000 refugees. It lacked the resources to house and feed them all. Because of delays in federal funding, hundreds of thousands of people went for months without hot meals or government food rations. Only international aid prevented mass starvation. It was then that Chechens began leaving for Europe and other countries. Before the war, the only established Chechen diaspora was in Jordan.

For Moscow, a new phase was beginning: holding the territory amid a guerrilla war. Western experts predicted serious difficulties, noting that Russia “had never developed a doctrine for conducting protracted counterinsurgency campaigns, which was one of the main reasons for its defeat in the First Chechen War.”

There was, indeed, no such doctrine. But there was a Soviet legacy of suppressing guerrilla movements in the 1940s: the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) in western Ukraine and the Forest Brothers in the Baltic states. The NKVD and MGB had developed a classic Soviet counterinsurgency playbook: sweeps and raids, filtration camps, enforced disappearances, secret prisons, torture to extract information or recruit informants, collective punishment designed to deprive guerrillas of popular support, and amnesties intended to fracture the underground resistance. All of these methods were deployed from the earliest days of the Second Chechen War.

The leading role belonged not to the military but to the security services. Once the army had re-established control over most of the republic, the generals were pushed aside and strategic command passed to the FSB. From 2001, the Joint Group of Forces was headed by serving or former security service officers who had formally transferred to the Interior Ministry.

It was at this point that Igor Girkin and operatives like him began activities in Chechnya that remained too sensitive to publish even nearly 30 years later.

“The Rest Were Taken Away Without Trial…”

Russian human rights defender Alexander Cherkasov used the records of human rights violations compiled by the Memorial Human Rights Center since the beginning of the war to establish the date of Girkin’s meeting with the informant near Mesker-Yurt. He also established what happened after the report was submitted to Girkin’s superiors — and what the author had left out of his story.

In the early hours of November 15, 2000, Russian forces carried out a “cleansing operation” in Mesker-Yurt. This was the term used in Chechnya for military raids on populated areas. The pattern was always the same. Masked soldiers in armoured vehicles with no license plates or identifying insignia sealed off a village or neighbourhood. They broke into homes, searched them and often looted property in front of the residents. But most importantly, they took large numbers of people away to unknown destinations without any legal grounds.

Detainees were transported to temporary detention centres that were, in effect, secret prisons, where they underwent so-called “intensive interrogations” — in other words, interrogations involving torture.

Everyone was subjected to violence, regardless of age or sex, although most were “random” victims, to use Girkin’s terminology. After several days, they were released, often after their relatives had paid a ransom. But some disappeared without a trace.

On November 15, 2000, Ilyas Gachayev, Shamil Yashuyev, Adam Soltamuradov and Emedi Soltamuradov were detained in Mesker-Yurt. Most of the other villagers detained in the following days were released. These four never returned home. They joined the ranks of the forcibly disappeared, whose numbers in Chechnya ran into the thousands.

To this day, there are no precise figures for the victims of enforced disappearances during the Second Chechen War. Neither Russian nor Chechen authorities kept a tally. Human rights groups attempted to document the cases as far as their limited resources allowed. While Russia’s Interior Ministry was still reporting figures, the statistics showed that 5,500 people had been detained in the first five months of the campaign alone. In the first two years, Memorial documented the disappearance without a trace of more than 1,250 detainees.

Local residents discovered at least nine mass graves and several dozen bodies buried separately in shallow pits. The bodies bore signs of elaborate torture: scalps cut away, finger joints severed, ears cut off, skin flayed from people while they were still alive, eyes gouged out, throats slit and bones broken. Almost all the bodies showed gunshot wounds consistent with execution.

In the village of Starye Atagi, the bodies of abducted people were discovered during the cleaning of a collective farm irrigation canal. An excavator caught on a chair to which the body of a young Chechen man had been tied with ropes. He had been bound to the chair while still alive, shot as a target and buried with it.

Bodies, and sometimes living people, were thrown from helicopters into the Grozny Sea reservoir and Chechen rivers. On April 1, 2000, residents of the Ingush village of Arshty saw a military helicopter drop a man into the Assa River. His body was identified as that of Rustam Temirsultanov, 24. A forensic examination found one of his own eyeballs inside his mouth.

According to Memorial, between 3,000 and 5,000 Chechens became victims of enforced disappearance over the ten years of the Second Chechen War. Human rights defenders stressed that their monitoring covered only between a quarter and a third of the republic’s settlements, and even there, the documentation was incomplete.

A Crime Against Humanity

Russian criminal law contains no specific offence of enforced disappearance, meaning that there is no corresponding legal classification or penalty. Yet on December 18, 1992, Russia was among the states that approved United Nations General Assembly Resolution 47/133, adopting the Declaration on the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance. The declaration defines enforced disappearance as the deprivation of a person’s liberty by state agents or people acting with state authorisation, followed by a refusal to acknowledge the detention and the concealment of the person’s fate or whereabouts.

The declaration called on states to prevent such practices and to make enforced disappearance a separate criminal offence. When disappearances are widespread and systematic, and the state refuses to acknowledge them, investigate them or punish those responsible, they may constitute crimes against humanity, which are not subject to a statute of limitations. Article 7 states: “No circumstances whatsoever, whether a threat of war, a state of war, internal political instability or any other public emergency, may be invoked to justify enforced disappearances.”

In 2006, Russia reversed its position and refused to ratify the International Convention that had been developed on the basis of the declaration. By then, it had effectively become the second European country, after Bosnia and Herzegovina, in terms of the number of people who had been forcibly disappeared. Lawyers from the Legal Initiative organisation alone won more than 1,000 cases concerning disappearances in Chechnya before the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR).

In late August, Serbian general Ratko Mladić died while serving a life sentence imposed by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia for crimes against humanity. The tribunal found him guilty of the Srebrenica massacre, the largest mass killing in Europe since the Second World War. On Mladić’s orders, Bosnian Serb forces killed 8,372 men and boys from Bosniak Muslim families. Until their remains were found, exhumed and identified, the victims were considered forcibly disappeared. More than 40,000 people disappeared during the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia.

It is no coincidence that Russia has still not recognised the Srebrenica massacre as genocide, while its Foreign Ministry formally expressed condolences to Mladić’s family.

The “Health” Settlement

In early 2001, rumours spread across Chechnya about bodies found in the abandoned dacha settlement of Zdorovye, just over half a mile from Khankala, Russia’s main military base in the republic. Since January 2000, the headquarters of the Joint Group of Forces conducting the so-called counterterrorism operation had been based there. That was the official term used in Russia for the Second Chechen War. The settlement stood deserted, and people were afraid even to venture into it.

In early February, the family of Adam Chimaev, who had disappeared after being detained in December 2000, paid a Russian serviceman for information about the location of his body. Risking his life, Chimaev’s father found his son near a holiday cottage. The body bore signs of torture and three gunshot wounds to the chest. The father paid the military another $3,000 to retrieve the body and bury his son.

By the end of February, three more families had found the bodies of relatives who had disappeared during cleansing operations. The case then attracted widespread attention. Memorial and Human Rights Watch jointly produced a report titled The Dirty War: Disappearances, Torture and Extrajudicial Executions. The settlement was covered by Kommersant and Radio Liberty. Later, the Legal Initiative represented the victims’ relatives before the European Court of Human Rights after the state refused to investigate the crimes.

Technically, this was not a mass grave but a dumping ground, where the bodies of people tortured to death were discarded in place of rubbish. After the scandal broke, prosecutors opened an investigation and found around 60 bodies of men and women. Almost all were dressed in civilian clothes, and many had their hands and feet bound with wire. Most had gunshot wounds inflicted at close range to the abdomen, chest or head. The bodies were at different stages of decomposition, ranging from several weeks to a year. This meant the settlement had been used as a dumping ground for the dead for several months.

Immediately after the reports were published, the authorities cordoned off the settlement, claiming that militants had allegedly mined the area. The bodies were laid out for identification in a dilapidated hangar at an emergency services base in Grozny. Within two weeks, nearly 30 people had been identified. All had previously been detained by the military and then disappeared. Evidence indicated that at least five of them had been taken alive to the Khankala military base.

The last to be identified were three women: Nura Luluyeva, the wife of Chechen judge Said-Alvi Luluyev, and her cousins, Markha and Raisa Gakayev. According to the European Court of Human Rights judgment in Luluyev and Others v. Russia, on June 3, 2000, the women went to a market in Grozny and were caught up in a cleansing operation. Soldiers in camouflage uniforms and masks pulled sacks over the detainees’ heads and drove them away in a Ural military truck. The prosecutor’s office, Interior Ministry and FSB all claimed that the women did not appear on any list of detainees. When their bodies were found, sacks were still covering their heads — possibly the very ones used during their abduction.

The authorities then hurriedly buried the unidentified bodies in a mass grave on the outskirts of the cemetery in the village of Prigorodnoye.

The remains of Ilyas Gachayev and brothers Emedi and Adam Soltamuradov, who had been taken from Mesker-Yurt following the operational intelligence provided by Girkin, were identified by their relatives only after the mass burial, using photographs taken by forensic experts. The bodies were still clothed, with their hands bound behind their backs. Shamil Yashuyev was never identified, but one of the bodies gnawed by dogs was wearing a jacket resembling the one he had been wearing when he was taken from his home.

On August 21, 2001, Chechnya’s prosecutor, Vladimir Chernov, told the Interfax news agency: “There is no witness testimony confirming that federal forces were responsible for these killings. Therefore, the main theory pursued by investigators is that the mass grave was organised by Chechen militants.”

Mass Reburials

Chernov justified the hasty burials by citing the lack of facilities to store the bodies and claimed that the evidence collected would be sufficient for any future identification. Yet investigators failed to preserve the clothing or collect forensic evidence. They conducted no autopsies, established neither the causes of death nor injuries sustained before death, took no dental X-rays, recovered no bullets and collected no samples for DNA testing. The authorities did everything they could to ensure that the bodies would never be identified and the killers never found.

The remains of more than 30 people from the Zdorovye settlement still lie unidentified in a mass grave in Prigorodnoye.

The search for mass graves was long conducted by the General Lebed Peacekeeping Mission. According to its head, Alexander Mukomolov, who until recently was a member of the Human Rights Council under the Russian president, 119 mass burial sites were identified in Chechnya between 1999 and 2009. They may contain the remains of around 1,500 people: victims of enforced disappearances, Russian soldiers reported missing in action, and civilians killed in bombing raids and shelling.

Most of the burial sites remain unopened to this day. They are excavated only when they obstruct construction projects planned by the Chechen authorities. In such cases, the remains are dug up and reburied elsewhere. Reburial without identifying the victims of serious crimes has become standard practice in the republic.

For years, Russian and Chechen authorities have repeated the same explanation: Chechnya has no laboratory capable of identifying human remains, and Russia lacks the necessary specialists. In reality, Russia began building the infrastructure for identifying the dead, particularly soldiers, as early as 1995. American military personnel helped their counterparts in the Russian Defence Ministry master modern techniques and supplied equipment for DNA analysis.

The United States was a pioneer in this field. American anthropologists, forensic pathologists and criminal investigators played a crucial role in investigating crimes committed by military dictatorships in Latin America. FBI experts helped establish what became the world’s most advanced system for exhuming and identifying remains from mass graves in the former Yugoslavia. Mukomolov repeatedly cited the experience of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an international benchmark and urged the authorities to apply the same approach in Chechnya.

Russia itself drew on American expertise in 2008, immediately after the five-day war in Georgia. More than 100 Russian forensic specialists were deployed to South Ossetia, accompanied by a mobile laboratory. Russian authorities announced to the world that between 1,500 and 2,000 civilians had been killed in South Ossetia during the five-day war and attempted to accuse the Georgian authorities of genocide. In reality, the number of South Ossetian victims was ten times lower: 162 people. There was no need to deploy so many forensic specialists other than for propaganda purposes.

Two months before the war in Georgia, in June 2008, one of the largest burial sites in Chechnya was discovered in Grozny’s Leninsky district, near a Christian cemetery. It contained around 800 bodies. In July, another site containing several hundred bodies was found near the village of Goryacheistochnenskaya. But Viktor Ledenev, head of the Investigative Committee in Chechnya, refused to conduct exhumations, citing a shortage of specialists and inadequate infrastructure.

Even Nurdi Nukhazhiev, the former human rights ombudsman under the head of Chechnya, publicly identified what he saw as the real reason behind this policy of concealment:“It is precisely the Defence Ministry that is doing everything possible to obstruct the creation of an interagency commission to identify abducted and missing persons, as well as the establishment of a laboratory in the Chechen Republic to identify exhumed bodies…”

Freedom in Exchange for Danger

The official objective of the Second Chechen War was to combat terrorism. The authorities persistently referred to the campaign as a “counterterrorism operation,” rather than a war. This was largely a legal manoeuvre. Declaring martial law would have required the approval of a parliament that was still independent at the time and compliance with international obligations, above all the Geneva Conventions.

But in September 1999, public concern centred above all on security. Political scientists would later describe the social contract offered to citizens by the new prime minister, Vladimir Putin, as “freedom in exchange for security.” The public readily accepted it.

Initially, the West sharply criticised Russia’s methods. But those methods only drove more recruits into the militants’ ranks. The unrestrained brutality of the military and security services became one of the factors behind the emergence of shahidkas — women, often the widows and sisters of those killed, who were turned into “human bombs” after relatively rudimentary psychological and ideological conditioning.

After the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Vladimir Putin was the first foreign leader to call US President George W. Bush to offer his condolences. Putin stressed that Russia had already spent two years defending the civilised world against Islamist terrorism in Chechnya. Western attitudes began to shift. Basayev, Khattab, Umarov and the Caucasus Emirate they led were placed on US terrorist lists. The West definitively abandoned the idea of an international tribunal for Chechnya.

When Putin opened Russian airspace to NATO aircraft and raised no objections to US military bases in Central Asia, the Second Chechen War came to be regarded as one front in the global war on terror.

In reality, the West and Russia shared a record of war crimes in this conflict. When confronted with accusations of human rights abuses in Chechnya, Russia pointed to Guantánamo Bay, Abu Ghraib, secret CIA prisons in Europe, and civilian casualties in Afghanistan and Iraq.

But a comparison of how the United States and Russia protected their citizens from terrorist attacks suggests that counterterrorism was never a priority for the Russian authorities. After September 11, the United States overhauled its security system. In the quarter-century since, no terrorist organisation has come close to repeating Osama bin Laden’s “success.” In Russia, by contrast, terrorist attacks became a recurring feature of life: the 2002 Moscow theatre siege, the 2004 attacks in Ingushetia and the Beslan school hostage-taking, the 2005 assault on Nalchik, and countless bombings targeting cars, buildings, hospitals, markets, aircraft and metro stations.

The authorities exploited every attack to concentrate presidential power and strengthen the security services. But the goal was not to fight terrorists; it was to suppress political opposition and civic dissent.

It was not until 2013, on the eve of the Sochi Winter Olympics, that the security services managed to stabilise the situation in the Caucasus. International developments played a significant role. When the Islamic State (ISIS), founded by former members of Saddam Hussein’s Iraqi security services, seized parts of Iraq and Syria and declared a caliphate, radicals from around the world, including the North Caucasus, flocked to join it. Russian security services simply opened the border to them.

In March 2024, Islamic State followers stormed the Crocus City Hall concert venue, opened fire and set the building ablaze. The attack killed 151 people and injured more than 600. Foreign intelligence agencies had warned the FSB of an impending terrorist attack. Yet on March 19, three days before the assault, Russia’s leadership publicly dismissed the warnings as “outright blackmail by Western countries” and an attempt to destabilise society. The FSB did nothing to prevent the attack.

Today, in Russia, Ukrainians are branded terrorists, while Islamic State militants are no longer the primary focus.

The terrorist attack took place in a climate of complete public silence. There is nowhere left to ask the authorities what became of the social contract of September 1999, and no one left to ask the question. This is what became of it: the methods of terror honed in Chechnya have become a central instrument of Russian state policy, both at home and abroad.

The practices of filtration — enforced disappearances, secret prisons, torture and extrajudicial executions — became a principal means of “bringing the population into line” after the annexation of Crimea, and later across all the regions of Ukraine occupied by Russian forces in the first months of the war. According to human rights defenders, the practice of so-called “short-term enforced disappearances” has also spread beyond Chechnya to regions across Russia itself.

▇ Replace Chechens with Ukrainians in Anna Politkovskaya’s articles, Novye Aldy and Khatuni with Bucha, Izium or Kherson, and Grozny, Komsomolskoye, Argun and Shali with Mariupol, Bakhmut, Kharkiv or, right now, Kyiv, and her reporting will read as entirely contemporary — and entirely prophetic.

This article was produced in collaboration with the Memory Project, a civic initiative comprising Russian lawyers, human rights defenders and researchers who investigate enforced disappearances and preserve historical memory.

Exchange

World.title: Abkhazia-Russia police cooperation: ‘shameful incompetence’ or boost to effectiveness?
World.content:
Independent Abkhaz journalist Nizfa Arshba published agreements on cooperation between the interior ministries of Abkhazia and the Russian Federation on her Telegram channel, Aiaashara, sparking a political debate in Abkhazia’s public sphere.

The debate centres on signed cooperation plans that have drawn sharply opposing reactions: some accuse the authorities of surrendering sovereignty, while others argue that joint efforts to fight crime are necessary.

Accusations of incompetence and pressure

In her investigation, Nizfa Arshba draws on a 2024–2025 cooperation plan between the Russian and Abkhaz interior ministries that she obtained. She also refers to a similar document for 2026–2027, signed by Russian Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev and his Abkhaz counterpart, Robert Kiut.

The journalist strongly criticised the leadership of Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry, calling it incapable of doing its job. In her view, seeking help from another country’s ministry directly illustrates its inability to fulfil its own responsibilities.

Низфа Аршба

“The agency entrusted to Robert Kiut employs several thousand people and has a wide range of technical equipment, yet it can do nothing. It cannot independently monitor and analyse the country’s crime situation. It cannot assess its own effectiveness. It cannot manage the situation in border regions on its own,” Arshba writes.

The provision that angered her most concerns the transfer to Russia of information about individuals capable of “destabilising the situation in a border region”. She directly links this mechanism to the recent stripping of Abkhaz heroes and opposition politicians Levan Mikaa and Kan Kvarchia of their Russian citizenship.

Arshba believes that Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry, under Robert Kiut, alerted the relevant Russian agencies to the two men, “documenting the shameful surrender of Abkhaz citizens” and helping the authorities eliminate their opponents through the actions of another country.

The story has attracted further attention because Nizfa Arshba herself exposed the ministry documents. Although she is an Abkhaz citizen and does not hold Russian citizenship, Russia’s Justice Ministry previously added her to its register of “foreign agents”.

Civil society reacts

The public movement Apsuaa Rymch saw the published documents as a threat to the independence of Abkhazia’s institutions and issued a strongly worded statement.

In its view, the list of measures in the cooperation plans illustrates the Abkhaz Interior Ministry’s inability to handle basic tasks independently.

“If you put together everything the Abkhaz Interior Ministry cannot handle on its own under this plan, you end up with a complete list of the ministry’s responsibilities,” Apsuaa Rymch members said.

Like Arshba, they objected to the provisions on information sharing and search operations. Apsuaa Rymch drew a direct parallel between agreements to monitor people capable of destabilising border regions and what it called “punitive” decisions against individual Abkhaz public figures.

“The documents list the transfer of information about individuals destabilising the operational situation to relevant Russian agencies as one of the measures to be carried out… What is this, if not an example of shifting responsibilities and laying the groundwork for pressure?” Apsuaa Rymch asked, calling for a legal review of the agreements and the publication of their full texts.

Critics of the documents argue that the public and parliament have not received a full account of the details of the interagency agreements covering 2024–2025 and 2026–2027.

The Interior Ministry’s position

The Interior Ministry itself takes a very different view of the agreements and the actual results of cooperation between the two agencies.

In interviews with television channels, Interior Minister Robert Kiut explained the arrangements in detail. He stressed that the ministry’s work focuses strictly on protecting citizens and maintaining law and order, and remains separate from politics.

According to the minister, speculation surrounding the cooperation plans has no real basis because the mechanism rests on a long-standing legal framework.

Robert Kiut

“The current cooperation plan between the Abkhaz and Russian interior ministries introduces no new obligations. It operates within the framework of existing basic interstate agreements signed in 2009 and 2014.

Abkhaz law unquestionably retains priority. The mechanism has been in place for more than five years, and the coordination we have established serves exclusively to address practical security issues,” Kiut said.

The minister urged people to judge the cooperation by its concrete results rather than political slogans. In particular, Robert Kiut said that joint efforts with Russian colleagues had dismantled around four major drug supply routes in 2025–2026.

According to the minister, another major achievement for the Interior Ministry was resolving the issue of maternity capital.

“Thanks to cooperation with Russian law enforcement agencies, around 400 Abkhaz citizens who had previously been listed as suspects in the illegal cashing-out of [maternity capital] have been reclassified as witnesses, effectively shielding them from criminal prosecution,” Kiut said.

He also expects technological advances to mark a significant step forward. Joint projects at the new Information and Coordination Centre, which is under construction, will include a modern DNA laboratory. This will reduce the time needed to conduct forensic examinations from a year and a half to just a few days.

Public demand for transparency

Overall, the debate surrounding the Interior Ministry’s cooperation plans has highlighted public demand for greater transparency in government decision-making. People are calling for full openness and the protection of sovereignty, fearing any form of institutional secrecy.

The Abkhaz parliament will probably hold hearings on the interagency agreements in the near future. Some MPs believe the documents need to be checked for compliance with Abkhazia’s constitution.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: ‘The trail leads to Azerbaijan and Israel’: Yerevan’s take on new cyberattacks on Armenia
World.content:
Cyberattacks on Armenian government agencies

Several Armenian government agencies have come under cyberattack, according to Citizen Lab, a Canadian organisation that researches cybersecurity and digital censorship and works to protect human rights.

Information security expert Samvel Martirosyan said the attacks were targeted rather than random.

The targets included specific individuals and organisations, notably the office of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, the Central Bank and the Central Election Commission.

Investigators have identified the Israeli company Candiru as responsible for the cyberattacks. In 2021, the same company targeted Armenia, infecting computers with malware.

At the time, Candiru acted on behalf of Azerbaijan. Samvel Martirosyan says he cannot determine which country, if any, stands behind the latest cyberattack.

“My guess is that either Azerbaijan, Israel itself, or both countries are behind this. I don’t think any other interested party could afford to buy these services. Carrying out attacks of this kind requires authorisation from the Israeli military,” the expert said.

It remains unclear what data or information the hackers wanted to obtain and what they managed to access in the attacks.

Commentary

According to information security expert Samvel Martirosyan, the Canadian organisation Citizen Lab identified attacks similar to those recorded in the past. However, the earlier incidents did not involve exploits that require no user interaction, known as “zero-click” exploits.

He recalls that the Israeli company Candiru has previously carried out cyberattacks against Armenian government agencies.

This time, however, the attackers also infected devices through online s:

“They reached an agreement with an advertising network. Websites often use software from advertising networks to display ads, while the site owners receive a share of the revenue. In this case, a major advertising company effectively partnered with Candiru, using these ads to infect users.”

According to Martirosyan, the attacks targeted Windows computers as well as mobile phones. It remains unclear whether the hackers collected detailed, in-depth data from the phones. However, Martirosyan suspects they may use this information later to carry out “other types” of attacks.

“The attacks were widespread. Most infections occurred through the mamul.am website. Under no circumstances should anyone assume that the website itself had any involvement in what happened. The only issue was that it displayed banners from this advertising network. The ads appeared around one million times, and investigators classified 100,000 of those instances as targeted and malicious. The attackers used them to collect data or launch an attack.”

Martirosyan stressed that Candiru’s cyberattack was not the only incident of its kind in recent days.

Cybersecurity firms Cisco Talos and Recorded Future published a report describing an attack on Armenia by another hacking group.

Based on the group’s tactics, its interactions with other hacking groups and its time zone, the companies investigating cyber threats suspect that the attack originated in Kazakhstan.

“These hackers speak Russian. They may actually be based in Russia, but are trying to disguise their origins by posing as actors operating from Kazakhstan,” the expert said.

According to Samvel Martirosyan, Kazakhstan is an “unusual actor” in cases of this kind. He suspects that “other forces attempting to operate under the flag of Kazakhstan” may be behind the attack. In early 2026, the same hacking group attacked Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade.

However, Armenia is not its only target. The group also operates against targets in Tajikistan, Belarus and Russia.

“These are not sophisticated tools that work on a ‘zero-click’ basis, without user interaction. The hackers use phishing and then try to install malware on computers,” the expert added.
