World.title: Georgia’s party ban: Court to begin hearing government case against opposition on 21 October
World.content:
At noon on 21 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court will begin hearing on the merits a case brought by the ruling Georgian Dream party, which is seeking to ban five opposition parties and political groups. The hearings will take place in Batumi and continue on 22 and 23 October.

Four of the five parties intend to defend their positions in court, while the fifth will boycott the proceedings. Some opposition groups also plan to hold protests in Batumi and Tbilisi alongside the hearings.

The Constitutional Court’s full bench will hear the case, meaning all its sitting judges. The court has nine seats, but only seven judges currently serve on it, with two vacancies. On 13 October, Manana Kobakhidze, one of the founders of Georgian Dream, left the court. She had previously asked to recuse herself from the case, but the court rejected her request. Kobakhidze said she had made the decision to leave the court independently and for personal reasons.

Georgian Dream MPs Archil Gorduladze, Giorgi Kakhiani, Tengiz Sharmanashvili and Tornike Cheishvili will represent the party in court.

Under the law, the court must deliver its ruling by 24 June 2027.

Why is Georgian Dream seeking to ban the parties?

The claimants — 88 Georgian Dream MPs — argue that all five parties have violated Article 23 of the Constitution, which prohibits political parties that aim to overthrow or forcibly change the constitutional order.

According to information released by the court, the claimants cite alleged human rights violations between 2004 and 2012, when one of the parties, the United National Movement (UNM), was in power. They also point to the parties’ current refusal to recognise Georgian Dream’s legitimacy. The claimants say the parties have rejected the government’s legitimacy since 2016 and are pursuing a common goal.

The claimants also accuse the parties of attempting to overthrow the government. In the case of the United National Movement, they further allege that it undermined the country’s independence and territorial integrity, citing the August 2008 war.

The opposition parties reject all these accusations.

What do the parties facing a ban plan to do?

United National Movement

The party will attend the court hearings, said Irakli Pavlenishvili, chair of its governing council. He called on members of the public to gather outside the courthouse in Batumi on the days of the hearings.

The UNM’s jailed founder and Georgia’s third president, Mikheil Saakashvili, has also demanded that he attend the proceedings. In a statement released on 17 October, he said he wanted the authorities to bring him to Batumi so he could “fully expose this so-called court and its master for their historic betrayal”. Much of the case against the parties concerns Saakashvili’s time in power, from 2004 to 2012.

The party’s leader, Levan Khabeishvili, who is also in prison, has likewise demanded permission to attend the hearings.

The UNM belongs to the opposition alliance and takes part in its protests.

What is the Opposition Alliance? The Opposition Alliance “Unity for Victory” was formed by nine pro-Western Georgian parties on 2 March 2026, following months of negotiations. Its members are the United National Movement, Ahali, Girchi – More Freedom, Droa, the Federalists, European Georgia, Strategy Aghmashenebeli, Freedom Square and the National Democratic Party. The alliance says its goals are to end the rule of Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder and honorary chairman of Georgian Dream, restore Georgia’s Euro-Atlantic course, release political prisoners and form a coalition government after Georgian Dream loses a free election. The parties retain their ideological independence but have agreed on a joint strategy for protests and communications. The alliance’s largest rally to date took place in Tbilisi on 26 May 2026, Georgia’s Independence Day. Two other major opposition parties, Lelo and For Georgia, led by Giorgi Gakharia, have not joined the alliance. Lelo chose to operate independently, while For Georgia rejected an alliance with the United National Movement and parties that split from it.

Coalition for Change

The coalition will also take part in the hearings. Its member parties — Ahali, Girchi – More Freedom and Droa — also belong to the Opposition Alliance. On 15 October, Nika Gvaramia, leader of Ahali, announced the launch of a joint campaign by the alliance.

Gvaramia said their struggle would not be confined to the courtroom. “We will be everywhere, including on the streets of Tbilisi,” he promised.

Strong Georgia – Lelo

Lelo will attend the hearings and has asked the Public Defender (ombudsman) to submit a legal opinion on the case. As of 19 October, the ombudsman’s office had not responded.

Lelo is not a member of the alliance. The party’s political council says it has several scenarios and an action plan ready in case the court approves the ban.

For Georgia

The party announced in a statement on 20 October that it would take part in the proceedings. However, it insists that the court consider the case against it separately, rather than together with the other parties.

The party of former Georgian prime minister Giorgi Gakharia does not belong to the Opposition Alliance. It was the only one of the five parties that refused to surrender its parliamentary mandate in protest and nevertheless entered parliament.

The Federalists

The party has decided not to attend the hearings, saying it does not want to lend the proceedings a veneer of legal legitimacy.

According to party leader Tamara Chergoleishvili, the Federalists will travel to Batumi but protest against the court proceedings outside the courthouse rather than in the courtroom.

Why does it matter whether the parties attend the hearings?

The parties’ attendance could affect their chances of appealing the verdict to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in Strasbourg.

Sandro Baramidze, a lawyer with Transparency International Georgia, explains that the ECHR requires applicants to raise and document their arguments through domestic legal proceedings first. If a party does not attend the hearing, its application to the court in Strasbourg could therefore be declared inadmissible.

Who is organising the protests?

As Georgian Dream seeks to ban the parties listed above, the Opposition Alliance has announced a protest campaign.

The first demonstration will take place at 11:00 on 21 October in Batumi, outside the Constitutional Court. Freedom Square, a member of the alliance, is organising the protest.

At 19:00 on 25 October in Tbilisi, outside the first building of Tbilisi State University, the Opposition Alliance will launch a joint campaign aimed at organising a large demonstration in Tbilisi on 28 November.

As of 20 October, Lelo and For Georgia had not said whether they would join the protests.

What is the rest of the opposition doing?

In addition to the parties facing a ban, the Opposition Alliance includes European Georgia, Strategy Aghmashenebeli, Freedom Square and the National Democratic Party. These parties are not named in the lawsuit but take part in all the alliance’s protests.

Levan Tsutskiridze, leader of Freedom Square, believes that banning the parties would create a bigger problem for Georgian Dream itself.

He says a ban will not make the country’s problems disappear. Instead, it will “close off the political path to solving these problems and guarantee an even worse end for Georgian Dream”.

Viktor Kipiani, leader of the party For Georgia First, points to the same risk:

Banning opposition parties through the courts effectively brings the political process to a standstill, while making change through elections virtually impossible.

He believes this will accelerate radicalisation in the country.

The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association has now issued its independent legal assessment of the case for the third time, arguing that the lawsuit aims to eliminate political competition.

What is the European Union saying?

EU institutions have reacted strongly to the Georgian authorities’ attempt to ban opposition parties:

The European Parliament adopted another critical resolution, calling for the immediate withdrawal of the lawsuit and saying it was considering personal sanctions against those who initiated the proceedings.

Christian Wigand, a European Commission spokesman, said Brussels was closely monitoring developments. He said the attempt to abolish leading political forces, alongside the Georgian authorities’ earlier statements and legislative changes, pointed to a worrying instrumentalisation of the justice system. This directly threatens democratic pluralism and fundamental freedoms.

On 20 October, Georgia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded that questioning the legitimacy of the proceedings before the court had even examined the case amounted to an attempt to pressure the court and interfere in the country’s internal affairs. The ministry urged EU representatives to refrain from statements that prejudge the proceedings.

What happens if the court upholds the lawsuit?

If the court upholds the lawsuit, the five parties will legally cease to exist. According to official figures from the Central Election Commission, a total of 784,820 voters backed the five parties in the 2024 parliamentary election.

Under current legislation, the court may also, at the claimant’s request, ban people associated with the dissolved parties from engaging in political activity. The law also provides a 14-day procedure for banning a successor party.

The hearings scheduled for 21–23 October mark the first stage in the proceedings. It remains unclear how long the case will take or when the court will deliver its ruling.

World.title: Armenia considers restricting regional cars from entering Yerevan
World.content:
Cars from regions banned from Yerevan

A statement by Yerevan Deputy Mayor Suren Grigoryan has sparked widespread debate in Armenia. He said that one of the city administration’s strategic goals was to create car parks at the entrances to Yerevan, where drivers arriving from other regions could leave their vehicles and continue their journeys by public transport.

The proposal has prompted heated discussions among both experts and residents.

Traffic experts suggest increasing parking fees in the capital rather than restricting vehicle access. Meanwhile, residents have raised concerns that the initiative could limit freedom of movement and lead to discriminatory measures.

People are also questioning how they would navigate Yerevan using public transport if travelling with young children or elderly relatives, or bringing a family member to the capital for medical treatment.

What else did deputy mayor say?

Deputy Mayor Suren Grigoryan said the city administration had no plans to introduce restrictions immediately. He explained that creating car parks and expanding the public transport fleet would take time. Grigoryan did not specify when a possible ban on cars from other regions entering Yerevan might come into force.

According to him, the number of cars in Armenia has doubled from 500,000 in 2014 to one million. Meanwhile, the number of vehicles in Yerevan is increasing by around 15,000 or more each year.

The deputy mayor also addressed plans to purchase new vehicles for public transport. He said the city planned to acquire 171 new buses in the near future.

However, Grigoryan acknowledged that he could not say with certainty whether all residents of Armenia’s regions would be able to switch from private cars to public transport.

Clarifications following statement

Following a wave of outrage on social media, the deputy mayor issued further clarifications. He stressed that he had been referring not to a measure that would be introduced immediately, but to a strategic goal that would be implemented gradually.

“There has been a misunderstanding. Some citizens assumed that vehicles from the regions would be banned from entering Yerevan. I said nothing of the sort,” Suren Grigoryan emphasised.

He attributed the confusion to the headline of his interview:

“It had nothing to do with the actual content of the interview. This is a clear example of what happens when people judge a news story solely by its headline.”

Expert opinion

Traffic expert Artak Gaboyan believes that banning private cars from Armenia’s regions from entering the capital would make little sense:

“Nowhere in the world do authorities simply tell people they are banned from entering a city. Instead, they create conditions that make leaving a car outside the city a more convenient and financially attractive option.”

To ease congestion in central Yerevan, Gaboyan suggests increasing parking fees to 1,000 drams ($2.60) per hour, roughly three times the current rate.

“In addition, free shuttle buses should operate near the car parks [at the entrances to the city], taking drivers to the nearest transport hub, metro station or interchange where they can transfer to regular public transport services heading in different directions,” he explained.

Gaboyan also believes that implementing his proposal would require ensuring the “uninterrupted movement of public transport”.

As an example, he cited Isakov Avenue, one of the capital’s busiest roads, where one lane is reserved exclusively for public transport.

Social media reactions

“Are you now dividing society into Yerevan residents and people from the regions? How long will you continue dividing society? Instead, ease congestion in the capital and sort out the traffic problems.”

“This violates people’s right to freedom of movement. The current city administration has already made life unbearable for us.”

“And what about the fact that many people are simply too lazy to travel one or two stops by public transport and prefer to use their own cars?”

“We come to Yerevan with small children and loads of bags. How does he expect us to get around on public transport?”

“Why not simply ban people from the regions from entering Yerevan unless they carry an ID card, an income declaration, a CV and at least three letters of recommendation? And then, why not require people from the regions to obtain police permission before leaving their villages?”

“The deputy mayor could start setting an example today: take public transport home, use it to get to work tomorrow, take his children to school and then go to the doctor. All by public transport. In short, let him try living like that for at least a week, and then we’ll see.”

“According to the deputy mayor, implementing this idea would require building car parks at the entrances to the capital and introducing dedicated public transport lanes. Given that over the past eight years the city administration has made no progress beyond a single dedicated lane on one avenue — failing to establish a proper network of such lanes or make progress in expanding the metro system — expecting them to resolve the issue of restricting cars from the regions from entering Yerevan is simply wishful thinking.”

World.title: South Ossetia’s new authorities seek to crack down on illegal trade in ‘award’ weapons
World.content:
The new president of South Ossetia, Marat Kambolov, has ordered an investigation into the legality of the circulation of civilian, service and military firearms, as well as bladed weapons.

The Prosecutor General’s Office is carrying out the president’s order. Kambolov’s fellow villager, Soslanbek Kozhiyev, was recently appointed first deputy prosecutor general.

A smuggled ‘award’

The authorities will pay particular attention to a practice that took hold under previous presidents: handing out Glock and Beretta pistols left, right and centre under the pretext of awarding them as honours. Smugglers brought the pistols into South Ossetia from Georgia.

Officials often used these supposed “awards” as a cover to sell the weapons to members of the criminal underworld or simply to anyone who wanted one. And plenty of people in South Ossetia want a gun “just in case”. However, Kambolov believes this “tradition”, which dates back to the 1990s, has run its course. He says that civilian gun ownership no longer serves a relevant purpose and that real security risks no longer justify it.

“Today, South Ossetia leads a peaceful life and is building a state governed by the rule of law. In a peaceful state, the law — not tradition, personal merit, official position or private arrangements — must determine the right to own a gun.

The republic has suspended all awards of weapons until the investigation ends. The state must know exactly where each weapon is, to whom and on what grounds it was issued, how it was registered and who is responsible for it,” the president said.

At the same time, he proposes extending permits to possess and carry most types of civilian firearms to ten years, while retaining mandatory checks and periodic permit renewals:

“This approach will allow us to bring order to the firearms register without imposing excessive bureaucracy on law-abiding owners. The republic’s Security Council will make the final decision on this matter, following a proposal from the prosecutor general.”

A rifle as a gift

These measures come amid criminal proceedings against former Interior Minister Erislav Mamiyev and his first deputy, Atsamaz Sagkayev.

Investigators suspect that Sagkayev “gifted” his boss, Mamiyev, a sniper rifle and an assault rifle in 2025 and 2026.

Authorities have opened two criminal cases against Sagkayev on suspicion of “abuse of official powers for personal gain or other personal motives”, an offence under the Criminal Code.

Some Telegram channels claim that over those two years, Sagkayev used the pretext of awarding weapons to sell 400 firearms to unknown buyers.

Both Sagkayev and Mamiyev lost their jobs at the Interior Ministry in August 2026, when Marat Kambolov, then prime minister, launched the first stage of a purge of South Ossetia’s security agencies.

The roots of the problem

Many consider Erislav Mamiyev a close friend of local crime boss Alexander (Alik) Gagloyev, the brother of former president Alan Gagloyev.

Social media has also circulated claims that Alan Gagloyev and his team planned to use his gangster brother and their friends, armed with weapons presented as “awards”, to hold on to power by force if he lost the 2027 presidential election.

But that scenario never materialised. In mid-2026, the Kremlin itself ousted Gagloyev from the presidency and effectively installed its own envoy, Marat Kambolov, in his place.

The new president is now trying to clean up his predecessor’s “legacy” and deliver on his promise to restore order, a pledge he repeatedly made to the people of South Ossetia over the past several months.

However, Alan Gagloyev was not the only former president involved in illegal arms trafficking. His predecessor, Leonid Tibilov, also had a record of such activity. One case came to light relatively recently, in autumn 2025. The major scandal that erupted at the time also implicated former Interior Minister Akhsar Lavoyev and Russian debt collector Eduard Budantsev, alongside Tibilov.

It emerged that back in December 2015, Budantsev and several former colleagues had exchanged gunfire in central Moscow using award weapons from South Ossetia. He had acquired the weapons through Tibilov and his inner circle.

“The trade in Glocks and Berettas in South Ossetia became a well-oiled operation under Tibilov and his associates. Gagloyev and his people simply continued the lucrative business,” a local expert said on condition of anonymity.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: TV host gets 30-day detention in Georgia over Facebook post: reactions
World.content:
Journalist jailed over Facebook post in Georgia

Popular Georgian TV host Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 30 days’ administrative detention on 19 October over social media posts deemed insulting to government officials.

The lawsuit was filed by the Department for Monitoring Hate Speech and Aggressive Statements, which recently became part of the Interior Ministry. Sanaia was accused of insulting Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and MP Vladimir (Lado) Bozhadze in his Facebook posts and videos.

This is the third sentence handed down to the Formula TV host on similar charges since July this year, and his second term of detention.

Vakho Sanaia

Sanaia did not attend the court hearing, saying that prosecuting him for his posts was absurd. Police arrested him at his home.

“They want to force society into silence, but society will never be silent. We will overthrow this regime, however long it takes. This will certainly end in our victory,” Sanaia said as he was being arrested.

Why was Vakho Sanaia punished

The case centres on three social media posts about parliament speaker Shalva Papuashvili and ruling-party MP Vladimir Bozhadze.

The posts included censored profanities referring to the two politicians.

In a post on 22 July, shortly before he was detained in an earlier case, Sanaia wrote: “For 14 days, don’t call Shalva [Papuashvili] and Lado [Bozhadze] [censored insult] – when I get out, I’ll deal with that.”

In another post on 5 August, he referred to his earlier remarks, writing: “I wrote that you shouldn’t call Papuashvili and Bozhadze [censored insult], and they arrested me.”

On 24 September, Sanaia published a video address whose title also contained a censored profane reference to Papuashvili. Sanaia has described the proceedings as an attempt to restrict freedom of expression.

The case is being brought under Article 173¹⁶ of Georgia’s Code of Administrative Offences, which penalises insulting a political office-holder. The provision allows for a fine of 2,500 to 6,000 lari ($930–$2,220) or administrative detention for between five and 60 days.

This is the third administrative case against Sanaia. In July, he was fined 6,000 lari and sentenced to 14 days in detention over earlier posts involving the same two politicians.

The government agency that monitors social media

The Interior Ministry’s Division for Combating Hate Speech began operating on 1 June. It monitors public statements, including social media posts, and refers cases to court. Local media report that the unit often acts without a complaint from the person allegedly insulted. Cases brought by the division have led to dozens of fines and several detentions.

The case comes amid deteriorating relations between Georgia and the West. In November 2024, the government halted EU accession talks until 2028, triggering mass protests. Georgia has also fallen to 135th place out of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 Press Freedom Index, down from 77th in 2022.

Sentence draws criticism in Georgia and abroad

European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand has commented on the arrest of Vakho Sanaia:

“We have been very vocal in our criticism of Georgian Dream’s actions aimed at suppressing the political opposition, journalists and activists. Unfortunately, they continue to restrict civic space. The Georgian authorities must immediately release all unjustly detained politicians, journalists and activists and repeal repressive legislation.”

The Georgian Charter of Journalistic Ethics described the sentence as unjust, saying the authorities are using legislation and the courts to silence critical voices and restrict independent media.

“Through legislative amendments and, subsequently, the way these amendments are enforced, Georgian Dream has abandoned its obligation to tolerate criticism,” the charter said.

The Media Advocacy Coalition said the third case brought against the same journalist points to a pattern of persecution targeting critical media and dissenting voices. The coalition also expressed solidarity with the Formula TV team.

PEN Georgia called for the detention ruling to be overturned immediately. “In a country where journalists and citizens are jailed for criticising the government, and free speech becomes grounds for punishment, democracy no longer exists,” the organisation said.

Transparency International Georgia said Sanaia was being punished for exposing billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of Georgian Dream and widely seen as Georgia’s shadow ruler, and for supporting the country’s European future.

Parliament speaker: “Obscenity is not freedom of expression”

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said obscene language in public was unacceptable and could carry legal consequences.

“Obscenity has nothing to do with expressing an opinion and is not protected by freedom of expression,” he said.

Papuashvili said he did not follow individual cases. According to him, the Interior Ministry’s unit operates automatically, and those targeted often learn about decisions only after they have been made.

He also cited Germany, saying people can face criminal charges for insulting others on social media, including following a personal complaint by the chancellor.

Papuashvili also criticised the EU ambassador, claiming that “he himself promotes hatred” and that “some people may try to win his favour.”

“If he has the audacity to use obscene language in public, he should also have the courage to face the consequences,” Papuashvili said of Sanaia.

News in Georgia

World.title: Opinion: ‘Irakli Bzhinava’s arrest in Russia is blow to freedom in Abkhaz society’
World.content:
Abkhaz Foreign Minister Oleg Bartsits discussed the fate of Abkhaz lawyer Irakli Bzhinava, who has been in a Russian prison since February 2026, with his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov.

Irakli Bzhinava

Irakli Bzhinava holds dual Abkhazian and Russian citizenship and lives in Russia. The initial grounds for his arrest stemmed from a social media post he published on 23 December 2022, in which he criticised an agreement to transfer a famous state-owned holiday residence in Abkhazia to Russia. Russian authorities accuse Bzhinava over the post of “criminal intent to make public calls for activities directed against the security of the Russian Federation”.

In mid-September 2026, Russia’s Investigative Committee opened a second criminal case against Bzhinava, accusing him of “publicly justifying terrorist Shamil Basayev on the internet”.

According to Oleg Bartsits, Abkhazia’s Foreign Ministry remains in regular contact with the Russian side and also liaises with Bzhinava’s relatives and lawyers. The Abkhaz consul in Russia recently visited Irakli Bzhinava, and the authorities also arranged a meeting between him and his mother.

Bartsits adds that some issues remain unresolved, but they fall under the jurisdiction of Russian law enforcement agencies, and the Abkhaz side respects this. Since Bzhinava is a Russian citizen, Abkhazia’s authorities have limited scope for action, although members of the public are urging them to do everything possible to help their compatriot.

Prominent Abkhaz public figure Akhra Bzhania explains in his blog why Irakli Bzhinava’s case matters so much to Abkhaz society. In his view, by punishing Bzhinava for his dissenting views, Russia is trying to intimidate all Abkhaz people who share his position. And there are many of them.

Most Abkhaz people oppose agreements under which Russia seeks to take something from Abkhazia or derive some benefit from it. The issue of Shamil Basayev is also controversial: he received the title of “Hero of Abkhazia” for his participation in the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war. In short, many other Abkhaz people could have made — and have made — the statements that led to Bzhinava’s arrest.

Akhra Bzhania: “An effective state is possible only when society is free and responsible. Society acts as a reservoir, supplying the state with everything it needs: personnel, money and a worldview. It also holds the state to account through the press and political institutions.

This model works wherever society is free and confident in its natural rights. To a large extent, it works in Abkhazia too. Our society delegates power to the authorities not as a sacred function, but to represent its real interests. When the authorities begin to disregard those interests, a correction follows: the government resigns, and the overall political course returns to a path guided by our own sovereign interests.

A free and politically active society is what makes us strong, allowing us to advance our own agenda under the most difficult circumstances. Our freedom is our immunity against everything that threatens us — a fence that marks where other people’s interests end and ours begin.

Irakli Bzhinava’s arrest is an attack on this very immunity.

I do not believe there are any naive people in Abkhazia who think the charges against our compatriot are purely personal. Almost our entire society could face the same accusations on entirely legitimate grounds, because the overwhelming majority of us think exactly as he does.”

Therefore, Bzhinava’s arrest and the extremely harsh conditions of his detention aim not to counter his personal views, but to control the ideological climate in Abkhazia.

From now on, anyone who dares to criticise agreements between Russia and Abkhazia must consider the possibility of arrest on charges of “making public calls for activities directed against the security of the Russian Federation”.

We must respond appropriately to this, if only out of an instinct for self-preservation, not to mention civic solidarity. This applies to everyone: political parties, public movements, creative unions and parliament. In this case, the strength of our response will determine the extent of our freedom. We must defend Irakli Bzhinava not for his sake, but for our own.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

The case of Irakli Bzhinava

World.title: Serdar Berdimuhamedov’s energy strategy - What are the priorities of OGT 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 21. The 31st International Conference and Exhibition “Oil and Gas of Turkmenistan - 2026” (OGT 2026) opens in Ashgabat on October 21, bringing together more than 1,700 delegates from 75 countries and representatives of around 450 companies. The event will focus on the development of the oil and gas sector, attracting foreign investment, diversifying export routes, and strengthening international energy cooperation.

The forum will run through October 23 at the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Turkmenistan under the theme “Energy. Partnership. Progress.” It is organized by the state concerns Turkmengaz and Turkmennebit and the state corporation Turkmengeology in partnership with Turkmen Energy Forum. The State Oil Company of Azerbaijan (SOCAR) is the event’s general partner, underscoring the importance of regional cooperation in developing energy resources and infrastructure.

Serdar Berdimuhamedov’s strategy: From expanding hydrocarbon production to technological modernization

OGT 2026 comes as Turkmenistan pursues an energy strategy aimed at increasing hydrocarbon production, modernizing industrial facilities, expanding processing capacity, and diversifying export markets. President Serdar Berdimuhamedov has consistently identified the development of the oil and gas sector as a key priority of state policy, emphasizing the adoption of advanced technologies and the attraction of international partners.

At a meeting of the Halk Maslahaty in 2026, the president stressed the need to modernize the sector and implement major projects.

“One of the key tasks is to modernize the operations of the oil and gas complex based on advanced achievements. Major projects for the production, processing, and export of hydrocarbons, as well as the development of new fields, are being implemented on a programmatic basis,” Berdimuhamedov said.

A central pillar of this strategy is the development of the Galkynysh gas field, one of the largest in the world. In April 2026, Turkmenistan launched the fourth phase of its development in cooperation with China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC). The project includes a gas processing facility with an annual capacity of 10 billion cubic meters, as well as production wells. Its cost is estimated at approximately $5.1 billion.

The development of Galkynysh is expected to boost natural gas production, expand the country’s industrial capacity, and strengthen its position in international energy markets.

In his address to participants of OGT 2025, the president also highlighted the international dimension of Turkmenistan’s energy policy.

“Our independent, neutral Motherland, possessing enormous hydrocarbon resources, seeks to use its natural resources not only in its national interests, but also in the interests of other peoples of the region and the world,” Turkmen president said.

This approach reflects Ashgabat’s ambition to align its domestic economic priorities with regional energy cooperation, expand export opportunities, and reinforce the country’s position as a reliable energy supplier.

Preparations for OGT 2026 have also received the president’s direct attention. At a Cabinet of Ministers meeting on October 17, Berdimuhamedov instructed Deputy Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers Guvanch Agajanov to ensure that the 31st International Conference and Exhibition was organized to a high standard. The directive continues the government’s policy of supporting international industry platforms designed to promote the development of the oil and gas sector and expand cooperation with foreign partners.

What to Expect from OGT 2026

The business program will focus on further development of Galkynysh, the Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India (TAPI) gas pipeline project, and the expansion of offshore activities in the Caspian Sea.

Participants will discuss the prospects for subsequent phases of Galkynysh development, progress on the Afghan section of TAPI, and opportunities for international companies to participate in the development of Caspian fields. Particular attention will also be paid to gas processing, petrochemicals, hydrocarbon monetization, and energy infrastructure development.

Another key area will be the adoption of advanced technologies. The agenda includes digitalization, artificial intelligence, methane emissions reduction, low-carbon technologies, and renewable energy. These topics reflect the sector’s efforts to improve operational efficiency and adapt to the changing requirements of global energy markets.

The international exhibition will open on October 21, showcasing the capabilities of oil and gas companies, engineering firms, and technology providers. For the first time, the event will feature a national pavilion from Malaysia, bringing together more than 20 companies. The forum will also mark 30 years of PETRONAS operations in Turkmenistan and 20 years of cooperation between Turkmenistan and CNPC.

Participants include SOCAR, Dragon Oil, XRG, PETRONAS, CNPC, Eni, SLB, TotalEnergies EP Turkmenistan, and other international companies. In addition to plenary sessions and industry discussions, the program will feature business-to-business (B2B) and business-to-government (B2G) meetings, creating opportunities for new investment arrangements and joint projects.

Although no major contracts scheduled for signing during the forum have been announced in advance, OGT 2026 will provide a platform for discussing promising initiatives and strengthening business ties.

The conference will give Turkmenistan an opportunity to present the progress made in implementing its energy strategy, outline further plans for expanding hydrocarbon production and processing, and attract potential investors. A key challenge remains turning the country’s substantial natural resources into a foundation for long-term economic growth, export diversification, and stronger regional energy connectivity.

World.title: Sudanese drone strike on market kills more than 150
World.content:
South Sudan has accused Sudan of carrying out a series of lethal drone strikes that killed more than 150 people at a market as Sudan's war spills across its borders.

The attack on Monday targeted the Amiet market in the oil-rich Abyei region, disputed territory nestled between the two countries.

Abyei's caretaker minister of information, Yohana Akol Ngor, said 153 had been killed and that the death toll was likely to rise. He said some bodies had been burned to ashes.

"The fire is still burning, so the recovery process ‌of the dead ones is still continuing. The situation is terrible," Mr Ngor said.

A person wounded in the drone strike is carried into Ameth Bek Hospital. (Medecins Sans Frontieres via Reuters)

As residents returned to inspect the damage, flames still billowed from one building and charred vehicles could be seen next to destroyed buildings.

Sudan has been in the grip of a civil war since 2023, but escalating drone strikes between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have increasingly threatened the security of neighbouring countries.

Rubble left after a drone strike on Almiet market in disputed territory along the border between South Sudan and Sudan. (Via Reuters)

The United Nations condemned Monday's drone strike, which took the death toll from attacks in recent days to more than 250.

Three diplomatic sources, an aid ‌worker and an expert on the conflict told Reuters the strike hit a fuel depot in the market. The sources said the depot had been used in the past by Sudan's RSF for supplies.

The RSF and Sudan's armed forces did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Struggle to retrieve bodies

An eyewitness said he heard five large explosions ‌before the fuel depot caught fire.

"People started evacuating the casualties. ‌They had injuries from shrapnel on their stomach and legs … in one site, I saw 28 bodies that were burnt," he said, asking not to be named for safety reasons.

The witness said he did not see Sudan's RSF or other uniformed fighters in the market, where goods such as sugar, flour and biscuits are sold.

The market in March 2025 (top) and October 2026, after the strike. (Planet Labs via Reuters)

Mr Ngor said about 8,000 people were displaced by the attack and that the fires were hindering emergency workers efforts to retrieve dead bodies.

Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) said it was treating more than 20 wounded, some with burns, at the nearby Ameth Bek Hospital.

Photographs shared by MSF show bandaged patients lying on the floor.

Medical workers treated injured people at Ameth Bek Hospital. (Medecins Sans Frontieres via Reuters)

UN condemns attack

South Sudan's foreign ministry said it had summoned the Sudanese ambassador over the attack.

Increase in drone strikes leads to 1,000 civilian deaths in Sudan The United Nations has condemned an increase in drone attacks in conflict-torn Sudan.

South Sudan's government says it has not taken sides in its neighbour's civil war, but experts say Abyei has been established as a crucial transit point for RSF logistics.

Monday's drone strikes and escalating attacks elsewhere drew condemnation from the UN.

"We remain alarmed by the relentless drone attacks across Sudan, as well as the damage they are causing to critical infrastructure," spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said.

"These attacks are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling ‌with the consequences of more than three years of conflict."

Reuters

World.title: Christmas 'culture war' goes against premier's 'nice guy' image
World.content:
October is too early to be talking about Christmas.

Even the stores that are ever ready to capitalise on the Christmas spirit have barely started to sneak in themed goods.

And yet Christmas seems to be the only thing Tasmania can talk about right now.

Thanks largely to a social media post by the leader of the state just over a week ago, where he alerted his constituents to an apparent attempt by a school to "remove all references to Christmas in end-of-year school celebrations".

"Whatever your religion or heritage, Christmas is part of our way of life," he wrote.

"Acknowledging other traditions is important.

"But that's not a reason to abandon our own."

In the post, Mr Rockliff said he had asked the education department to step in.

The problem is, the post did not have all the facts right.

Tasmanian premier Jeremy Rockliff's Facebook post. (Facebook: Jeremy Rockliff)

School still had Christmas events in its calendar

While the government did not name an individual school (and continues to claim it's a broader issue), it became apparent, due to a social media post by Pulse Media minutes before Mr Rockliff's, that it was referring to one particular case.

The school was planning to change the name of just one event from 'Christmas on the Hill' to 'End of Year Extravaganza' and swap out carols for some pop songs.

But its calendar, which contains multiple references to Christmas, indicated there was no attempt to "remove all references to Christmas in end-of-year school celebrations".

Santa, carols and other Christmas elements will still be part of end of year celebrations at the school in question. (ABC News: Jane Cowan)

The premier's post may have been rather general, gone to an effort not to identify the school and even moderated comments, but a predictable culture war over "cancelling Christmas" unfolded from there.

It was never going to be hard to work out which school it was.

Media outlets including the Daily Mail, Sunrise and Pulse named the school, with some identifying the acting principal.

She is now on stress leave, which is pretty understandable; having a decision you made be called out publicly by the most senior person in the state, by name or not, would rattle most people.

Tasmanian minister Felix Ellis' post to Facebook earlier this week. (Facebook: Felix Ellis)

As an education department employee, the acting principal is not allowed to defend themselves and the reasons for the end-of-year changes in the same public manner.

Certain senior Liberal MPs, including the education minister, have been conspicuously silent on the issue, but elements of the party's right faction have taken it up with glee.

Treasurer Eric Abetz posted an AI-generated image of a parent consoling a child about a cancelled nativity play, while minister Felix Ellis posted a straw man argument along with a still from the iconic Christmas movie, The Grinch.

Tasmanian Treasurer Eric Abetz's full Facebook post. (Facebook: Eric Abetz)

They were just two in the very public Liberal pile-on.

Education union launches petition

The Australian Education Union (AEU) claims staff are upset and being harassed.

There are also reports of security being required at the school because of the heated online climate.

The AEU, along with Unions Tas and other MPs, are calling on the premier to apologise for his public handling of the issue, with the AEU even launching a petition.

Of course every new piece of discourse, including this one, keeps the conversation going and continues to add to the stress some are experiencing.

Almost a week on from the story breaking, the premier went public again, doubling down on his earlier comments and not apologising.

Jeremy Rockliff says "we expect our schools to acknowledge and celebrate Christmas". (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

"I believe that I have a right to voice that opinion, on behalf of our community," he wrote on Tuesday.

"Concerned parents contacted me regarding a school's decision to remove references to Christmas.

"The school's response confirmed changes were being made, out of concerns about exclusion."

Labor, which was a little slow to the party, has fully joined the parade now.

Deputy Leader Janie Finlay was on the radio earlier this week claiming that Jeremy Rockliff had lost his "nice guy" mantle.

While Labor Leader Josh Willie called out the premier for getting the facts wrong and leaning into culture wars.

"The Education Department had already confirmed there would be carols, Christmas performances and a visit from Santa, just like every other year. He knew that. He just didn't care," wrote Mr Willie.

"Words have consequences, especially when they come from the premier.

"Leaders need to hold themselves to a higher standard."

Labor's Josh Willie has joined the criticism of Jeremy Rockliff's actions. (ABC News)

In the context of a conversation about the political climate nationally, Federal Assistant Minister Rebecca White said politicians needed to dial the temperature down and lead by example.

"I know that he knows better than that," she said.

"I'd call on him to make amends for that, because I think that is a really tangible example of how we as community leaders can put forward a really civil conversation and lead by example."

For some, this whole saga feels out of character for Mr Rockliff — a man who promised to "lead with heart".

His almost quarter-of-a-decade in politics has earned him the decent guy title that Ms Finlay wants to take away.

Row over 'cancelled' Christmas deepens The row over a Tasmanian primary school's alleged "cancelling" of Christmas deepens, with government ministers doubling down with AI-generated images and other posts on social media.

When the federal Liberals leaned into the culture wars around the Voice to Parliament referendum in 2023, Mr Rockliff urged Tasmanians to support it.

Amid heightened debate over migration levels, Mr Rockliff spoke about how important migrants are and how they'll always be welcome in Tasmania.

And it was just a few months ago that he said "culture wars, frankly, do not pay the rent".

How he's found himself not only smack bang in the middle of one, but also a co-instigator of a culture war seems at odds with who he is.

Even if Mr Rockliff's intentions are good, they have ultimately caused distress for a school that even he admitted was simply making changes "out of concerns about exclusions".

For a leader who's all about inclusion, which one might argue is the intention of Christmas, this whole situation seems to be in the wrong spirit.

World.title: Fortescue senior executive sacked after sexual harassment probe
World.content:
A senior executive at Andrew Forrest's Fortescue Metals Group has been sacked following an investigation into allegations of sexual harassment and bullying at the iron ore miner.

The executive, who was not named by Fortescue in its short statement about the matter, "breached Fortescue’s policies, as well as our values", it said.

Fortescue had engaged law firm MinterEllison to examine a series of allegations about the employee's conduct.

"Sexual harassment, bullying, and other behaviour that makes people feel unsafe has no place at Fortescue," the company said.

Mining magnate Dr Andrew Forrest is the founder of Fortescue. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

" Everyone, regardless of their role or seniority, is expected to meet the standards set by our values. "

It said it would provide "ongoing support" to those who took part in the investigation.

In August, Reuters reported Fortescue had allowed the executive to continue working at the firm while the MinterEllison investigation was underway.

The company's energy chief Gus Pichot told the wire service the company was "quite confident we are following the proper process" in allowing it.

Class action by women workers

It comes after a group of female Fortescue employees launched a class action in the Federal Court against the company in June, alleging rape, sexual assault and stalking at remote FMG mine sites in WA's Pilbara.

The allegations included drink spiking, promotions offered in exchange for sexual favours and a widespread culture of sexual harassment and denigration.

Andrew 'Twiggy' Forrest warns Fortescue staff after sexual harassment class action In an email sent to all staff, Mr Forrest said: "Anyone who thinks this behaviour has a place at Fortescue is in the wrong company."

The sacking comes despite a 2023 deal with WorkSafe WA in which Fortescue agreed to spend $1.4 million on addressing inappropriate workplace behaviour after allegedly failing to supply documents about dozens of sexual harassment allegations to the work safety regulator.

Widespread harassment

FMG is not the first mining company to face claims of unsafe work practices and a toxic culture.

Hundreds of women have come forward in the two years since BHP and Rio Tinto were taken to federal court over similar allegations.

A 2022 report into the sexual harassment of women in the mining industry by a parliamentary committee found nearly three quarters of women in mining had experienced sexual harassment at work in the past five years, and that it was generally accepted in workplaces.

The scathing report found mining companies failed to recognise the problem or act on it, and while the government accepted its recommendations, not all have been enacted.

Some of these included changes to equal opportunities laws, which the WA government yesterday announced it would introduce, four years on from the landmark report.

World.title: McDonald's bid for Phillip Island restaurant knocked back by council
World.content:
An application by McDonald's to build a restaurant in the Victorian tourist hotspot of Phillip Island has been rejected after councillors voted to refuse it a planning permit.

The fast-food giant lodged its application earlier this year with the Bass Coast Shire Council to build a new restaurant in Cowes, which has a population of 6,593.

But councillors unanimously voted to reject the application, saying it was inconsistent with the local planning scheme.

The public gallery was full at Bass Coast Shire Council's meeting. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

Island ward councillor Tim O'Brien said the proposal failed the community "on so many levels".

"Where is the community benefit?" Mr O'Brien said.

"This will be muscling its way into a part of a market it had no part in building."

Councillor Mat Morgan, who is a Greens candidate at the upcoming Victorian election, said the application "should obviously be rejected" because of inappropriate residential development.

"There are a thousand ethical and moral reasons to throw this in the bin," he said.

" We don't want this, we don't need this. "

Island residents celebrate after Bass Coast Shire council's rejection of the planning permit. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

'Just so wrong'

The proposal raised the ire of thousands of residents, with more than 5,800 people signing a petition rejecting the proposal, citing traffic concerns and the threat to small businesses in town.

The no vote came after a recommendation by council officers to grant McDonald's a planning permit, which they found "acceptable" after assessing it against the planning scheme.

Councillor Jan Thompson told the meeting that the decision would likely be overturned on appeal to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT), but voted to reject the application anyway.

The plan to build a McDonald's on Phillip Island has angered some community members. (Supplied: Say No To McDonald's Cowes group)

The council received 1,543 objections and 32 submissions relating to the McDonald's application.

The proposed site is home to a petrol station and a vacant plot of land.

Cowes is the main township on Phillip Island. (Supplied: Bass Coast Shire Council)

Cowes resident and business owner, Trevor Ware, said the community's concerns were heard by the council in rejecting the proposal.

"We didn't need this and I think the community has done very well to fight it," he said.

Trevor Ware says the community has been heard. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

"There's still a big track ahead and [McDonald's] are going to push very hard. We just can't let it just ride through.

"The way it's been approached and the area that they put it in so close to the school, everything was just so wrong."

McDonald's Australia has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Cairns rape trial judge retires to consider verdict
World.content:
A judge has retired to consider whether a teenager who held a man at knifepoint during a Cairns home invasion is also guilty of raping the man's partner.

The judge-only, three-day trial in the Childrens Court of Queensland, sitting in Cairns, hinged on one question: whether the boy heard a co-offender tell the woman he intended to sexually assault her.

The defendants and victims cannot be identified for legal reasons.

Evidence heard in closed court by Judge Joshua Treviño KC included pre-recorded evidence from the couple and the boy, as well as evidence from police.

The teenager was one of three boys who broke into a home in the Cairns suburb of Manunda about 3am on February 21 last year.

The couple were woken by burglars in their bedroom.

The court heard while the defendant held the man at knifepoint, his two co-accused took the woman to other parts of the house and raped her multiple times.

The two co-accused have pleaded guilty to rape, and their cases remain before the courts.

The defendant has pleaded guilty to six charges, including stealing, going armed in company and detaining the couple in their home, but has pleaded not guilty to five counts of rape.

Manunda is an inner suburb of Cairns, Queensland. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

Police interview played in court

Yesterday, the court was shown the boy's police interview after his arrest, in which he appeared shocked when Detective Senior Constable Damon Smalley told him the details of the rape.

"I did not know anything about that. I was in the room with the other person and holding him in the room," the boy said.

When Senior Constable Smalley, from the Police Child Protection and Investigation Unit, asked whether he had at any point tried to stop anything happening to the woman, the boy replied: "No."

Damon Smalley leaves Cairns Courthouse after a video of his interview with the defendant was shown in the Queensland Childrens Court trial. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

Defence barrister Timothy Grau argued his client never intended to be involved in a sexual assault and instead believed his co-offenders were only robbing the woman.

He told the court the boy either did not hear or did not understand what one of his co-accused said about the woman before she was led from the bedroom.

"At that point, that she's being removed from the bedroom to leave the room, at that point the conversation, it's about [stealing] wallets and money," Mr Grau said.

"So, the purpose of his detention … is a robbery."

The court also heard the boy believed he would be stabbed by his co-accused if he did not detain the man.

Timothy Grau (left) argued his client failed to hear and understand his co-offenders would rape the victim. (ABC Far North: Conor Byrne)

Crown case

Crown prosecutor Nicole Friedewald told the court her case relied on the evidence of the woman's partner.

She said the man heard one of the co-accused say he intended to sexually assault the woman as she was led from the bedroom at knifepoint to get her wallet.

The court heard the boy was told to get a knife from the kitchen and hold the man in the room.

"The suggestion he did not hear that statement … and did not respond to it, as [the man] has given evidence, defies logic and belief," Ms Friedewald said.

The trial included lengthy exchanges between the judge, prosecution and defence over how the rape charge would or would not apply to someone who had no physical contact with the victim.

Ms Friedewald argued the boy was criminally responsible under Section 7 of the Queensland Criminal Code, because he aided and enabled the rapes by keeping the woman's partner from stopping them.

"He was, in those circumstances, the only person who could have intervened, who could have protected that complainant, and he was prevented by this defendant from doing so," she said.

Joshua Treviño is presiding over the judge-only trial in the Cairns Courthouse. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

Her alternative argument relied on Section 8 of the code, which says those who share a common intention to carry out an unlawful purpose can be held responsible for offences committed along the way.

She also pointed to provisions of the Evidence Act 1977, recognising that people involved in non-consensual sexual activity may give differing accounts and respond in different ways, and that victims do not need to have been physically injured or threatened.

Judge Treviño told the court he intended to reach a decision as soon as possible.

The Queensland government added rape to its adult crime, adult time reforms three months after the offending alleged in this case took place.

World.title: Child safety failed to recognise coercive control in Struhs case, inquest hears
World.content:
Child safety workers failed to recognise the significant coercive control that Elizabeth Struhs's mother and fringe church group were subjecting on her father when assessing the eight-year-old's future risk of harm, an inquest has heard.

Elizabeth Struhs's body was found at her Toowoomba home in January 2022 after her father Jason Struhs stopped providing her insulin for her type 1 diabetes.

Elizabeth Struhs died in 2022 after her parents withheld her insulin for her type 1 diabetes. (Supplied)

He had recently converted to a sect named The Saints, which his wife Kerrie Struhs was a member of.

The group holds anti-medical intervention views and instead believed that God would save Elizabeth.

Limited focus on coercive control

An inquest probing various government agencies' involvement in the case has so far run for a week and a half and heard from more than 20 witnesses.

Today a child safety worker gave evidence about various mistakes she said were made in Elizabeth's initial risk assessment and resulting case plan.

"Child safety were too narrowly focused on Elizabeth's diabetes management and failed to identify the power imbalance of Mr and Mrs Struhs," she said.

Jason and Kerrie Struhs were each sentenced to 14 years for their daughter's manslaughter, after first being acquitted of murder. (ABC News: Sharon Gordon)

According to the child safety witness, staff "failed to identify the serious risk of harm Mrs Struhs's beliefs surrounding medical intervention could have had on Elizabeth", as well as the presence of domestic and family violence.

She said the case plan identified just one form of abuse, when there were two.

"Exposure to domestic and family violence in terms of coercive control," she said.

Religious group members found guilty of causing 8yo's death All 14 members of a fringe religious group have been found guilty of the manslaughter of eight-year-old Elizabeth Struhs, who died after her insulin was withheld.

The woman said if staff had recognised that factor they would have looked at other ways to support Jason Struhs.

"To withstand the coercive control, if possible, that was occurring in relation to the importance of the religious beliefs of Mrs Struhs and their older children which then weighed heavily on Jason," she said.

The Brisbane Corconer's Court heard on Friday, Elizabeth risk of future neglect should have also been flagged at various stages, including when Mrs Struhs was questioned by a doctor and two child safety workers.

The child safety worker said, while every person has a right to their own beliefs, they must still, by law, ensure a child's protection and safety.

Jason Struhs stopped providing his daughter with insulin for her type 1 diabetes following his conversion to the same religious sect as his wife.

Missed chance to intervene

In mid-2019 Elizabeth was taken to hospital in a comatose state by her father against her mother's wishes, which is when the Child Safety Department became involved, and required the couple to sign an intervention with parental agreement (IPA) which stipulated Mr Struhs would continue providing Elizabeth with her lifesaving medicine, and that Kerrie Struhs wouldn't intervene.

In 2021 Kerrie Struhs spent several months in jail over the incident.

It was at this stage, the inquest heard, that her husband converted to the sect, falling "into their hold, coercive control and belief system", which was a "very significant event in terms of what caused or contributed to Elizabeth's death".

The family signed an agreement that Jason Struhs would continue providing Elizabeth with her lifesaving medicine, and that Kerrie Struhs would not intervene. (Supplied: Supreme Court of Queensland)

Counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris questioned the child safety worker over whether the department should have intervened when Kerrie Struhs was first sent to jail.

She said that fact would have been viewed as a positive that would have reduced Elizabeth's risk rather than increased it, and pointed to Jason Struhs's swift conversion to the sect as a major complicating factor.

"It would have been very hard to predict."

In 2025 Mr and Mrs Struhs were each sentenced to 14 years for their daughter's manslaughter, after first being acquitted of murder.

Eleven other members of The Saints were sentenced to between six and nine years in prison for their involvement.

World.title: Plea offer rethink for man accused of harassing federal MP
World.content:
Prosecutors are reconsidering a plea offer put to a man accused of sending multiple harassing emails to a South Australian MP due to recent events, a court has heard.

Ronald Dean Munro, 74, was today scheduled to enter pleas in the Adelaide Magistrates Court to 10 counts of using a carriage service in a harassing or offensive way for allegedly sending "menacing" emails to the member for Spence, Matt Burnell.

But, prosecutors told the court they were re-thinking their position on the matter.

"We have previously had some negotiations in relation to this matter, but prosecution is presently reconsidering the plea offer put to consolidate the charges and is not presently in a position to maintain our previously foreshadowed agreement," the prosecutor said.

Federal Labor MP Matt Burnell was elected in 2022 to the seat of Spence in Adelaide's northern suburbs. (ABC News)

The development in the case came two days after an unrelated incident where a man allegedly drove his vehicle into federal MP Helen Haines in Wangaratta outside her electorate office.

Mr Munro's defence lawyer, James Caldicott, told the court he was in the process of taking instructions from his client about the proposed plea deal when he was informed about the prosecution's change of position.

"Dynamically things have changed in recent times which has caused a reconsideration by the Commonwealth director as to how matters of this type ought to proceed," Mr Caldicott said.

He said the matter was now "destined for trial".

According to court documents, Mr Munro, of Elizabeth South in Adelaide's northern suburbs, allegedly sent emails that "reasonable persons would regard as being, in all the circumstances, menacing, harassing or offensive" between May 2023 and December 2025.

They alleged emails were sent to Mr Burnell's official email address twice in 2023, on May 2 and November 30, and three times in 2024, on May 12, August 4 and August 20.

They further alleged Mr Munro sent a further five emails in 2025, on June 6 and 17, July 14 and 15 and on December 31.

Mr Munro did not enter any pleas and the matter was adjourned for two weeks.

Ronald Dean Munro spoke briefly outside of court to media today. (ABC News)

Outside court, Mr Munro said he would be pleading not guilty to the charges.

At the time of his arrest in February, AFP detective and acting superintendent Simon Lalic said the federal agency took all allegations relating to the safety and security of Australian parliamentarians "seriously".

"The AFP supports freedom of speech and political expression, but does not tolerate criminal behaviour, including threats and harassment," he said.

The AFP today said no further comment could be made as the matter was before the courts.

World.title: Prisoner allegedly shackled, separated from newborn after C-section
World.content:
An Indigenous woman has allegedly been shackled and separated from her newborn baby at a north Queensland hospital.

The woman delivered her baby via caesarean section at Townsville Hospital on October 10 while in custody.

Prison officers allegedly restrained her in the maternity unit following the birth while her newborn was taken to the neonatal intensive care unit.

Nurses and midwives involved in the care escalated concerns about the use of restraints to Queensland Corrective Services (QCS).

A QCS spokesperson said it was reviewing the management of the patient because "restraints are only ever used as a last resort on pregnant prisoners".

The woman was not restrained during labour or surgery.

Minister for Corrective Services Laura Gerber said she had been briefed by her department on the incident.

"A pregnant woman can only be restrained as a last resort due to public safety," she said.

"In this instance … the woman was not restrained during the delivery of the baby."

Laura Gerber says she has been made aware of the incident. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

The investigation comes as Queensland MP Jonty Bush this week launched a petition to prohibit the use of restraints on women during labour, childbirth and immediately after birth.

Queensland Nurses and Midwives' Union assistant secretary Fridae King said the union strongly opposed shackling during childbirth and labour.

"The use of restraints during labour and birth is traumatising and may compromise care," Ms King said.

"There must be a national prohibition on the use of restraints in pregnancy, childbirth and post birth, and the upholding of the human rights and dignity of women."

'What does last resort mean?'

Townsville-based female prisoner advocate Tahlia Isaac said prison officers made a "values-based judgement" when deciding to restrain prisoners.

She said that in her experience working with female prisoners, restraints had never been used as a last resort.

"They're saying it's used as a last resort, but what does it actually mean?" Ms Isaac said.

"It's up to the individual officer's determination as to whether it's an exceptional circumstance."

Tahlia Isaac wants to see a ban on restraining pregnant prisoners during childbirth. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

She said there were psychological impacts on the child if their mother was restrained.

"The child is trying to bond with its mother," she said.

"The impact that has on the child … it can last for years."

Last week in the Senate, Labor and the Coalition voted down Victorian senator Lidia Thorpe's bill prohibiting shackling during childbirth.

Musician Lily Allen has cancelled a concert in Auckland hours before it was due to take place, citing ill health, two days before she is due to start her Australian tour.

The artist is touring her album West End Girl, which in part tracks the breakdown of her relationship with actor David Harbour, and was scheduled to perform at Auckland’s Spark Arena before heading to Australia for a series of concerts in Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne and Perth.

Lily Allen performs West End Girl in April in Los Angeles. Getty Images for Live Nation

There are presently no publicly stated changes to her planned Australian schedule, which is due to start on Friday October 23 at the Brisbane Entertainment Centre.

A spokesperson for tour promoter Frontier said on Wednesday afternoon: “Lily is resting and recuperating, with the full intention of completing the rest of the tour in Australia as planned.”

World.title: Victoria Barracks must stay in public hands, with greater public access
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life Editorial Victoria Barracks must stay in public hands, with greater public access The Herald's View Editorial October 21, 2026 — 4:24pm

October 21, 2026 — 4:24pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Victoria Barracks is one of the jewels in Sydney’s crown. Convict labour built the elegant buildings quarried from Hawkesbury sandstone and the site, regarded as the spiritual and historical home of the Australian Army, is poised to begin an uncertain new life. Following an independent audit of the national defence estate, Defence Minister Richard Marles last February announced Victoria Barracks was part of a plan to divest the government of 67 Defence properties, including other Victoria Barracks in Melbourne and Brisbane. Matt Golding The aim was to raise $3 billion and avoid $100 million annual upkeep costs, with savings ploughed back into the Defence budget. Marles said Victoria Barracks needed to be returned to Sydneysiders and Australians, and dismissed objections to the sale by retired generals – including former governor general Sir Peter Cosgrove – by likening the historic facility to a glorified wine cellar that was a watering hole for old officers. “It is not my priority for Defence to be a heritage organisation. It’s not my priority to see Defence manage the oldest wine cellar in Australia,” he said. “It’s nice that it’s at Victoria Barracks Sydney, but it’s not core interest in terms of defending the country.”



Related Article Note From The Editor Sydney can change while preserving its treasures His comments caused an uproar and followed heavy and sometimes orchestrated pushbacks from veterans’ groups, former prime ministers Paul Keating, John Howard and Tony Abbott, Premier Chris Minns and federal, state and local politicians from across the spectrum, business and respected military leaders and heritage bodies. RSL NSW said Australia could not afford to permanently surrender such an important piece of military heritage – particularly at a time of increasing global uncertainty. Its location close to the Sydney CBD also gave the site continuing strategic value, including the potential to support Defence operations and responses to future security incidents or emergencies affecting the nation’s largest city. The Herald’s Matthew Knott reported Marles was aiming for the Australian Army to be out by Christmas. On Sunday, the Save Victoria Barracks Alliance will rally to pressure Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to intervene and stop the sale and keep it a Defence facility over concerns about losses of public land, military heritage and morale among serving members.



At present, the site houses the Headquarters Forces Command, Headquarters 2nd Health Brigade, offices, a museum, cadet training facilities and residential accommodation. While Victoria Barracks remains an active military establishment, the public currently has limited access to the museum or to undertake guided tours. High sandstone walls and a strong security regimen keep the site mostly locked away from citizens. The value of the site to the modern defence forces is debatable. But its value to the community is undeniable. The only way it can be truly protected in perpetuity is to ensure it does not pass into private ownership. The magnificent architecture and elegant grounds are a singular and great link with Sydney’s past; a torch passed down the generations. The barracks must remain in public hands, and the public given far greater access to this historic gem. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.
