World.title: Reserve Bank in ‘nightmare’ position as it considers another rate rise in November
World.content:
PoliticsFederalRBA Reserve Bank in ‘nightmare’ position as it considers another rate rise in November Shane Wright October 21, 2026 — 4:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Reserve Bank’s deputy governor has warned mortgage holders and businesses the bank is facing “hard choices” in its bid to bring down inflation amid warnings it risks pushing the country into recession. Andrew Hauser used an event in Sydney on Wednesday to argue the RBA was facing a “central bankers’ nightmare” with signs that some businesses believe an inflation rate of between 3 and 3.5 per cent could be the new norm for Australia – well above the bank’s 2-3 per cent target it has struggled to hit over the past four years. RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser says the battle to bring down inflation is a hard task. Dominic Lorrimer A key factor is the surge in global oil prices which overnight touched $US110 a barrel. The Reserve, in its most recent set of economic forecasts released in August, had expected oil to be around $US80 a barrel. Hauser said the nation’s inflation pressures were not improving.



“I don’t know for sure, but a few things are clear, and the inflation outlook looks materially worse than we projected in August,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

Interest rates RBA’s worst nightmare as oil pushes up inflation threat “The challenge that’s facing the board and has done for some time is do you do more to tackle higher inflation, recognising that that means weaker activity, weaker labour market,” he said. “[Or] do we hold our horses to protect the labour market, try and protect some of the labour market … but accept the risk in so doing is that this upside inflation risk embeds, and that becomes more expensive to deal with? “Those are hard choices; they’re not where we’d like to be ideally as the central bank.”



The comments had an immediate impact on financial markets which had put the chance of a rate rise next month at one in four. They are now closer to 50-50. Hauser, who sits on the RBA’s interest rate setting committee that will next meet on November 2 and 3, said the war in Iran - and its impact on oil prices - had dragged on far longer than most central banks had been expecting. This had added to the inflation pressures caused by the AI data centre building boom and overall demand across the economy. But he noted that the bank’s four rate rises this year were having an impact. “Monetary policy is working,” he said.



“The labour market is easing, consumption growth is quite tepid, but there are still pockets of growth, and the inflation outlook has deteriorated. So that’s a pretty tricky balance.” Commonwealth Bank chief economist Luke Yeaman this week warned the Reserve could push the economy “over the edge” if it lifted interest rates to 4.85 per cent at its November meeting. On Wednesday, Betashares chief economist David Bassanese joined Yeaman in warning the RBA was risking an Australian recession with tight monetary policy. “The RBA seems increasingly prepared to risk a recession to get inflation down – given it has been above target for an extended period and it is sensing evidence of rising inflation expectations within the community,” he said. “The RBA – along with other central banks – has likely become less confident the Iran war will end anytime soon and more appreciative of the upside inflation pressures the AI boom is causing, at least in the short term.”



An ongoing concern for the bank has been low productivity growth, prompting demands from the business community for the federal government to put in place measures to boost productivity. But Hauser, who previously worked with the Bank of England, said local businesses had their role to play. He said it appeared “something of an Australian thing” to demand the government solve a problem when there had been a sharp fall in business investment over recent years which was probably a factor in low productivity growth. “There is a joint obligation, I think, not just on government but also on business to get their arms around this productivity challenge and to embrace what could actually be a very positive future for Australia,” he said.



Treasurer Jim Chalmers, in an interview with CNBC, said the war in the Middle East was causing problems for all economies due to its impact on oil prices. “The war in the Middle East has been pushing up inflation around the world, and in Australia, it’s been weighing on growth around the world and in Australia as well, and pushing up borrowing costs at the same time,” he said. “So, from an economic point of view, the war in the Middle East has created a very difficult set of conditions for a lot of countries, including ours. You can see it in our inflation, which is a bit higher than we would like. We can see it in our growth. You can see it in other areas as well.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: ‘Got away with murder’: Man faces trial over 2014 death of Kirra-Lea McLoughlin
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts ‘Got away with murder’: Man faces trial over 2014 death of Kirra-Lea McLoughlin Cloe Read October 21, 2026 — 4:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A man accused of killing his partner told a new girlfriend he felt guilty of the death after having gone into a violent rage, smashing her head into the ground or a wall over claims she had slept with a teenage neighbour, a court has heard. Kirra-Lea McLoughlin, 27, died in July 2014 after an argument with her partner Paul Alan McDonald, who is accused of manslaughter. Wolvi mother Kirra-Lea McLoughlin. Facebook For much of McDonald’s first day of trial in the Supreme Court in Brisbane on Wednesday, he sat looking down, at times shaking his head slightly at some of the evidence being heard. In the hours before McLoughlin died in her Wolvi home, near Gympie, north of Brisbane, there had been a physical fight between her and McDonald’s sister after things had escalated following discussions about McLoughlin’s relationship with a 17-year-old neighbour, the court heard.



Key evidence in the prosecution case is that four years after McLoughlin’s death, McDonald had spoken with a new girlfriend, Jade Vandenberg, about the night of McLoughlin’s death. She told police McDonald had claimed he felt guilty for letting his sister feel responsible for McLoughlin’s death. Crown Prosecutor David Nardone told the court McDonald had confided in Vandenberg, who has since died, about him going into a violent rage before grabbing McLoughlin by the shoulders. “He told Ms Vandenberg that he was upset with [McLoughlin] for having had sex with the neighbour, that he became violent, banging and shaking her head into the floor or a wall,” Nardone said. Ms Vandenberg said in a message to McDonald’s sister the accused said he “kept smashing her head into the floor and panicked when she wouldn’t wake up and tried putting her in the shower”, the court heard.



Years later, in a phone call with his mother discussing his conversations with Vandenberg, McDonald said he feared she would dob him in, Nardone said. McDonald had told the new girlfriend that night he had ended up “sorting it out” with McLoughlin and the pair had had sex that night, the court heard. “She described himself as having got away with murder,” Nardone said. He told his mother it was Vandenberg’s word against his, and he had done “nothing wrong”, the court heard. That night neighbours reported hearing yelling and banging from the home, Nardone said.



McDonald’s sister, Tamiqua McDonald, testified that she had heard the pair talking about how McLoughlin had a relationship with the 17-year-old neighbour, and that McDonald wanted a lie detector test. She said her brother and McLoughlin got into an argument, with McLoughlin hitting her brother in the face. McLoughlin threw a glass at the back of Tamiqua’s head after she intervened in the altercation, she told the court. She then punched McLoughlin in the face, causing her to fall. “She was just yelling she was going to kill me,” she said. The court heard McDonald was trying to defuse the situation when McLoughlin had grabbed a baseball bat and went to swing at him.



Tamiqua intervened, throwing the bat off the veranda. Another member of the family also intervened, throwing red paint, causing both McDonald and McLoughlin to slip. Several people left the property, with McLoughlin staying at the house. Later that evening about 11pm, she could be heard yelling in the background of one of McDonald’s calls. At 2.46am the following morning, a call was made from the house to 13HEALTH, which appeared to be a hang-up call. Another call was also made to another health line for 36 seconds, but the content of the calls were not known, the court heard. The following day, July 17, 2014, about 1pm, McDonald phoned his brother telling him McLoughlin was unresponsive. The brother advised calling 13HEALTH.



At 2.06pm, McDonald called the health line, explaining that McLoughlin had taken more than 20 pills. McDonald called triple zero, and McLoughlin was rushed to hospital, where medical teams found she had more than 100 bruises, and a spongy area on her scalp. She was airlifted to the Gold Coast for treatment, where it was determined she had suffered a severe brain injury. Medical tests did not show signs of an overdose. McLoughlin died the following day on July 18. The judge-alone trial before Justice Peter Davis continues.



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service (1800RESPECT) on 1800 737 732. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Worse and worse’: Data centre backlash threatens billions in building boom
World.content:
Updated PoliticsFederalInvestigations ‘Worse and worse’: Data centre backlash threatens billions in building boom Clay Lucas and Nick Toscano Updated October 21, 2026 — 4:16pm ,first published 11:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

What began as a community protest in Melbourne’s inner west over giant electricity poles being installed on quiet residential streets has now rocked the nation’s highest-profile data centre developer, as it scrambles to find a new way to supply energy to its flagship facility. On Wednesday, ASX-listed NextDC announced it would slash its expected profits and construction spending, as it deals with delays in getting more electricity supply into its West Footscray M3 data centre. NextDC’s M3 data centre in West Footscray. Joe Armao The news triggered a share price collapse that wiped about $3 billion off the company’s valuation and sparked a warning from investors and analysts that a mounting community backlash across Australia against data centres posed a worsening threat to the booming sector. Plans to build dozens of new data centres across the country are running into social opposition, partly due to the vast amounts of electricity needed to run their high-intensity computing and cooling systems, and the proximity of some sites to people’s homes.



“Community concerns around data centre developments present a real risk to the timing of delivery of contracted capacity for data centre owners,” said RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Beadle, pointing to NextDC’s earnings cut and warning that local opposition could disrupt projects. Some of the new Jemena power lines in a Yarraville residential street, with the NextDC data centre in the background (left), which caused locals to rally against them. Joe Armao One of the new power poles alongside an existing wooden pole. Jason South That residential pushback has hit other projects nationwide: developer Green Square was recently forced to pull a proposed project in Western Australia, Goodman Group shelved a $1.2 billion facility in Sydney’s Lane Cove, and private developer Firmus was forced to abandon a planned $44 billion stock market float. The news for the data centre industry “keeps getting worse and worse”, Ten Cap portfolio manager Jun Bei Liu said, particularly for developers with unbuilt facilities where customers hold contract-termination rights if projects are delayed.



Last week, Microsoft pulled out of a deal to anchor a flagship facility in the United Kingdom following power-supply delays. “What’s happening with NextDC highlights the risk for companies that have secured energy and water, but whose facilities are not yet built,” she said. “These risks are playing out in real time. There will definitely be more investor scrutiny now.” NextDC came out of its two-day trading halt on Wednesday, warning investors that the next stages of the politically contentious M3 development – which sits just metres from some West Footscray residents’ front gates – would also not be approved until after next month’s Victorian election. A community blockade in September, revealed by this masthead, hit electricity distributor Jemena’s rollout of 15-metre-tall 66,000-volt residential power poles. Direct action by residents included blockading streets by parking cars and light trucks where power poles were to be installed, co-ordinating via WhatsApp groups to ignore door-knocks from contractors, and filling excavation pits with green waste.



The protests, and subsequent local political backlash, saw Jemena halt powerline construction until at least February. It will leave NextDC without extra power it needs to keep expanding its West Footscray data centre. Yarraville resident Milco Bogoevski was among those who led the community protest to halt Jemena. He said while he was sympathetic to data centre operators – “no one here wants to see industry fail” – what had happened was the direct result of power companies and businesses not listening to residents. A sign in Sanderson Street, Yarraville, in September. Jason South “These power lines, this material, it was going to be in our street, we were going to have to deal with it for decades after they left – power operators like Jemena, and businesses like NextDC, they’re going to need to engage more with the community.” Bogoevski said community opposition to the West Footscray data centre and the impact of other data centres in Melbourne’s west could help swing seats in the November 28 election. “The state government is responsible for electricity – it comes down to them. There’s a good chance an issue like this could flip this seat away from Labor,” he said.



The market reaction against NextDC was sharp: its shares collapsed on Wednesday to as low as $5.07 – down more than 40 per cent from their Monday closing price of $9.57. The price recovered slightly and shares were trading at $5.53 at about 3.30pm, still a far cry from the peak of $17.22 a year ago. NextDC also revealed it was putting the brakes on its wider construction pipeline, in a move that could alarm state and federal governments as data centre construction has provided a rare bright spot in the sluggish Australian economy. The company had planned to spend up to $5.75 billion on construction in the coming financial year, but will now spend between $4.5 billion and $5 billion. NextDC chief executive Craig Scroggie said the company, as well as pausing expectations from its West Footscray project, would also halt speculative expansion projects and land buys not already locked in. “With [West Footscray] revenue deferred, we have paused projects not backed by customer contracts and put that capital behind the capacity our customers have already contracted,” he said.



Scroggie said the company was working with Jemena on community consultation and considering other options. “We’re working with them on alternative routes that may be feasible, and alternative locations for such poles and undergrounding,” he said, although noting that undergrounding the cables would take more time. He also flagged political uncertainty as a challenge for the project as NextDC awaits planing approval for the final expansion at M3. “It has been with the Victorian government and planning minister for a very long time, and when the Victorian government went through recent portfolio changes and the Premier changed, obviously the decisions in relation to approvals and other things slowed down,” he said. NextDC’s market shock represents the clearest evidence yet that Victoria’s rapid push to attract power-hungry artificial intelligence infrastructure has run into severe grid constraints and suburban backlash.

World.title: ‘Where will they go?’: Barracks eviction sparks fears for families and morale
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life ‘Where will they go?’: Barracks eviction sparks fears for families and morale David Barwell October 21, 2026 — 4:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Military families face being evicted from Sydney’s historic Victoria Barracks by the end of the year as the federal government’s push to sell the historic site sparks mounting concerns over the use of public land, heritage and Defence Force morale. Critics of the proposed sale warn plans to relocate up to 12 families, including children, are being rushed, without arrangements to secure alternative accommodation alongside the hundreds of other personnel who live, work and serve at the Paddington site. RSL NSW President Vince Williams has criticised plans to relocate personnel before suitable replacement accommodation has been secured. Sitthixay Ditthavong The concerns have united a group of politicians, business leaders, sporting identities and senior military figures under the Save Victoria Barracks Alliance, which will hold a public rally on Sunday urging Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to keep the site in public hands. Former prime minister John Howard said he would speak at the rally on Sunday to demonstrate the “depths of community resentment” over the proposal.



The rally follows the government’s decision to include Victoria Barracks among 67 Defence properties earmarked for full or partial sale after an independent review of ageing and underused military assets. The program aims to raise up to $3 billion for other Defence priorities. The demonstration also comes after a separate rally this month when hundreds turned out at Balmoral to oppose the partial sale of the HMAS Penguin. Skywriting over Balmoral Beach during the HMAS Penguin protest earlier this month. Oscar Colman But critics question whether the financial benefits justify selling a site that remains operational and has played a central role in Australian military history for 178 years. As of December 2025, up to 250 permanent Australian Defence Force personnel were based at the barracks, alongside 50-100 public servants, 150-200 reservists and 50-100 cadets.



The site also houses the Headquarters Forces Command, Headquarters 2nd Health Brigade, offices, a museum, cadet training facilities and residential accommodation. Defence has proposed moving administrative personnel to Defence Plaza Sydney, about two kilometres away, while cadets could relocate to Randwick Barracks or community facilities and schools. However, the department has not publicly detailed the intended location of every operational unit or affected military household. Political and community leaders including Business Sydney executive director Paul Nicolaou, former Wallabies captain Simon Poidevin, Manly MP James Griffin, Coogee MP Marjorie O’Neill, RSL NSW president Vince Williams, Senator Jessica Collins, Woollahra Mayor Sarah Dixson, and Wentworth MP Allegra Spender urge the federal government to reverse its controversial decision to sell off the Victoria Barracks. Sitthixay Ditthavong Uncertainty has been compounded by conflicting signals over the timetable. In September, a Defence planning order requiring personnel to leave by December 19 was rescinded, with the department describing it as having been “erroneously” issued after details emerged publicly. Defence later said relocations would begin in the fourth quarter of the year, subject to workforce and operational requirements, and that no final decisions had been made about where personnel would be based.



A Defence spokesperson said in a statement a consultation process had begun, with most personnel expected to move off-site before the end of 2026. “The transition and divestment of Victoria Barracks Sydney will be managed carefully and sensitively, supporting our people, families and the broader Defence community while preserving its heritage, history and legacy,” the spokesperson said. The proposed sale of the Paddington barracks has sparked debate between those pushing for more housing and those who believe it is too special to touch. Wolter Peeters Defence Minister Richard Marles has signalled the government wants to move quickly. Questioned last month, he said he expected Defence would leave the affected sites “as soon as possible”. Liberal Senator Jess Collins, who is chairing a Senate inquiry into the planned sales, said serving personnel were unable to publicly express their views despite growing concern about the consequences.



“The army has been gagged. The Defence Force cannot speak up about it,” Collins said. Retired vice-admiral Vince Williams, president of RSL NSW, which represents 33,000 former and serving Defence personnel, criticised plans to relocate personnel before suitable replacement accommodation had been secured. Defence Minister Richard Marles at the historic Victoria Barracks in Paddington Peter Rae “It’s appalling, kicking people out in a hurry and sticking them into an office tower in Pitt Street, or into bunk beds in Randwick Barracks without having replacement full-time accommodation sorted out beforehand,” he said. “It’s the message it’s sending that is terrible for morale.”



The alliance has attracted support from state and federal politicians crossing party lines, as well as business and sporting figures. Marjorie O’Neill, the NSW Labor member for Coogee, has described Victoria Barracks as the army’s “spiritual home”. Independent federal MP for Wentworth Allegra Spender said community sentiment favoured retaining the site in public hands. Related Article City life Why this slice of land on Sydney Harbour might be harder to sell than expected “This is not something that needs to be turned into a boutique hotel or a wedding venue,” she said. Former Wallabies captain Simon Poidevin, whose grandfather served at the barracks during World War I, said finding replacement housing in the expensive eastern suburbs at short notice was a serious concern.



“They’ve got kids and families, they’re active members of surf clubs and sporting groups and they’re now asking where will they go,” he said. “They love working here. They’re proud to work here. They don’t want to go and work in a soulless city building which has no connection to the Defence Force.” The financial case for the sale has also come under scrutiny. Defence has declined to disclose estimates of the expected proceeds, telling the Senate inquiry that releasing the figures could “diminish” the Commonwealth’s negotiating position in achieving market value. The Department of Finance, which is coordinating the sales program, told the inquiry that spending on external advisers had totalled $2.72 million as of August 31, including $1.66m in management fees paid to KPMG as its strategic industry partner. Organisers of Sunday’s rally say the event could attract thousands. Originally planned outside the barracks’ main gates, the demonstration has been relocated to Moore Park near Kippax Lake on advice from NSW Police about crowd size and public safety.



Howard on Wednesday said he would “strongly oppose” any attempt to sell off the site. “Like many in the community I resent the Albanese government’s indifference to our proud national and military history in proposing the sale of sites which are part of that history,” Howard said in a statement. World.title: Heart attacks to premature births: Experts are sounding the alarm on Melbourne’s next hot summer
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaMelbourne Assembly Heart attacks to premature births: Experts are sounding the alarm on Melbourne’s next hot summer Melissa Cunningham October 21, 2026 — 4:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As another El Nino summer approaches, health experts are raising the alarm over the potentially fatal consequences of higher temperatures and an increased number of hot days expected around the state. Mounting research showing soaring temperatures can increase rates of stillbirth and premature birth, trigger heart attacks, worsen mental health and exacerbate chronic illnesses comes amid warnings that Victorian emergency departments remain severely underprepared for a surge in heatwaves that are forecast to lead to record-shattering death tolls. The sun rises over Melbourne on a hot morning last year. Jason South As part of this week’s Melbourne Assembly civic forum, The Age has been exploring big ideas for the future of the city, including how infrastructure and housing can be transformed to protect residents from the rise in dangerously high temperatures. Professor Ollie Jay, academic director of the Heat and Health Research Centre at the University of Sydney, said extreme heat cost the Australian economy more than $6 billion in lost productivity every year.



“Basically, we’ve got this hazard, which is extreme heat and chronic hot weather that is growing undeniably in Australia,” Jay says. Related Article Sorry, your browser doesn't support embedded videos. City life As Melbourne gets hotter, some suburbs suffer more than others “On top of that, you’ve also got a shift in the population where we have a progressively ageing population, and we’ve got an increased prevalence of chronic diseases like cardiovascular disease and kidney disease.” A growing body of research has laid bare the implications of extreme heat on ageing populations, with a landmark study published in The Lancet Planetary Health in August warning the impacts of heatwaves on people aged 60 and over have been underestimated. Researchers found people in this group face an increase in serious health risks directly linked to rising temperatures, and will bear the brunt of increasingly frequent spells of extreme heat.



But it’s not just the heat. Rising humidity also hinders sweat from evaporating, which is the body’s primary physiological mechanism to keep cool. Related Article Melbourne Assembly ‘As tall as you can go’: The NYC-style density plan for Melbourne’s future Wind can also affect human thermal states, and direct sun exposure can make an environment feel at least 15 degrees hotter than the official shade temperature reading. “What most people don’t realise is that official temperatures are recorded in the shade,” Jay says. Protecting people from rising extreme heat requires urgent action now, he says, including implementing targeted building and landscape interventions – such as external shutters and reflective roofs – to reduce heat risk.



As part of their work, Jay and a team of researchers have reviewed global literature to evaluate over 70 cooling interventions, grading more than 20 building-level strategies based on cost, effectiveness, and scientific evidence. Among the top interventions measured by effectiveness are air conditioning; street trees and urban canopies; outdoor shade structures such as arcades; and reflective roofs (also known as cool roofs) designed to bounce back more sunlight and absorb less heat than standard dark roofs. Jay says that among the greatest challenges for a city like Melbourne is tackling the urban heat island effect – a phenomenon created by poorly designed buildings, roads and footpaths, which can make temperatures vary by as much as 6 degrees across different parts of the city, particularly in fast-growing suburbs. Researchers Dr Sarah Robertson (left) and Dr Rebecca Olive at RMIT University’s Centre for Urban Research. Chris Hopkins Extreme heat is a conundrum that Dr Sarah Robertson, a research fellow at RMIT University’s Centre for Urban Research, has dedicated years to, as she examines ways to make climate resilient and safe housing.



Robertson says one of the biggest day-to-day issues is much of Victoria’s existing housing was built before the introduction of energy efficiency and thermal performance standards came in. “We need to focus on improving the quality of our existing housing so it’s thermally comfortable, energy efficient, and affordable for people,” she says, adding that existing housing should be retrofitted or upgraded. Related Article Climate solutions The simple fix that will cool our streets – if only we get it right Robertson also says the introduction of minimum standards for rental properties, which will come into effect from next year, will be a catalyst for change. “It means for the first time, rental properties have to have ceiling insulation [and] be draft proof, so gaps and around doors and windows sealed up, and have fixed cooling in the living room installed at the point of lease or sale,” she says.



Robertson’s colleague, research fellow Dr Rebecca Olive, has focused her attention on outdoor public spaces and “cooling commons”, examining how swimmable urban waterways and shade can protect communities from extreme heat while also keeping people socially connected. “Often we’re told in extreme heat to stay indoors, pull down the blinds, and stay cool ... but this creates great inequities and social isolation, which can link directly to heat-related fatalities,” she says. Related Article Exclusive

Climate crisis Energy shock: families choose between cooling their homes and driving Olive says many local outdoor pools are deteriorating and have costly leaks, forcing councils into difficult financial decisions and highlighting the urgent need for government funding to upgrade or shade these vital community spaces. Olive has also joined four Melbourne councils in a united push to make the Yarra River safe and clean enough for public swimming by 2050.



The government’s recently announced plan to plant 100,000 trees across Melbourne in suburbs where exposure to heat is higher was welcomed by Robertson and Olive. Some of the biggest projects will include more than 15,000 trees in Bayview Park in Narre Warren North, and 14,000 trees at Cranwell Park in Braybrook – a move aimed at improving outdoor community spaces. Related Article Melbourne Assembly Victoria lands $350m federal bonus to improve liveability New research commissioned by Bupa and undertaken by the RedBridge Group found nearly three-quarters of Australians experienced the negative health effects of extreme heat over the past year, emotional and psychological stress being ranked as the single largest health threat. Nearly four in five respondents said hot temperatures were affecting their sleep quality. Despite 98 per cent of households among the 3000 people surveyed saying they had home cooling, about three-quarters said they were forced to limit its use due to rising electricity costs. World.title: Inside Ben Roberts-Smith’s media campaign for support
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing Inside Ben Roberts-Smith’s media campaign for support Calum Jaspan October 21, 2026 — 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Disgraced war hero Ben Roberts-Smith has launched a coordinated publicity blitz over the past week that will be capped off by a 150-minute interview with 2GB’s Ben Fordham broadcast on Thursday morning. Currently out on bail as he prepares to fight five counts of war crimes murder charges, Roberts-Smith’s public relations offensive also includes launching a clothing line and Instagram page. Ben Roberts-Smith’s 2GB interview will premiere on YouTube. Getty Images The Victoria Cross (VC) recipient and former SAS soldier has become a lightning rod for division across politics and culture since launching and later losing a defamation case against this masthead, where he unsuccessfully contested he’d ordered and committed war crimes in Afghanistan. He now faces war crimes charges which could land him behind bars for the rest of his life.



Where the VC holder would give his first major interview had been the subject of intense competition with conservative broadcasters Karl Stefanovic and Kyle Sandilands both vying for the exclusive. Related Article Roberts-Smith case Ben Roberts-Smith launches personal brand to fund legal costs But he chose to work with the newly formed Tapt, the radio stations formerly owned by Nine, and it’s headline star Fordham. While he is not paid for the interview, promotional pictures released by 2GB show him wearing his new clothing line Epic 1 Two in the video recording, which will be premiered in full on YouTube in video format at 9am. The network is using the long form interview format as part of a new strategy to find audiences on digital platforms outside traditional radio.



The interview, which spans two and a half hours, is the first since Roberts-Smith was charged with war crimes offences. It presents an opportunity for him to put his side of the story to the public, according to those familiar with the process not authorised to speak publicly, although Roberts-Smith did give several interviews before charges were laid and has in the past engaged media managers. Roberts-Smith has drawn support from sections of the population, in particular those aligned with Pauline Hanson’s One Nation. Prospective voters of the party view him more favourably than they do their only lower house MP Barnaby Joyce, recent polling showed. Ben Fordham’s interview with Ben Roberts-Smith will be released on Thursday. Louise Kennerley Roberts-Smith launched Epic 1 Two last week, which is a reference to his military call sign, positioning himself as the “underdog”. It has prompted a renewed push of public support for him, largely from sections of the right aligned with One Nation. “EPIC 1 TWO is forged in adversity. It is for the people who know what it means to be counted out. To have the odds stacked against them,” the brand’s website says. “EPIC 1 TWO is for the underdog who refuses to stay down.”



As part of the agreement between Roberts-Smith and 2GB, Fordham was free to ask Roberts-Smith whatever he wanted. For Roberts-Smith, it is an opportunity to get his side of the story across, at length. Related Article Australian War Memorial Ben Roberts-Smith joins politicians, veterans as Albanese marks 25 years since start of Afghanistan war But there is also a risk that a spike in publicity could ultimately lead to the argument there is no possibility of a fair trial, says former Media Watch host and publisher of legal journals Justinian and Gazette of Law and Journalism, Richard Ackland. “If you can poison the well enough, then they will make a plea to drop the charges against him,” Ackland says. “I think that’s a reality.” Representatives for Roberts-Smith were approached for comment.



The Roberts-Smith case has already infiltrated the heart of Australian politics. One Nation has adopted Roberts-Smith as a central figure in the party’s push to be viewed as that of the battler, of veterans and of those punished by the establishment. One Nation has used Roberts-Smith’s image on campaign material and he, like the party, enjoys significant support from Australia’s richest person, Gina Rinehart. Opening a new apartment block for veterans in Brisbane this past weekend, Rinehart was introduced by Roberts-Smith. Mining billionaire Gina Rinehart has named a block of villas after ex-soldier, Ben Roberts-Smith. “He’s fighting a fight that most of us don’t realise is a fight against the deep state,” Rinehart said of charges he is facing, according to an opinion piece written by veteran journalist Des Houghton in The Courier Mail.



The piece was republished on Rinehart’s website with the alternative headline Three Aussie Heroes, referring to the billionaire, Roberts-Smith and Daniel Keighran VC, who the apartments were named after. While Roberts-Smith’s fashion brand says it is for the underdog, Roberts-Smith was born to wealthy parents, his father being a Supreme Court judge and major general in the Army Reserves. He went to Perth’s oldest boarding school. He towers over most at 6 foot 7 inches. He has been financially backed by one of Australia’s richest people, Kerry Stokes, and enjoys the support of Rinehart and the political party she is a major donor to, One Nation, which is currently preferred by a quarter of Australia’s population. Kerry Stokes (right) has previously backed Roberts-Smith financially. Michael Howard He has supporters across wide sections of the media at News Corp’s influential news channel News24, has received favourable coverage from outlets controlled by Stokes, including The West Australian newspaper, and is being handed two and half hours on Sydney’s number one radio network to tell his side of the story.



Since launching a social media account this week, Roberts-Smith has received support online from News24 presenter Peta Credlin, a former chief of staff to Tony Abbott. Related Article On Background Is Karl Stefanovic now Australia’s most famous small business owner? Podcaster Karl Stefanovic has also posted a picture of himself and BRS donning the new merch, and has become a vocal supporter of the former soldier since leaving Nine, the owner of this masthead. There has also been support from One News Australia, a news outlet this masthead revealed was previously a One Nation Supporters Facebook group, as well as The Noticer, a white supremacy-affiliated news outlet. The chief executive of Tapt Media, which owns 2GB and 3AW, Tom Malone said the interview showcases the company’s digital transformation in its new era owned by pokies and publican billionaire family, the Laundys. Whether it moves the dial for 2GB or Roberts-Smith, will have to wait. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Musician Lily Allen has cancelled a concert in Auckland hours before it was due to take place, citing ill health, two days before she is due to start her Australian tour.

The artist is touring her album West End Girl, which in part tracks the breakdown of her relationship with actor David Harbour, and was scheduled to perform at Auckland’s Spark Arena before heading to Australia for a series of concerts in Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne and Perth.

Lily Allen performs West End Girl in April in Los Angeles. Getty Images for Live Nation

There are presently no publicly stated changes to her planned Australian schedule, which is due to start on Friday October 23 at the Brisbane Entertainment Centre.

A spokesperson for tour promoter Frontier said on Wednesday afternoon: “Lily is resting and recuperating, with the full intention of completing the rest of the tour in Australia as planned.”

World.title: Reserve Bank in ‘nightmare’ position as it considers another rate rise in November
World.content:
PoliticsFederalRBA Reserve Bank in ‘nightmare’ position as it considers another rate rise in November Shane Wright October 21, 2026 — 4:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Reserve Bank’s deputy governor has warned mortgage holders and businesses the bank is facing “hard choices” in its bid to bring down inflation amid warnings it risks pushing the country into recession. Andrew Hauser used an event in Sydney on Wednesday to argue the RBA was facing a “central bankers’ nightmare” with signs that some businesses believe an inflation rate of between 3 and 3.5 per cent could be the new norm for Australia – well above the bank’s 2-3 per cent target it has struggled to hit over the past four years. RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser says the battle to bring down inflation is a hard task. Dominic Lorrimer A key factor is the surge in global oil prices which overnight touched $US110 a barrel. The Reserve, in its most recent set of economic forecasts released in August, had expected oil to be around $US80 a barrel. Hauser said the nation’s inflation pressures were not improving.



“I don’t know for sure, but a few things are clear, and the inflation outlook looks materially worse than we projected in August,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

Interest rates RBA’s worst nightmare as oil pushes up inflation threat “The challenge that’s facing the board and has done for some time is do you do more to tackle higher inflation, recognising that that means weaker activity, weaker labour market,” he said. “[Or] do we hold our horses to protect the labour market, try and protect some of the labour market … but accept the risk in so doing is that this upside inflation risk embeds, and that becomes more expensive to deal with? “Those are hard choices; they’re not where we’d like to be ideally as the central bank.”



The comments had an immediate impact on financial markets which had put the chance of a rate rise next month at one in four. They are now closer to 50-50. Hauser, who sits on the RBA’s interest rate setting committee that will next meet on November 2 and 3, said the war in Iran - and its impact on oil prices - had dragged on far longer than most central banks had been expecting. This had added to the inflation pressures caused by the AI data centre building boom and overall demand across the economy. But he noted that the bank’s four rate rises this year were having an impact. “Monetary policy is working,” he said.



“The labour market is easing, consumption growth is quite tepid, but there are still pockets of growth, and the inflation outlook has deteriorated. So that’s a pretty tricky balance.” Commonwealth Bank chief economist Luke Yeaman this week warned the Reserve could push the economy “over the edge” if it lifted interest rates to 4.85 per cent at its November meeting. On Wednesday, Betashares chief economist David Bassanese joined Yeaman in warning the RBA was risking an Australian recession with tight monetary policy. “The RBA seems increasingly prepared to risk a recession to get inflation down – given it has been above target for an extended period and it is sensing evidence of rising inflation expectations within the community,” he said. “The RBA – along with other central banks – has likely become less confident the Iran war will end anytime soon and more appreciative of the upside inflation pressures the AI boom is causing, at least in the short term.”



An ongoing concern for the bank has been low productivity growth, prompting demands from the business community for the federal government to put in place measures to boost productivity. But Hauser, who previously worked with the Bank of England, said local businesses had their role to play. He said it appeared “something of an Australian thing” to demand the government solve a problem when there had been a sharp fall in business investment over recent years which was probably a factor in low productivity growth. “There is a joint obligation, I think, not just on government but also on business to get their arms around this productivity challenge and to embrace what could actually be a very positive future for Australia,” he said.



Treasurer Jim Chalmers, in an interview with CNBC, said the war in the Middle East was causing problems for all economies due to its impact on oil prices. “The war in the Middle East has been pushing up inflation around the world, and in Australia, it’s been weighing on growth around the world and in Australia as well, and pushing up borrowing costs at the same time,” he said. “So, from an economic point of view, the war in the Middle East has created a very difficult set of conditions for a lot of countries, including ours. You can see it in our inflation, which is a bit higher than we would like. We can see it in our growth. You can see it in other areas as well.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: ‘Got away with murder’: Man faces trial over 2014 death of Kirra-Lea McLoughlin
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts ‘Got away with murder’: Man faces trial over 2014 death of Kirra-Lea McLoughlin Cloe Read October 21, 2026 — 4:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A man accused of killing his partner told a new girlfriend he felt guilty of the death after having gone into a violent rage, smashing her head into the ground or a wall over claims she had slept with a teenage neighbour, a court has heard. Kirra-Lea McLoughlin, 27, died in July 2014 after an argument with her partner Paul Alan McDonald, who is accused of manslaughter. Wolvi mother Kirra-Lea McLoughlin. Facebook For much of McDonald’s first day of trial in the Supreme Court in Brisbane on Wednesday, he sat looking down, at times shaking his head slightly at some of the evidence being heard. In the hours before McLoughlin died in her Wolvi home, near Gympie, north of Brisbane, there had been a physical fight between her and McDonald’s sister after things had escalated following discussions about McLoughlin’s relationship with a 17-year-old neighbour, the court heard.



Key evidence in the prosecution case is that four years after McLoughlin’s death, McDonald had spoken with a new girlfriend, Jade Vandenberg, about the night of McLoughlin’s death. She told police McDonald had claimed he felt guilty for letting his sister feel responsible for McLoughlin’s death. Crown Prosecutor David Nardone told the court McDonald had confided in Vandenberg, who has since died, about him going into a violent rage before grabbing McLoughlin by the shoulders. “He told Ms Vandenberg that he was upset with [McLoughlin] for having had sex with the neighbour, that he became violent, banging and shaking her head into the floor or a wall,” Nardone said. Ms Vandenberg said in a message to McDonald’s sister the accused said he “kept smashing her head into the floor and panicked when she wouldn’t wake up and tried putting her in the shower”, the court heard.



Years later, in a phone call with his mother discussing his conversations with Vandenberg, McDonald said he feared she would dob him in, Nardone said. McDonald had told the new girlfriend that night he had ended up “sorting it out” with McLoughlin and the pair had had sex that night, the court heard. “She described himself as having got away with murder,” Nardone said. He told his mother it was Vandenberg’s word against his, and he had done “nothing wrong”, the court heard. That night neighbours reported hearing yelling and banging from the home, Nardone said.



McDonald’s sister, Tamiqua McDonald, testified that she had heard the pair talking about how McLoughlin had a relationship with the 17-year-old neighbour, and that McDonald wanted a lie detector test. She said her brother and McLoughlin got into an argument, with McLoughlin hitting her brother in the face. McLoughlin threw a glass at the back of Tamiqua’s head after she intervened in the altercation, she told the court. She then punched McLoughlin in the face, causing her to fall. “She was just yelling she was going to kill me,” she said. The court heard McDonald was trying to defuse the situation when McLoughlin had grabbed a baseball bat and went to swing at him.



Tamiqua intervened, throwing the bat off the veranda. Another member of the family also intervened, throwing red paint, causing both McDonald and McLoughlin to slip. Several people left the property, with McLoughlin staying at the house. Later that evening about 11pm, she could be heard yelling in the background of one of McDonald’s calls. At 2.46am the following morning, a call was made from the house to 13HEALTH, which appeared to be a hang-up call. Another call was also made to another health line for 36 seconds, but the content of the calls were not known, the court heard. The following day, July 17, 2014, about 1pm, McDonald phoned his brother telling him McLoughlin was unresponsive. The brother advised calling 13HEALTH.



At 2.06pm, McDonald called the health line, explaining that McLoughlin had taken more than 20 pills. McDonald called triple zero, and McLoughlin was rushed to hospital, where medical teams found she had more than 100 bruises, and a spongy area on her scalp. She was airlifted to the Gold Coast for treatment, where it was determined she had suffered a severe brain injury. Medical tests did not show signs of an overdose. McLoughlin died the following day on July 18. The judge-alone trial before Justice Peter Davis continues.



Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service (1800RESPECT) on 1800 737 732. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Worse and worse’: Data centre backlash threatens billions in building boom
World.content:
Updated PoliticsFederalInvestigations ‘Worse and worse’: Data centre backlash threatens billions in building boom Clay Lucas and Nick Toscano Updated October 21, 2026 — 4:16pm ,first published 11:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

What began as a community protest in Melbourne’s inner west over giant electricity poles being installed on quiet residential streets has now rocked the nation’s highest-profile data centre developer, as it scrambles to find a new way to supply energy to its flagship facility. On Wednesday, ASX-listed NextDC announced it would slash its expected profits and construction spending, as it deals with delays in getting more electricity supply into its West Footscray M3 data centre. NextDC’s M3 data centre in West Footscray. Joe Armao The news triggered a share price collapse that wiped about $3 billion off the company’s valuation and sparked a warning from investors and analysts that a mounting community backlash across Australia against data centres posed a worsening threat to the booming sector. Plans to build dozens of new data centres across the country are running into social opposition, partly due to the vast amounts of electricity needed to run their high-intensity computing and cooling systems, and the proximity of some sites to people’s homes.



“Community concerns around data centre developments present a real risk to the timing of delivery of contracted capacity for data centre owners,” said RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Beadle, pointing to NextDC’s earnings cut and warning that local opposition could disrupt projects. Some of the new Jemena power lines in a Yarraville residential street, with the NextDC data centre in the background (left), which caused locals to rally against them. Joe Armao One of the new power poles alongside an existing wooden pole. Jason South That residential pushback has hit other projects nationwide: developer Green Square was recently forced to pull a proposed project in Western Australia, Goodman Group shelved a $1.2 billion facility in Sydney’s Lane Cove, and private developer Firmus was forced to abandon a planned $44 billion stock market float. The news for the data centre industry “keeps getting worse and worse”, Ten Cap portfolio manager Jun Bei Liu said, particularly for developers with unbuilt facilities where customers hold contract-termination rights if projects are delayed.



Last week, Microsoft pulled out of a deal to anchor a flagship facility in the United Kingdom following power-supply delays. “What’s happening with NextDC highlights the risk for companies that have secured energy and water, but whose facilities are not yet built,” she said. “These risks are playing out in real time. There will definitely be more investor scrutiny now.” NextDC came out of its two-day trading halt on Wednesday, warning investors that the next stages of the politically contentious M3 development – which sits just metres from some West Footscray residents’ front gates – would also not be approved until after next month’s Victorian election. A community blockade in September, revealed by this masthead, hit electricity distributor Jemena’s rollout of 15-metre-tall 66,000-volt residential power poles. Direct action by residents included blockading streets by parking cars and light trucks where power poles were to be installed, co-ordinating via WhatsApp groups to ignore door-knocks from contractors, and filling excavation pits with green waste.



The protests, and subsequent local political backlash, saw Jemena halt powerline construction until at least February. It will leave NextDC without extra power it needs to keep expanding its West Footscray data centre. Yarraville resident Milco Bogoevski was among those who led the community protest to halt Jemena. He said while he was sympathetic to data centre operators – “no one here wants to see industry fail” – what had happened was the direct result of power companies and businesses not listening to residents. A sign in Sanderson Street, Yarraville, in September. Jason South “These power lines, this material, it was going to be in our street, we were going to have to deal with it for decades after they left – power operators like Jemena, and businesses like NextDC, they’re going to need to engage more with the community.” Bogoevski said community opposition to the West Footscray data centre and the impact of other data centres in Melbourne’s west could help swing seats in the November 28 election. “The state government is responsible for electricity – it comes down to them. There’s a good chance an issue like this could flip this seat away from Labor,” he said.



The market reaction against NextDC was sharp: its shares collapsed on Wednesday to as low as $5.07 – down more than 40 per cent from their Monday closing price of $9.57. The price recovered slightly and shares were trading at $5.53 at about 3.30pm, still a far cry from the peak of $17.22 a year ago. NextDC also revealed it was putting the brakes on its wider construction pipeline, in a move that could alarm state and federal governments as data centre construction has provided a rare bright spot in the sluggish Australian economy. The company had planned to spend up to $5.75 billion on construction in the coming financial year, but will now spend between $4.5 billion and $5 billion. NextDC chief executive Craig Scroggie said the company, as well as pausing expectations from its West Footscray project, would also halt speculative expansion projects and land buys not already locked in. “With [West Footscray] revenue deferred, we have paused projects not backed by customer contracts and put that capital behind the capacity our customers have already contracted,” he said.



Scroggie said the company was working with Jemena on community consultation and considering other options. “We’re working with them on alternative routes that may be feasible, and alternative locations for such poles and undergrounding,” he said, although noting that undergrounding the cables would take more time. He also flagged political uncertainty as a challenge for the project as NextDC awaits planing approval for the final expansion at M3. “It has been with the Victorian government and planning minister for a very long time, and when the Victorian government went through recent portfolio changes and the Premier changed, obviously the decisions in relation to approvals and other things slowed down,” he said. NextDC’s market shock represents the clearest evidence yet that Victoria’s rapid push to attract power-hungry artificial intelligence infrastructure has run into severe grid constraints and suburban backlash.

World.title: ‘Where will they go?’: Barracks eviction sparks fears for families and morale
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life ‘Where will they go?’: Barracks eviction sparks fears for families and morale David Barwell October 21, 2026 — 4:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Military families face being evicted from Sydney’s historic Victoria Barracks by the end of the year as the federal government’s push to sell the historic site sparks mounting concerns over the use of public land, heritage and Defence Force morale. Critics of the proposed sale warn plans to relocate up to 12 families, including children, are being rushed, without arrangements to secure alternative accommodation alongside the hundreds of other personnel who live, work and serve at the Paddington site. RSL NSW President Vince Williams has criticised plans to relocate personnel before suitable replacement accommodation has been secured. Sitthixay Ditthavong The concerns have united a group of politicians, business leaders, sporting identities and senior military figures under the Save Victoria Barracks Alliance, which will hold a public rally on Sunday urging Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to keep the site in public hands. Former prime minister John Howard said he would speak at the rally on Sunday to demonstrate the “depths of community resentment” over the proposal.



The rally follows the government’s decision to include Victoria Barracks among 67 Defence properties earmarked for full or partial sale after an independent review of ageing and underused military assets. The program aims to raise up to $3 billion for other Defence priorities. The demonstration also comes after a separate rally this month when hundreds turned out at Balmoral to oppose the partial sale of the HMAS Penguin. Skywriting over Balmoral Beach during the HMAS Penguin protest earlier this month. Oscar Colman But critics question whether the financial benefits justify selling a site that remains operational and has played a central role in Australian military history for 178 years. As of December 2025, up to 250 permanent Australian Defence Force personnel were based at the barracks, alongside 50-100 public servants, 150-200 reservists and 50-100 cadets.



The site also houses the Headquarters Forces Command, Headquarters 2nd Health Brigade, offices, a museum, cadet training facilities and residential accommodation. Defence has proposed moving administrative personnel to Defence Plaza Sydney, about two kilometres away, while cadets could relocate to Randwick Barracks or community facilities and schools. However, the department has not publicly detailed the intended location of every operational unit or affected military household. Political and community leaders including Business Sydney executive director Paul Nicolaou, former Wallabies captain Simon Poidevin, Manly MP James Griffin, Coogee MP Marjorie O’Neill, RSL NSW president Vince Williams, Senator Jessica Collins, Woollahra Mayor Sarah Dixson, and Wentworth MP Allegra Spender urge the federal government to reverse its controversial decision to sell off the Victoria Barracks. Sitthixay Ditthavong Uncertainty has been compounded by conflicting signals over the timetable. In September, a Defence planning order requiring personnel to leave by December 19 was rescinded, with the department describing it as having been “erroneously” issued after details emerged publicly. Defence later said relocations would begin in the fourth quarter of the year, subject to workforce and operational requirements, and that no final decisions had been made about where personnel would be based.



A Defence spokesperson said in a statement a consultation process had begun, with most personnel expected to move off-site before the end of 2026. “The transition and divestment of Victoria Barracks Sydney will be managed carefully and sensitively, supporting our people, families and the broader Defence community while preserving its heritage, history and legacy,” the spokesperson said. The proposed sale of the Paddington barracks has sparked debate between those pushing for more housing and those who believe it is too special to touch. Wolter Peeters Defence Minister Richard Marles has signalled the government wants to move quickly. Questioned last month, he said he expected Defence would leave the affected sites “as soon as possible”. Liberal Senator Jess Collins, who is chairing a Senate inquiry into the planned sales, said serving personnel were unable to publicly express their views despite growing concern about the consequences.



“The army has been gagged. The Defence Force cannot speak up about it,” Collins said. Retired vice-admiral Vince Williams, president of RSL NSW, which represents 33,000 former and serving Defence personnel, criticised plans to relocate personnel before suitable replacement accommodation had been secured. Defence Minister Richard Marles at the historic Victoria Barracks in Paddington Peter Rae “It’s appalling, kicking people out in a hurry and sticking them into an office tower in Pitt Street, or into bunk beds in Randwick Barracks without having replacement full-time accommodation sorted out beforehand,” he said. “It’s the message it’s sending that is terrible for morale.”



The alliance has attracted support from state and federal politicians crossing party lines, as well as business and sporting figures. Marjorie O’Neill, the NSW Labor member for Coogee, has described Victoria Barracks as the army’s “spiritual home”. Independent federal MP for Wentworth Allegra Spender said community sentiment favoured retaining the site in public hands. Related Article City life Why this slice of land on Sydney Harbour might be harder to sell than expected “This is not something that needs to be turned into a boutique hotel or a wedding venue,” she said. Former Wallabies captain Simon Poidevin, whose grandfather served at the barracks during World War I, said finding replacement housing in the expensive eastern suburbs at short notice was a serious concern.



“They’ve got kids and families, they’re active members of surf clubs and sporting groups and they’re now asking where will they go,” he said. “They love working here. They’re proud to work here. They don’t want to go and work in a soulless city building which has no connection to the Defence Force.” The financial case for the sale has also come under scrutiny. Defence has declined to disclose estimates of the expected proceeds, telling the Senate inquiry that releasing the figures could “diminish” the Commonwealth’s negotiating position in achieving market value. The Department of Finance, which is coordinating the sales program, told the inquiry that spending on external advisers had totalled $2.72 million as of August 31, including $1.66m in management fees paid to KPMG as its strategic industry partner. Organisers of Sunday’s rally say the event could attract thousands. Originally planned outside the barracks’ main gates, the demonstration has been relocated to Moore Park near Kippax Lake on advice from NSW Police about crowd size and public safety.



Howard on Wednesday said he would “strongly oppose” any attempt to sell off the site. “Like many in the community I resent the Albanese government’s indifference to our proud national and military history in proposing the sale of sites which are part of that history,” Howard said in a statement. World.title: Heart attacks to premature births: Experts are sounding the alarm on Melbourne’s next hot summer
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaMelbourne Assembly Heart attacks to premature births: Experts are sounding the alarm on Melbourne’s next hot summer Melissa Cunningham October 21, 2026 — 4:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As another El Nino summer approaches, health experts are raising the alarm over the potentially fatal consequences of higher temperatures and an increased number of hot days expected around the state. Mounting research showing soaring temperatures can increase rates of stillbirth and premature birth, trigger heart attacks, worsen mental health and exacerbate chronic illnesses comes amid warnings that Victorian emergency departments remain severely underprepared for a surge in heatwaves that are forecast to lead to record-shattering death tolls. The sun rises over Melbourne on a hot morning last year. Jason South As part of this week’s Melbourne Assembly civic forum, The Age has been exploring big ideas for the future of the city, including how infrastructure and housing can be transformed to protect residents from the rise in dangerously high temperatures. Professor Ollie Jay, academic director of the Heat and Health Research Centre at the University of Sydney, said extreme heat cost the Australian economy more than $6 billion in lost productivity every year.



“Basically, we’ve got this hazard, which is extreme heat and chronic hot weather that is growing undeniably in Australia,” Jay says. Related Article Sorry, your browser doesn't support embedded videos. City life As Melbourne gets hotter, some suburbs suffer more than others “On top of that, you’ve also got a shift in the population where we have a progressively ageing population, and we’ve got an increased prevalence of chronic diseases like cardiovascular disease and kidney disease.” A growing body of research has laid bare the implications of extreme heat on ageing populations, with a landmark study published in The Lancet Planetary Health in August warning the impacts of heatwaves on people aged 60 and over have been underestimated. Researchers found people in this group face an increase in serious health risks directly linked to rising temperatures, and will bear the brunt of increasingly frequent spells of extreme heat.



But it’s not just the heat. Rising humidity also hinders sweat from evaporating, which is the body’s primary physiological mechanism to keep cool. Related Article Melbourne Assembly ‘As tall as you can go’: The NYC-style density plan for Melbourne’s future Wind can also affect human thermal states, and direct sun exposure can make an environment feel at least 15 degrees hotter than the official shade temperature reading. “What most people don’t realise is that official temperatures are recorded in the shade,” Jay says. Protecting people from rising extreme heat requires urgent action now, he says, including implementing targeted building and landscape interventions – such as external shutters and reflective roofs – to reduce heat risk.



As part of their work, Jay and a team of researchers have reviewed global literature to evaluate over 70 cooling interventions, grading more than 20 building-level strategies based on cost, effectiveness, and scientific evidence. Among the top interventions measured by effectiveness are air conditioning; street trees and urban canopies; outdoor shade structures such as arcades; and reflective roofs (also known as cool roofs) designed to bounce back more sunlight and absorb less heat than standard dark roofs. Jay says that among the greatest challenges for a city like Melbourne is tackling the urban heat island effect – a phenomenon created by poorly designed buildings, roads and footpaths, which can make temperatures vary by as much as 6 degrees across different parts of the city, particularly in fast-growing suburbs. Researchers Dr Sarah Robertson (left) and Dr Rebecca Olive at RMIT University’s Centre for Urban Research. Chris Hopkins Extreme heat is a conundrum that Dr Sarah Robertson, a research fellow at RMIT University’s Centre for Urban Research, has dedicated years to, as she examines ways to make climate resilient and safe housing.



Robertson says one of the biggest day-to-day issues is much of Victoria’s existing housing was built before the introduction of energy efficiency and thermal performance standards came in. “We need to focus on improving the quality of our existing housing so it’s thermally comfortable, energy efficient, and affordable for people,” she says, adding that existing housing should be retrofitted or upgraded. Related Article Climate solutions The simple fix that will cool our streets – if only we get it right Robertson also says the introduction of minimum standards for rental properties, which will come into effect from next year, will be a catalyst for change. “It means for the first time, rental properties have to have ceiling insulation [and] be draft proof, so gaps and around doors and windows sealed up, and have fixed cooling in the living room installed at the point of lease or sale,” she says.



Robertson’s colleague, research fellow Dr Rebecca Olive, has focused her attention on outdoor public spaces and “cooling commons”, examining how swimmable urban waterways and shade can protect communities from extreme heat while also keeping people socially connected. “Often we’re told in extreme heat to stay indoors, pull down the blinds, and stay cool ... but this creates great inequities and social isolation, which can link directly to heat-related fatalities,” she says. Related Article Exclusive

Climate crisis Energy shock: families choose between cooling their homes and driving Olive says many local outdoor pools are deteriorating and have costly leaks, forcing councils into difficult financial decisions and highlighting the urgent need for government funding to upgrade or shade these vital community spaces. Olive has also joined four Melbourne councils in a united push to make the Yarra River safe and clean enough for public swimming by 2050.



The government’s recently announced plan to plant 100,000 trees across Melbourne in suburbs where exposure to heat is higher was welcomed by Robertson and Olive. Some of the biggest projects will include more than 15,000 trees in Bayview Park in Narre Warren North, and 14,000 trees at Cranwell Park in Braybrook – a move aimed at improving outdoor community spaces. Related Article Melbourne Assembly Victoria lands $350m federal bonus to improve liveability New research commissioned by Bupa and undertaken by the RedBridge Group found nearly three-quarters of Australians experienced the negative health effects of extreme heat over the past year, emotional and psychological stress being ranked as the single largest health threat. Nearly four in five respondents said hot temperatures were affecting their sleep quality. Despite 98 per cent of households among the 3000 people surveyed saying they had home cooling, about three-quarters said they were forced to limit its use due to rising electricity costs.
