World.title: Inside Ben Roberts-Smith’s media campaign for support
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing Inside Ben Roberts-Smith’s media campaign for support Calum Jaspan October 21, 2026 — 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Disgraced war hero Ben Roberts-Smith has launched a coordinated publicity blitz over the past week that will be capped off by a 150-minute interview with 2GB’s Ben Fordham broadcast on Thursday morning. Currently out on bail as he prepares to fight five counts of war crimes murder charges, Roberts-Smith’s public relations offensive also includes launching a clothing line and Instagram page. Ben Roberts-Smith’s 2GB interview will premiere on YouTube. Getty Images The Victoria Cross (VC) recipient and former SAS soldier has become a lightning rod for division across politics and culture since launching and later losing a defamation case against this masthead, where he unsuccessfully contested he’d ordered and committed war crimes in Afghanistan. He now faces war crimes charges which could land him behind bars for the rest of his life.



Where the VC holder would give his first major interview had been the subject of intense competition with conservative broadcasters Karl Stefanovic and Kyle Sandilands both vying for the exclusive. Related Article Roberts-Smith case Ben Roberts-Smith launches personal brand to fund legal costs But he chose to work with the newly formed Tapt, the radio stations formerly owned by Nine, and it’s headline star Fordham. While he is not paid for the interview, promotional pictures released by 2GB show him wearing his new clothing line Epic 1 Two in the video recording, which will be premiered in full on YouTube in video format at 9am. The network is using the long form interview format as part of a new strategy to find audiences on digital platforms outside traditional radio.



The interview, which spans two and a half hours, is the first since Roberts-Smith was charged with war crimes offences. It presents an opportunity for him to put his side of the story to the public, according to those familiar with the process not authorised to speak publicly, although Roberts-Smith did give several interviews before charges were laid and has in the past engaged media managers. Roberts-Smith has drawn support from sections of the population, in particular those aligned with Pauline Hanson’s One Nation. Prospective voters of the party view him more favourably than they do their only lower house MP Barnaby Joyce, recent polling showed. Ben Fordham’s interview with Ben Roberts-Smith will be released on Thursday. Louise Kennerley Roberts-Smith launched Epic 1 Two last week, which is a reference to his military call sign, positioning himself as the “underdog”. It has prompted a renewed push of public support for him, largely from sections of the right aligned with One Nation. “EPIC 1 TWO is forged in adversity. It is for the people who know what it means to be counted out. To have the odds stacked against them,” the brand’s website says. “EPIC 1 TWO is for the underdog who refuses to stay down.”



As part of the agreement between Roberts-Smith and 2GB, Fordham was free to ask Roberts-Smith whatever he wanted. For Roberts-Smith, it is an opportunity to get his side of the story across, at length. Related Article Australian War Memorial Ben Roberts-Smith joins politicians, veterans as Albanese marks 25 years since start of Afghanistan war But there is also a risk that a spike in publicity could ultimately lead to the argument there is no possibility of a fair trial, says former Media Watch host and publisher of legal journals Justinian and Gazette of Law and Journalism, Richard Ackland. “If you can poison the well enough, then they will make a plea to drop the charges against him,” Ackland says. “I think that’s a reality.” Representatives for Roberts-Smith were approached for comment.



The Roberts-Smith case has already infiltrated the heart of Australian politics. One Nation has adopted Roberts-Smith as a central figure in the party’s push to be viewed as that of the battler, of veterans and of those punished by the establishment. One Nation has used Roberts-Smith’s image on campaign material and he, like the party, enjoys significant support from Australia’s richest person, Gina Rinehart. Opening a new apartment block for veterans in Brisbane this past weekend, Rinehart was introduced by Roberts-Smith. Mining billionaire Gina Rinehart has named a block of villas after ex-soldier, Ben Roberts-Smith. “He’s fighting a fight that most of us don’t realise is a fight against the deep state,” Rinehart said of charges he is facing, according to an opinion piece written by veteran journalist Des Houghton in The Courier Mail.



The piece was republished on Rinehart’s website with the alternative headline Three Aussie Heroes, referring to the billionaire, Roberts-Smith and Daniel Keighran VC, who the apartments were named after. While Roberts-Smith’s fashion brand says it is for the underdog, Roberts-Smith was born to wealthy parents, his father being a Supreme Court judge and major general in the Army Reserves. He went to Perth’s oldest boarding school. He towers over most at 6 foot 7 inches. He has been financially backed by one of Australia’s richest people, Kerry Stokes, and enjoys the support of Rinehart and the political party she is a major donor to, One Nation, which is currently preferred by a quarter of Australia’s population. Kerry Stokes (right) has previously backed Roberts-Smith financially. Michael Howard He has supporters across wide sections of the media at News Corp’s influential news channel News24, has received favourable coverage from outlets controlled by Stokes, including The West Australian newspaper, and is being handed two and half hours on Sydney’s number one radio network to tell his side of the story.



Since launching a social media account this week, Roberts-Smith has received support online from News24 presenter Peta Credlin, a former chief of staff to Tony Abbott. Related Article On Background Is Karl Stefanovic now Australia’s most famous small business owner? Podcaster Karl Stefanovic has also posted a picture of himself and BRS donning the new merch, and has become a vocal supporter of the former soldier since leaving Nine, the owner of this masthead. There has also been support from One News Australia, a news outlet this masthead revealed was previously a One Nation Supporters Facebook group, as well as The Noticer, a white supremacy-affiliated news outlet. The chief executive of Tapt Media, which owns 2GB and 3AW, Tom Malone said the interview showcases the company’s digital transformation in its new era owned by pokies and publican billionaire family, the Laundys. Whether it moves the dial for 2GB or Roberts-Smith, will have to wait. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Clouds, but no rain? Moth swarms bamboozle the weather radar
World.content:
NationalNSWAnimals Clouds, but no rain? Moth swarms bamboozle the weather radar Angus Dalton October 21, 2026 — 3:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In an epic clash between migration and meteorology, vast swarms of moths are suspected to have bamboozled the state’s weather radars, appearing as rain clouds in a phenomenon that could help scientists save one of Australia’s most infamous and under-threat insects. Bogong moths are flying south to shelter in the cool caves of the Australian Alps over summer, in thick throngs conservationists are celebrating as a sign their populations are climbing back from a catastrophic crash in 2017. Bogong moths are suspected to be showing up as widespread light rainfall across NSW. BOM So mighty are the moth numbers that the Bureau of Meteorology’s instruments are detecting “clouds” on evenings with clear skies and no rain. “It is possible that radars across eastern New South Wales are detecting bogong moths,” the bureau said in a statement. “The bureau’s radars are not malfunctioning … large numbers of insects can look like very light widespread rain, particularly near sunrise and sunset.”



ABC meteorologist Tom Saunders reported widespread rain lighting up the weather radar like “clockwork” each evening for the past few weeks. “The only problem is that on most nights, skies are not cloudy and it certainly has not been raining for a month straight,” he wrote, attributing the false signals to bogongs taking flight each evening. Bogong moths arriving at their summer sites in the Australian Alps. Bogong moths blanket mountain caves where they spend their summer; up to 17,000 roost within a single square metre. Eric Warrant Radar works by blasting out pulses of radio waves, a type of electromagnetic radiation. These radio waves reflect off water particles and “echo” back to the radar antenna.



The timing and the strength of the returning signal allows the bureau to see whether rain, hail or a thunderstorm is on the way. Those radio waves, however, can also bounce off things that aren’t precipitation, including smoke, ash, birds – and moths. “We can confirm that there has been increased ‘echoes’ displaying on radars across eastern New South Wales that aren’t precipitation,” the bureau said, adding the signals may not be completely caused by moths and there could be other atmospheric factors at play. ‘Now we can go back through the records as long ago as World War II to look for signatures of big clouds of moths.’ Kate Umbers, Western Sydney University If the phenomenon is caused by moths, it could serve as critical data used to save the species, which is suffering from a lack of data. “It’s brilliant – it provides us with an example of what the moths look like on satellite radars,” said Associate Professor Kate Umbers, a moth researcher from Western Sydney University.



“Now we can go back through the records as long ago as World War II to look for signatures of big clouds of moths. My goodness, it’s such an important observation.” Efforts to list the moths as endangered federally were knocked back in 2025 by then-Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek due to gaps in monitoring and population data. Having a clear signature of what the moths look like on radar could help reconstruct their populations and movements back through the decades, using historical radar signals to help address those critical knowledge gaps. This season’s bogong moth sightings as gathered by Moth Tracker. Moth Tracker/Zoos Victoria Radar could also help track down more of the moths’ remote and undiscovered roosts in the alps.



The last well-publicised time moths were detected on radar was during the 2000 Sydney Olympics, when organisers panicked as rain clouds encroached on the closing ceremony, only to be revealed as swarms of bogongs attracted by the stadium lights. Umbers and her team tagged 14,000 of the moths earlier this year at Mount Kosciuszko. The idea was to find at least some of them as they spread around Australia to finally untangle the mystery of their movements – but every single one went missing. “The thing is, we don’t know where bogong moths come from, and we don’t know where they go,” Umbers said. Associate Professor Kate Umbers and her team have tagged some bogongs blue in the hope they’re spotted by the public and reveal crucial data about the migration. Western Sydney University “There’s lots of stories that are repeated all the time that they come from Queensland and fly 1000 kilometres … but there’s no evidence. We’ve never tracked a single moth from one place to the other.”



The lack of hard data about the bogong moth populations has stifled efforts to get the insect listed as threatened under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act. The bogong moth is listed as endangered on the international IUCN red list, but not because of its actual population number, which isn’t known. Related Article Insects Naked and afraid: The extraordinary reason moths are haunting your shower The bogongs are listed under Criterion B, which covers species threatened because of fragmentation or destruction of their geographic range. For the moths, the listing recognises the alpine caves they shelter within over summer are vulnerable to warming due to climate change.



“Their threatened status has nothing to do with how many there are,” Umbers said. “It has all to do with the declining quality of the habitat that they require.” In a renewed effort to track moth movement, Umbers and her team recently caught 500 bogongs in the Blue Mountains and dabbed blue paint on their wings. The hope is that someone will spot a blue-marked bogong, snap a photo and report its location to bogong.org. Doing so would reveal much-needed information about a migration that is apparently mighty this year, but is constantly under threat. “The first time we find one of these [tracked moths], it’s going to be just remarkably valuable information about where that one little moth has come from and gone to,” Umber said. The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Sign up to get it each week.

World.title: Puberty blocker restrictions for gender-diverse youth overturned by High Court
World.content:
The High Court has ruled regulations banning new prescriptions of puberty blockers for young people with gender dysphoria were unlawful.

In 2025, the Government sought to introduce regulations stopping doctors from making new prescriptions of puberty blockers for children and adolescents with gender dysphoria or gender incongruence.

The Ministry of Health undertook public consultation in 2024 on whether there should be additional safety measures for the prescribing of puberty blockers in young people with gender-related health needs.

The majority of public submissions opposed further restrictions on the prescribing of puberty blockers.

In November 2025, the minister recommended the regulations be made in light of the potential harm caused by puberty blockers. The regulations prohibited new prescriptions to treat gender dysphoria or gender incongruence in children and adolescents.

However, the prescription of puberty blockers remained available to pause puberty for young people with other medical conditions, and for use in gender-affirming care for those who had been prescribed them prior to the regulations.

The following month, the Professional Association for Transgender Health Aotearoa (PATHA) applied for judicial review of the regulations. Court orders were granted preventing enforcement of the regulations pending final resolution of the proceedings.

In a decision released today, the court found the Government failed to adequately consult those affected by failing to consult on the substance of the regulations and failing to directly consult with gender diverse young people.

It also found the restrictions unlawfully discriminated against gender-diverse young people, breaching the Bill of Rights.

It found there was differential treatment between young people with gender-related health needs and those who could access puberty blockers for other health conditions.

"This differential treatment imposed a material disadvantage on young people with gender-related health needs, as they are at high risk of seriously poor health outcomes, particularly self-harm and suicide."

It found while there was a rational basis to impose restrictions on access to puberty blockers for some, a complete prohibition on prescriptions for new patients was a disproportionate response to the potential harm caused by puberty blockers.

The court did not accept that the Minister abdicated his decision-making power to Cabinet and acted for an improper purpose of advancing New Zealand First's "anti-woke" agenda.

It ruled that the regulations were unlawful and invalid, and made an order setting them aside.

When it launched its legal action, PATHA - an interdisciplinary professional organisation that promotes the health, wellbeing and rights of transgender people - said the ban would "cause immense harm, both directly and indirectly, to transgender children and their whānau".

But Family First NZ said it was "shocked" by the decision, and that the High Court was siding with activists instead of vulnerable children.

Chief executive Bob McCoskrie said there was no settled scientific consensus supporting gender-affirming care for minors.

"The stakes could not be higher. These treatments can have life-altering consequences for young people. The Government has a responsibility to ensure that policies are guided by the strongest available evidence and not by pressure from advocacy groups."

A spokesperson for the Health Minister said the government will continue to take an evidence-based approach to this matter and was seeking advice on next steps.

World.title: Photos only a part of 'overwhelming' case against Scott Watson, Crown says
World.content:
Crown lawyers in the Supreme Court today say a photo montage at the heart of Scott Watson's appeal is only one piece of evidence in an "overwhelming" case against him.

Watson is appealing his conviction for the murders of Ben Smart and Olivia Hope in Marlborough Sounds on New Years' Day in 1998.

His lawyers argue the evidence of water taxi driver Guy Wallace - used in the original trial - who picked out Watson in "Photo Montage B" as the man seen boarding a boat with the young pair, is inadmissible.

Crown lawyer Madeleine Laracy said the Crown always relied on a "large volume of evidence" - not just a photo montage.

"This was and is an overwhelming case."

Laracy referred to the Court of Appeal's judgment in 2024 - which rejected a previous bid by Watson to quash his convictions.

The Court of Appeal had found there were just too many factors pointing to Watson, Laracy said.

"If Mr Watson was not the man on the Naiad, then the lone man, like Mr Watson, happened to be alone, happened to have a yacht, happened to have moored his yacht out from the jetty, happened to be in the same age range, late twenties or early thirties, happened to have an appearance that was so like Mr Watson's as to mislead Mr Wallace into thinking it was the same man."

Crown lawyer Stuart Baker said Wallace's evidence did not solely rely on picking him out of a photo montage.

"This was not a case of a fleeting glance by Mr Wallace, rather Mr Wallace observed the male at the lodge for some time throughout the evening, both in the main bar and the garden bar."

Baker said Wallace gave descriptions of the "lone man", prior to going to the wharf, including who was on the naiad, where exactly they went, what was said, and a description of rafted boats in the bay, where the three people disembarked.

The justices questioned Baker on Watson's lawyers argument that police pressured Wallace to identify Watson in an interview in early January, 1998.

"It was inappropriate, wasn't it?" Justice Joe Williams asked.

"I've never in all the trials I did read an interview like that.

"I accept that the officer... that the questioning was challenging, and was at a level that quite clearly wouldn't be dealt with at the present day."

Baker said he did not succumb to pressure at the time to identify Watson, and ended up identifying him due to other reliable factors.

Another key issue that came up in the hearing was the photo police used of Watson in Montage B.

Watson had his eyes half-closed in this photograph, and his lawyers said yesterday it unfairly stood out and led to Wallace and others identifying him.

Chief Justice Helen Winkelmann put to Baker that this was "quite an extraordinary photograph", and asked him whether it was acceptable for police to choose a photo that most closely matched witness descriptions.

Baker replied that he thought it was acceptable, but the other photos in the montage needed to have other similar characteristics.

He said it did not have the effect of substantially leading people to choose Watson, because only half of the 53 people shown the photo in Montage B chose Watson.

Laracy said a major point in the Crown's case at the original trial was motive.

"The motive is a long-harboured intention to kill a woman," she said, and in her address she referred to witnesses who had pointed to such comments expressed in different words and different places.

"[That motive] suffused throughout this Crown case, and the way it's held together, it's a very important aspect of the Crown's case for identity."

Watson's Court of Appeal bid sought to overturn his convictions on the question of reliability of DNA evidence of two blonde hairs found on Watson's boat, as well as the photo montage evidence.

The Supreme Court is only considering the question of whether a miscarriage of justice arose from the decision of the original trial judge to admit Wallace's photo ID evidence.

Tuesday's hearing concludes the Supreme Court appeal, with the justices reserving their decision.

World.title: Hawke's Bay vet nurse challenges politicians to live on her income for a month
World.content:
Audio player for " Hawke's Bay mother challenges politicians to live on her income " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2057953%2Fhawke-s-bay-vet-nurse-challenges-politicians-to-live-on-her-income-for-a-month

Hawke's Bay mother challenges politicians to live on her income Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

A Hawke's Bay vet nurse and mother of two has challenged politicians to live on her income for a month.

Kayla Knibb wrote in to RNZ's Checkpoint saying she was sick of politicians arguing while families struggled to get by.

"I am angry, I am exhausted and quite frankly, I am sick of watching politicians argue over election polls while families like mine are drowning," she wrote.

Knibb spoke to the programme on Wednesday and said her family were struggling to make ends meet.

"You shouldn't be having to make these choices, you're meant to be working people, full-time jobs, we should be in a better place than where we are."

Knibb and her husband both work, earning about $100,000 to $130,000 a year before tax.

They've been making decisions on what they can go without in order to manage bills, she said.

"I can't really remember the last time I really bought packets of meat at the supermarket, we've gone to lentils, and chickpeas, and things because they're really cheap.

"There's just so many things that we have to try and juggle to make things a little bit better, and I don't really know what else there is."

Knibb was also fundraising for her son who has a chronic lung condition and was on IV antibiotics.

They've been declined additional financial help from anywhere else, she said.

"We work too much and we've been told we earn too much money to have any help from any external means," she said.

She said they've been trying to upgrade there home, so it can be a healthy home for her son.

"I had no idea that working hard, and kind of being put in this position, that it's not something that we're going to ever be able to do."

It was especially tough for families with children, she said.

"You've got to juggle daycare, food, working, sick leave, annual leave, it just all adds up and there's nothing left to give at the end."

Knibb wanted to see a politician try and survive on her income.

"I don't think they've ever had to be in that position, I don't think they've ever had to choose, or if it was, it was a very, very, very long time ago" she said.

World.title: Fire crews called to central Auckland blaze
World.content:
Emergency services are responding to a fire in Auckland's central city this afternoon.

Crews were called at about 4pm to the scene on Greys Avenue.

A St John spokesperson says they assessed one person in a minor condition.

Kainga Ora has confirmed the fire was in a Te Mātāwai unit.

Fire and Emergency have been approached for comment.

Members of the Professional Fire Fighters Union on strike around the corner from the fire on Greys Ave. RNZ / Jess Hopkins

World.title: Cancerous chemical at centre of callout revealed
World.content:
Fire and Emergency have revealed last week's callout to a Christchurch chemical company was sparked by the reported spill of 200 litres of a carcinogenic industrial degreaser.

Three people were taken to hospital, including one in a critical condition.

But the company involved disputes that and said there was no spill and one of its workers tripped and fell.

Emergency services were called to Solvent Rescue in Coleridge Street in the suburb of Sydenham about 3.50pm last Thursday.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said firefighters found one person unconscious and had to rescue two people from the building.

FENZ revealed on Wednesday the callout was for a chemical spill of about 200 litres of trichloroethylene.

Trichloroethylene is a non-flammable, colourless liquid used mainly as a solvent to remove grease from metal parts. But it is also used as an ingredient in adhesives, paint removers, typewriter correction fluids and spot removers.

Solvent Rescue director Chris Bathurst told RNZ there was no spill.

"Our distillation operator was cutting open a cold 210-litre drum of chemical waste paint thinner. He appears to have tripped and fallen on the concrete floor," Bathurst said, in an emailed statement.

"There was no chemical spill or release of vapours into the atmosphere.

"St John assessed all three of us and we were taken to the emergency department for observation, but everyone is recovering well."

Following subsequent inquiries from RNZ, Bathurst said the drum still contained 200 litres of the chemical and nothing was spilled or removed.

World.title: Family, police appeal to public for help finding PhD student Sam Newton-Jones whose car was found at Piha's Mercer Bay loop track
World.content:
The family of a man whose car was found at a well-known walking track in West Auckland are urging the public to come forward with information.

Sam Newton-Jones, a 33-year-old PhD student, was last seen at his workplace in Henderson on Tuesday.

Police said his car was later found at the Mercer Bay Loop carpark near Piha but there was no sign of Newton.

Newton-Jone's family said he was a much-loved son, husband and father-of-two, and his disappearance was "deeply concerning".

Police wanted to speak to anyone who had seen Newton walking on the track or in the Piha area on Tuesday afternoon or evening.

A spokesperson said Newton-Jones also visited the track on the morning of October 19.

"Members of the public may have noticed him in the area on that day, and we would like to hear from them."

A statement from his family said Newton-Jones was "warm, empathetic and incredibly generous".

"He plays a significant role in the lives of his family and friends. They are deeply concerned that he is missing."

Newton-Jones had been an engineer, but decided in his mid-20s to re-train as a psychologist.

"He is currently in the final stages of completing his PhD. He has a passion for working with children and young adults and helping them to navigate adversity.

"Like many New Zealanders, Sam has experienced his own mental health challenges. However, he recently described himself as feeling optimistic about the year ahead."

The family said his disappearance is highly out of character.

"Sam's family urge members of the public to contact police with any sightings, observations or information that may help to locate him. Sam's car was last seen at Mercer Bay, so Piha locals in particular are asked to stay aware of Sam. The family appreciate prayers and support at this difficult time."

Newton-Jones was about 185cm tall and wears glasses. He was known to be wearing a white shirt, black pants and black sneakers.

World.title: Lake Omapere gets $3 million boost to tackle algal bloom
World.content:
An ambitious project to restore Northland's largest - and most polluted - lake has received a $3 million boost from the government's Regional Infrastructure Fund.

Regional Development Minister Shane Jones made the announcement at Lake Ōmāpere, just north of Kaikohe, on Wednesday afternoon.

Jones said the funding would pay for consents, road access, a weir to regulate lake levels and design work for future water storage infrastructure.

He said the project would "go a long way" towards improving Northland's water and economic resilience while also restoring the lake's health.

The 1200-hectare lake was once regarded as the food bowl of Ngāpuhi for its vast numbers of eels and freshwater mussels.

However, deforestation in the 1800s, followed by expansion of farming, triggered a steady decline in water quality.

Lake Ōmāpere, north of Kaikohe, is Northland’s largest lake. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Since the 1980s the lake, which is little more than two metres deep, has been blighted by regular algal blooms, killing aquatic life and making the water unusable for drinking, recreation or irrigation.

Jones said local communities had long regarded Lake Ōmāpere as a taonga.

"Restoring the lake's health is about honouring that connection while supporting communities, businesses and future development. This investment is an important step towards realising that long-term vision."

Associate Minister Mark Patterson said a reliable water supply was critical if Northland was to remain productive during dry periods.

"By helping advance this project, we're supporting the long-term resilience of the region and its ability to respond to future water challenges, as well as helping revive a precious taonga," he said.

"A healthy Lake Ōmāpere has the potential to support local communities by enabling strengthened food production and creating opportunities for Māori economic development."

The first stage of the project was expected to cost around $5.9m with funding from multiple partners.

Called He wai ora, he iwi ora (If the water is well, the people are well), the project is led by Lake Ōmāpere GP Limited on behalf of the Lake Ōmāpere Trust.

Northland MP Grant McCallum said the $3 million investment was "fantastic news" for Northland.

He said Lake Ōmāpere Trust chair Marise Stuart, the trustees and locals had worked tirelessly for many years.

"Their commitment to restoring this precious lake and securing a better future for their community deserves real recognition."

McCallum said the trust's wider restoration vision included sediment traps, riparian planting, wetland restoration and addressing decades of sediment build-up.

World.title: Body found after man in kayak went into the sea at Waihi Beach
World.content:
A body had been found in the search for missing kayaker at Waihi Beach on Coromandel Peninsula.

Police said the body is believed to be that of the man who was last seen on Tuesday though formal identification is yet to take place.

A search and rescue operation began at the beach after the man was reported missing about 5.40pm.

World.title: How Antonelli can become F1's youngest world champion this weekend
World.content:
Italian F1 driver Kimi Antonelli has his first chance to win the world championship this weekend, as the 20-year-old closes in on a maiden title in just his second season.

The Mercedes driver has been a class above the rest in 2026, with eight grand prix wins and a further six podium places across 17 rounds.

This Monday's (AEDT) United States Grand Prix will be Antonelli's first match point where he can officially seal a championship that has felt like his for many months.

The equation for Kimi Antonelli is very simple: win and hope for other results.

Antonelli enters this weekend's grand prix on 340 points, 102 more than teammate George Russell and 111 ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.

The Italian needs to have a lead of 125 points or more to seal the drivers' championship at the United States Grand Prix.

That will happen if Antonelli wins the race, Russell finishes ninth or worse, and Hamilton finishes fifth or worse.

Antonelli Russell Hamilton Championship result Win 9th or lower 5th or lower Antonelli becomes champion Win 8th or better 5th or lower Hamilton eliminated Win 9th or lower 4th or better Russell eliminated Win 8th or better 5th or lower Championship remains alive 2nd or lower Any Any Championship remains alive

After this weekend, there will be five grands prix left in the season — Mexico, Brazil, Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

There will be a maximum of 125 points left to win.

If Antonelli finishes exactly 125 points ahead of either Russell or Hamilton in Texas, mathematically either of those drivers could end the season level on points — if they won every race and Antonelli failed to score another point.

Even in that unlikely scenario, Antonelli would still become champion through a tie-break, having won more grands prix than the others.

6:30am: ACDT: South Australia

World.title: Australians run 80 hours or more in 'crazy' race with no finish line
World.content:
It sounds like a metaphor for torture: a running race with no finish line.

About 900 runners from 67 nations, including 15 Australians, crossed the start line of the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship at 11pm on Saturday AEDT at Kembla Grange in the New South Wales Illawarra.

In a deceptively simple test of physical and mental grit, each athlete completes a 6.7-kilometre course loop on the hour, every hour, until one runner remains.

They squeeze food and minutes of sleep into the remaining time, in an event that can stretch beyond four days.

Jonathan Ash was the first Australian to pull out, succumbing to injury on Monday afternoon after he exceeded the hour limit on his 41st lap.

He told the event's live stream that knee bursitis and muscle tightness from the 16th lap slowed him down.

"Basically every muscle in my body started to get knotted at some point," Ash said.

"We had to get a physio in to push that out.

"[It was] probably one of the most painful experiences of my life."

Jonathan Ash, 43, took up running in his 30s and is now one of Australia's top endurance athletes. (Supplied: Snapped Sport Pics)

The Shellharbour engineer is the second-ever Australian to complete 100 laps, equal to 670 kilometres, over four days in 2024, behind Phil Gore, who sits injured on the sidelines this year, tending to fellow athletes.

Gore broke the world record last year after running 119 laps, or 797.3km, after five days on a southern Queensland farm.

Each Australian runner has a team of supporters stationed in tents ready to provide first aid, food and water between loops. (Supplied: Snapped Sport Pics)

Melbourne's Brandon Lee Gretch tapped out after lap 73 about midnight on Wednesday and said he was proud of his effort, having achieved a personal best.

"I came in with 20 seconds to spare and had a shooting pain down my back. That was just killing me from about yard 67 onwards," he said.

"It was hell."

Brandon Lee Gretch, 32, described the world championship event as "running with 14 of my best friends". (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

The 32-year-old was cheerful as he snacked on chicken nuggets this morning with heavily bandaged feet.

"Myself as an eight-year-old would be so proud to know I got to put on the green and gold," Gretch said.

"It's weird because I am so sleep-deprived, I feel like my body automatically goes into recovery mode.

Dozens of local volunteers have helped coordinate the Backyard Ultra World Championship at the grassy Kembla Grange course. (Supplied: Snapped Sport Pics)

"The only bad thing is I always wake up [with] stiff legs, so I'll have to get moving again soon."

Backyard ultras were invented 15 years ago by Gary "Lazarus Lake" Cantrell and hosted at his Bell Buckle property in Tennessee.

"He wanted to challenge people to complete 100 miles in 24 hours," Australian race director Red Barnett said.

"It just grew in popularity as people pushed beyond the 24-hour mark.

"It is a bit of a crazy event."

Ash described the event as "the lesson that every person is incredibly capable of much more than they think they are".

"You don't know until you give it a shot," he said.

Dan Camac crossed the finishing line of lap 81 with about 10 minutes to spare on Wednesday morning, shortly after teammate Ben Nicholls. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Australian athletes have so far completed more than 1,000 laps, but the attrition rate has been severe.

"There's a mixture of fatigue, not getting their nutrition right, body ailments that are going on," Ms Barnett said.

"So unfortunately, we just had one after the other [drop out] and are left with two [Australian competitors].

" If all goes well, these guys [Dan Camac and Ben Nicholls] are hoping to get to 100 hours, which is Thursday morning. "

Red Barnett started hosting Backyard Ultras in Wollongong's south in 2020 and is now managing the Australian course of the World Championship. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

Ms Barnett said things would become "drastically harder" for the remaining Australians.

"When there is only two left, they really need to work together," she said.

"Having a lot of people around to support and cheer them on, even through the nights, all that really helps, but it's going to be a huge mental test."

World.title: PNG Chiefs unveil new logo ahead of 2028 NRL entry
World.content:
The PNG Chiefs have unveiled the club's inaugural logo ahead of its debut NRL season in 2028.

The club says the striking logo, designed by a team of graphic artists in Papua New Guinea, depicts what makes the Chiefs "strong and what makes us unique".

A supporters' jersey was also unveiled on Wednesday.

The new logo and jersey were described as a defining moment for the new club as it prepares to enter the NRL, based in a nation which is obsessed with rugby league.

PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said the unveiling of the logo marked "one of the most significant milestones in the journey of the PNG Chiefs".

"This is the first time that our club has its true, complete identity — a logo and jersey that our players, partners and fans can hold to as their own," McPherson said.

"The logo of the PNG Chiefs tells a story about Papua New Guinea — our people, what makes us strong and what makes us unique.

"The jersey of the PNG Chiefs is more than what players wear when they take to the field; it is a symbol of belonging, unity and the opportunity to represent millions of Papua New Guineans on the national stage.

"We know the responsibility that comes with establishing this club and we are incredibly proud to show our club to the world today.

"We strive for the PNG Chiefs to be something our country is proud of in every way — not because of the success that we will achieve on the field, but for the opportunities and legacy we will create for our country."

Elements of the PNG Chiefs logo

As per the PNG Chiefs media release

The feather headpiece: Inspired by Papua New Guinea's ceremonial plumes, the five feathers represent strength, beauty, chiefly status and national pride, with the Southern Cross connecting the club to the nation's flag.

The cassowary bone: Inspired by warrior traditions, the cassowary bone symbolises chiefly status, courage, power and the fighting spirit of the team.

The face: The chief's face represents the shape of Papua New Guinea, with ceremonial red paint showing a nation united through one warrior, one team and one purpose.

The kina shells: Representing traditional wealth, trade and prestige across Papua New Guinea's coastal, island and highland communities, the kina symbolises the value, legacy and future the club is building for the nation.

World.title: Snooker player in tears, hugged by presenter, after emotional and raw interview
World.content:
Former world number one snooker player Mark Allen has given an emotional and tearful interview, which involved a hug from the presenter and the admission that he may give up the game.

Allen, 40, took a break from playing after losing a dramatic semifinal in April's World Snooker Championship in April.

The Northern Irishman is understood to have taken time away from the game to deal with private matters, and it has cast doubt over the 40-year-old's future in the sport.

Loading Instagram content

Allen returned to the table for the first time since the world championship semi, where he missed a match-ball black that would have sent him to the decider, with a 4-2 defeat in the first round of the Northern Ireland Open to good friend Jordan Brown.

After the defeat, Allen did an interview with TNT Sports presenter Rachel Casey, where he admitted he was strongly considering throwing away the game he loved.

"I'm in a bad place at the minute, so even just to go out there and try was tough," Allen said.

"I think if I weren't playing Jordan, I wouldn't have come back.

"I felt like if I was going to play one last time, playing here at the Waterfront, where it all started in 2005, against one of my best mates — I thought that was a better way to sign out."

Asked if he was genuinely considering retirement, the winner of 12 ranking tournaments said it was a real possibility.

"I've been flooded with support but the problems are within. I just don't see a future with snooker in it, if I'm honest," he said.

"It's sad to say, because it's all I've loved to do since I was 12, but the last few months has been really difficult, and it's put snooker into perspective for me. At the minute, I'm just trying to survive."

In a touching moment, the interview was paused as Casey gave a clearly distraught Allen a comforting hug.

Allen also gave an interview with BBC Sport NI, where he said he was not prepared to retire now, but he had contemplated it "for a while".

Allen is a former world number one with 12 ranking titles in his career since turning professional in 2005.

He has won his home Northern Ireland Open twice, as well as two of the three Triple Crown events — Masters (2018) and the UK Championship (2022).

Loading Instagram content

Brown, who advances to the final 32 in Belfast with his win, described the match against his friend Allen as " the hardest match I've ever had to deal with".

"I don't even know what to say, I'm lost for words," he told Casey on TNT Sports.

"I've missed him, I love him. Just a great guy, through and through."

World.title: AFL sets date and time of AFL Origin between WA and SA
World.content:
The AFL has set the date for next year's State of Origin clash between Western Australia and South Australia.

The two states will clash at Perth Stadium on Saturday, February 27, marking South Australia's first Origin appearance in 28 years.

The match will begin at 4:40pm local time in Perth (7:10pm ACDT, 7:40pm AEDT).

"We are thrilled to officially confirm a date for AFL Origin in 2027, with Western Australia and South Australia set to reignite one of football’s greatest rivalries next February," AFL CEO Andrew Dillon said.

"[Perth] Stadium provided an incredible stage for AFL Origin's return earlier this year and we look forward to continuing to build on that momentum as we prepare for a meeting of two proud football states in Perth.

"We know football fans around the country will embrace the opportunity to celebrate the history, rivalry and unique spectacle that is AFL Origin."

WA and SA have not faced each other in a State of Origin since 1998, and the fixture coincides with the 150th anniversary of the SANFL competition.

State of Origin returned in 2026, with Victoria defeating WA by 36 points in Perth.

SA replaces Victoria for the 2027 edition, but the two old rivals will meet in 2028.

World.title: Ellis scores monster 47 points, most in WNBL game for over two decades
World.content:
Townsville's Abbey Ellis has produced one of the all-time great WNBL individual performances with a mammoth 47-point effort in the Fire's 86-68 away win over Adelaide.

The defending champions trailed 35-21 in the second quarter but outscored Adelaide 27-10 in the last term.

They improved to 1-1 while Adelaide dropped to 0-2.

Ellis kept her team afloat in the first half, scoring 25 of their first 33 points and their first 16 of the second quarter.

Her club record individual score, eclipsing the 45 points by Chandi Jones in 2005, was the equal fifth-highest in WNBL history and the largest in 21 years.

She joined league legends Lauren Jackson, Penny Taylor and Belinda Snell among the only players to record 47 points and six steals in a game.

"It's a pretty cool feeling," Ellis said.

She hit 16 of 24 from the field, nailing seven of 13 from three-point range.

"Credit to our team, we used the ball really well and found the hot hand," Ellis said.

Townsville coach Shannon Seebohm said Ellis was one of the bravest players he had coached.

"Abbey had probably one of the best games that I know I've ever seen In the WNBL, making huge shots, making big plays," Seebohm said.

"I said to her probably the thing I was most proud of her wasn't all the scoring, [it was] that she was fighting as hard as she could and defending her butt off."

Adelaide led by seven at quarter-time and Townsville scored the last seven points of the second quarter to get within three at the half.

As the game progressed, Townsville's defence improved and Ellis got more scoring support from Courtney Woods (14) and German centre Marie Gulich (13).

Alicia Froling grabbed 11 rebounds and Alexandra Fowler 10 to help Townsville collect 11 more boards.

Adelaide were shooting at 62 per cent from the field at half-time, but that dropped to 45 per cent by the end, as they scored just 25 points after half-time.

"We had a tough second half," Lightning coach Aja Parham-Ammar said.

Tayla Brazel led Adelaide's offence with a personal WNBL career-high of 19, at 72 per cent from the field.

Shay Ciezki tallied 13 points, Zitina Aokuso 12 and Opals star Steph Talbot had 11 and nine assists in her first game back from WNBA duties.

AAP

World.title: Gardner smashes 84 as Australia retains Rose Bowl over NZ
World.content:
Australia has retained the Rose Bowl with a comfortable 40-run victory in the Twenty20 International against New Zealand at North Sydney Oval.

Led by a blazing 84 from vice-captain Ash Gardner, Australia scored a competitive 6-167 and held New Zealand to 8-127 on Tuesday night, claiming a 2-0 lead in the three-match series, with the remaining game on Thursday.

It was Australia's 12th T20 victory in a row, including an unbeaten run during the World Cup in the UK during June and July, prompting Gardner to credit surprise skipper Sophie Molineux with enhancing a winning culture.

Aussies beat New Zealand in first women's T20 Australia survives a scare to down New Zealand by two wickets in the first T20 at North Sydney Oval.

"It's led by Soph, who has brought this different mantra to the group, and the fun aspect as well," Gardner said.

"When you're enjoying yourself, and you're having fun, it creates an environment of growth and wanting to learn and challenge yourself."

Australia has held the Rose Bowl for more than 26 years, and the trophy is on the line again in March for a three-match one-day series. This will be the first time it has been contested twice in the same season.

Gardner dominated an otherwise stuttering Australian batting performance, hitting 10 fours and four sixes in 45 balls on the compact North Sydney Oval.

Beth Mooney looked good for the second time in the series without pressing on, well caught by a diving Maddy Green at long on for 39 from 28 deliveries, lofting a slower ball from Jess Kerr.

Australia then smothered New Zealand. White Ferns captain Melie Kerr top scored with 32 from 38 balls, while Australia's most successful bowler was leg-spinner Georgia Wareham, who claimed 3-18 from her four overs.

New Zealand named an unchanged team after giving Australia a fright in the opening game, with the home side scrambling to victory by two wickets in a tense finish.

There was no such tension this time, with New Zealand never mounting a serious challenge.

AAP

World.title: Bavuma's batting masterclass takes control from Australia
World.content:
A few days before this Test series began, a digitally manipulated image was doing the rounds on social media.

Modelling South Africa's new Test playing kit, a pensive expression on his face, Proteas skipper Temba Bavuma was flanked by teammates Ryan Rickelton and Marco Jansen.

The visual punchline, in this case, was that Bavuma had been shrunk even smaller than his already-diminutive self, dwarfed by his teammates, even though he was standing on a superimposed shoe-shine box. My sides!

Australia on the ropes in second Test Temba Bavuma's sensational century turns the second Test on its head and leaves Australia on the ropes after day three.

Never mind that 5'4" Bavuma's batting inspiration, Sachin Tendulkar, stands only an inch taller, nor that the previous owner of India's "Little Master" moniker, Sunil Gavaskar, is the same height as Bavuma. Nor, indeed, that a certain lad from Bowral who did kind of OK in the 1930s and 40s was only 5'7". None faced quite the same level of condescension or fixation on their physical stature as Bavuma.

In reality, Bavuma is, by a few key measures, as big as anyone in the story of South African cricket in the post-apartheid decades. On the world stage he captained his country to victory in the 2025 World Test Championship decider, banishing years of big-tournament heartbreak.

Australians, apt to wipe such unexpected defeats in crunch games from the collective memory, are thus obliged to bracket Bavuma with a select group of figurehead skippers of recent decades — Clive Lloyd, Sourav Ganguly, Michael Vaughan, Virat Kohli — who've engineered famous and important victories against great Australian Test sides in their pomp.

Now Australia reckons with his batting. On day three of the second Test at Gqeberha, Bavuma played an innings that, for context and quality, ranks among the highest calibre; a towering and important century that any of the all-timers above would envy.

Beginning the day on 41, with his side wobbling away at 5-97, Bavuma finished it with a stunning set of numbers next to his name: 179 runs from 334 deliveries in a total of 9-425 declared.

Temba Bavuma's (right) presence is towering over the second Test match. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Due to the rain and delays of the opening stages of this game, Bavuma's epic stretched across three days, clocked in at a shade under 10 hours and required nothing less than the total psychological and physical mastery of the most complete pace attack in world cricket. Australians scoff at the mere concept of moral victories, but here Bavuma and South Africa claimed a resounding one.

It was the highest score of Bavuma's career, his fourth century (out of five all up) since becoming captain and moving up the order, and it means that a game in which Australia fancied skittling the Proteas on a green pitch is very unlikely to be won by the tourists — and possibly worse.

The "possibly worse" part got its preview sequence in the final moments of the day, when South Africa's returning paceman Kagiso Rabada marauded his way through Nic Maddinson to leave Australia one wicket down at stumps. Had bad light not limited Bavuma to the use of spinners in the final three overs of the day, the carnage could have been worse.

Quick hits: Jansen hit where it hurts as Bavuma grinds Aussies into the dirt Here are the quick hits from day three of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.

It has been said that the Australians respect but don't particularly warm to Bavuma. By this theory, he is aloof, undemonstrative and unlikely to engage in banter, verbal sparring or fun. In that way, he is more like a bowler who always had Australia's measure, Curtly Ambrose. "Curtly talks to no-one," Ambrose once said. It worked out just fine for him, too.

Bavuma's knock was a masterpiece of the kind of tempo batting that makes Test cricket tragics swoon. His watchful first 50, comprised almost entirely of judicious nudges, nurdles and leaves, took 140 deliveries.

His second, which grew to encompass sumptuous on drives, square drives and a cracking pull shot off Pat Cummins to reach his century, took only 86 balls. His third, a by-product of an acceleration phase when he and Simon Harmer removed any thoughts of an Australian victory, came from just 73 balls.

It was hard to believe this was the same player who'd scratched around for a combined total of four runs in 45 tortured deliveries last week in Durban. But like Matt Renshaw in that game, it was not just Bavuma's own runs that turned this contest on its head but the partnerships he forged with his side's highly capable tailenders.

Loading Instagram content

There was a thrilling stand of 132 from 186 with Marco Jansen, whose 85 came at almost a run a ball and, to be fair, presented a truly arresting example of cricket's capacity to attract all shapes and sizes. Paired with the 6'8" beanpole, Bavuma brought to mind the famous photo of NBA basketballers Muggsy Bogues and Manute Bol.

Even more profitable — game-defining, most likely — was Bavuma's union with Harmer, the spinner whose surprising selection reprieve suddenly seemed completely sensible as he hammered his way through a sparkling knock of 82 from 157 deliveries. Their partnership of 183 traversed 46 overs and was South Africa's highest eighth-wicket stand ever — not the sort of record with which this Australian squad likes to be associated.

In the final analysis, 315 runs came after the fall of South Africa's sixth wicket. It was a total wipe-out for the Aussies.

What did Cummins get wrong? There were some indefensibly defensive field placements, in truth, especially in the crucial phase when Jansen went berserk and Bavuma fed him the strike with easy singles to men stationed in the deep.

But as Richie Benaud once said, the best attribute a captain can have is luck, and there wasn't much on offer here for Cummins. Josh Hazlewood, missing with illness on day two, was thus obliged not to bowl for the first two hours of the day. The green pitch, which had promised carnage early in the game, turned docile and offered minimal lateral movement even for Scott Boland. And after the second new ball brought the wicket of Jansen — Boland's fifth — very little else transpired, so the field spread again.

Of the Australian bowlers, Boland was clearly the pick with 5-81 from 29 overs, and the overall picture of gloom rather rubbished the claim that his otherworldly Test statistics could be attributed to being slotted into an attack that was always firing from the other end (and anyway, by that logic, Andy Bichel, as the last backup quick to receive acclaim like that heaped on Boland, would have easily maintained a bowling average far lower than 32).

In the Boland years, as in the Bichel ones, sometimes even great sides have to admit it has not been their day. That was Australia today; at the mercy of the biggest small man in cricket, who doesn't have to open his mouth to say something profound.

Tech.title: YouTube might be testing hiding the dislike button
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

YouTube appears to be testing hiding the dislike button on videos, as reported by 9to5Google. At least two users on X have recently shared screenshots of the dislike button now being placed in the three-dots submenu, and a user on Reddit also shared an image of the dislike button being absent for them.

Right now, for me, the dislike button sits right next to the like button under a video. Moving it to a submenu would make it considerably more of an effort to access, meaning that fewer people would likely use it.

It’s unclear how widely this apparent test may be rolled out, and Google didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

YouTube has shown a willingness to make changes to the dislike button. In 2021, it hid the public dislike count on videos to help “protect creators from harassment,” though creators can still see dislike counts. Earlier this year, YouTube removed the dislike button from YouTube Shorts, suggesting instead that users take advantage of options in the three-dots menu.

Tech.title: Judge dismisses Sam Altman’s sister’s sexual abuse lawsuit
Tech.content:
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

On Tuesday, US District Judge Zachary Bluestone dismissed the lawsuit Ann Altman filed last year alleging that her brother, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, had sexually abused her throughout her childhood. As reported earlier by The Guardian, the judge wrote that over the past year, Ann had failed to appear for an independent medical examination or meet other deadlines despite warnings that it would result in the case being dismissed.

When the case was filed last year, a statement shared by Sam Altman, his mother, and his brothers said, “Annie has made deeply hurtful and entirely untrue claims about our family, and especially Sam… All of these claims are utterly untrue. This situation causes immense pain to our entire family.”

Bluestone granted Sam Altman’s motion to dismiss the case with prejudice, meaning it can’t be refiled in that court, while denying Sam’s request for attorney fees and costs. Santos Perez, a lawyer who had represented Ann until withdrawing this month, told The Guardian in a statement that “I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie.”

Tech.title: Trump is giving Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million fraud bounty program
Tech.content:
is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance said on Tuesday that the Trump administration was giving right-wing YouTuber Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million bounty program for members of the public to report fraud.

In December 2025, Shirley published a viral video alleging fraud at daycares in Minnesota that were operated by members of the local Somali community. Shirley lingered in parking lots and asked to enter childcare centers, taking refusals as evidence that the centers weren’t actually caring for children. The video quickly went viral, triggering a massive governmental response: Federal immigration agents descended on the Minneapolis area, and the Trump administration froze Minnesota’s federal funding for childcare. Shirley has since visited other states in the US under similar pretenses, showing up unannounced to grocery stores and hospice centers in search of evidence of fraud. Vance and others in the administration publicly praised Shirley, who has since become a mainstay in the MAGA-aligned content creator ecosystem. He’s helped popularize a genre of so-called independent journalism popular on the right in which content creators and influencers confront businesses or people they suspect of fraud or crime as the basis for their online content. Harassment — or even immigration crackdowns — often follow.

The administration told Fox News that it was also launching the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program (WHIP), a pool of $25 million open to anyone who believes they’ve witnessed fraud. A “particular emphasis” is placed on fraud in hospice, home healthcare, daycares, and special services, a government website says. A chatbot collecting responses instructs the reporting party: “Briefly describe what you saw, heard, or read. A few sentences are enough. Include names, dates, amounts, or records if you have them, and how you know. Note any details you’re unsure about.”

According to Fox News and the reporting portal, members of the public who flag fraud are eligible to get up to $30,000 if a tip submitted leads to a conviction or significant federal action. But speaking on Tuesday, Trump contradicted the $30,000 ceiling.

”If you turn somebody in and … you find $1 billion, we are giving a commission to that person of 1 percent,” Trump said today. (One percent of $1 billion would exceed the $30,000 cap.) “And if it’s $10 billion, $200 billion, $400 billion, we’re giving a 1 percent commission to that person,” Trump continued.

The White House didn’t immediately clarify how the $10,000 payment to Shirley was calculated or how the program is being funded in the first place.

Shirley’s methods have been criticized particularly in Minnesota, where sweeping fraud investigations were already taking place before he arrived to make content. He accused businesses of faking childcare services based on little more than being denied entry to facilities, and — to the frustration of many — acted as if his video was the first fraud investigation in the state. Subsequent state official visits to the centers Shirley featured found them operating “as expected.”

Tech.title: Google’s more personalized Gemini AI is heading to your car
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search.

As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.”

Google brought its Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year before rolling it out to cars with Google built-in in April. Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps.

Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says.

Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months.

Tech.title: Tesla and SpaceX are discussing a possible merger, Musk says
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger, Elon Musk said during the latter’s third quarter earnings call Tuesday.

Musk, who serves as CEO of both companies, said the special committees were formed at the request of shareholders and consist of independent directors (though he did not name them). He also noted that he is not a member of either committee, nor involved in any of the discussions.

“Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” Musk said. “So it’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation.”

The groups have not reached agreement on the terms of any transaction — and there’s no guarantee that they will. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this,” he continued. “And particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50 percent vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that’s quite a high hurdle to try to achieve.”

That said, Musk called the possibility of a Tesla-SpaceX merger a “good idea.” He continued:

I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity. And there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the TeraFab, obviously robotics, mass to orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity. So I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies. They’ve got to come up with something and then that’s going to be put to the shareholders as a vote.

A Tesla-SpaceX merger would be a blockbuster corporate deal creating a mega-entity valued upwards of $3.6 trillion. But combining Musk’s car and energy company with his AI and rocket company would not be without its tradeoffs. A lot depends on which company absorbs the other. To buy SpaceX, Tesla would have to create millions of new stock shares, which for current Tesla owners would mean owning a smaller slice of a much larger pie. SpaceX’s launch goals require tens of billions of dollars every year — extra spending that could drain Tesla’s ability to build new car factories and battery plants.

That said, most Wall Street analysts and legal experts believe SpaceX would acquire Tesla (or absorb it through a stock swap) rather than vice versa. Since its IPO, SpaceX has maintained a higher valuation than Tesla. A merger in that direction would allow SpaceX shareholders to hold the majority control of the combined mega-entity. Some Tesla shareholders may balk at this deal.

But it would also create one company for those who believe in Musk’s vision of the future — robot cars, humanoid robots, AI super-intelligence, and human habitats on Mars — in which to place their investments. And Tesla shareholder approved Musk’s enormous pay package last year — even after a Delaware judge tossed it over lack of independence.

Earlier this month, Barclays published a client note suggesting a potential Tesla-SpaceX combination could be announced ahead of Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting scheduled for December 3, 2026.

Tech.title: SpaceX will try catching Starship and its booster for first time, Musk says
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said the company would attempt to catch Starship and its booster next month, with the goal of recovering the entire orbital launch system for the first time. If successful, Musk said, the attempt would mark the first time in history an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered.

“This is a profound technology milestone in the history of civilization consciousness,” he said during the company’s third quarter earnings report Tuesday.

But he also allowed for the possibility of a failure. “Success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight,” Musk said. “And if not, we have a steady stream of Starship flight attempts through the end of this year and then accelerating next year.”

“Success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.” — Elon Musk

Starship is a two-stage system, composed of the Super Heavy booster (first stage) and the Starship spacecraft (second stage). It stands approximately 120 meters (around 400 feet) tall with a 9-meter diameter, and is powered by SpaceX’s Raptor engines burning liquid methane and liquid oxygen. Starship, which was first introduced in 2018, was designed to return to the launch site, where launch towers with mechanical “chopstick” arms catch the vehicle mid-air.

Last month’s Starship launch represented two firsts for its next gen rocket: send the spacecraft into Earth orbit, and insert a few dozen of SpaceX’s larger and more capable V3 satellites into the Starlink constellation for the first time. Still, the launch wasn’t without its snafus: one Raptor engine shut down prematurely during ascent, prompting mission control to adapt and complete the climb on remaining. Because of the issue, SpaceX cut the planned 10-hour, 6-orbit mission short after about 3 hours and 2 Earth orbits.

The Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico, while the Starship upper stage executed a de-orbit burn and ended with a fiery vertical splashdown in the Pacific Ocean north of Hawaii. Neither piece was recovered.

Tech.title: Netflix is telling investors not to worry, even though you’re watching less and less
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Netflix is making monetization a top priority amid reports of falling viewing time. As part of its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, Netflix lists improvements to monetization as one of its main focuses going forward, alongside efforts to boost entertainment value and leverage new technology.

The streaming giant doesn’t say exactly how it plans to improve its monetization, but the company notes that these goals will help Netflix “create member value that lets us occasionally raise prices, and increase advertiser demand.” Netflix also highlighted plans to push further into original titles, live events, and third-party programming as it faces an “intense competition and an explosion of content competing for consumer attention.”

An analysis from financial firm Jefferies estimated that Netflix’s monthly viewing time per member dropped to 49 hours in the first half of this year, down from 66 hours in the first half of 2023, according to a report from Reuters. At the same time, Netflix made up 7.8 percent of US viewing time in the US in July, a one-percentage-point dip from the same time last year, The New York Times reports.

During an earnings call, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos pointed to success abroad when answering a question about the company’s content strategy. “We see titles across Latin America, EMEA (Europe, the Middle East and Africa), APAC (Asia-Pacific), driving engagement, subscriber growth, revenue, and profit,” Sarandos said. “Now, the US is also working. It’s just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we’d like.”

Related Netflix is pivoting away from prestige

In its letter to investors, Netflix mentions its upcoming lineup of NFL games, its Grand Theft Auto VI preview, and its partnership with French TV station TF1 as evidence of opening its platform to a wider breadth of content. The company reported earning $12.9 billion over the past few months, marking a 12 percent year-over-year increase. It also plans to bring its ad-supported tier — which raked in $1.5 billion last year — to 15 new countries in 2027.

In the coming months, Netflix may be facing tougher competition from HBO Max and Paramount Plus following the Skydance megamerger, as co-CEO David Ellison has said that he plans to combine the two apps into a single service. The streamer struck deals with several creators as it competes with YouTube, which has reportedly offered channels “millions of dollars” not to post their videos on Netflix.

Netflix has also weighed making even bigger changes to its app, including integrating other third-party streamers, such as Peacock and Fox One, as well as adding always-on channels, according to reports from The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal.

Update, October 20th: Added a quote from Sarandos.
