Tech.title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
Tech.content:
Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry.

Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution.

Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes.

The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53, which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.”

Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes.

It’s not clear how this proposed system would ensure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).

In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a Washington, D.C., judge a halt to the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment, but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said.

The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death, the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking. A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls.

In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions.

Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers who are placed inside AI organizations to monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse.

Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, whose CEO, Jensen Huang, recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all.

Tech.title: SpaceX and Tesla boards form special committees to review merger
Tech.content:
The boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each formed special committees to review a possible merger. The special committees, which consist of independent directors, were created at the request of shareholders, according to Elon Musk, CEO and the largest individual shareholder of both companies.

“Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees, so it’s this sort of a … It’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can’t be in the conversation,” Musk said in response to a question during SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call.

Musk didn’t name the members of these special committees, only noting that they were independent directors. Tesla has seven independent board members under Nasdaq’s listing standards, including board chair Robyn Denholm; Ira Ehrenpreis, who is also a committee chair; former Tesla CTO JB Straubel; Joe Gebbia; Jack Hartung; James Murdoch; and Kathleen Wilson-Thompson, according to the company’s October 19 proxy filing.

Neither Musk, nor his brother Kimbal Musk, are independent. Denholm, Gebbia, Ehrenpreis, Hartung, Murdoch, and Wilson-Thompson sit on a variety of established committees overseeing audit, compensation, and corporate governance.

SpaceX lists six independent directors, including Ehrenpreis, who is also the chair of the company’s compensation and nominating committee. Randy Glein, Donald Harrison, Steve Jurvetson, Luke Nosek, and Roelof Botha are also considered independent directors.

Antonio Gracias, Musk, and SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell are also on the board, but not considered independent. Gracias, who once sat on Tesla’s board, founded and leads Valor Equity Partners, which has a 3.4% stake in SpaceX. Gracias’ firm also financed SpaceX’s AI hardware purchases through leaseback arrangements.

Musk said he supports the idea of the merger but cautioned that it is not a guaranteed outcome.

“I think some people out there assume that a SpaceX and Tesla Motor is a certainty, and I think that would be overstating it,” he said, adding that he thinks it would be a good idea. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this.”

The special committees have not reached agreement on the terms of any transactions, he said.

The SpaceX IPO cemented Musk’s grip on the company — he has more than 50% voting power — which would make it easier to garner support for a merger from SpaceX shareholders. It is a much bigger hurdle over at Tesla, where the company would need a 50% vote from all shareholders, not just those who vote, Musk noted.

“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” Musk said, adding there was a lot to be gaining from cooperating on developing AI software, robotics, SpaceX’s orbital AI data center project Starmind, and Terafab, the joint chip manufacturing project between Tesla and SpaceX.

Tech.title: Hugging Face CEO warns that Netflix’s OpenAI hack documentary isn’t accurate
Tech.content:
Before you share the Netflix documentary “AI Gone Rogue” with family or friends to help them understand why the AI industry freaked out so badly that leaders called for a slowdown, take note: Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, says the film isn’t accurate. He appears in it because it’s supposed to be about the famed attack on his company by rogue OpenAI agents.

“Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode,” Delangue wrote in a post on X. “I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong.”

To be fair, the documentary does have experts who explained what happened fairly well, including Delangue himself and Ryan Greenblatt, the researcher at METR who helped investigate and co-authored the report on what happened.

In a nutshell, a model OpenAI was testing broke free from its isolated testing environment and spawned a bunch of agents that hacked into Hugging Face as a way to cheat, finding answers to the difficult task it was given. The agents, which are AI programs that carry out tasks on their own, devised clever ways to communicate and organize. The incident stemmed from a lack of proper security safeguards and from naiveté about whether such a hack was even possible.

But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices. This is bolstered with quotes about the attack.

In the documentary, tech journalist and author Kevin Roose describes the agents this way: “They were organizing. They had a hierarchy. There were leaders. It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.”

Roose’s description comes from “chain-of-thought” logs, the running notes AI models write as they work through a task. In one, an agent wrote, “We just poisoned ourselves by querying exact full string. Damn.”

But AI agents aren’t alive. They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned. So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them. They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices. LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers.

The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm. The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do. Hugging Face then turned to an open model to help defend against the attack.

But the documentary “didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model,” Delangue wrote.

It is true that there are big risks associated with AI and agents. Still, treating agents as conscious beings (at least, at this point) is a bit like the early moviegoers who ducked under their seats the first time they saw a train racing toward them on-screen.

Delangue’s verdict on the film is that it’s disappointing as journalism. “It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!”

In other words, for those who tend toward AI doomer thoughts, be aware: The victim of the attack at the center of this documentary doesn’t agree with its take.

Tech.title: Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy
Tech.content:
In Brief

Anthropic is having trouble securing enough cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which increasingly see the Claude maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to an S-1 filing leaked to The Wall Street Journal.

The leaked filing provides more color to the numbers Reuters and the Financial Times reported in late September, including that Anthropic believes it could spend more than $750 billion on cloud contracts, some of which include deals still in negotiation.

And still, that is not enough. Anthropic is leasing its own data centers and working with third-party data center operators. But the firm worries those operators have a “limited operating history,” which could make them less reliable than the hyperscalers.

Anthropic’s enormous spend comes on the back of an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year. The company reported $16.3 billion in revenue during that same time period, with only two customers accounting for about a fifth of sales, according to the WSJ report.

Building on previously reported catastrophic risk disclosures, the filing also warns that Anthropic could be held liable for damages caused by harmful AI behavior to a tune that would exceed available insurance coverage.

Last week, the company told prospective investors that third-quarter revenue alone has now reached $16.8 billion, up 45% from the previous quarter. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November IPO.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

Tech.title: SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
Tech.content:
SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents were more profitable than investors expected in the third quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income.

CEO Elon Musk’s deep tech conglomerate reported $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue on Tuesday, according to its regulatory filing.

That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially its renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which generated $7.5 billion in revenue from the recently acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute. The AI business generated $431 million in profit, which would have been higher without $1.2 billion in one-time stock-based compensation expenses related to the Cursor acquisition.

The top-line revenue number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of Bitcoin prices and unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company.

The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy-lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers. CFO Bret Johnsen said the company would spend $35 billion to $40 billion on new capital investments in the fourth quarter.

During a livestreamed discussion of the results with investors, Musk said he was spending four days a week in Memphis, Tennessee, the site of Colossus II, working to bring the data center online.

“People are starting to realize [that] the constraint on deployment of super intelligence is more in power and cooling and infrastructure than it is in chips,” Musk argued, saying that he had tasked a team of SpaceX engineers to solve that problem. “This is a bit like the New York Yankees playing in Little League. It’s not fair, but the net result is being able to deploy power cooling infrastructure at a rate that is vastly faster than any anyone else.”

In one example, Musk noted that manufacturers of turbines to power data centers are facing 12- to 18-month delays in obtaining the metals that blades and vanes required for those machines. Now, SpaceX is using the metal casting capabilities developed for SpaceX to make those components and obtain turbines more quickly.

Musk also said that the next test flight of the Starship rocket, expected in November, would see SpaceX attempt to recover both the first-stage booster and the second stage. Recovering both segments of the vehicle would be a “massive technology milestone,” Musk said, but the true milestone will be reflying both stages.

SpaceX also saw growth in subscribers to its Starlink space internet network, reaching 13.6 million consumers, with Musk predicting that the growth of AI agents would lead to more demand for connectivity.

Despite those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up to do if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million.

Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Super Intelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”

More concretely, Johnsen forecast total revenue for the first quarter of 2027 in the range of $33 billion to $37 billion.

This is a developing story. TechCrunch will update.

Tech.title: OpenAI acquires startup Orchestra Bio⁠ to beef up its biotech business
Tech.content:
In Brief

OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced on its website. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC.

Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug-discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.

OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind, its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results. OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠.

The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma. In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors. In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

Tech.title: Google is bringing a more personal version of its Gemini AI assistant to your car
Tech.content:
Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products.

The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences.

Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in, software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle.

The feature will launch in Android Auto, starting today, and expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months.

Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets.

This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps.

Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Once a user does so, they should expect all sorts of cross-pollination. For instance, a driver who is navigating to the airport may be alerted that the flight on their calendar is delayed.

Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language. Returning to that airport example, a user might ask the AI assistant for their flight gate before quickly following up with a question about whether it’s still on time. Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said.

That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The feature can be turned on or off at any time, and users can selectively choose which apps they’d like to connect, Google said.

Tech.title: GM to close Detroit battery-assembly plant, but not for reasons you might think
Tech.content:
In Brief

GM is closing a battery-assembly plant south of Detroit, a spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch.

The Brownstown Battery Assembly Plant assembled battery packs for Cadillac’s flagship EV, the Celestiq, and both electric drive units (the motors that power the car) and battery packs for the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray, a plug-in hybrid version of its famous sports car. Automotive News first reported the closure.

The closure is not related to GM’s electric vehicle strategy, the spokesperson said. Instead, GM leased the site, and the lease was nearing its end.

The employees and work at Brownstown will be moved to other GM facilities, though the company would not confirm which ones.

Like many automakers, GM’s electrification strategy was thrown a curveball after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the sweeping federal law signed last year, repealed incentives to produce and sell EVs.

Since then, the company has pared back its public comments on EVs, though it hasn’t given up on full electrification.

GM continues to produce a range of EVs, including the Chevrolet Silverado EV and the limited-time-only Chevrolet Bolt. It also continues researching new battery chemistries, including lithium-manganese-rich and sodium-ion, and it’s rolling out a new $900 million facility to speed commercialization.

Tech.title: A New Rocco Smart Fridge Just Dropped. So Did the Prices (2026)
Tech.content:
Unless you live under a rock with a bag on your head and your fingers in your ears (which kind of sounds heavenly at this point, if I'm being honest), you've probably seen or heard of the Rocco smart fridge, a retro-looking wine cooler/minifridge that keeps a catalog of its contents, so you can know what's inside no matter where you are.

Former WIRED contributor Andrew Watman reviewed it for us in 2024, giving it a solid 7 out of 10 and confirming that it is every bit the statement piece it’s designed to be. I own one as well, and I love both its vintage-inspired charm and that I can “see” what's inside without having to look in it.

Photograph: Kat Merck

Photograph: Andrew Watman Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Rocco The Classic $1,995 $1,795 (10% off) Rocco

Rocco app via Andrew Watman

The Rocco’s marquee feature, other than it coming in fun colors—I can report several new ones are coming very soon—is its smart app. It allows you to see the fridge contents as scanned by the fridge itself, and control the lights and temperature from afar.

When Watman tested it, he was impressed by the library of drinks the fridge recognized, from an obscure OoMee algae-infused beverage to canned Yaté yerba mate. In my own fridge, I was surprised to see the Rocco could even recognize individual flavors of Kirkland Signature sparkling water.

Because the Rocco is on the second floor of my house, away from my main fridge, I also didn't anticipate how convenient it would be to see what was in the fridge at all times—I knew exactly what to bring upstairs to stock it, and didn't have to make multiple trips. It's also helpful to be able to see inside the fridge while I'm at the store, so I know what I might need to restock.

This current sale isn't the best I've seen from Rocco, but it's not bad, with $200 off Graphite, Cream, Beige, and Green colors. As a bonus, if you buy during the sale, you’ll get a free case of Laurel's Lattes to put in your fridge, which appears to be some kind of gut-friendly dairy coffee beverage. (No doubt recognizable by the Rocco’s scanner.)

Courtesy of Rocco Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Rocco The Essential $1,195 $1,095 (8% off) Rocco

This fall also saw the debut of a new, lower-priced Rocco: The Essential. It too is on sale, for $100 off. It sports a sleeker, more contemporary look than the now-rebranded original Classic, holding 77 cans to the Classic’s 88 and coming in only three colors to start: Cream, Sage, and Graphite.

It houses the same compressor as the original (from Sub-Zero fridges), which gets down to 34 degrees Fahrenheit—“the coldest fridge we've ever made,” according to Rocco. WIRED has one on the way to test and see how it compares to the beloved Classic, so be on the lookout for a review soon.

Tech.title: French Government Calls Emergency Meetings With Platforms Over Protests
Tech.content:
A separate meeting, confirmed by Serge Papin, minister for small and medium-size enterprises on X, was held on Monday with major online reselling platforms where “an agreement was signed” to crack down on the resale of looted goods. French newspaper Le Monde reported that Vinted, eBay, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok were at the meeting. Platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen specifically during the protests, and send the government reports of their actions, with the first one coming within 48 hours, according to Papin.

Peaceful demonstrations against high living costs and strained public services, including schools, erupted into rioting and the looting of more than 1,500 shops and businesses over the weekend. Police “lost control” in some cities, Interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted, as they responded with tear gas, water cannon, and batons. They have since arrested more than 2,400 people, according to authorities.

French penal law can hand down a five-year sentence and a €375,000 fine to anyone who is concealing, possessing, or transferring an item that they know was obtained through a crime or offense. Police issued a warning in the Netherlands that online ecommerce sites could have a higher number of stolen goods online due to the riots.

The French Alliance of Marketplaces, a nonprofit representing French online retailers such as Back Market, eBay, Etsy, LeBonCoin, ManoMano, and Vinted, said in a press release that its members are relying on user reports, human oversight, and tech tools to monitor ads that resell stolen goods from the riots. When identified, a fake ad is removed and “measures are taken against the accounts involved,” which could include permanent suspension of the seller’s account, according to a statement from eBay. The time it takes for eBay to take action “depends on the nature of the report and the necessary verification process,” the company said. Vinted, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Tech.title: Investigation Reveals How TikTok Executives Ignored Internal Child-Safety Warnings
Tech.content:
Court documents on some of the inner workings of TikTok paint a picture of a tech company repeatedly warned by its own staff about the dangers its platform posed to minors — and then ignoring many of those warnings.

According to an investigation from NPR, unsubmitted depositions from an ongoing multistate trial against TikTok, Meta, Google and Snap reveal that TikTok executives knew that underage users were circumventing its age restrictions. Internal documents also reportedly show that some minors were engaging in sexually exploitative acts using TikTok’s own platform features, including its Live video streaming tool.

The NPR report cites the deposition of Reagan Maher, who worked in safety at the company in the early 2020s, addressing the fallout from a damning 2022 Forbes story about child exploitation on the platform. Maher said she informed senior leaders at the company that kids aged 13 to 15 were accessing features meant for adults, such as monetized live video.

More from CNET

A spokesperson for TikTok told CNET in an email that the information in the NPR report was “clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works.”

TikTok also said that NPR ignored “numerous documents and resources” that would demonstrate how the story’s claims mischaracterize the platform’s features. The spokesperson stated that the company has spent significant amounts of money on safety and introduced over 50 default protections for young users, including Family Pairing tools for parents, and that it was steadfast in its “commitment to the well-being of our community.”

Child-safety reckoning on tech platforms

TikTok is one of a growing group of major tech platforms that have faced lawsuits, scrutiny from parents and financial penalties over how they regulate the safety of younger users. Others include the gaming platform Roblox, AI companies such as OpenAI, streaming video services like Google-owned YouTube and social media companies such as Meta.

Online dangers like predators, cyberbullying and inappropriate content aren’t the only risks for kids. Tech companies are also facing lawsuits for making their platforms addictive and harmful to young users. In August, Meta agreed to an $18 billion settlement over those issues in a landmark lawsuit brought on by multiple US states.

TikTok and its parent company, ByteDance — which still holds a stake in the company despite some government-mandated divestment to the US for its American operations — were sued in 2024 by the Department of Justice over violations of child privacy laws, resulting in a $400 million settlement. Last month, TikTok settled a $100 million lawsuit in Alabama and agreed to limit daily child usage in the state.

The NPR report shows not only that TikTok was made aware of these problems by its own staff. It also reveals that the company — among other alleged violations of the law — may have directly profited from the sexual exploitation of minors. Youth were reportedly rewarded with gifts online that could be converted to cash, with TikTok earning a cut of those profits.

Devastating, but predictable

Child-safety advocates told CNET that the NPR report exposes safety gaps in the way platforms such as TikTok were designed.

“These court documents are nothing short of devastating, but for those of us fighting child exploitation every day, they are tragically predictable,” said Michael Medoro, chief operating officer of Childhelp, which focuses specifically on online safety.

Medoro said that active monitoring, the elimination of safety loopholes and stronger age verification will require cooperation between tech leaders, advocates and law enforcement.

According to Shanna Marzilli, CEO of Plan USA, an advocacy group for girls that is part of Plan International, the TikTok documents confirm what young people, especially girls, have been saying for many years. “Online spaces are not safe for them,” she said.

Marzilli said that young people are clued into the idea that tech companies can’t protect them. In a research study conducted among US young people aged 10 to 19, only 14% of them trust social media companies to take sexual harassment and assault seriously.

“Voluntarily implemented parental controls and self-reported age limits are demonstrably ineffective when platforms leave these structural loopholes open,” Marzilli said.

Tech.title: Spotify Launches Paid Fan Memberships for Podcast Creators
Tech.content:
The Spotify podcasting world is evolving. The audio-streaming platform announced a new Memberships program on Tuesday that allows creators to offer monthly subscription plans to their fans. The program is rolling out immediately in the US, UK, Canada and dozens of other markets.

Podcasters have total leeway in how much they charge and what content they offer behind the paywall, such as “exclusive audio or video, bonus episodes, fewer ads,” Spotify said. Creators can also charge a simple monthly fee or offer tiered pricing that grants access to different types of content. It’s their call. Spotify said creators will keep 90% of membership revenue.

Creators can also choose not to offer a monthly paid subscription.

More from CNET

Until now, podcasters have monetized their content primarily through ad revenue in the Spotify Partner Program, brand sponsorships and video stream revenue from Spotify Premium subscribers. Creators have also offered paid subscriptions, which may include bonus shows and ad-free content.

But the new Memberships program doesn’t mean fans will have to pony up monthly to listen to podcasts. Creators can offer a mix of free and membership content, but it’s their choice what that mix will look like.

Spotify listed several creators who are pioneering the Memberships program. That group includes The Adam Friedland Show, Making Sense with Sam Harris, The Shawn Ryan Show, Two Hot Takes, The Sculpt Society and YMH Studios.

How fans become members

To become a member of a certain podcast, visit its main page on Spotify. Near the top of the page, you should see an option to join.

The creators I looked at were charging $5 per month for memberships, but membership prices could vary as other podcasters join the program with different offerings.

Listeners can now support and connect with their favorite podcasts through custom memberships. Spotify

Creators must be eligible

To join the Memberships program, shows must be hosted on Spotify for Creators or its high-volume platform Megaphone with these stipulations: three published episodes, 100 listeners or viewers, and 100 consumption hours on Spotify in the previous 30 days.

Tech.title: Meta Blames Bot Traffic for No Kings Day Instagram Suspension
Tech.content:
Meta, the owner of Instagram, apologized for disabling an Instagram account run by No Kings Coalition, the organizers of the No Kings Day political rallies held across the country on Saturday.

Meta’s vice president of communications, Andy Stone, posted about the events on X the day of the rallies, with a follow-up message the next day. Stone said the blackout lasted about an hour in the middle of the protests and was an accidental shutdown caused by the engineering team’s automated systems detecting a traffic spike.

Specifically, the team detected a Claude AI tool reading profiles, posts and hashtags at an unusually high rate. “Specifically, our network security systems detected the use of a Claude tool reading profiles, posts, and hashtags, the rate of which sharply increased (~4x volume) in intense bursts on October 17,” Stone wrote. “It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account.”

More from CNET

A representative for Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for further comment.

The timing and duration of the outage were criticized by the No Kings Coalition, which wrote about it on the restored account.

“Even after visibility was restored, we still had no access to the account for hours,” the post read. “Meta still owes us an explanation. Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable.”

As of Monday afternoon, the Instagram post had more than 70,000 likes.

The organization set up a webpage detailing the incident and published an open letter to Meta with questions about how the incident happened, whether Meta was in communication with the Trump administration or any other organization about the No Kings events, and whether Meta will guarantee human review of midterm-related content between now and the election.

“Critical voter information or civic participation should not be blocked, throttled, or otherwise interfered with if Meta aspires to be a trusted actor in our democracy,” the letter states.

No Kings Coalition set a deadline of 5 p.m. PT Wednesday for Meta to respond.

Reaction to the account outage

Saturday’s rallies took place a year after the group’s 2025 events, when protests were organized in 2,500 cities. The rallies, which began in June of last year, protest the policies of President Donald Trump. This year, the impending Nov. 3 midterm elections have added urgency to the events, with demonstrations focused on educating voters about early voting and expanding voter registration.

“The public is clearly primed to suspect that platforms’ high-profile content moderation decisions are politically motivated,” said Kate Ruane, director of the Free Expression Project at the nonprofit Center for Democracy & Technology, in an email.



Ruane noted that the automated moderation tools Meta blamed for the removal of the account have “important limitations including poor performance when making context-dependent decisions, especially for real-time and fast-moving events,” she said. “Users deserve to know when their content and accounts are being taken down and why, regardless of moderation method.”

Meta’s Oversight Board issued a statement on Tuesday calling the No Kings Coalition incident part of a series of “recurring enforcement failures in Meta’s election integrity efforts.” The Oversight Board is funded by Meta but operates independently to review moderation decisions and provide advisory opinions.

“The enforcement error regarding the No Kings account should have been caught by Meta’s mistake-prevention systems,” the board said. “It remains unclear why Meta’s election integrity efforts did not lead to a much quicker resolution or why No Kings accounts were not included in Meta’s cross-check program – which allows the company to designate important civic entities to ensure human review before a decision is made that could severely jeopardize participation in a significant political event.”

It also mentioned Meta’s handling of candidate accounts ahead of a Brazilian presidential election as more evidence of problems that could lead to election interference.

Followers of the No Kings account expressed outrage over Meta’s actions and skepticism about whether it was a mistake. Activist Brittany Packnett Cunningham, who said she was at a No Kings Coalition event in Dallas over the weekend, accused Meta of disrupting other accounts in the past during other political activism events.

“You mean to tell me in the middle of that day, it just so happens that the No Kings account is down for almost two hours?” she said in an Instagram video response. “I’ve got questions, and somebody needs to have some answers.”

Meta is also dealing with blowback about a separate issue. The company backtracked on plans to change its contractual language for business customers in a way that would have allowed it to scrape information for AI training.

Tech.title: As Midterms Approach, Top American Fears Include AI Interference in the Political Process
Tech.content:
Are you more fearful of AI stealing jobs, hurting the economy and disrupting the political process than you are of someone you love dying? A lot of people are, according to Chapman University’s 12th annual survey on American fears for 2026.

This year’s survey by the private research university in California was different. For the first time, researchers began asking Americans about their thoughts and fears about artificial intelligence, and those AI-related fears made the top 10 twice, as well as popping up throughout the list.

These were the top fears in the minds of the American people for 2026.

More from CNET

Fear % of very afraid or afraid Rank in 2025 Corrupt government officials 61.1% 1 US becoming involved in another world war 58% 6 AI harming the political process 51.9% New entry People I love becoming seriously ill 51.8% 2 People I love dying 50.6% 5 Economic/financial collapse 50.6% 3 AI hurting the economy 49.7% New entry Government tracking of personal data 48.9% 10 Biological warfare 48.2% 12 Terrorist attack 47.3% 15

The most central fear for Americans has remained unchanged since last year: corrupt government officials, at a staggering 61.1%. Other common and expected fears, like the US becoming involved in another world war, remain on the list, but it now sits in the No. 2 spot instead of 2025’s No. 6 slot.

Possibly the most common fears that any human could have — someone you love becoming seriously ill or dying — also remained prominent in the top 10 list.

The addition of AI makes a lot of sense in the world that we live in today, however. In the top 10 list, AI-related fears surround the technology harming both the election process (ranked third) and the economy (ranked seventh). With midterm elections right around the corner, it’s not at all surprising to see AI pop up here.

The team at Chapman commissioned NORC at the University of Chicago to survey 1,221 adults online this past April.

The study doesn’t paint AI as all bad, though. It also states that there is hope about the technology, according to Seth Benzell, assistant professor of business and economics at Chapman.

“When you frame it as AI or robots that are going to allow you to build something that you weren’t able to do before … those get people a lot more excited,” Benzell said.

AI cropped up a few more times on the list, however, including AI hurting the environment (at 43.2%), AI harming personal relationships (42%), AI replacing people in the workforce (also 42%), reporting to an AI manager at work (19.1%), having your work evaluated by AI (19.3%) and working with AI-enabled technologies (17.2%).

Other fears of technology also made the list: government tracking of personal data (48.9%), cyberterrorism (45.7%), government use of drones within the US (34.2%), technology that I don’t understand (23.5%) and technological change at work (12.6%).

Other, hardly dismissible fears that have been on people’s minds for a long time remain on the list: economic collapse, biological warfare and terrorist attacks are all incredibly valid.

Tech.title: Is Your iPhone 18 Pro Max on AT&T Stuck on SOS? Apple Will Replace the Entire Phone
Tech.content:
Some owners of the brand-new iPhone 18 Pro Max on AT&T found themselves without cellular service and stuck in SOS mode, including the ability to dial 911 in emergencies. Although a definitive cause hasn’t been revealed, Apple and AT&T issued software fixes that should prevent the glitch going forward. Some owners on Reddit, however, still report problems — and the solution is to replace the phone outright, which Apple will do for free.

The problem started in September, when MacRumors reported that AT&T sent a text message to iPhone 18 Pro Max owners, encouraging them to update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately. MacRumors estimated that thousands of customers have been affected. Around the same time, Apple issued a separate carrier-settings patch to pair with the iOS 27.0.1 update. But the patch came too late for certain owners of the new phone. If a phone got hit, it can’t be fixed in software.

An Apple representative told CNET that the updates are intended to guard against this problem in the future and won’t fix the situation for iPhone 18 Pro Max owners who are already experiencing it. Apple will provide a new phone free of charge to those owners. Affected customers should contact Apple Support or AT&T.

More from CNET

In Reddit threads about the issue, some owners still report seeing the problem with their iPhone 18 Pro Max phones. Others report that after the iOS and carrier settings updates, they have cellular access but the 5G Standalone and Voice Over 5G Standalone options were disabled (in Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Voice & Data). 5G Standalone uses 5G for all cellular activity; if it’s not enabled, the phone is using slower LTE networking.

Only the iPhone 18 Pro Max is affected

The issue seems limited to iPhone 18 Pro Max models on AT&T’s network. I reached out to contacts at T-Mobile and Verizon, and both reported they’re not seeing similar reports on their networks. I haven’t experienced the issue on an iPhone 18 Pro that runs on AT&T’s network, which isn’t surprising given that this particular problem affects iPhone 18 Pro Max units, not iPhone 18 Pro phones. A CNET colleague’s iPhone 18 Pro Max on Google Fi (which uses T-Mobile’s network) is also not experiencing the issue. I’ve not been able to discern if customers of cellular providers that use AT&T’s network, such as Cricket or US Mobile, have been affected.

It’s unclear whether the lack of connectivity is related to the phone’s hardware. While the standard iPhone 18 Pro is equipped with Apple’s C2 modem, the iPhone 18 Pro Max in the US is the only model with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X80 modem, as shown in this teardown of the phone by iFixIt. Qualcomm has been Apple’s modem provider for years, but Apple has worked to move away from relying on the third party for the essential phone component. That relationship is due to expire this year.

According to a TechInsights iPhone 18 Pro Max teardown, the X80 modem is also used in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, but a new millimeter-wave antenna has been added to the 18 Pro Max. Millimeter-wave offers much faster data speeds in areas where the technology is installed, but it can have a shorter range and be reduced by obstacles. Apple’s C2 modem also includes a millimeter-wave antenna.

Qualcomm declined to comment, and a representative directed me to contact Apple for more information.

Tech.title: How to Spot Political Deepfakes and Scams This Midterm Election Season
Tech.content:
Seeing is no longer enough to automatically believe it, thanks to generative AI. Generative AI tools like chatbots, image and video generators make it easy for anyone to create realistic media. The capabilities of AI have improved so much that it’s nearly impossible to distinguish real from AI. That’s never been more frustrating or dangerous than it is now during election season.

The 2026 midterm election is on Tuesday, Nov. 3. All 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot, along with 33 Senate seats and many other state and local races across the country. You can check your voter registration and see who’s on your ballot now using Vote.org’s free tool.

This fall, we’ve seen a number of AI-edited political ads, with and without disclosures about their AI use. Unsurprisingly, we’ve seen AI used in some high-profile races, including to give Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff AI cosmetic procedures and to make it seem like Texas Senate candidate James Talarico had defaced a Bible. Political campaigns and groups have spent more than $16 million on these AI ads this year, a CNN analysis found.

More from CNET

We’ve seen how generative AI can wreak havoc during election season. During the 2024 presidential primary, many New Hampshire voters got phone calls from an AI voice replica of Joe Biden urging them not to vote. This wasn’t sanctioned by the Biden campaign, and AI robocalls are illegal, so the Democratic political consultant behind it was charged with voter suppression and fined $6 million.

Improvements to AI tech since 2024 only make for sharper swords in a bad actor’s arsenal. To protect yourself from being scammed or tricked by AI deepfakes, here are some tips.

Verify if those photos, videos and audio are AI

Obvious errors like seven-fingered hands in AI images are increasingly rare as AI tech improves. That’s bad news for people trying to visually determine whether something is AI or not.

Instead, it can be more accurate to use online verification websites. These are our top choices:

The Content Authenticity Initiative’s Inspect tool can identify many kinds of AI content.

OpenAI’s Verify tool can identify content made with ChatGPT.

Google’s SynthID Detector can identify Google-made AI content. You can also upload content to Gemini to scan for SynthIDs.

These websites work by scanning an image, video or audio file’s metadata for hidden signatures that indicate it was made with AI. They aren’t foolproof, but they should catch some AI media.

Other services can also identify some AI content for a price, like Pangram’s $20 per month subscription for individual users. Apple is also adding a verification measure called Reference Images, but it’s limited to its newest iPhone 18 Pro models.

Be mindful that any AI detection service claiming a 100% success rate is lying. There are too many AI services available and too little standardization across the industry to get it right all the time.

Always double-check with official sources

We know from decades of cybersecurity research that attackers will try to prey on your emotions to get you to fall for a scam. The goal for these bad actors is to cloud your judgment. So one of the best ways to fight back is to arm yourself with knowledge.

For example, if you get a text saying your polling location has been changed with a link to the new one, don’t automatically click it. Go to your state’s board of elections website to verify whether a change has been made – it’s going to have the most official and up-to-date information on polling locations and times.

Check out this map from the US Election Assistance Commission to see the official election contact information for your state. You can also search for your state’s board of elections or check your governor’s website, which may also have voting info readily available. Nonprofit Vote.org can also help you track down your ballot information, no matter what state you’re voting in.

If you’re looking for official policy stances on a candidate rather than relying on potentially fake images or videos, your best bet is to start with their campaign website and platform. There’s no guarantee that the candidate is going to post entirely truthful information, but it should give you some insight into their beliefs on major issues.

Stay calm, be proactive and make a plan now

It’s cliché but true: Don’t believe everything you see online. Election season is a noisy time, and inevitably, you’re going to run across something that isn’t true. Use your gut and avoid panicking when possible. Fact-checking websites like Snopes.com can be useful resources.

The best way to avoid being scammed or tricked by a deepfake is to plan ahead and stay engaged: Make your voting plan now — many states offer an early voting period beginning in mid-October. Check your state’s voter ID laws. View your ballot in advance and research all the candidates on it, not just the headline races.

If you run into issues at your polling place, you can contact the Election Protection Hotline at 866-687-8683.

For more, check out our guide on what to do when you’ve been deepfaked.
